A good definition does part of the work of a theorem. Take the number 1. If 1 were a prime number, the factorization of 6 would not be unique: 6 = 2 · 3 = 1 · 2 · 3. So the definition of a prime leaves 1 out, and the theorem needs no exception.

This page collects 6709 cases of this kind, in 63 subjects of the Mathematics Subject Classification. Open an entry to read it. Each subject also has its own page, listed under "Sections" at the end. Each entry gives the definition in plain words, the problem it solves, how it solves it, a quote that supports it, and the original papers.

## How to read an entry

Each entry has the same parts, in the same order:

- **A line to remember.** One sentence that holds the definition in your head. It shows under the title.
- **The kind of help.** There are three kinds, described below. The colour of the dot shows the kind.
- **Definition.** The definition in plain words.
- **Problem.** The theorem or property that the definition is for.
- **How the definition helps.** Why the definition makes the theorem easy, and what stays hard.
- **Quote and pages.** A sentence from the nLab, Wikipedia, or a paper or page in the TheoremSearch data set that supports the entry, and links to the pages.
- **Sources.** Papers on the definition or the theorem. Most are the original papers. A few are surveys, books or histories.

The entries come from three places. 1531 come from the [nLab](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/HomePage), a wiki on category theory and the mathematics around it. 2744 come from [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/). 2434 come from the [TheoremSearch data set](https://huggingface.co/datasets/uw-math-ai/theorem-search-dataset) ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05216)). It holds 1.34 million theorem statements from openly licensed arXiv papers, ProofWiki, the Stacks Project and some open textbooks. Use the source menu to see one source at a time.

## Tags and order

Each entry has three tags:

- **MSC2020 codes.** The [Mathematics Subject Classification](https://msc2020.org/) of zbMATH Open and Mathematical Reviews. The first code is the main subject of the definition. For example, 54D30 is compactness in general topology.
- **arXiv categories.** The [arXiv subject classes](https://arxiv.org/category_taxonomy), such as math.GN for general topology. The first one is the main category.
- **A level.** Where a student usually first meets the definition: 1 is early undergraduate, 2 is later undergraduate, 3 is graduate, and 4 is research.

The entries are always in the same order. They are sorted first by the main MSC subject, then by level, then by the finer MSC code, and then by title. Any filter keeps this order. So when you filter by a tag, each subject reads from the basic entries to the research ones. "Copy as notes" copies the entries that match, in this order, as Markdown.

## Three kinds of help

**True by definition** (3190 entries). The definition builds the result in. The [homotopy hypothesis](#the-homotopy-hypothesis-is-a-tautology-or-a-theorem-depending-on-definitions) says that ∞-groupoids are the same as spaces. If you define an ∞-groupoid to be a space, the hypothesis is "of course a tautology", as the nLab says. This kind of definition does not remove the work. It moves the work into a second theorem. That theorem says that the new definition agrees with the old one, or that the objects you care about meet the definition. Take [Weil cohomology](#weil-cohomology-gives-rationality-and-the-functional-equation-of-zeta-functions). The Lefschetz trace formula follows from the axioms. The hard part is to prove that ℓ-adic cohomology satisfies the axioms.

**Rules out counterexamples** (1521 entries). The definition adds a condition that removes a known bad case. Then the theorem holds with no exceptions. [Brown representability](#brown-representability-needs-connected-pointed-spaces) is false for spaces that are not connected. Freyd and Heller found a counterexample with Thompson's group F. If the definition asks for connected spaces with a base point, the theorem is true.

**Makes the theorem clean to state or prove** (1998 entries). The definition lets you state the theorem at all, or it makes a long argument short. Take the [compactly generated spaces](#compactly-generated-spaces-make-the-exponential-law-hold-for-all-spaces). For any two of them, maps X × Y → Z are the same as maps X → Map(Y, Z). For all topological spaces, this is true only for some X and Y. Another example is [Lawvere's fixed point theorem](#lawveres-fixed-point-theorem-gives-cantor-russell-and-gdel-from-one-definition). With it, the diagonal arguments of Cantor, Russell, Tarski and Gödel are one short argument. For Gödel and Tarski, you still must show that arithmetic meets the hypothesis.

## Patterns that repeat

The same few ideas solve many different problems.

1. **Leave out the trivial case.** Then the theorem has no exception. The number 1 is [not prime](#leaving-1-out-of-the-primes-makes-factorization-unique). The trivial group is [not simple](#the-trivial-group-is-not-simple-so-composition-factors-are-unique). The empty space is [not connected](#the-empty-space-and-the-empty-category-are-not-connected). A zero object is [not simple](#a-zero-object-is-not-simple-so-schurs-lemma-has-no-exception). The ring with one element is [not a field](#maximal-ideals-are-exactly-the-ideals-whose-quotient-is-a-field). The graph with no vertices is [not a tree](#the-graph-with-no-vertices-is-not-a-tree).
2. **Change the category, not the objects.** Do not ask every space to be nice. Choose a category in which the constructions behave well. Examples are [compactly generated spaces](#compactly-generated-spaces-make-the-exponential-law-hold-for-all-spaces), [Delta-generated spaces](#delta-generated-spaces-form-a-convenient-category-that-is-locally-presentable), [diffeological spaces](#diffeological-spaces-make-spaces-of-smooth-maps-smooth-again), [condensed abelian groups](#condensed-abelian-groups-form-an-abelian-category), [convenient vector spaces](#testing-smoothness-on-curves-gives-the-exponential-law-for-smooth-maps) and [quasi-Borel spaces](#quasi-borel-spaces-give-probability-a-cartesian-closed-category). In analysis, the [Lebesgue integral](#the-lebesgue-integral-lets-limits-pass-inside-the-integral) and [Sobolev spaces](#sobolev-spaces-make-dirichlets-principle-true) do the same for functions.
3. **Keep the isomorphisms.** If you forget the symmetries of an object, a theorem fails. If you keep them as part of the data, the theorem holds. Examples are [moduli stacks](#moduli-stacks-give-fine-moduli-spaces-for-objects-with-automorphisms), [van Kampen's theorem for groupoids](#van-kampens-theorem-works-for-a-set-of-base-points), [anafunctors](#with-anafunctors-fully-faithful-and-essentially-surjective-means-equivalence-without-choice), [univalent categories](#univalent-categories-make-fully-faithful-essentially-surjective-functors-equivalences-without-choice) and [complete Segal spaces](#completeness-makes-complete-segal-spaces-see-equivalences-correctly).
4. **Define the object by the property you want.** Then the theorem follows quickly, or you can at least state it precisely. The real work moves into another theorem, such as a comparison of two definitions. Examples are the [homotopy hypothesis](#the-homotopy-hypothesis-is-a-tautology-or-a-theorem-depending-on-definitions), [Weil cohomology](#weil-cohomology-gives-rationality-and-the-functional-equation-of-zeta-functions), [sifted categories](#sifted-categories-are-defined-by-the-theorem-they-satisfy), [Waldhausen K-theory](#waldhausens-s-construction-makes-short-exact-sequences-add-in-k-theory) and the [cobordism hypothesis](#fully-dualizable-objects-make-the-cobordism-hypothesis-a-precise-statement).
5. **Ask for exactly what the proof uses.** Find the weakest condition that makes the argument work. Examples are the point-surjective maps in [Lawvere's theorem](#lawveres-fixed-point-theorem-gives-cantor-russell-and-gdel-from-one-definition), the formal diagrams in [Mac Lane's coherence theorem](#mac-lanes-coherence-theorem-is-true-for-formal-diagrams-only), the [monoid axiom](#the-monoid-axiom-gives-a-model-structure-on-monoids), [uniform integrability](#uniform-integrability-is-exactly-what-l-convergence-needs) and [localizable measures](#localizable-measures-are-exactly-where-the-main-measure-theorems-hold). For localizable measures, the condition is necessary as well as sufficient.
6. **Drop the points.** A locale is a space that is described only by its open sets. With locales, some theorems that need the axiom of choice for spaces get proofs without it. Examples are [Tychonoff's theorem](#tychonoffs-theorem-holds-for-locales-without-the-axiom-of-choice), the [Heine–Borel theorem](#heineborel-holds-constructively-for-the-locale-of-real-numbers) and [Gelfand duality](#locales-make-banachalaoglu-hahnbanach-and-gelfand-duality-constructive). Locales also help with the [Banach–Tarski paradox](#with-sublocales-as-parts-the-banachtarski-pieces-overlap). As sublocales, its pieces overlap, so a measure need not add up over them.
7. **Add what is missing.** Some theorems fail because the objects are too few. Add the missing objects, and the theorem holds. Bézout's theorem counts the [intersection points of two curves](#counting-complex-points-at-infinity-makes-bzouts-count-exact) exactly once you add complex points and points at infinity. Every linear map has an eigenvector over an [algebraically closed field](#over-an-algebraically-closed-field-every-linear-map-has-an-eigenvector). Nash equilibria always exist once [players may randomize](#letting-players-randomize-makes-nash-equilibria-exist).

## How this list was made

The nLab text comes from its public mirror, [ncatlab/nlab-content](https://github.com/ncatlab/nlab-content), as of 26 November 2026. That is about 20,800 pages. The Wikipedia text comes from the live English Wikipedia, read from 26 to 27 November 2026. The TheoremSearch data set was downloaded on 27 November 2026. All the work was done by research agents. A research agent is one instance of an AI model with a single task. Most agents were Claude models. Some were OpenAI Codex models.

The work had seven steps:

1. **nLab.** Thirty-one agents searched the nLab. The later group of 22 agents alone read about 3,800 pages. The pages were found first by a phrase search for words such as "by definition", "tautology", "convenient category", "rules out" and "counterexample". They followed links between pages and wrote one entry for each case that the page supports.
2. **Wikipedia.** Twenty-eight agents searched Wikipedia. Each agent covered one narrow subject, such as group theory, measure theory or graph theory.
3. **TheoremSearch.** The data set was split into 34 slices by arXiv subject, with ProofWiki, the Stacks Project and the textbooks as their own slices. A keyword score ranked the papers in each slice. One agent read each slice. It used the abstracts and the theorem statements, and searched the whole slice for more.
4. **True by definition.** Fifty more agents each searched one subject in all three sources at once. They looked only for theorems that a good definition makes true by definition, or nearly so. Each entry had to say where the work went, for example into a theorem that two definitions agree. They found 1,580 entries, and the check below kept 1,148 of them.
5. **Tags.** Ten agents gave every earlier entry its MSC2020 codes, arXiv categories and level. A script checked every code against the official lists. The agents in step 4 tagged their own entries, and the checkers corrected the tags.
6. **Check.** A second set of agents checked every entry as a referee. In step 4, a different model checked each entry: Claude checked the Codex entries, and Codex checked the Claude entries. They made sure that the quote is on the page and that the page supports the entry. They corrected the mathematics, for example by adding missing conditions or by fixing a wrong counterexample. They dropped entries about open conjectures, entries that only fix a name, and entries that repeat another entry. They looked up the sources through Crossref, arXiv or the publisher's page.
7. **Plain English.** Agents rewrote the entries in short sentences, and explained each technical term the first time it appears. Their short explanations of terms come from the models' own knowledge, and nobody checked them a second time.

Where an entry gives a counterexample or an argument that is not on the page, the entry says "our own". A source marked "link not checked" was not opened. Some entries have no source, because no primary source with a working link was found.

The list is long, but it is not complete. It contains only cases where the page says, or clearly shows, that the definition does the work. Entries from research papers rest on the paper's abstract and theorem statements, not on a full reading of the paper. Each quote is copied from the page, but formulas are changed to plain symbols, and links and emphasis are removed. Nobody checked the entries by hand. An entry with medium or low confidence has weaker support. Read the linked papers before you rely on a claim.
