Without the degree bound, x − x² vanishes on {0,1} despite its nonzero linear term (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Additive colorings of planar graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.0667v2). It says: “Suppose that there is a nonvanishing monomial x₁ᵏ¹⋯xₙᵏⁿ in P such that k₁+⋯+kₙ=deg(P).”

**Sources:**

- [Noga Alon, Combinatorial Nullstellensatz (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0963548398003411)

### Stable subset laws survive conditioning

**Remember:** Set a variable to zero for absence, and differentiate for presence.

*True by definition.* MSC 05D40 (Probabilistic methods in extremal combinatorics, including polynomial methods (combinatorial Nullstellensatz, etc.)). arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Encode a random subset of a finite set by a polynomial. Each subset contributes its probability times the product of its variables. The law is strongly Rayleigh when this polynomial has no zero with every variable in the open upper half-plane.

**Problem.** Conditioning a strongly Rayleigh random subset on inclusion or exclusion of an element preserves the property if the event has positive probability.

**How the definition helps.** Encoding subsets as monomials turns conditioning into operations on one polynomial (our own). Setting a variable to zero selects subsets missing its element (our own). Differentiating in that variable, then multiplying it back, selects subsets containing the element (our own). Dividing by the event probability normalizes, and the work lies in proving that these operations preserve stability (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Stable multivariate Narayana polynomials and labeled plane trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.15058v2). It says: “Given i,j ∈ \[n\], the following operations preserve real stability of f ∈ ℝ\[x\]:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A ratio of alternating determinants makes Schur polynomials symmetric

**Remember:** Swapping variables flips both determinant signs, so the ratio stays fixed.

*True by definition.* MSC 05E05 (Symmetric functions and generalizations). arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A partition λ with at most n parts gives a decreasing list λ₁, …, λₙ, padded with zeros. Define its Schur polynomial by dividing the determinant with entries xᵢ raised to λⱼ + n − j by the determinant for λ = 0. Another definition sums one monomial per filling of the rows of lengths λᵢ by labels from 1 to n. Labels never decrease along rows and strictly increase down columns, and each label i contributes a factor xᵢ.

**Problem.** The determinant ratio is a polynomial that is invariant under every permutation of the variables.

**How the definition helps.** The ratio makes symmetry immediate because swapping variables swaps two rows of each determinant, changing both signs. The denominator is the product of the differences xᵢ − xⱼ for i &lt; j. Every difference divides the numerator, since setting the corresponding variables equal gives two equal rows (our own). For the filling definition, a separate bijection can exchange the counts of adjacent labels (our own). The work moves into proving divisibility and showing that the two definitions agree.

**nLab:** [Schur function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Schur+function). It says: “Then the Schur polynomial attached to λ is the quotient”

**Wikipedia:** [Schur polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_polynomial). It says: “This is a symmetric function because the numerator and denominator are both alternating, and a polynomial since all alternating polynomials are divisible by the Vandermonde determinant.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Increasing indices merge quasisymmetric products

**Remember:** Merge index lists and add exponents at shared indices.

*True by definition.* MSC 05E05 (Symmetric functions and generalizations). arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a list α = (α₁, …, αₖ) of positive integers, the monomial quasisymmetric function M\_α is the sum of x<sub>i₁</sub><sup>α₁</sup>⋯x<sub>iₖ</sub><sup>αₖ</sup> over all i₁ &lt; ⋯ &lt; iₖ.

**Problem.** M\_α M\_β is the sum of M\_γ over all quasi-shuffles γ of α and β, counted with multiplicity. A quasi-shuffle merges the two lists in an order-preserving way and may add one entry of α to one entry of β.

**How the definition helps.** In the product, the only question is which variable indices of the two monomials coincide (our own). Each quasi-shuffle records exactly one pattern of shared indices, and shared indices add their exponents (our own). Once the merge is fixed, summing over the actual indices gives M\_γ (our own).

**nLab:** [quasi-symmetric function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quasi-symmetric+function). It says: “Let X be a totally ordered set of indeterminants.”

**Paper or page:** [The Bernstein homomorphism via Aguiar-Bergeron-Sottile universality](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.02969v2). It says: “Mα₁Mα₂⋯Mαₖ = ∑\[A ∈ ℕᵏ˒• Cred, (Aɡ,•)ʳᵉᵈ = αɡ for each g\] Mcolumn A.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ordered variables split quasisymmetric functions

**Remember:** Two ordered lists cut each exponent list once.

*True by definition.* MSC 05E05 (Symmetric functions and generalizations). arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a list α of positive integers, the monomial quasisymmetric function M\_α sums the monomials that place the entries of α, in order, on strictly increasing variable indices. Its coproduct evaluates it on two ordered variable lists, with every variable of the first list before every variable of the second, and reads the result as a tensor.

**Problem.** The coproduct of M\_α is the sum of M\_β ⊗ M\_γ over all ways to cut α into a first piece β and a second piece γ. Here M of the empty list is 1.

**How the definition helps.** Evaluation on consecutive lists forces each increasing index sequence to cross between lists at most once (our own). Each cut point therefore gives a product of independent sums (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The Bernstein homomorphism via Aguiar-Bergeron-Sottile universality](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.02969v2). It says: “Let γ ∈ Comp and k ∈ ℕ. Then, Δ⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾Mγ = ∑\[(γ₁, γ₂, …, γₖ) ∈ Compᵏ, γ₁γ₂⋯γₖ = γ\] Mγ₁ ⊗ Mγ₂ ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ Mγₖ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Power sums make the symmetric function involution immediate

**Remember:** Apply the same sign twice to recover each generator.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 05E05 (Symmetric functions and generalizations). arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over the rationals, the symmetric function ring uses symmetric polynomials in arbitrarily many variables, compatible under setting extra variables to zero. Its free polynomial generators pₖ sum the kth powers of the variables. Define the ring map ω by multiplying pₖ by (−1) to the power k − 1. Another definition sends the sum eₖ of square-free degree-k monomials to the sum hₖ of all degree-k monomials.

**Problem.** Applying ω twice gives the identity.

**How the definition helps.** The power-sum definition makes the second application of ω cancel the sign on every generator (our own). Starting with eₖ sent to hₖ, one instead uses the relations between the two families to prove that ω sends hₖ back to eₖ. The work moves into deriving the signed action from those relations (our own). This definition also needs the fact that the power sums freely generate the ring over the rationals. Over the integers the power sums do not generate the ring.

**Wikipedia:** [Ring of symmetric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_symmetric_functions). It says: “The fact that ω is an involution of Λ<sub>R</sub> follows from the symmetry between elementary and complete homogeneous symmetric functions expressed by the first set of relations given above.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Schur characters make Littlewood–Richardson coefficients nonnegative

**Remember:** Multiply characters and count how often each irreducible piece occurs.

*True by definition.* MSC 05E05 (Symmetric functions and generalizations), 05E10, 20G05. arXiv math.CO, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use complex polynomial representations of the group of invertible n by n matrices. Each representation assigns matrices acting on a vector space, with entries polynomial in the original matrix entries. Define the Schur polynomial for a partition λ with at most n parts as the trace on diagonal matrices in the corresponding irreducible representation. An irreducible representation has no proper nonzero invariant subspace.

**Problem.** The product of two Schur polynomials in n variables expands in the Schur basis with nonnegative integer coefficients. These are the Littlewood–Richardson coefficients for the partitions with at most n parts.

**How the definition helps.** The character definition makes each coefficient a count of irreducible summands (our own). The product of two traces is the trace on the tensor product, where each original matrix acts on both factors (our own). Over the complex numbers, the tensor product splits into irreducible polynomial representations. The determinant or tableau definition needs a separate proof of nonnegativity. The work here is the splitting theorem and the character formula that identifies the traces with the Schur polynomials.

**Wikipedia:** [Schur polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_polynomial). It says: “In representation theory they are the characters of polynomial irreducible representations of general linear groups.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Tableau weights explain the Cauchy identity

**Remember:** One matrix gives two tableaux of the same shape.

*True by definition.* MSC 05E05 (Symmetric functions and generalizations). arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Draw left-aligned rows of boxes whose lengths decrease weakly. Fill them with variable indices that increase weakly across rows and strictly down columns. Each filling contributes the product of the variables in its boxes. The Schur polynomial sums these products for one shape.

**Problem.** The sum over all shapes λ of s\_λ(x₁, x₂, …) s\_λ(y₁, y₂, …) equals the product of 1/(1 − xᵢyⱼ) over all pairs i, j.

**How the definition helps.** The filling definition lets both sides count matrices by their row and column sums (our own). Expanding each geometric series chooses one nonnegative matrix entry (our own). The Robinson–Schensted–Knuth bijection turns each matrix into two fillings of equal shape with those variable counts (our own). The work lies in proving the bijection and identifying the filling sum with the usual determinant ratio (our own).

**nLab:** [Schur function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Schur+function). It says: “the corresponding Schur polynomial sλ is equal to the sum over the monomials”

**Paper or page:** [Growth diagram proofs for the Littlewood identities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04014v1). It says: “\\sum<sub>\\lambda</sub> s\_\\lambda(\\mathbf{x})s\_\\lambda(\\mathbf{y}) &amp;= \\prod\_{\\substack{1 \\leq i \\leq n \\\\ 1 \\leq j \\leq m}} \\frac{1}{1-x<sub>iy</sub><sub>j</sub>},”

### Tableaux make Kostka numbers nonnegative

**Remember:** Each coefficient counts fillings of a fixed shape and weight.

*True by definition.* MSC 05E05 (Symmetric functions and generalizations), 05E10. arXiv math.CO, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let λ be a partition, a decreasing list of row lengths allowing ties. A tableau here fills those rows with labels from 1 to n that never decrease along rows and strictly increase down columns. Define the Schur polynomial by adding one monomial per tableau, with a factor xᵢ for each occurrence of i. Another definition takes a ratio of two alternating determinants, which change sign under a swap of variables.

**Problem.** The Schur polynomial expands in monomial symmetric polynomials with nonnegative integer coefficients called Kostka numbers. Each basis polynomial sums all distinct monomials whose exponents are permutations of a fixed list.

**How the definition helps.** The filling definition makes positivity immediate because each monomial coefficient counts fillings with the prescribed label counts. Symmetry makes the coefficients equal for monomials in the same basis polynomial. In the determinant definition, the quotient of signed sums does not show that the coefficients are nonnegative. The work moves into proving that the filling sum equals the determinant ratio, which also gives symmetry.

**Remember:** Weight vertices by the leading eigenvector.

**Definition.** Let ν be the Perron eigenvector of the adjacency matrix, the unit eigenvector for the largest eigenvalue λ₁ with nonnegative entries. Give each vertex u the weight νᵤ. In our own explanation, split ν restricted to S into its projection onto ν and a perpendicular part. The projections give the main term, λ₁ times the two set weights. The perpendicular parts give the error, at most λ times their lengths. Each length is the square root of the weight of a set times that of its complement, since ν has length one.

### The 1-Laplacian makes Cheeger's constant an exact eigenvalue

**Remember:** Absolute values, not squares, turn Cheeger's bounds into an equality.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 05C50 (Graphs and linear algebra (matrices, eigenvalues, etc.)), 35P30. arXiv math.SP, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a function x on the vertices of a graph, let I(x) be the sum over edges of \|x(i) − x(j)\|. The 1-Laplacian Δ₁ is the set-valued derivative of I, because I is not smooth. Its eigenvalues are the critical values of I on the set where the sum of d(i)\|x(i)\| is 1, with d(i) the degree. The Cheeger constant h(G) is the smallest ratio of cut edges to the volume of the smaller side.

**Problem.** For every connected graph, the first nonzero eigenvalue μ₂ of the 1-Laplacian equals the Cheeger constant h(G).

**How the definition helps.** The energy I uses absolute values, which is the same shape as the count of cut edges in the Cheeger constant (our own reason). On the indicator function of a vertex set, I is exactly the number of edges that leave the set (our own remark). So the eigenvalue problem and the cut problem become one problem (our own). The usual Laplacian uses squares, and it only gives the two-sided Cheeger inequalities.

**Paper or page:** [Spectrum of the 1-Laplacian and Cheeger's constant on graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.1150), [Spectrum of the 1-Laplacian and Cheeger's constant on graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.1150). It says: “Cheeger's constant, which has only some upper and lower bounds in linear spectral theory, equals to the first non-zero Δ₁ eigenvalue for connected graphs.”

**Remember:** Allow each vertex to serve two models.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 05C83 (Graph minors), 05C35. arXiv math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A model of a graph H in a host graph G assigns disjoint connected vertex sets to the vertices of H. Sets for adjacent vertices of H must be joined by an edge. In a half-integral packing of models, each vertex of G lies in at most two models. A cover is a set of vertices of G that meets every model of H.

**Problem.** For every graph H there is a function f with the following property. Every graph G has either a half-integral packing of k models of H, or a cover of at most f(k) vertices.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing each vertex to lie in two models restores the packing-or-cover alternative for every H. With disjoint models, Robertson and Seymour showed that the alternative holds exactly when H is planar. Their constructions give counterexamples for every nonplanar H. Liu proved the half-integral version, which confirmed a conjecture of Thomas, and his proof is hard and nonconstructive. The cited paper reports this and studies constructive versions.

**Paper or page:** [Delineating Half-Integrality of the Erdős-Pósa Property for Minors: the Case of Surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16647v1). It says: “Recently, Liu confirmed a conjecture of Thomas and showed that every graph has the half-integral Erdős-Pósa property for minors.”

**Sources:**

- [Christophe Paul, Evangelos Protopapas, Dimitrios M. Thilikos, Sebastian Wiederrecht, Delineating Half-Integrality of the Erdős-Pósa Property for Minors: the Case of Surfaces, arXiv:2406.16647 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16647v1)
- [Neil Robertson and Paul Seymour, Graph minors. V. Excluding a planar graph, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1016/0095-8956(86)90030-4)

### Requiring pairwise shared vertices makes strict brambles detect cycles exactly

**Remember:** With shared vertices required, order one everywhere means no cycles.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 05C83 (Graph minors), 05C38. arXiv math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A strict bramble is a nonempty family of connected subgraphs, each two of which share a vertex. Its order is the least number of vertices needed to meet every member. In an ordinary bramble, two subgraphs joined by an edge also count as touching.

**Problem.** A graph with at least one vertex is a forest exactly when every strict bramble has order one.

**How the definition helps.** Requiring shared vertices lets the Helly property of subtrees apply, so pairwise-meeting subtrees of a tree share a vertex. In a forest this gives every strict bramble order one. For the converse, in our own construction, split a cycle into three nonempty arcs and take the three unions of two arcs. These are connected, meet pairwise, and no vertex lies in all three, so the order is two. Ordinary brambles fail here, since one edge gives two touching single vertices with no common vertex. The paper's harder results describe graphs with larger strict bramble number.

**Paper or page:** [On Strict Brambles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.05783v1). It says: “The strict bramble number of G can be seen as a way to extend the notion of acyclicity, departing from the fact that (non-empty) acyclic graphs are exactly the graphs where every strict bramble has order one.”

**Sources:**

- [Emmanouil Lardas, Evangelos Protopapas, Dimitrios M. Thilikos, Dimitris Zoros, On Strict Brambles, arXiv:2201.05783 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.05783v1)
- [Emmanouil Lardas, Evangelos Protopapas, Dimitrios M. Thilikos and Dimitris Zoros, On Strict Brambles, Graphs and Combinatorics 39 (2023), article 24](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00373-023-02618-y)

### Requiring nonempty families makes the cross-intersecting size bound nontrivial

**Remember:** An empty family forces no intersection at all.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 05D05 (Extremal set theory). arXiv math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Two families cross-intersect if each set from one meets each set from the other. In a nonempty pairwise cross-intersecting collection, every family has at least one member and each pair of families cross-intersects.

**Problem.** Take nonempty cross-intersecting families A and B of k-element subsets of an n-element set, with n ≥ 2k. Then \|A\| + \|B\| is at most the larger total of two constructions. Either both families are all sets through one point, or A is one set F and B is all k-sets meeting F.

**How the definition helps.** The nonempty condition rules out the trivial answer of one full family and one empty family. In our own example, with n = 5 and k = 2, all ten pairs fit in A when B is empty. With both nonempty, the bound is 8, reached by either construction. The hard part is proving that no other choice does better.

**Paper or page:** [Non-empty pairwise cross-intersecting families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03473v2). It says: “If 𝒜₁, 𝒜₂, …, 𝒜ₜ ⊂ \[n\] choose k are non-empty pairwise cross-intersecting families”

**Sources:**

- [Yang Huang, Yuejian Peng, Non-empty pairwise cross-intersecting families, arXiv:2306.03473 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03473v2)

### Double posets make the antipode of quasisymmetric functions reverse one order

**Remember:** The antipode reverses the first order and gives sign −1 for odd size.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 05E05 (Symmetric functions and generalizations), 06A11, 16T05. arXiv math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A double poset is a finite set E with two partial orders &lt;₁ and &lt;₂. Consider maps φ from E to the positive integers that weakly increase along &lt;₁. They must strictly increase on pairs e &lt;₁ f with f &lt;₂ e. The generating function adds, for each such map, the product over e of the variable indexed by φ(e).

**Problem.** Suppose the second order is total. Then the antipode sends the generating function of (E, &lt;₁, &lt;₂) to that of (E, &gt;₁, &lt;₂), times −1 when E has odd size. The antipode is the inversion map of the Hopf algebra of quasisymmetric functions, an algebra that also has a rule for splitting elements.

**How the definition helps.** Two independent orders let one recipe describe both sides of the formula, with only the first order reversed. Many classical functions are special cases, including Schur functions and P-partition enumerators. So one antipode formula covers them all. The formula restates a result of Malvenuto and Reutenauer, and the paper gives a new self-contained proof that produces the sign.

**Paper or page:** [Double posets and the antipode of QSym](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.08355v3), [Double posets and the antipode of QSym](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.08355v3). It says: “We prove a formula for the antipode of this function that holds under certain conditions (which are satisfied when the second order of the double poset is total, but also in some other cases)”

**Sources:**

- [Darij Grinberg, Double posets and the antipode of QSym, arXiv:1509.08355 (2017). The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 24(2) (2017), \#P2.22 (published with minor changes to Section 2 and without ancillary file)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.08355v3)

### Orbit counts constrain cyclic sieving

**Remember:** Fixed counts must grow along divisibility, not merely stay nonnegative.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 05E18 (Group actions on combinatorial structures), 05A15. arXiv math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a cyclic group of order m acting on a finite set, and choose a primitive mth root of unity. Cyclic sieving means that evaluating a polynomial at each power of the root counts the points fixed by the corresponding generator power.

**Problem.** If a cyclic group of order m acts on X with cyclic sieving for f, then for each divisor d of m the number ∑<sub>j∣d</sub> μ(d/j) f(ωₘʲ) is nonnegative. So nonnegative integer values of f at the roots of unity do not suffice.

**How the definition helps.** Points fixed by the jth power of the generator are those in orbits whose size divides j (our own). Möbius inversion over divisors recovers the number of points in orbits of each size, which cannot be negative (our own). For m = 4, f = 4 + 2q + 2q³ gives 4 at i but 0 at −1, yet every point fixed by the generator is fixed by its square (our own). The converse also needs each recovered count to be divisible by its orbit size (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Skew Schur polynomials and cyclic sieving phenomenon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.12394v3). It says: “Then there exists an action of a cyclic group C of order m on X such that (X, C, f(q)) exhibits the cyclic sieving phenomenon if and only if for each d ∣ m, ∑\[j ∣ d\] μ(d/j)f(ωₘʲ) ≥ 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A useless edge makes both path complexes cones, hence contractible

**Remember:** An edge on no path can join every face.

*True by definition.* MSC 05E45 (Combinatorial aspects of simplicial complexes), 05C38. arXiv math.CO, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a directed graph with chosen vertices s and t. Its path-free complex consists of the edge sets that contain no directed path from s to t. Its path-missing complex consists of the edge sets whose complement contains such a path. A useless edge lies on no directed path from s to t.

**Problem.** If the graph has a useless edge e and some directed path from s to t, then both complexes are cones with apex e. So both complexes are contractible.

**How the definition helps.** Membership in either complex depends only on which paths from s to t an edge set contains, and a useless edge lies on none. So adding e to any face of either complex gives another face (our own explanation). This settles the contractible case of the paper's result that each complex is contractible or homotopy equivalent to a sphere.

**Paper or page:** [The path-missing and path-free complexes of a directed graph](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07894v3). It says: “Assume that G has a useless edge e. Then, both 𝒫ℱ(G) and 𝒫ℳ(G) are cones with apex e.”

**Sources:**

- [Darij Grinberg, Lukas Katthän, Joel Brewster Lewis, The path-missing and path-free complexes of a directed graph, arXiv:2102.07894 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07894v3)

### Effective resistance as an orthogonal projection makes Foster's theorem a trace identity

**Remember:** The trace of a projection counts the directions it keeps.

*True by definition.* MSC 05E45 (Combinatorial aspects of simplicial complexes), 05C50, 55U10. arXiv math.CO, math.AT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a finite weighted simplicial complex, a p-chain is a real combination of oriented p-simplices. The paper defines the effective resistance r(σ) of a simplex σ by a bilinear form taken from circuit theory. It proves that the resistance operator ∂\*(∂\*)⁺ is the orthogonal projection onto the chains perpendicular to all cycles, the chains with zero boundary.

**Problem.** For a finite weighted simplicial complex and each degree p, the sum of w(σ)·r(σ) over all p-simplices σ equals the rank of the boundary map. Here w(σ) is the weight and r(σ) the effective resistance of σ. For a graph and p = 1 this is Foster's theorem: the sum equals the number of vertices minus the number of connected components.

**How the definition helps.** Once resistance is a projection, the weighted sum is the trace of that projection, the sum of its diagonal entries. In our own explanation, a projection has only the eigenvalues 0 and 1, so its trace equals its rank. Its image is the image of ∂\*, whose dimension is the rank of the boundary map. The real work comes earlier, in showing that the operator is this projection and that its diagonal entries are the products w(σ)·r(σ).

**Paper or page:** [Effective Resistance in Simplicial Complexes as Bilinear Forms: Generalizations and Properties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10749v1), [Effective Resistance in Simplicial Complexes as Bilinear Forms: Generalizations and Properties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10749v1). It says: “The p-th effective resistance operator 𝒯ₚ = ∂ₚ∗(∂ₚ∗)⁺ on chains is the orthogonal projection”

**Sources:**

- [Inés García-Redondo, Claudia Landi, Sarah Percival, Anda Skeja, Bei Wang, Ling Zhou, Effective Resistance in Simplicial Complexes as Bilinear Forms: Generalizations and Properties, arXiv:2511.10749 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10749v1)

## 06 Order, lattices, ordered algebraic structures

### Lexicographic comparison gives total orders

**Remember:** The first difference settles the comparison.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A05 (Total orders). arXiv math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Compare two tuples of a fixed finite length at their first unequal coordinate. A total order compares every pair, so this rule differs from requiring every coordinate to be at most its counterpart.

**Problem.** Lexicographic comparison of tuples from totally ordered sets gives a total order.

**How the definition helps.** The first difference always decides which of two distinct tuples comes first. For transitivity, use the earlier of the two first differences (our own). If they coincide, transitivity in that coordinate decides the comparison (our own). Coordinatewise comparison leaves (0, 1) and (1, 0) incomparable (our own).

**nLab:** [lexicographic order](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lexicographic+order). It says: “if x, y ∈ L and x ≠ y, then x &lt; y iff xᵢ &lt; yᵢ where i is the least element in the set {j ∈ I : xⱼ ≠ yⱼ}.”

**Paper or page:** [Lexicographic Order on Pair of Totally Ordered Sets is Total Ordering](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Lexicographic_Order_on_Pair_of_Totally_Ordered_Sets_is_Total_Ordering). It says: “is a total ordering on S₁ × S₂”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Well-ordering gives strong induction

**Remember:** Any failure would have a first failure.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 06A05 (Total orders). arXiv math.LO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A well-order is a total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element. Totality alone says only that every pair can be compared.

**Problem.** A claim about natural numbers holds everywhere if its truth at all smaller numbers implies its truth at each number.

**How the definition helps.** The well-ordering of the natural numbers supplies a first counterexample whenever the claim fails (our own). All earlier elements then satisfy the claim and force it to hold at that counterexample (our own). On the integers, the claim that every integer is nonnegative satisfies the earlier-elements implication but is false (our own). For any integer there is a smaller negative integer, so the premise of that implication never holds (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Well-order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-order). It says: “the standard ordering ≤ of the integers is not a well ordering”

**Paper or page:** [Well-Ordered Induction](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Well-Ordered_Induction). It says: “That is, if a property passes from the initial segment of x to x, then this property is true for all x ∈ A.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Antisymmetry makes least elements unique

**Remember:** Two least elements each lie below the other.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 06A06 (Partial orders, general). arXiv math.LO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A preorder is a reflexive and transitive comparison. A partial order also requires antisymmetry, which means that x ≤ y and y ≤ x force x = y.

**Problem.** Any subset of a partially ordered set has at most one least element.

**How the definition helps.** Antisymmetry turns the two comparisons between least elements into equality (our own). Each least element is at most every element of the subset, including the other least element (our own). Divisibility on all integers lacks antisymmetry and has two least elements, 1 and −1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Partially ordered set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set). It says: “i.e. no two distinct elements precede each other.”

**Paper or page:** [Smallest Element is Unique](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Smallest_Element_is_Unique). It says: “If S has a smallest element, then it can have only one.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The order dual gives every order theorem a second theorem free

**Remember:** Turn the Hasse diagram upside down and every theorem still holds.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A06 (Partial orders, general). arXiv math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** The dual of a partially ordered set P is the same set with the order reversed. So x ≤ y in the dual exactly when y ≤ x in P. The dual of a statement reverses every order relation and swaps each notion for its dual, such as join for meet.

**Problem.** If a statement holds for all partially ordered sets, then its dual statement also holds for all partially ordered sets. This is the duality principle.

**How the definition helps.** The axioms of a partial order do not change when the order is reversed, so the dual of a partially ordered set is again one. A statement true for all partially ordered sets is then true for every dual, and read in the original set this is the dual statement. So each theorem about least upper bounds gives a theorem about greatest lower bounds with no new proof. The principle needs a class of orders closed under duals; Heyting algebras, for example, are not (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Duality (order theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duality_%28order_theory%29). It says: “The importance of this simple definition stems from the fact that every definition and theorem of order theory can readily be transferred to the dual order.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ties turn preorders into partial orders

**Remember:** Treat mutual comparisons as ties, then order the tie classes.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A06 (Partial orders, general). arXiv math.LO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A preorder is a reflexive and transitive relation. Group elements into classes by putting x and y together when x ≤ y and y ≤ x. Order the class of x below or equal to the class of y when x ≤ y.

**Problem.** The classes of a preorder under mutual comparison form a partially ordered set.

**How the definition helps.** Classes make antisymmetry automatic because comparison both ways puts the representatives in the same class. Transitivity makes the comparison independent of the representatives (our own). For integer divisibility, each class consists of an integer and its negative (our own).

**nLab:** [preorder](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/preorder). It says: “Then the quotient set P / ∼ is a poset.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cover relations recover finite orders

**Remember:** Follow upward steps to recover comparisons.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 06A07 (Combinatorics of partially ordered sets). arXiv math.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a partially ordered set, y covers x if x &lt; y and nothing lies strictly between them. A Hasse diagram draws only these steps and leaves out comparisons that follow by transitivity.

**Problem.** In a finite partially ordered set, x &lt; y exactly when a path of one or more upward cover steps leads from x to y.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping only covers still records every comparison because each finite interval can be crossed in immediate steps (our own). Choose the next element as a minimal element above the current one and at most y (our own). Each step rises, so finiteness forces arrival at y (our own). In the rational numbers, every two distinct numbers have another between them, so there are no covers (our own).

**nLab:** [Hasse diagram](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hasse+diagram). It says: “its Hasse diagram encodes the minimal amount of information necessary to reproduce the ordering relation.”

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse diagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_diagram). It says: “a type of mathematical diagram used to represent a finite partially ordered set”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining transitive closure as the smallest transitive relation gives existence for free

**Remember:** Smallest by definition, chains by theorem.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A15 (Galois correspondences, closure operators (in relation to ordered sets)), 03E20. arXiv math.CO, math.LO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** The transitive closure R⁺ of a relation R on a set S is the smallest transitive relation on S that contains R. The chain description says x R⁺ y when there is a finite chain x = s₀ R s₁ R … R sₙ = y with n ≥ 1.

**Problem.** Every relation has a transitive closure, and it is the chain relation.

**How the definition helps.** With the smallest-relation definition, existence is immediate: the intersection of all transitive relations containing R is one, and S × S ensures the family is not empty. The work moves to the theorem that the chain relation is that smallest relation. The chain relation is transitive and lies inside every transitive relation that contains R, by induction on chain length.

**Paper or page:** [Equivalence of Definitions of Transitive Closure of Relation/Union of Compositions is Smallest](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Equivalence_of_Definitions_of_Transitive_Closure_of_Relation/Union_of_Compositions_is_Smallest), [Equivalence of Definitions of Transitive Closure of Relation/Finite Chain is Smallest](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Equivalence_of_Definitions_of_Transitive_Closure_of_Relation/Finite_Chain_is_Smallest). It says: “Then ℛ⁺ is the smallest transitive relation on S that contains ℛ.”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Equivalence of Definitions of Transitive Closure of Relation/Union of Compositions is Smallest](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Equivalence_of_Definitions_of_Transitive_Closure_of_Relation/Union_of_Compositions_is_Smallest)
- [ProofWiki, Equivalence of Definitions of Transitive Closure of Relation/Finite Chain is Smallest](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Equivalence_of_Definitions_of_Transitive_Closure_of_Relation/Finite_Chain_is_Smallest)

### Absorption makes lattice orders agree

**Remember:** Absorption makes meet and join agree about which element is larger.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 06B05 (Structure theory of lattices). arXiv math.RA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** An algebraic definition of a lattice uses two commutative and associative operations, ∧ and ∨. Each operation gives x when applied to x twice. The absorption laws are x ∧ (x ∨ y) = x and x ∨ (x ∧ y) = x.

**Problem.** The two operations determine one order in which ∧ is greatest lower bound and ∨ is least upper bound.

**How the definition helps.** Absorption makes the two order tests agree. Define x ≤ y when x ∧ y = x. Absorption makes this equivalent to x ∨ y = y. The operation laws then make ∧ the greatest lower bound and ∨ the least upper bound. Without absorption, both operations could be minimum on {0, 1}, giving opposite orders (our own).

**nLab:** [lattice](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/lattice). It says: “Notice that the absorption laws guarantee that these two descriptions of ≤ agree.”

**Paper or page:** [Structure with Commutative Idempotent Associative Operations satisfying Absorption Laws is Lattice](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Structure_with_Commutative_Idempotent_Associative_Operations_satisfying_Absorption_Laws_is_Lattice). It says: “Then there exists a unique lattice ordering ≼ on S such that”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dedekind completeness is exactly what makes closed bounded sets compact

**Remember:** In ℚ, the rationals between 0 and 2 are closed, bounded and not compact.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 06A05 (Total orders), 06B23, 54D30. arXiv math.GN. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A linearly ordered space is a totally ordered set with the order topology, which open rays generate. It is Dedekind complete when every nonempty subset that is bounded above has a least upper bound.

**Problem.** In a linearly ordered space, every closed and bounded subset is compact exactly when the order is Dedekind complete.

**How the definition helps.** Dedekind completeness is the exact condition for the Heine–Borel property, not only one sufficient condition. Our own example: in ℚ, the set of rationals between 0 and 2 is closed and bounded. It is not compact, because a sequence of rationals that tends to √2 has no subsequence that converges in it. Our own remark: the direction from completeness to compactness copies the proof for \[a, b\] in ℝ.

**Paper or page:** [Heine-Borel iff Dedekind Complete](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Heine-Borel_iff_Dedekind_Complete). It says: “every closed, bounded subset of X is compact.”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Heine-Borel iff Dedekind Complete](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Heine-Borel_iff_Dedekind_Complete)

### Dedekind completeness skips the empty set, whose supremum is a least element

**Remember:** The supremum of nothing is the bottom, and ℝ has no bottom.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 06A05 (Total orders), 06B23. arXiv math.CO, math.LO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** An ordered set is Dedekind complete when every nonempty subset that is bounded above has a supremum. A complete lattice is an ordered set in which every subset, the empty set included, has a supremum and an infimum.

**Problem.** In an ordered set S, every element is an upper bound of the empty set, so sup ∅ exists exactly when S has a least element. Hence ℝ, which has no least element, is Dedekind complete only because the definition skips the empty set.

**How the definition helps.** The word nonempty removes the one subset that would make ℝ fail. With the nonempty clause, Dedekind completeness is self-dual: it is the same as asking for infima of nonempty sets bounded below. A Dedekind complete set with a top and a bottom is a complete lattice, with the bottom as sup ∅ and the top as inf ∅. Our own example: the extended real line is such a complete lattice.

**Paper or page:** [Infimum of Empty Set is Greatest Element](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Infimum_of_Empty_Set_is_Greatest_Element), [Supremum of Empty Set is Smallest Element](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Supremum_of_Empty_Set_is_Smallest_Element), [Dedekind Completeness is Self-Dual](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Dedekind_Completeness_is_Self-Dual), [Dedekind-Complete Bounded Ordered Set is Complete Lattice](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Dedekind-Complete_Bounded_Ordered_Set_is_Complete_Lattice). It says: “Suppose that inf ∅, the infimum of the empty set, exists in S. Then ∀s ∈ S: s ⪯ inf ∅. That is, inf ∅ is the greatest element of S.”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Infimum of Empty Set is Greatest Element](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Infimum_of_Empty_Set_is_Greatest_Element)
- [ProofWiki, Supremum of Empty Set is Smallest Element](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Supremum_of_Empty_Set_is_Smallest_Element)
- [ProofWiki, Dedekind Completeness is Self-Dual](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Dedekind_Completeness_is_Self-Dual)
- [ProofWiki, Dedekind-Complete Bounded Ordered Set is Complete Lattice](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Dedekind-Complete_Bounded_Ordered_Set_is_Complete_Lattice)

### Excluding endpoints makes every countable dense order isomorphic to the rationals

**Remember:** No ends and no gaps: every countable such order is ℚ.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 06A05 (Total orders), 03C15, 03C35. arXiv math.LO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A linear order is dense if between any two elements there is a third. It is unbounded if it has no least and no greatest element.

**Problem.** Every nonempty countable dense linear order without endpoints is isomorphic to the rational numbers. In model theory, the theory of such orders has exactly one countable model.

**How the definition helps.** Without endpoints, the back-and-forth method can always place the next element, because there is always room above, below and between. The excluded counterexamples are the rationals in \[0, 1\] and in \[0, 1) (our own example). Both are countable and dense, but neither is isomorphic to ℚ or to the other. The word nonempty excludes the empty order, which is dense and unbounded by default.

**Wikipedia:** [Cantor's isomorphism theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor%27s_isomorphism_theorem). It says: “Cantor's isomorphism theorem states that every two nonempty countable dense unbounded linear orders are order-isomorphic.”

**Sources:**

- [Cantor, G. (1895). Beiträge zur Begründung der transfiniten Mengenlehre. Mathematische Annalen 46, 481–512.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02124929)

### Möbius functions of posets unify inclusion–exclusion

**Remember:** The Möbius function is the inverse of 'is less than or equal to'.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 06A07 (Combinatorics of partially ordered sets), 06A11. arXiv math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a locally finite poset, functions of pairs x ≤ y form the incidence algebra, with product (f∗g)(x, y) = ∑ f(x, z)g(z, y) over x ≤ z ≤ y. The zeta function is ζ(x, y) = 1 for x ≤ y. The Möbius function μ is the inverse of ζ under this product.

**Problem.** Möbius inversion: in a poset where every element has finitely many elements below it, g(y) = ∑<sub>x≤y</sub> f(x) for all y exactly when f(y) = ∑<sub>x≤y</sub> μ(x, y) g(x) for all y. Inclusion–exclusion, classical Möbius inversion and the finite difference calculus are special cases.

**How the definition helps.** Defining μ as the inverse of ζ turns all three results into special cases of one formula. For finite subsets ordered by inclusion, μ(S, T) = (−1)ᵏ with k the size of T ∖ S, so Möbius inversion is inclusion–exclusion. For positive integers ordered by divisibility, μ is the classical Möbius function. For the natural numbers in their usual order, Möbius inversion is the backward difference operator.

**Wikipedia:** [Incidence algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_algebra). It says: “whenever S and T are finite subsets of E with S ⊆ T, and Möbius inversion is called the principle of inclusion-exclusion.”

**Sources:**

- [Gian-Carlo Rota, On the foundations of combinatorial theory I. Theory of Möbius functions, Zeitschrift für Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und Verwandte Gebiete 2 (1964) 340–368](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00531932)

### Defining floor by a Galois connection gives its rules by reasoning

**Remember:** Floor is the best integer below x, and that defines everything.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A15 (Galois correspondences, closure operators (in relation to ordered sets)). arXiv math.CO, math.CT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A monotone Galois connection between partial orders A and B is a pair of maps, F from A to B and G back. They satisfy F(a) ≤ b exactly when a ≤ G(b). F is the lower adjoint and G the upper adjoint. The floor function is the upper adjoint of the inclusion of the integers into the real numbers.

**Problem.** For every real x and integer n, ⌊x + n⌋ = ⌊x⌋ + n.

**How the definition helps.** The rule m ≤ x exactly when m ≤ ⌊x⌋, for integers m, turns each claim about floors into a chain of equivalences. Take any integer m (our own steps). Then m ≤ ⌊x + n⌋ exactly when m − n ≤ x, so exactly when m − n ≤ ⌊x⌋, so exactly when m ≤ ⌊x⌋ + n. Two integers with the same integers below them are equal, so the rule follows with no case analysis.

**Wikipedia:** [Galois connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_connection). It says: “The well-known properties of the floor function, such as ⌊x+n⌋=⌊x⌋+n, can be derived by elementary reasoning from this Galois connection.”

**Sources:**

- [Ore, O. (1944). Galois connexions. Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 55, 493–513.](https://doi.org/10.2307/1990305)

### Galois connections give the shape of every correspondence theorem

**Remember:** Keep only the closed elements, and every Galois connection is a perfect correspondence.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A15 (Galois correspondences, closure operators (in relation to ordered sets)), 18A40. arXiv math.CT, math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Galois connection between posets P and Q is a pair of order-reversing maps f : P → Q and g : Q → P. They satisfy p ≤ g(q) exactly when q ≤ f(p). The closed elements are those fixed by g∘f (in P) or by f∘g (in Q).

**Problem.** For every Galois connection, f and g restrict to inverse order-reversing bijections between the closed elements of P and of Q. The fundamental theorem of Galois theory and the correspondence between radical ideals and Zariski-closed sets are instances.

**How the definition helps.** The bijection between closed elements takes two lines, so the shape of every correspondence theorem holds by definition. The real work in each case is to find the closed elements. For a finite Galois extension L/K, every intermediate field is closed because L is Galois over it, and every subgroup is closed by Artin's lemma. For k algebraically closed, the statement that the closed ideals are the radical ideals is the strong Nullstellensatz.

**nLab:** [Galois connection](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Galois+connection), [Galois theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Galois+theory), [Zariski topology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Zariski+topology). It says: “others reserve it for its restriction to its fixed points, where it becomes an adjoint equivalence.”

**Sources:**

- [Øystein Ore, Galois connexions, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 55 (1944) 493–513](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1944-0010555-7)

### Lower adjoints of Galois connections preserve all existing joins

**Remember:** Lower adjoints keep joins, upper adjoints keep meets, by one line.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A15 (Galois correspondences, closure operators (in relation to ordered sets)). arXiv math.CO, math.CT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a monotone Galois connection, F is the lower adjoint and G the upper adjoint when F(a) ≤ b exactly when a ≤ G(b).

**Problem.** A lower adjoint preserves every join that exists: F(sup S) = sup of the F(s) for s in S. For example, the image map of a function preserves unions.

**How the definition helps.** The defining equivalence turns the claim into a statement about upper bounds, so the proof is one chain of equivalences. F(sup S) ≤ b holds exactly when sup S ≤ G(b), so exactly when s ≤ G(b) for every s in S, so exactly when F(s) ≤ b for every s (our own steps). The image map is the lower adjoint of the preimage map (our own example). Dually, upper adjoints preserve all existing meets.

**Wikipedia:** [Galois connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_connection), [Complete lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_lattice). It says: “Another important property of Galois connections is that lower adjoints preserve all suprema that exist within their domain.”

**Sources:**

- [Ore, O. (1944). Galois connexions. Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 55, 493–513.](https://doi.org/10.2307/1990305)

### Taking the diamond isomorphism as the definition of a modular lattice

**Remember:** In every diamond a ∧ b, a, b, a ∨ b, opposite sides match.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 06B05 (Structure theory of lattices), 06A15. arXiv math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Take a lattice and two elements a and b in it. The map z ↦ z ∧ b goes from the interval \[a, a ∨ b\] to the interval \[a ∧ b, b\], and the map w ↦ a ∨ w goes back. In any lattice, these two maps are adjoint (a Galois connection). The lattice is modular if, for all a and b, these two maps are inverse to each other.

**Problem.** A lattice is modular exactly when its order dual is modular.

**How the definition helps.** Reversing the order swaps the two intervals and the two maps, so the definition is unchanged (our own). The work moves into the proof that this definition agrees with the usual modular law: if a ≤ b, then (a ∨ z) ∧ b = a ∨ (z ∧ b). The nLab proves this equivalence in a few lines. Examples are the lattices of subspaces of a vector space and of normal subgroups of a group.

**nLab:** [modular lattice](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/modular+lattice). It says: “This is perhaps the most memorable definition for a category theorist: it is a precise expression of the slogan given in the Idea section.”

**Sources:**

- [Richard Dedekind, Ueber die von drei Moduln erzeugte Dualgruppe, Mathematische Annalen 53 (1900) 371–403](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01448979)

### Asking for all joins gives all meets of a complete lattice

**Remember:** The meet of a set is the join of its lower bounds.

*True by definition.* MSC 06B23 (Complete lattices, completions). arXiv math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A complete lattice is a partially ordered set in which every subset, the empty set included, has a least upper bound, its join, and a greatest lower bound, its meet.

**Problem.** A partially ordered set in which every subset has a join is a complete lattice. Every subset then also has a meet.

**How the definition helps.** The meet of a set X is simply the join of the set of all lower bounds of X. Each element of X is an upper bound of those lower bounds, so this join is below every element of X and is the greatest lower bound. The empty set is needed, since its join gives the least element. So a family of subsets that is closed under all intersections is a complete lattice (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Completeness (order theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completeness_%28order_theory%29), [Complete lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_lattice). It says: “The best-known example is the existence of all suprema, which is in fact equivalent to the existence of all infima.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### In a complete lattice every order-preserving map has a fixed point

**Remember:** Every subset has a supremum, even the empty one, so a bottom always exists.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 06B23 (Complete lattices, completions), 47H10. arXiv math.CO, math.LO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A complete lattice is a partially ordered set in which every subset has a supremum (least upper bound) and an infimum (greatest lower bound). This includes the empty set. So a complete lattice has a least and a greatest element, and it is never empty.

**Problem.** Every order-preserving map f from a complete lattice to itself has a fixed point. (Order-preserving means that x ≤ y implies f(x) ≤ f(y).) It even has a least and a greatest fixed point.

**How the definition helps.** Completeness supplies the supremum that the proof needs. The supremum of all x with x ≤ f(x) is a fixed point, and in fact the greatest one. Tarski proved more: the fixed points form a complete lattice, which is never empty. Davis proved the converse: a lattice in which every order-preserving map has a fixed point is complete.

**Wikipedia:** [Knaster–Tarski theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knaster%E2%80%93Tarski_theorem). It says: “If every order-preserving function f : L → L on a lattice L has a fixed point, then L is a complete lattice.”

**Sources:**

- [Alfred Tarski, A lattice-theoretical fixpoint theorem and its applications, Pacific Journal of Mathematics 5 (1955)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1955.5.285)
- [Anne C. Davis, A characterization of complete lattices, Pacific Journal of Mathematics 5 (1955)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1955.5.311)

### The meet definition makes least-fixed-point induction immediate

**Remember:** The meet of all candidates lies below each one.

*True by definition.* MSC 06B23 (Complete lattices, completions), 03B70. arXiv cs.LO, math.LO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let f preserve order on a complete lattice, one where every subset has a greatest lower bound and a least upper bound. A prefixed point is an x with f(x) ≤ x. Define μf as the meet, or greatest lower bound, of all prefixed points.

**Problem.** μf is the least fixed point of f. Moreover, Park induction holds: if f(x) ≤ x, then μf ≤ x.

**How the definition helps.** The meet definition gives the induction rule immediately because a meet lies below every term in it. A different construction applies f repeatedly starting from the least element. That construction needs extra conditions or a way to continue past the finite stages. The work here lies in proving that μf actually is a fixed point. For every prefixed x, monotonicity gives f(μf) ≤ f(x) ≤ x, so f(μf) ≤ μf. Applying f gives f(f(μf)) ≤ f(μf), so f(μf) is prefixed and μf ≤ f(μf).

**Wikipedia:** [Knaster–Tarski theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knaster%E2%80%93Tarski_theorem). It says: “⋀P = ⋀{ x ∈ L ∣ x ≥ f(x) } as the least fixpoint of f.”

**Sources:**

- [Alfred Tarski, A lattice-theoretical fixpoint theorem and its applications, Pacific Journal of Mathematics (1955)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1955.5.285)

### Distributivity implies modularity by substitution

**Remember:** Distribute first, then absorb the smaller element.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 06D05 (Structure and representation theory of distributive lattices), 01A60. arXiv math.CO, math.HO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a lattice, two elements have a greatest lower bound, their meet ∧, and a least upper bound, their join ∨. A distributive lattice satisfies both distributive laws for these operations.

**Problem.** Every distributive lattice is modular. If a ≤ b, then (a ∨ z) ∧ b = a ∨ (z ∧ b).

**How the definition helps.** The distributive law expands (a ∨ z) ∧ b into (a ∧ b) ∨ (z ∧ b). In our own calculation, a ≤ b gives a ∧ b = a, proving the modular law. Birkhoff also characterized distributivity by excluding two five-element lattices, the diamond and the pentagon, as subsets closed under meet and join. Starting from that description puts the work in Birkhoff’s equivalence.

**nLab:** [distributive lattice](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/distributive+lattice), [modular lattice](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/modular+lattice). It says: “A lattice L is distributive if and only if there is no embedding of N₅ or M₃ into L that preserves binary meets and binary joins.”

**Paper or page:** [On complemented, uniquely complemented and uniquely complemented nondistributive lattices (a historical and epistemological note about a mathematical mystery)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04506). It says: “Any distributive lattice is modular.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The bottom element is not join-irreducible, so Birkhoff's representation is exact

**Remember:** The bottom is the empty join, as 1 is the empty product.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 06D05 (Structure and representation theory of distributive lattices), 06B15. arXiv math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** In a lattice, an element is join-irreducible if it is not the join of a finite set of other elements. The bottom element is the join of the empty set, so it is not join-irreducible. A lower set of a poset is a set that contains everything below each of its elements.

**Problem.** Every finite distributive lattice is isomorphic to the lattice of lower sets of its poset of join-irreducible elements. The bottom of the lattice matches the empty lower set.

**How the definition helps.** Leaving the bottom out makes the map from lower sets to elements one-to-one, as leaving 1 out of the primes makes factorizations unique. Suppose the bottom counted as join-irreducible (our own example). Then the empty lower set and the set holding only the bottom would both map to the bottom. With the convention, each element corresponds to the set of join-irreducibles below it, and the bottom to the empty set. The theorem then uses distributivity to show that join-irreducible elements are join-prime. Infinite distributive lattices need more, such as Priestley duality.

**Wikipedia:** [Birkhoff's representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%27s_representation_theorem). It says: “Equivalently, x is join-irreducible if it is neither the bottom element of the lattice (the join of zero elements) nor the join of any two smaller elements.”

**Sources:**

- [G. Birkhoff, Rings of sets, Duke Mathematical Journal 3 (1937) 443–454](https://doi.org/10.1215/S0012-7094-37-00334-X)

### The median identity makes distributivity visibly self-dual

**Remember:** Swapping meet and join only exchanges the two sides.

*True by definition.* MSC 06D05 (Structure and representation theory of distributive lattices). arXiv math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The usual distributive law is x∧(y∨z) = (x∧y)∨(x∧z). An equivalent definition uses the median identity (a∧b)∨(a∧c)∨(b∧c) = (a∨b)∧(a∨c)∧(b∨c).

**Problem.** The order dual of a distributive lattice is distributive. Its order is reversed, so meet and join exchange roles.

**How the definition helps.** The median definition makes duality immediate because exchanging meet and join just swaps the two sides of the identity. With the one-sided law, one must prove the other law separately. The work lies in showing that the median identity and the usual distributive law are equivalent.

**nLab:** [distributive lattice](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/distributive+lattice). It says: “A lattice is distributive if and only if the identity (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c) ∨ (b ∧ c) = (a ∨ b) ∧ (a ∨ c) ∧ (b ∨ c) is satisfied.”

**Wikipedia:** [Distributive lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributive_lattice). It says: “It is a basic fact of lattice theory that the above condition is equivalent to its dual”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Atoms exclude zero, so finite Boolean algebras are power sets

**Remember:** Atoms play the part of singletons, and the empty set is no singleton.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 06E05 (Structure theory of Boolean algebras), 06B05. arXiv math.CO, math.LO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let P be a partially ordered set with least element 0. An atom of P is an element a with 0 &lt; a and nothing strictly between 0 and a. So 0 is never an atom. Atoms are the order-theory version of one-element sets.

**Problem.** Every finite Boolean algebra is isomorphic to the power set of its set of atoms. So the number of elements of a finite Boolean algebra is a power of two.

**How the definition helps.** Atoms are the nonzero minimal elements, so they behave exactly like the singletons of a power set. In a finite Boolean algebra, each element is the join of the atoms below it, and the map to that set of atoms is an isomorphism (our own). If 0 counted as an atom, a set of atoms with 0 and the same set without 0 would have the same join (our own). Infinite Boolean algebras can have no atoms, and then Stone's representation theorem is needed (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Atom (order theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom_%28order_theory%29), [Boolean algebra (structure)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29). It says: “It can be shown that every finite Boolean algebra is isomorphic to the Boolean algebra of all subsets of a finite set.”

**Sources:**

- [Stone, M. H. (1936). The theory of representation for Boolean algebras. Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 40, 37–111.](https://doi.org/10.2307/1989664)

### Distributivity makes complements unique, so negation is an operation

**Remember:** Distributive lattices allow at most one complement per element.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 06E05 (Structure theory of Boolean algebras), 06B05. arXiv math.CO, math.LO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let L be a lattice with least element 0 and greatest element 1. A complement of an element a is an element b with a ∧ b = 0 and a ∨ b = 1. A Boolean algebra is a complemented distributive lattice.

**Problem.** In a bounded distributive lattice, each element has at most one complement. So in a Boolean algebra, complementation is a well-defined operation.

**How the definition helps.** Distributivity forces two complements of the same element to be equal. Let b and c both be complements of a (our own steps). Then b = b ∧ (a ∨ c) = (b ∧ a) ∨ (b ∧ c) = b ∧ c, and in the same way c = b ∧ c. The condition excludes lattices such as the diamond lattice M₃, where each middle element has two complements (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Complemented lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complemented_lattice). It says: “In bounded distributive lattices, complements are unique.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Truth tables count the elements of finitely generated free Boolean algebras

**Remember:** Count the truth tables, one output bit for each input tuple.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 06E05 (Structure theory of Boolean algebras), 03G05. arXiv math.LO, math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Boolean algebra has meet, join, complement and constants 0 and 1, as in the algebra of subsets. The free algebra on n generators allows any assignment of them to extend uniquely to a homomorphism. For finite n we can take its elements to be functions from n bits to one bit, with the operations applied to each value. The other construction takes expressions modulo the Boolean algebra laws.

**Problem.** The free Boolean algebra on n generators has 2 raised to the power 2ⁿ elements.

**How the definition helps.** The function definition reduces the count to choosing a bit for each of the 2ⁿ inputs. The work moves into proving that these functions really give the free algebra. In our own argument, each truth table is a join of elementary terms, one for each row with output 1. Each such term is the meet that chooses the variable or its complement in every position. The Boolean laws put every expression into this form, so its truth table determines it in every Boolean algebra.

**Wikipedia:** [Free Boolean algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Boolean_algebra). It says: “Another way to see why the free Boolean algebra on an n-element set has 2<sup>2<sup>n</sup></sup> elements is to note that each element is a function from n bits to one.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Boolean rings make lattice ideals into ring ideals

**Remember:** Turn the Boolean algebra into a ring, and ring theory does the rest.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 06E20 (Ring-theoretic properties of Boolean algebras), 06E15. arXiv math.CO, math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Boolean ring is a ring in which every element x satisfies x·x = x. A Boolean algebra becomes a Boolean ring with symmetric difference as addition and meet as multiplication. The two constructions are inverse to each other.

**Problem.** A subset of a Boolean algebra is an order ideal exactly when it is a ring ideal of the associated Boolean ring. The same holds for prime ideals and for maximal ideals.

**How the definition helps.** With this correspondence, the ring theory of ideals, quotients and prime ideals applies directly. For example, every prime ideal of a Boolean ring is maximal, since the quotient is an integral domain with x·x = x, so it is the field with two elements. This is what Stone needed to represent Boolean algebras as algebras of sets. What stays hard is to show that there are enough prime ideals, which needs the Boolean prime ideal theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Boolean ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_ring), [Boolean algebra (structure)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_algebra_%28structure%29). It says: “Furthermore, a subset of a Boolean ring is a ring ideal (prime ring ideal, maximal ring ideal) if and only if it is an order ideal (prime order ideal, maximal order ideal) of the Boolean algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [Stone, M. H. (1936). The theory of representation for Boolean algebras. Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 40, 37–111.](https://doi.org/10.2307/1989664)

### Chain-complete posets give inflationary maps fixed points without choice

**Remember:** Bourbaki–Witt is Zorn's lemma with the choice taken out.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 06A06 (Partial orders, general), 03E25. arXiv math.LO, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A partially ordered set is chain complete if every chain (totally ordered subset) has a least upper bound. A function f is inflationary if f(x) ≥ x for every x.

**Problem.** If X is a chain-complete partially ordered set and f is an inflationary map on X, then f has a fixed point. The proof does not use the axiom of choice.

**How the definition helps.** The theorem isolates the part of Zorn's lemma that needs no choice, so choice shrinks to one step. In a chain-complete set with no maximal element, a choice function picks some y &gt; x for each x. This gives an inflationary map with no fixed point, which is a contradiction. Applied to the chain-complete set of all chains of an order, this gives a maximal chain and hence Zorn's lemma.

**Wikipedia:** [Bourbaki–Witt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourbaki%E2%80%93Witt_theorem). It says: “Note the above argument does not rely on the axiom of choice. (In the case of a proof of Zorn's lemma, Choice is used to define an inflationary map.)”

**Sources:**

- [Bourbaki, N. (1949). Sur le théorème de Zorn. Archiv der Mathematik 2, 434–437.](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02036949)
- [Witt, E. (1950). Beweisstudien zum Satz von M. Zorn. Mathematische Nachrichten 4, 434–438.](https://doi.org/10.1002/mana.3210040138)

### An up and down relation gives the path count n!

**Remember:** Commuting down past up produces the factors n, n − 1, and so on.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A07 (Combinatorics of partially ordered sets), 05A19. arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A differential poset is a graded poset with a least element. The up operator U sends an element to the sum of the elements that cover it, and the down operator D sends it to the sum of the elements it covers. The poset is 1-differential when DU − UD = I.

**Problem.** In a 1-differential poset, exactly n! paths go up n steps from the least element and then back down n steps to it. For partitions ordered by adding one box, this counts pairs of ways to build the same n-box shape.

**How the definition helps.** The operator relation makes each down step after n up steps contribute a factor n on the least element (our own). Moving D past the n copies of U gives DUⁿ = UⁿD + nUⁿ⁻¹, and D sends the least element to zero (our own). Repeating gives n!, since matrix entries of these operator products count paths (our own). The work moves to checking the relation, which for partitions is a count of the ways to add and remove boxes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Differential poset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_poset). It says: “Then the second and third conditions may be replaced by the statement that DU − UD = r I (where I is the identity).”

**Sources:**

- [R. P. Stanley, Differential posets, Journal of the American Mathematical Society 1 (1988) 919–961](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0894-0347-1988-0941434-9)

### Möbius inversion on divisor intervals gives the prime formula

**Remember:** Factor a divisor interval into prime-power chains and multiply their Möbius values.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A07 (Combinatorics of partially ordered sets), 11A25. arXiv math.CO, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Möbius function of a finite poset is the inverse of its zeta matrix, where ζ(x, y) = 1 when x ≤ y and 0 otherwise. The arithmetic Möbius function μ(n) is zero if a squared prime divides n, and otherwise (−1) to the number of primes dividing n.

**Problem.** The Möbius value from 1 to n in the divisibility order equals the arithmetic Möbius function at n.

**How the definition helps.** The inverse definition makes the prime formula a product, because the inverse for a product of orders is the product of their inverses. Unique prime factorization makes the divisors of n a product of chains of prime powers (our own). In a chain the inverse has 1 on the diagonal, −1 one step above it, and zero elsewhere. The arithmetic definition instead starts from the prime formula and leaves a check that it gives the inverse (our own).

**nLab:** [Möbius inversion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/M%C3%B6bius+inversion). It says: “The Möbius function of the cartesian product P × Q of two posets P and Q is the product of their Möbius functions:”

**Wikipedia:** [Incidence algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_algebra). It says: “Now the Möbius function of D is the product of the Möbius functions for the factor posets, computed above, giving the classical formula:”

**Sources:**

- [G.-C. Rota, On the foundations of combinatorial theory I. Theory of Möbius functions, Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie verw. Gebiete 2 (1964) 340–368](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00531932)

### Taking Euler's relation as a definition extends Dehn–Sommerville to Eulerian posets

**Remember:** Euler's relation on every interval is the whole definition of Eulerian.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 06A07 (Combinatorics of partially ordered sets), 52B05. arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A graded poset has a rank function that goes up by one along each covering step. It is Eulerian if every nontrivial interval has as many elements of even rank as of odd rank. Equivalently, its Möbius function is μ(x, y) = (−1) raised to the rank difference.

**Problem.** For every Eulerian poset of rank d + 1, Stanley's toric h-vector satisfies the Dehn–Sommerville equations hₖ = h\_(d−k). Face lattices of polytopes, simplicial homology spheres and intervals of Bruhat orders are Eulerian.

**How the definition helps.** The definition keeps exactly the property that the Dehn–Sommerville proof uses, so the proof works in the general setting (our own remark). For a polytope, each interval of the face lattice is itself a face lattice, so the even–odd balance is Euler's formula (our own remark). The empty face and the whole polytope must be included, or the intervals would not all be of this form. For simplicial polytopes the toric h-vector is the usual h-vector.

**Wikipedia:** [Eulerian poset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eulerian_poset). It says: “The face lattice of a convex polytope, consisting of its faces, together with the smallest element, the empty face, and the largest element, the polytope itself, is an Eulerian lattice.”

**Sources:**

- [R. P. Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 1, second edition, Cambridge University Press (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139058520)

### Well-quasi-orders keep the order on subsets well-founded

**Remember:** A well-quasi-order is well-founded and has no infinite antichain.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 06A07 (Combinatorics of partially ordered sets), 03E05. arXiv math.CO, math.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A quasi-order is a reflexive and transitive relation ≤. A well-quasi-order is a quasi-order in which every infinite sequence x₀, x₁, … has some i &lt; j with xᵢ ≤ xⱼ. This is stronger than being well-founded (having no infinite strictly descending chain). It also forbids infinite antichains, which are infinite sets of elements that are pairwise incomparable.

**Problem.** If ≤ is a well-quasi-order on X, then the order on subsets of X, with A ≤⁺ B when each element of A is below some element of B, is well-founded.

**How the definition helps.** An infinite antichain can make the subset order descend forever, and a well-quasi-order has no infinite antichain. Our own example: an infinite antichain a₁, a₂, … gives the descending chain {a₁, a₂, …} &gt;⁺ {a₂, a₃, …} &gt;⁺ ⋯. So well-foundedness of the original order alone is not enough. The subset order need not itself be a well-quasi-order, which leads to better-quasi-orders (our own remark).

**Wikipedia:** [Well-quasi-ordering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-quasi-ordering). It says: “One can show that this quasiordering on P(X) need not be well-founded, but if one takes the original quasi-ordering to be a well-quasi-ordering, then it is.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A geometric series for the Möbius function counts chains

**Remember:** Expand the inverse as a geometric series to count chains with alternating signs.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A11 (Algebraic aspects of posets), 06A07. arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the incidence algebra of a finite poset, write ζ = δ + η, where δ is the identity and η(x, y) = 1 when x &lt; y and 0 otherwise. The Möbius function μ is the inverse of ζ.

**Problem.** For x &lt; y, μ(x, y) is the sum of the numbers of strict chains from x to y, with sign (−1) to their lengths. The length counts the steps in the chain.

**How the definition helps.** Defining μ as an inverse gives the geometric series δ − η + η² − ⋯ (our own). The power ηⁱ(x, y) counts the chains from x to y with i steps (our own). The powers vanish beyond the longest chain, so the series is finite and inverts δ + η (our own). Starting from the recursion instead leaves a check that the alternating chain count obeys it (our own).

**nLab:** [Möbius inversion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/M%C3%B6bius+inversion). It says: “A Möbius function of P is defined as an inverse to the zeta function with respect to the convolution product.”

**Wikipedia:** [Incidence algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incidence_algebra). It says: “This can be shown using Philip Hall's theorem, relating the value of μ(0,1) to the number of chains of length i.”

**Sources:**

- [P. Hall, The Eulerian functions of a group, Quarterly Journal of Mathematics os-7 (1936) 134–151](https://doi.org/10.1093/qmath/os-7.1.134)
- [G.-C. Rota, On the foundations of combinatorial theory I. Theory of Möbius functions, Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie verw. Gebiete 2 (1964) 340–368](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00531932)

### Möbius inverses give both recursions and reverse the order

**Remember:** The inverse identity works on both sides and survives reversing the order.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A11 (Algebraic aspects of posets), 06A07. arXiv math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let P be a partially ordered set with finite intervals \[x, y\]. Multiply functions on comparable pairs by summing f(x, z)g(z, y) over z in \[x, y\]. The Möbius function μ is the two-sided inverse of the function ζ that equals 1 on all comparable pairs x ≤ y. Another definition starts with μ(x, x) = 1 and chooses μ(x, y) so that the sum of μ(x, z) over \[x, y\] is zero.

**Problem.** For x &lt; y, both the sum of μ(x, z) and the sum of μ(z, y) over z in \[x, y\] vanish. Reversing the order exchanges the two arguments of μ.

**How the definition helps.** The two-sided inverse definition gives both sums at once, because multiplying by ζ on either side gives zero off the diagonal. Reversing the order interchanges the factors in every product, so it also reverses the inverse identity (our own). Starting with one recursion leaves the opposite identity to prove (our own). The work moves into constructing the inverse. Each recursion constructs a one-sided inverse, and associativity makes the two inverses equal (our own).

**nLab:** [Möbius inversion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/M%C3%B6bius+inversion). It says: “A Möbius function of P is defined as an inverse to the zeta function with respect to the convolution product.”

**Sources:**

- [G.-C. Rota, On the foundations of combinatorial theory I. Theory of Möbius functions, Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie verw. Gebiete 2 (1964) 340–368](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00531932)

### An adjoint description makes closed elements determine closure

**Remember:** An element closes to the least closed element above it.

*True by definition.* MSC 06A15 (Galois correspondences, closure operators (in relation to ordered sets)). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.
