### Relative class numbers keep odd characters

**Remember:** Divide by the real class number to keep only odd characters.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11M20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, let K be the field generated over ℚ by a primitive p-th root of unity. Its real subfield K⁺ consists of the elements fixed by complex conjugation. The relative class number is h⁻ = h(K)/h(K⁺), where h counts ideal classes.

**Problem.** Put n = (p−1)/2, and let R and R⁺ be the regulators of K and K⁺. Then h⁻ = p(√p/π)ⁿ(R⁺/R) times the product of L(1,χ) over the characters χ modulo p with χ(−1) = −1.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the ratio cancels exactly the factors indexed by even characters, those satisfying χ(−1) = 1. In our own derivation these characters index the zeta factors of K⁺, while all characters index those of K. The analytic class number formula expresses the ratio of residues at one in terms of class numbers and regulators. The absolute discriminants have ratio exp(n log p), and the fields contain 2p and 2 roots of unity respectively. These identities give the stated constant.

**Wikipedia:** [Class number formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_formula). It says: “there is a further formulation possible, as shown by Kummer.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Root discriminants ignore unramified extensions

**Remember:** The root cancels the extension degree.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a basis of the ring of integers over ℤ, form the matrix of field traces of pairwise basis products. Its determinant is the field discriminant. For a number field of degree n, the root discriminant is the nth root of its absolute discriminant value.

**Problem.** The root discriminant stays constant in extensions unramified at every finite prime. This means that no prime ideal acquires a repeated factor in the larger ring of integers.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the degree root cancels the power in the ordinary discriminant tower law (our own). The relative discriminant is the unit ideal because no finite prime ramifies (our own). The tower law therefore raises the absolute discriminant value to the extension degree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Discriminant of an algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant_of_an_algebraic_number_field). It says: “The relation between relative discriminants in a tower of fields shows that the root discriminant does not change in an unramified extension.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Tameness gives different exponent e − 1

**Remember:** Tame ramification contributes exactly its index minus one.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a number field extension, let e be the exponent of a prime ideal in the factorization of the prime below it. Ramification is tame there if the residue characteristic does not divide e. The different is the inverse ideal of elements whose products with all integers have integral trace.

**Problem.** At a tame prime of ramification index e, the different has exponent e − 1.

**How the definition helps.** Tameness keeps the leading coefficient e of the derivative nonzero in the residue field (our own). After completing and removing the unramified part, the integers have a generator π whose minimal polynomial is Eisenstein of degree e (our own). At π the term eπ<sup>(e−1)</sup> of the derivative has valuation e − 1, strictly below every other term (our own). In the wild extension ℚ₂(√2), the derivative 2√2 has valuation three although e = 2 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “The precise exponent to which a ramified prime P divides δ is termed the differential exponent of P and is equal to e − 1 if P is tamely ramified”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The different ideal shows exactly which primes ramify

**Remember:** The different's prime factors are exactly the ramified primes upstairs.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R32. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L be a number field with ring of integers O. The inverse different is the set of x in L such that the trace of xy is in ℤ for every y in O. The different is the inverse of this fractional ideal. It measures how far the trace pairing (x, y) ↦ Tr(xy) is from identifying O with its dual.

**Problem.** A prime ideal of L is ramified when it appears to a power above 1 in the factorization of the prime below. This happens exactly when it divides the different.

**How the definition helps.** The different is an ideal upstairs in L, so it can name the ramified primes of L one by one. The discriminant lives in the base field and only says which primes below have some ramified prime above them. The exact exponent of a prime in the different is e − 1 for tame ramification and at least e for wild ramification. What stays hard is the local computation of that exponent in the wild case.

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “Pi divides the relative different δL / K if and only if Pi is ramified, that is, if and only if the ramification index e(i) is greater than 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Richard Dedekind, Über die Discriminanten endlicher Körper, Abhandlungen der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen 29 (1882)](http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/en/dms/load/img/?IDDOC=39145)

### The narrow class group decides which primes a norm form represents

**Remember:** Signs matter for norm forms, so count ideals with positive generators.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R11, 11E16. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An element of a number field is totally positive when it is positive under every embedding into the real numbers. The narrow class group is the group of fractional ideals modulo principal ideals with a totally positive generator. The ordinary class group allows any generator.

**Problem.** Let K = ℚ(√d) have trivial narrow class group and discriminant D, and let q be the norm form of an integral basis. A prime p equals q(x,y) for some integers exactly in three cases. Either p divides D, or p = 2 and D ≡ 1 mod 8, or p is odd and (D/p) = 1.

**How the definition helps.** The narrow class group tracks the sign of a norm, and the ordinary class group does not. A split prime gives a principal ideal (α) with p = ±N(α), and a totally positive generator makes the sign positive (our own). The field ℚ(√6) shows the difference: its class group is trivial but its narrow class group has order 2. There −2 = 2² − 6·1², but 2 is not of the form x² − 6y², since squares are never 2 mod 3 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Narrow class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow_class_group). It says: “However, this statement is false if we focus only on p and not −p (and is in fact even false for p = 2), because the narrow class group is nontrivial.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Fröhlich and M. J. Taylor, Algebraic Number Theory, Cambridge University Press, 1991](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139172165)

### Trace determinants square lattice indices

**Remember:** A basis change enters a trace determinant twice.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An order in a number field is a subring containing 1 that has full rank inside the ring of integers. Choose a ℤ-basis of the order. Its discriminant is the determinant of the matrix of field traces of pairwise basis products.

**Problem.** If one order has index m in another order of the same field, its discriminant is m² times the larger order’s discriminant.

**How the definition helps.** Using the trace matrix makes the basis change appear twice in one determinant (our own). If C expresses the smaller basis in the larger basis, the matrix changes from T to CᵀTC (our own). The lattice index theorem identifies the absolute determinant of C with m (our own). This avoids computing how each entry in the alternative matrix of field embeddings changes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Discriminant of an algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant_of_an_algebraic_number_field). It says: “The discriminant of an order in K with integral basis b₁,…,bₙ is defined in the same way.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Trace duals multiply in towers

**Remember:** Trace maps compose, so trace duals multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The trace dual for L/K consists of elements x of L for which every integer y of L gives an integral field trace Tr(xy). Its inverse fractional ideal is the different. A fractional ideal becomes an ordinary ideal after multiplication by a nonzero integer.

**Problem.** In a tower L/K/F, the different of L/F is the product of the different of L/K and the extended different of K/F.

**How the definition helps.** The trace dual turns the tower formula into two integral trace tests (our own). Traces compose, and the integers of L contain the integers of K (our own). Thus x passes the combined test exactly when every Tr(xy) from L to K belongs to the trace dual for K/F (our own). Locally that dual has one generator, which factors out of the test (our own). Inverting the resulting product gives the formula without computing generators from polynomial derivatives (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “In a tower of fields L/K/F the relative differents are related by δL/F = δL/K δK/F.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Unit signs explain narrow classes

**Remember:** The only signs that disappear come from units.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fractional ideals are ideals with denominators allowed. In the ordinary class group, two such ideals represent the same class if one is a nonzero scalar multiple of the other. In the narrow class group, the scalar must also be positive under every real embedding.

**Problem.** Forgetting positivity maps narrow classes onto ordinary classes. Its kernel is the group of sign patterns at the real embeddings modulo the signs of units.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping positivity in the quotient leaves only the signs of a principal generator to track (our own). Two generators differ by a unit, so their signs agree modulo unit signs (our own). Weak approximation, which lets one prescribe signs at all real embeddings, gives every sign pattern (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Narrow class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow_class_group). It says: “where now Pₖ⁺ is the group of totally positive principal fractional ideals”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Decomposition groups turn counting prime factors into orbit counting

**Remember:** Primes above p form one orbit; the stabilizer is the decomposition group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L over K be Galois with group G and P a prime of L above p. The decomposition group of P is the set of elements of G that send P to itself. The inertia group is the part that acts trivially on the residue field.

**Problem.** In a Galois extension, all primes above p have the same ramification index e and residue degree f. With g primes above p, the degree is e·f·g, and g is \|G\| divided by \|D\|.

**How the definition helps.** Once G acts on the primes above p, their number is an orbit size, so the orbit-stabilizer formula gives g = \|G\|/\|D\|. The work moves into the fact that G acts transitively on these primes. Transitivity also makes e and f the same for every prime above p. Then D maps onto the Galois group of the residue field extension, with kernel the inertia group.

**Wikipedia:** [Splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splitting_of_prime_ideals_in_Galois_extensions). It says: “the decomposition group of Pj, is the subgroup of elements of G sending a given Pj to itself.”

**Sources:**

- [David Hilbert, Die Theorie der algebraischen Zahlkörper, Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung 4 (1897)](http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002115344)

### Frobenius as a conjugacy class makes Chebotarev's theorem statable

**Remember:** Each prime picks a conjugacy class; classes are hit in proportion to size.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory), 11R45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let p be a prime number that does not ramify in a Galois extension of ℚ. Its Frobenius element acts as x ↦ xᵖ on the residue field of a prime above p. Different primes above p give conjugate elements, so p gives a conjugacy class.

**Problem.** Let L/ℚ be a finite Galois extension with group G, and let C be a conjugacy class of G. The unramified primes whose Frobenius class is C have density \|C\|/\|G\|.

**How the definition helps.** A prime only fixes its Frobenius element up to conjugation, so a conjugacy class is the invariant of p that a theorem can count. The Frobenius element of one prime above p depends on that choice, and taking the class removes the choice. For cyclotomic fields the theorem gives Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions (our own). What stays hard is the analytic proof.

**Wikipedia:** [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem). It says: “The statement of the more general Chebotarev density theorem is in terms of the Frobenius element of a prime (ideal), which is in fact an associated conjugacy class C of elements of the Galois group G.”

**Sources:**

- [Nikolai Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören, Mathematische Annalen 95 (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01206606)

### Frobenius defined by a pth-power congruence restricts to Frobenius below

**Remember:** Restrict the same power map to the smaller residue field.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L be a Galois number field and 𝔓 a prime ideal of its integers above the prime p. Suppose 𝔓 is unramified, so it appears with exponent one when the ideal generated by p is factored. Define the Frobenius of 𝔓 as the unique automorphism σ of L with σ(x) ≡ xᵖ modulo 𝔓 for every algebraic integer x in L. Another definition lifts the map x ↦ xᵖ, which generates the Galois group of the residue field.

**Problem.** Let L ⊃ K be number fields, both Galois over ℚ, and let 𝔓 in L lie over 𝔭 in K, both unramified. The Frobenius of 𝔓 restricts on K to the Frobenius of 𝔭.

**How the definition helps.** With the congruence definition, the restricted automorphism already passes the test that defines the Frobenius of 𝔭 (our own). For an algebraic integer x of K, σ(x) ≡ xᵖ modulo 𝔓, and both sides lie in the integers of K (our own). So the congruence holds modulo 𝔭, which is 𝔓 intersected with the integers of K (our own). Uniqueness of the Frobenius of 𝔭 then gives equality (our own). The work moves to proving that such a unique automorphism exists at an unramified prime (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Theorem 6.1. (Restrictions of Frobenius elements)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “Assume L/ℚ and K/ℚ are both Galois. Let 𝔓 and 𝔭 be unramified as above.”

### Restricted products put Poitou–Tate duality in one sequence

**Remember:** Almost everywhere unramified makes the infinite product locally compact.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois module M over a number field k, take the local cohomology groups H¹(kᵥ, M) over all places v. Their restricted product keeps only the families whose entry lies in the unramified subgroup at almost every place.

**Problem.** Global cohomology of M and of its twisted dual M′ = Hom(M, μ) fit into a nine-term exact sequence through restricted products of local cohomology. Summing the local pairings gives a perfect pairing of the restricted products for M and M′.

**How the definition helps.** The restriction makes the product locally compact, so Pontryagin duality applies to it (our own). Global classes are unramified almost everywhere, so they land in the restricted product (our own). The work went into the global duality theorems of Poitou and Tate.

**Wikipedia:** [Tate duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_duality). It says: “where ∏′ denotes a restricted product with respect to the unramified cohomology groups.”

**Sources:**

- [Jürgen Neukirch, Alexander Schmidt and Kay Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, Springer (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-37889-1)

### Artin and Hecke factors agree

**Remember:** The same Frobenius value gives both factors wherever the units act trivially.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11S40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An idele is a tuple of nonzero local elements, almost all units. A Hecke character is a continuous multiplicative character of ideles that is trivial on global elements. Given a one-dimensional finite Galois character, define its Hecke character by composition with global reciprocity. Normalize local reciprocity so a generator of the maximal ideal acts on residues by arithmetic Frobenius.

**Problem.** At every finite place of a number field, the Artin and Hecke Euler factors of these characters agree. An Euler factor is the local term in the product defining an L-function.

**How the definition helps.** Composition with reciprocity makes both definitions use the same character value (our own). Local units map onto inertia, the subgroup acting trivially on residues (our own). If the character is nontrivial on inertia, both factors equal one (our own). Otherwise both use its value on arithmetic Frobenius, which raises residues to the size of the base residue field (our own). Compatibility of global and local reciprocity supplies the comparison (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_reciprocity). It says: “connects Artin L-functions associated to abelian extensions of a number field with Hecke L-functions”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Artin kernels turn composita into intersections

**Remember:** The compositum keeps only the classes that fix both fields.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An idele class is a tuple of nonzero elements of the completions, almost all units, modulo simultaneous multiplication by a global element. For a finite abelian extension of number fields, the Artin map sends each class to a Galois automorphism. Its kernel describes the subgroup of norms on idele classes.

**Problem.** Take two finite abelian extensions of the same number field inside one algebraic closure. The norms on idele classes from their compositum form the intersection of their two norm subgroups.

**How the definition helps.** The kernel description turns the norm identity into a fixed field test (our own). An automorphism fixes the compositum exactly when it fixes both fields (our own). Global reciprocity supplies the hard step by identifying each kernel with the image of the idele class norm (our own).

**nLab:** [class field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/class+field+theory). It says: “by relating them to the idele class group.”

### Brauer reciprocity forces even ramification

**Remember:** Each nonsplit place contributes one half to a zero sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11S45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At each completion of ℚ, a quaternion algebra either becomes a matrix algebra or remains a division algebra. Call the former place split and the latter ramified. The local Brauer invariant records these cases by zero and one half respectively, modulo the integers.

**Problem.** A quaternion algebra over ℚ ramifies at an even number of places, counting the real place when it is nonsplit.

**How the definition helps.** The invariant converts a parity question into addition modulo the integers (our own). Only finitely many places ramify, and global Brauer reciprocity makes the sum of all local invariants zero (our own). Each ramified place contributes one half, so their number is even (our own). Reciprocity supplies the global step (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Quaternion algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternion_algebra). It says: “The number of places where a quaternion algebra over the rationals ramifies is always even”

### Cyclicity repairs the norm principle

**Remember:** Cyclic extensions turn everywhere local norms into global norms.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite Galois extension is cyclic if one automorphism generates its Galois group. A norm is the product of the conjugates of a nonzero field element. At a place of the base field, a local norm is a norm from a completion of the extension above that place.

**Problem.** An element of a number field that is a local norm everywhere from a finite cyclic extension is a global norm.

**How the definition helps.** Cyclicity lets one test the norm equation by checking each completion. For a cyclic extension, the norm equation has a solution exactly when its associated cyclic algebra is a matrix algebra (our own). The local-global theorem for these algebras supplies the hard step (our own). Hasse found that 3 is a local norm everywhere from ℚ(√−3, √13) but is not a global norm.

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse norm theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_norm_theorem). It says: “Hasse gave the counterexample that 3 is a local norm everywhere for the extension ℚ(√−3, √13)/ℚ but is not a global norm.”

**Paper or page:** [A Projective Twist on the Hasse Norm Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11159v1). It says: “\\mathrm {HNP}<sub>K</sub>(L) holds whenever L/K is cyclic.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Herbrand quotients make the first inequality computable

**Remember:** Herbrand quotients multiply and ignore finite pieces, so compute them on lattices.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 20J06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A be a module over a cyclic group G. Its Herbrand quotient h(A) is the order of Tate cohomology in degree 0 over that in degree 1. It is defined when both groups are finite.

**Problem.** For a cyclic extension L/K of number fields of degree n, the idele class group of L has Herbrand quotient n. So the index of the norm group in the idele class group of K is at least n.

**How the definition helps.** The quotient is multiplicative and ignores finite modules, so one may cut the idele class group into S-units and local unit groups (our own). Each cohomology group alone is hard to find, but the quotient for the S-units follows from Dirichlet's unit theorem (our own). The degree 0 group is the norm index, which gives the inequality.

**Wikipedia:** [Class formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_formation), [Herbrand quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbrand_quotient). It says: “It is fairly straightforward to prove, because the Herbrand quotient is easy to work out, as it is multiplicative on short exact sequences, and is 1 for finite modules.”

### Moduli with real places let conductors tell real abelian fields apart

**Remember:** Put the real place in the modulus to record whether signs matter.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11R20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A modulus of a number field is a formal product of finite primes with powers and of some real places. Congruence modulo a real place means that the quotient a/b is positive there.

**Problem.** Every abelian extension of a number field has a conductor, the smallest modulus whose ray class field contains it. Over ℚ, let n be the smallest number with K inside the n-th cyclotomic field. The conductor of K is n if K is real and n times ∞ otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** A real place in the modulus records a sign condition, and that is exactly ramification at infinity. For example, ℚ(ζ₅) has conductor 5 times ∞, and its real subfield ℚ(√5) has conductor 5 (our own). Without real places, every ray class field over ℚ would be real, so ℚ(ζ₅) would have no conductor (our own). What stays hard is the existence theorem of class field theory.

**Wikipedia:** [Modulus (algebraic number theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulus_%28algebraic_number_theory%29), [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “the conductor of K is then n if K is fixed by complex conjugation and n ∞ otherwise.”

### Outside the special case, local powers are global

**Remember:** Only 2-adic cyclotomic accidents stop local n-th powers from being global.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For s ≥ 2 let ηₛ be 2cos(2π/2ˢ). A field is s-special if it contains ηₛ but none of i, ηₛ₊₁ and iηₛ₊₁. The special case occurs when K is s-special with 2ˢ⁺¹ dividing n, and S contains the 2-adic primes p where Kₚ is s-special.

**Problem.** Let S be a finite set of primes of a number field K. Outside the special case, an element that is an n-th power at every prime outside S is an n-th power in K.

**How the definition helps.** The special case names exactly where the Hasse principle fails, so the theorem has no further exceptions. ℚ is 2-special, so Wang's example appears: 16 is an 8th power at every odd prime but not in ℚ. Even then the failure is a group of order 2. The work went into Wang's corrected proof, which uses class field theory (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Grunwald–Wang theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunwald%E2%80%93Wang_theorem). It says: “In the special case the failure of the Hasse principle is finite of order 2”

### Ray moduli bound composita

**Remember:** The stricter modulus maps onto both weaker ray class groups.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An idele is a tuple of nonzero local elements, almost all units. Idele classes identify tuples that differ by a common global factor. A modulus prescribes congruences at finite primes and positivity at selected real places. Its ray class group divides the idele class group by local units satisfying these conditions, allowing unrestricted factors at the remaining infinite places.

**Problem.** The compositum of two ray class fields lies in the ray class field for the least common multiple of their moduli.

**How the definition helps.** Using one group for all moduli turns comparison of separate ideal groups into inclusion of subgroups. The least common multiple imposes both sets of conditions, so its subgroup lies in each original subgroup (our own). Class field theory reverses these inclusions, placing both fields inside the field for the least common multiple (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ray class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_class_field). It says: “They are sometimes easier to handle theoretically because they are all quotients of a single group, and thus easier to compare.”

### The transfer reduces the principal ideal theorem

**Remember:** Extending ideals is the transfer, and the transfer to the commutator subgroup vanishes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 20J06, 11R29. arXiv math.NT, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let H be a subgroup of finite index in a group G. The transfer is a homomorphism from the abelianization of G to the abelianization of H, built by choosing coset representatives.

**Problem.** Every ideal of a number field K becomes principal in the Hilbert class field of K.

**How the definition helps.** Through Artin reciprocity, extending ideal classes from K to its Hilbert class field becomes the transfer from G to its derived subgroup. Here G is the Galois group of the second Hilbert class field over K (our own). So the theorem becomes the claim that this transfer is trivial. Furtwängler proved this group-theoretic claim in 1929, and that is where the work went.

**Wikipedia:** [Principal ideal theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal_theorem). It says: “he showed that it would follow if the transfer from a finite group to its derived subgroup is trivial.”

### Unramified at real places, the Hilbert class field matches the class group

**Remember:** Unramified everywhere, including at infinity, gives exactly the class group.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Hilbert class field of a number field K is its largest abelian extension that is unramified at every place. Unramified at a real place means that the real embedding stays real in the larger field.

**Problem.** The Galois group of the Hilbert class field over K is isomorphic to the ideal class group of K. Its degree is the class number.

**How the definition helps.** Counting real places as places that can ramify makes the extension match the ordinary class group. The page gives the bad case K = ℚ(√3), which has class number 1: its extension K(i) is unramified at every finite prime, but the real embeddings become complex. If K(i) were allowed, the extension would be larger than the class group predicts; K(i) is in fact the narrow class field of K. Furtwängler proved that the Hilbert class field exists.

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_class_field). It says: “That is, every real embedding of K extends to a real embedding of E, rather than to a complex embedding of E.”

### Centering pairs Hadamard factors

**Remember:** Center the reflection and the linear terms cancel.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Λ be the Dedekind zeta function of a number field with the discriminant and gamma factors from its functional equation. Set F(z) = (z²+¼)Λ(½+iz). The quadratic factor removes the poles at s = 0 and s = 1.

**Problem.** F is even, and F(z) = c·zᵐ ∏(1 − z²/w²) with a nonzero constant c. Here m is the order of vanishing of F at 0, and the product has one factor for each pair w, −w of nonzero zeros, counted with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** Centering at ½ turns the functional equation into F(z) = F(−z), pairing opposite zeros. This replaces separate factors for individual zeros of Λ. Hadamard’s theorem expresses the entire function F of order one as a product over zeros times an exponential of a linear polynomial. In our own calculation, the exponential corrections at w and −w cancel. The zero at the origin has even multiplicity, so evenness forces the remaining exponential to be constant.

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function). It says: “producing an entire function, and moves the critical line to the real line.”

### Equal zeta functions fix class number times regulator

**Remember:** Equal zeta functions force equal class number times regulator.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Dedekind zeta function sums inverse powers of the sizes of the quotients by nonzero integral ideals. Two fields are arithmetically equivalent if these functions agree. Equivalently, almost every rational prime gives the same list of residue field degrees in both fields.

**Problem.** Arithmetically equivalent number fields have the same class number times regulator. The class number counts ideal classes, and the regulator measures the volume of the lattice formed from logarithms of units.

**How the definition helps.** The zeta function definition makes the two residues at one equal before any prime factorizations are compared (our own). The residue is the coefficient of the simple pole there (our own). The analytic class number formula expresses it using the class number, regulator, discriminant, roots of unity, and counts of real and complex embeddings (our own). The cited invariance theorem matches these other factors, leaving equal products (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Notes on Explicit Constructions of Arithmetically Equivalent Global Function Fields via Torsion Points On Drinfeld Modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.08250v1), [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “product of regulator and class-number reg(𝒪ₖ)hₖ = reg(𝒪ₗ)hₗ”

### Finite-place logarithms absorb missing zeta factors

**Remember:** Finite-place logarithms account for the deleted Euler factors at zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let S contain every infinite place of a number field and finitely many finite primes. An S-unit is a field element with valuation zero outside S at every finite prime. Tabulate the logarithmic absolute values at S of a basis of S-units modulo roots of unity, doubling the logarithm at each complex place. Delete one row and call the absolute determinant R(S).

**Problem.** The S-zeta function omits prime factors at S. Its first nonzero Taylor coefficient at zero equals −h(S)R(S)/w. Here w counts roots of unity and h(S) counts ideal classes after allowing denominators at the finite primes in S.

**How the definition helps.** The finite-prime rows incorporate the logarithms from the omitted zeta factors into one regulator, in our own calculation. The row at a prime with residue field of size q records valuations multiplied by −log q. The valuation vectors have index equal to the number of ordinary ideal classes generated by the omitted primes. In the determinant this index cancels the corresponding decrease in the class number. The ordinary analytic class number formula supplies the starting identity.

**Paper or page:** [Special values of L-functions on regular arithmetic schemes of dimension 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00811). It says: “We obtain from the analytic class number formula for the S-zeta function of K (the arithmetic zeta function of U)”

### Gamma factors cancel trivial zeta zeros

**Remember:** Reflection moves negative integers into the region where the prime product converges.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a number field F with discriminant D, start with \|D\| raised to s/2 times its Dedekind zeta function. For each real embedding multiply by π raised to −s/2 times Γ(s/2), where Γ is Euler’s gamma function. For each conjugate pair of nonreal embeddings multiply by (2π) raised to −s times Γ(s). Call the resulting function Λ.

**Problem.** The completed function satisfies Λ(s) = Λ(1−s). In particular it is finite and nonzero at every negative integer, although the Riemann zeta function vanishes at −2.

**How the definition helps.** Completion puts all gamma factors inside one function, so the functional equation becomes a reflection, in our own explanation. Proving that equation is the analytic work. Reflection sends each negative integer to a real number greater than one. There the convergent product over primes and the gamma factors are all nonzero and finite.

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function). It says: “The functional equation for the Dedekind zeta function implies a set of trivial zeroes which cancel poles of the gamma factors in the equation”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Integrating over ideles proves Hecke's functional equation by Poisson summation

**Remember:** One Poisson summation on the adeles gives every Hecke functional equation.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields), 11R56. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The adeles of a number field are a restricted product of all its completions, and the ideles are their units. Tate's zeta integral is the integral over the ideles of a test function times a character times a power of the absolute value. The ideles carry a Haar measure, a measure that does not change under translation. For a test function that is a product of local functions, the integral splits into one factor per place.

**Problem.** Every Hecke L-function of a number field extends to a meromorphic function on the whole complex plane. It satisfies a functional equation that relates s and 1 − s. It has poles only when the character is a power of the idele norm (our own).

**How the definition helps.** The zeta integral turns the L-function into an integral over a group, and there Poisson summation applies directly. Inside the adeles, the number field is a discrete subgroup with compact quotient (our own). The local factor at each place, including the gamma factor at infinite places, comes from one local integral (our own). Hecke had used theta series for a lattice in the ring of integers. What stays hard is computing the local integrals at ramified places (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Tate's thesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%27s_thesis). It says: “Using harmonic analysis, more precisely the Poisson summation formula, he proved the functional equation and meromorphic continuation of the zeta integral and the Hecke L-function.”

### Nontrivial monomial characters give entire L-functions

**Remember:** Induce nontrivial characters and no zeta pole appears.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let G be the Galois group of a finite Galois extension of number fields. A one-dimensional character assigns a nonzero complex scalar to each group element and preserves multiplication. Induce such a character from a subgroup to G by taking a copy of its line for each coset. Form direct sums using only characters that are nontrivial on their inducing subgroup.

**Problem.** The Artin L-function of this direct sum is entire, meaning holomorphic on the whole complex plane.

**How the definition helps.** Excluding trivial characters removes the zeta factors that can have poles, in our own explanation. Artin’s induction formula converts each summand into a one-dimensional L-function over the field fixed by its subgroup. Hecke’s theorem makes each nontrivial factor entire. A trivial character instead gives that field’s zeta function, which has a pole at one.

**Paper or page:** [Equivariant algebraic K-theory and Artin L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03578). It says: “this meromorphic continuation is entire if ρ is a direct sum of inductions of non-trivial abelian characters on subgroups.”

### Norm-one classes exclude shifted poles

**Remember:** Test nontriviality on norm-one classes to avoid shifted poles.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An idele chooses a nonzero element in each completion of a number field, with a unit at almost every finite prime. Idele classes identify choices differing by one global field element. Multiplying the normalized local absolute values gives their norm. A unitary Hecke character is a continuous homomorphism from these classes to the unit circle.

**Problem.** If the character is nontrivial on the subgroup of norm one, its completed Hecke L-function is holomorphic everywhere.

**How the definition helps.** Our own test on norm-one classes excludes precisely the characters that depend only on the norm. Tate’s continuation theorem shows that only those characters can give poles. In our own example, χ(a) = exp(it log N(a)) weights each ideal of norm N(a), with real t ≠ 0. Its L-function is the Dedekind zeta function at s − it, with a pole at 1 + it.

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_character). It says: “Hecke proved these L-functions have a meromorphic continuation to the whole complex plane, being analytic except for a simple pole of order 1”

### Permutation representations factor intermediate zeta functions

**Remember:** A fixed field becomes a permutation representation.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L/K be a finite Galois extension of number fields with group G. For a subgroup H, let E be the field that H fixes. Give a complex vector space one basis vector per left coset of H. Let G act by permuting this basis.

**Problem.** The Dedekind zeta function of E equals the Artin L-function of this representation over K. Decomposing the representation into irreducible pieces factors the zeta function, with one factor per piece.

**How the definition helps.** The coset basis encodes all embeddings of E at once, in our own explanation. Its representation is the one induced from the trivial representation of H. Artin’s induction formula identifies their L-functions over K and E respectively. The trivial representation over E has the zeta function of E, and direct sums give products.

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function). It says: “Without the assumption that the extension is Galois, the formula becomes more complicated, but is also possible to obtain a similar factorization using the normal closure of the larger field and induced representations.”

### Prime-power traces give Artin log derivatives

**Remember:** Taking traces on fixed vectors includes the ramified primes.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ρ be a complex representation of the group of a finite Galois extension of number fields. At each prime 𝔭, inertia consists of local automorphisms acting trivially on residues. On vectors fixed by inertia, Frobenius represents raising residues to the power q, the base residue field size. Weight 𝔭ᵐ for m ≥ 1 by log(q) times the trace of the mth Frobenius power, and give other ideals weight zero.

**Problem.** For Re s &gt; 1, sum each weight times exp(−s log N𝔞) over nonzero integral ideals 𝔞, where N𝔞 counts residue classes. The sum equals −L′(s,ρ)/L(s,ρ) for the Artin L-function of ρ.

**How the definition helps.** Traces on fixed vectors make the prime-power weights agree with the logarithm of each Artin determinant factor, even at ramified primes. A character value on the full representation can depend on the chosen Frobenius lift there. Averaging over inertia gives the trace on fixed vectors. Our own calculation expands the logarithm of the determinant using its eigenvalues. Differentiation cancels the denominator m and supplies the factor log(q).

**Paper or page:** [A new bound on the relative error in the Chebotarev density theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01802v2). It says: “\\tilde {\\chi }(g)=\\frac {1}{\|I\|}\\sum <sub>\\alpha \\in I</sub>\\chi (g\\alpha ).”

### Primitive completion restores reflection

**Remember:** The smallest modulus keeps every factor needed for reflection.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite-order Hecke character χ assigns roots of unity multiplicatively to ideals coprime to its conductor, the smallest modulus through which it factors. Its primitive L-function includes every prime factor allowed by that conductor. Form Λ(s,χ) by multiplying by the gamma factors from the embeddings and by exp((s/2)log(DN𝔣)). Here D is the absolute field discriminant and N𝔣 is the conductor norm.

**Problem.** For a finite-order character, the completed function satisfies Λ(s,χ) = ε(χ)Λ(1−s,χ̄), with \|ε(χ)\| = 1. The same completion need not work if one drops factors at extra primes.

**How the definition helps.** Using the smallest modulus keeps the local factors needed on both sides of Hecke’s functional equation. Our own example deletes one prime of norm q from the trivial character’s product. This multiplies the completed zeta function by 1 − exp(−s log q). The multiplier has different absolute values at 2 and −1, so reflection cannot hold with a constant of absolute value one.

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_character). It says: “Hecke showed these L-functions satisfy a functional equation relating the values of the L-function of a character and the L-function of its complex conjugate character.”

### Summing over ideals gives the Dedekind zeta function an Euler product

**Remember:** Sum over ideals, factor over prime ideals.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Dedekind zeta function of a number field sums N(a)⁻ˢ over all nonzero ideals a of the ring of integers. Here N(a) is the number of elements of the quotient ring. The sum converges when the real part of s is greater than 1.

**Problem.** For Re s &gt; 1, the Dedekind zeta function is the product over all nonzero prime ideals P of 1/(1 − N(P)⁻ˢ).

**How the definition helps.** Ideals factor uniquely into prime ideals and the norm is multiplicative, so the Euler product follows as for the Riemann zeta function. The page says this directly. A sum over elements up to units would have no such product when unique factorization of elements fails (our own). So the zeta function sees prime ideals, not prime elements. What stays hard is the analytic continuation and the class number formula at s = 1.

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function). It says: “The norm function is multiplicative with respect to multiplication of ideals, which implies that the Dedekind zeta function has an Euler product over all non-zero prime ideals”

### Using inertia-fixed vectors makes the Artin local factor independent of Frobenius lift

**Remember:** Two lifts differ by inertia, which acts as the identity on fixed vectors.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ρ be a Galois representation with finite image on a vector space V, and p a prime whose residue field has N(p) elements. Inertia is the subgroup acting trivially on the residue field, and a Frobenius lift Frob acts on it by raising to the power N(p). The local Artin factor is the inverse of det(1 − Frob·N(p)⁻ˢ) on the inertia-fixed part of V. Using a Frobenius lift on all of V would depend on the lift.

**Problem.** The local Artin factor does not depend on the chosen lift of Frobenius, even at a ramified prime.

**How the definition helps.** Restricting to inertia-fixed vectors removes the choice, because two lifts of Frobenius differ by an inertia element, which acts as the identity there (our own). The fixed part is stable under the decomposition group, since inertia is normal in it (our own). On all of V the choice matters: for a ramified quadratic character, inertia acts by −1, so two lifts give opposite values (our own). A different prime above p gives a conjugate operator, so the determinant does not change (our own).
