### Generating functions give Landau’s asymptotic

**Remember:** The gamma factor starts with z, so k primes leave k minus one logarithms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let ω(n) count distinct prime divisors. Define S(x,z) by adding z raised to ω(n) over all positive integers n≤x. The coefficient of degree k counts integers with exactly k distinct prime divisors.

**Problem.** Fix an integer k≥1 and put L=log log x. As x grows, the count with ω(n)=k is asymptotic to xLᵏ⁻¹/((k−1)! log x).

**How the definition helps.** The generating function reduces the fixed-count problem to extracting one coefficient (our own calculation). The Selberg–Delange theorem estimates S(x,z) uniformly near zero, with leading term x exp(zL)G(z)/(Γ(z) log x). Here Γ is the gamma function, and G is analytic near zero with G(0)=1 by the theorem’s prime product. Since 1/Γ(z)=z+O(z²), the leading contribution comes from degree k−1 in exp(zL). Cauchy’s coefficient formula on the circle \|z\|=1/L bounds the error.

**Paper or page:** [Probabilistic interpretation of the Selberg--Delange Method in analytic number theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17535v1). It says: “Let f: ℕ → ℂ be an admissible function with average value ρ.”

### Poisson normalization yields a product

**Remember:** Remove the Poisson term and each prime leaves a summable error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For s&gt;1, give N probability 1/(ζ(s)nˢ) at each positive integer n, where ζ(s)=∑ 1/nˢ. Let ω(N) count distinct prime factors and put μ(s)=∑ 1/pˢ over primes. Divide E\[exp(zω(N))\] by exp(μ(s)(exp(z)−1)), the corresponding expectation for a Poisson variable with mean μ(s).

**Problem.** As s decreases to 1, the quotient converges locally uniformly for complex z. Its limit is the product over primes of (1+w/p)exp(−w/p), where w=exp(z)−1.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by the Poisson factor cancels the linear term at each prime (our own calculation). Independent prime divisibility gives the factor (1+w/pˢ)exp(−w/pˢ). On each bounded set of z, its difference from one is O(1/p²). The sum of these error bounds converges, so the product converges uniformly there as s decreases to one.

**Paper or page:** [Large deviations for number of irreducible divisors of the Dirichlet series distribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14234v1). It says: “The random variables ω(Xₛ), s &gt; 1, converges mod-Poisson as s ↘ 1”

### Sparse exceptions permit bounded values

**Remember:** A nonunit prime value matters through its divisibility probability.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions), 11N64. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be positive integer valued and multiplicative. Call a prime exceptional for this test when f(p) ≠ 1. Measure the exceptional primes by the sum of their reciprocals, without counting how large f(p) is.

**Problem.** For a finite C, consider the fraction of integers n ≤ X satisfying f(n) ≤ C. For some C this fraction has positive limit superior exactly when the exceptional primes have finite reciprocal sum.

**How the definition helps.** Our own reading is that every exceptional prime occurring exactly once multiplies the value by at least two. Thus the local test needs no knowledge of the size of a nonunit value. The cited theorem proves the density criterion with all prime powers. Our own simplification drops higher powers because the sum of their reciprocals converges.

**Remember:** A zero between two signs is not a sign.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N64 (Other results on the distribution of values or the characterization of arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Count sign changes by first deleting the zeros of a real sequence. Count each pair of successive remaining terms whose product is negative.

**How the definition helps.** Skipping zeros lets the theorem count changes even when every pair of neighboring integers contains a zero. Our own example repeats the values 1,0,−1,0, starting at n=1. Its nonzero values alternate, giving one change about every two integers. Corollary 3 proves the criterion.

### Uniform distance gives one model

**Remember:** A uniformly close model can be chosen once.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N64 (Other results on the distribution of values or the characterization of arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be multiplicative, with \|f(n)\| ≤ 1. ### Counting remainders continue Beurling zeta

**Remember:** Subtract the linear count so that the smaller remainder sets the convergence line.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N80 (Generalized primes and integers). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give each generalized prime a real size greater than one, with sizes tending to infinity. Let N(x) count unordered prime products of size at most x, counting the empty product and distinguishing factorizations. Set R(x)=N(x)−κ(x−1) for x≥1. The Beurling zeta function sums exp(−s log v) over these products, where v is their size.

**Problem.** Suppose κ &gt; 0 and \|R(x)\| is bounded by a constant times x to the power θ, with θ &lt; 1. Then ζ extends to Re s &gt; θ, with only a simple pole at 1 of residue κ.

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting the linear count isolates the pole that the original zeta series hides (our own). For Re s&gt;1, the linear term contributes κ/(s−1) (our own). Integration by parts expresses the remainder as s times the integral of R(x) exp(−s log x) against dx/x from one to infinity (our own). The growth bound makes this integral holomorphic for Re s&gt;θ (our own). The main arithmetic work lies in proving that growth bound (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Distribution of Beurling primes and zeroes of the Beurling zeta function I. Distribution of the zeroes of the zeta function of Beurling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.09045v3). It says: “\|ζ(s) − κ/(s−1)\| ≤ A\|s\|/(σ−θ)”

### Prime labels preserve Möbius inversion

**Remember:** Invert each labeled prime factor before combining products of equal size.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11N80 (Generalized primes and integers). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Assign each prime label a real size greater than one, with sizes tending to infinity. Count unordered products of labels separately even when their sizes agree. Give a product Möbius weight zero if a label repeats and weight (−1)ᵏ otherwise, where k counts its labels. Include the empty product of size and weight one.

**Problem.** Form the Beurling zeta series by summing exp(−s log v) over all products of size v, including multiplicities. Wherever this series converges absolutely, its reciprocal equals the same series with each term multiplied by its Möbius weight.

**How the definition helps.** Distinct labels give each product exactly one factorization, so multiplying the inverse prime factors gives its Möbius weight (our own). For prime sizes 2 and 4, the prime of size 4 contributes −1, while the repeated factor 2 contributes zero (our own). Grouping only by size requires adding those contributions (our own). Absolute convergence justifies multiplying and regrouping the series (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Beurling zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beurling_zeta_function). It says: “A Beurling generalized integer is a number that can be written as a product of Beurling generalized primes.”

**Paper or page:** [The average order of the Möbius function for Beurling primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.06866v2). It says: “Here Mℙ(x) is the partial sum of the Möbius function over 𝒩 not exceeding x.”

### Relative density excludes Goldbach obstructions

**Remember:** Measure density inside the prime class that can reach the target.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let P contain all primes congruent to 1 modulo 3 and take A ⊆ P. Define its relative lower density as the limit inferior of \|A ∩ \[1,X\]\|/\|P ∩ \[1,X\]\| as X tends to infinity.

**Problem.** Suppose A has relative lower density greater than one half in P. Then every sufficiently large odd multiple of 3 is a sum of three elements of A. This can fail at density one half.

**How the definition helps.** In our own comparison, measuring density inside P gives a sharp threshold even though every subset of P has density zero among integers. Keep just the primes in P congruent to 1 or −1 modulo 5. The prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions gives relative density one half. Three residues from {1,−1} never sum to zero modulo 5, so this set misses every odd multiple of 15. Alsetri’s theorem proves that density strictly above one half suffices.

**Paper or page:** [Density ternary Goldbach for primes in a fixed residue class](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09648v3). It says: “Then A+A+A contains every sufficiently large odd integer n which satisfies n ≡ 0 mod 3.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dickman weights isolate smooth density

**Remember:** The Dickman weight isolates the lost density on central arcs.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An integer is Z-smooth if every prime factor is at most Z. The Dickman function ϱ equals one on \[0,1\] and satisfies uϱ′(u) = −ϱ(u−1) for u &gt; 1. For integer degree d, give m weight ϱ(log m/(d log Z)) times m raised to (1/d − 1), divided by d. Let w(β) sum these weights times exp(2πiβm) over integers Zᵈ &lt; m ≤ Xᵈ.

**Problem.** Fix an integer d ≥ 3, B &gt; 0 and sufficiently small η &gt; 0, and set Z = X raised to η. For \|β\| &lt; (log X)ᴮ/Xᵈ, one has w(β) = ϱ(1/η)XI(Xᵈβ) + O(X/log Z + Z). Here I(t) = ∫₀¹ exp(2πitvᵈ) dv.

**How the definition helps.** The weight separates the density of smooth integers from the integral for unrestricted powers. In our own explanation, m raised to (1/d − 1), divided by d, comes from changing variables from x to m = xᵈ. Rome and Yamagishi estimate the error from replacing the Dickman factor by its value at m = Xᵈ. Their preceding lemma relates this weighted sum to the original sum over smooth bases.

**Paper or page:** [Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09256v2). It says: “Then w(β) = ϱ((d log X)/(d log Z)) X I(Xᵈβ) + O(X/log Z + Z).”

**Sources:**

- [N. Rome and S. Yamagishi, Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations (2026)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.2026.340.179)

### Disjoint supports multiply local sums

**Remember:** Functions on disjoint pieces vary independently, so their averages multiply.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a curve over a finite field K, a finite closed subscheme Z specifies finitely many points, possibly with multiplicities. Write R for its finite K-algebra of functions and λ for a K-linear map from R to K. Given an integer k ≥ 1, define S(Z,λ) as the average of ψ(λ(xᵏ)) over x in R. Here ψ maps addition in K to multiplication of complex numbers of modulus one and is not identically one.

**Problem.** If Z is the disjoint union of Z₁ and Z₂, then S(Z,λ) = S(Z₁,λ₁)S(Z₂,λ₂), where λᵢ applies λ to functions on Zᵢ extended by zero. Moreover, λ is nondegenerate, meaning that it factors through no proper quotient of R, exactly when λ₁ and λ₂ are nondegenerate.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, specifying the finite set with multiplicities lets the global average split into separate averages over its disjoint parts. Functions on the union are pairs of functions, one on each part; kth powers act componentwise, λ adds the two outputs, and ψ turns that sum into a product, so averaging over independent choices gives the factorization. In our own explanation, every ideal of the product ring splits into ideals of the two factors, which gives the nondegeneracy test. This is Sawin’s lemma for the trivial line bundle, where sections are ordinary functions.

**Paper or page:** [The asymptotic in Waring's problem over function fields via singular sets in the circle method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14053v1). It says: “Then we have \\\[ S<sub>Z</sub>(\\overline{\\alpha})=S<sub>Z<sub>1</sub></sub>(\\overline{\\alpha}<sub>Z<sub>1</sub></sub>)S<sub>Z<sub>2</sub></sub>(\\overline{\\alpha}<sub>Z<sub>2</sub></sub>) \\\]”

### Real solution density makes positivity local

**Remember:** A smooth zero with positive weight sends positive mass near zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F map ℝˢ smoothly to ℝʳ, and let w be a nonnegative smooth function with compact support. Integrate w over points whose images lie in a cube of side 2ε centered at zero. The real solution density is the limit of this integral divided by the cube’s volume as ε decreases to zero, when the limit exists.

**Problem.** Assume F has derivative of rank r at every zero in the support of w. Then the normalized mass has a finite limit, which is positive if w is positive at any zero.

**How the definition helps.** Measuring mass near zero makes positivity visible in a single neighborhood of a solution. In our own proof, the rank assumption gives local coordinates in which F selects the first r coordinates. Integration over the remaining coordinates gives a continuous density and a positive contribution wherever w is positive at a solution. Compactness lets finitely many neighborhoods cover the relevant zeros. The cited paper identifies a normalized integral with a real density in its particular quadratic setting.

### Residues modulo sixteen select sums of twelve fourth powers

**Remember:** Modulo sixteen, a fourth power records whether its base is odd.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Call a positive integer admissible if its remainder modulo 16 lies between 1 and 12 inclusive. Consider representations by exactly twelve positive fourth powers with at least one odd base.

**Problem.** Every sufficiently large admissible integer is a sum of twelve fourth powers of positive integers. No integer outside the admissible classes is such a sum with an odd base.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the remainder records exactly how many of the twelve bases are odd. An even fourth power is zero modulo 16, and an odd fourth power is one. Thus a remainder of zero forces all twelve bases to be even, while remainders 13 through 15 are impossible. Brüdern and Wooley prove existence for every sufficiently large admissible integer in Corollary 1.3.

**Wikipedia:** [Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem). It says: “any sufficiently large number congruent to 1 through 14 mod 16 could be written as a sum of 14 fourth powers”

**Sources:**

### Smooth cutoffs suppress Poisson tails

**Remember:** Smooth weights remove boundary terms in repeated integration by parts.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11L07. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F₁ and F₂ be fixed quadratic forms in s real variables and W a smooth function of compact support. Define I by integrating W(x/P)exp(2πi\[β₁F₁(x)+β₂F₂(x)−c·x/q\]) over ℝˢ. Here β = (β₁,β₂) is real, c is a real vector and q is a positive integer.

**Problem.** Fix δ &gt; 0 and take P sufficiently large. If \|c\| ≥ (q/P)(1+P²\|β\|)Pᵟ, then \|I\| ≤ C(A)Pˢ/(P\|c\|/q)ᴬ for each integer A ≥ 1. The constants may depend on the forms, W and δ.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, a smooth weight eliminates the boundary terms that prevent arbitrarily fast decay for a sharp cutoff. For example, integrating exp(2πitx) over \[0,1\] gives absolute value 1/(πt) at positive half-integers t. After scaling x by P, the frequency condition keeps the directional derivative of the phase away from zero throughout the support, and repeated integration by parts in the direction of c gives the stated decay. Frequencies below the threshold require separate estimates.

**Paper or page:** [A two-dimensional delta symbol method and its application to pairs of quadratic forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11355v1). It says: “I<sub>q</sub>(\\vec{\\mathrm{w}},\\mathbf{u})\\ll<sub>N</sub> P<sup>s</sup>(P\|\\mathbf{u}\|/q)<sup>-N</sup>\\ll P<sup>s-N\\delta</sup>”

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, an admissible exponent records the power lost in a moment estimate, so zero records the full expected saving. ### Bailey pairs generate identity chains

**Remember:** Keep the relation, and each new pair can start the next step.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P84 (Partition identities; identities of Rogers-Ramanujan type), 11B65. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Sequences α and β form a Bailey pair relative to a when βₙ is the sum of αᵣ/((q;q)ₙ₋ᵣ(aq;q)ₙ₊ᵣ) over 0 ≤ r ≤ n, for every n ≥ 0. Here (x;q)ₘ is the product of the m factors 1 − xqʲ with 0 ≤ j &lt; m, and a and q keep all denominators nonzero.

**Problem.** Bailey’s lemma turns each Bailey pair into another Bailey pair relative to the same a, with free parameters for which the denominators do not vanish. So one may iterate the limiting transformation to produce a chain of finite sum identities.

**How the definition helps.** A Bailey pair records the exact relation that each successive application of the lemma requires. The lemma gives formulas for two new sequences and proves that they satisfy the same relation. The work lies in that finite summation identity. In our own reading, preservation of the relation explains why every output can serve as the next input.

**Wikipedia:** [Bailey pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bailey_pair). It says: “This process can be iterated to produce an infinite sequence of Bailey pairs, called a Bailey chain.”

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Problem.** For every nonzero complex polynomial P(x,y), replacing x by B(x) preserves m(P). Here y denotes any number of additional variables.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, fixing zero preserves the circle average of every continuous function. Extend the function harmonically to the disk and compose with B; the composition is harmonic with the same value at zero, so it has the same boundary average, and this equality of measures also covers the integrable logarithm. Our own example B(z) = (z + ½)/(1 + z/2) moves zero to ½. For P(z) = z − 2 the average changes from log 2 to log(3/2).

**Remember:** The constant coefficient keeps exactly the walks that return to the origin.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

The coordinates u+v and u−v turn each step into independent increments of +1 or −1, so a return after 2j steps needs j positive increments in each coordinate, which gives Bⱼ² walks. No walk returns after an odd number of steps. Katagiri’s comparison with averages over roots of unity justifies using the constant coefficient.

**Remember:** Jensen keeps the exterior roots, and the regulator form reads their logarithms.

At a curve point write x = tᵐa and y = tⁿb, using a local coordinate t and nonvanishing factors a,b; the tame symbol there is (−1)ᵐⁿaⁿ/bᵐ evaluated at the point. If either order is nonzero, the terms of least order in the polynomial lie on one edge, and their cancellation makes the tame symbol a signed integer power of an edge root. **Remember:** Let the Euclidean algorithm run on ideals, and the class group becomes cyclic.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 13F07, 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The class group of a number field K measures how far its ring of integers is from having unique factorization. Lenstra’s notion, which the abstract calls a generalization of the Euclidean domain, puts the division condition on ideal classes, and Lenstra proved that a Euclidean class forces a cyclic class group. Our own note: what stays hard is to show that a given class is Euclidean. The paper does this for a family of biquadratic fields with class number 2.

### Pólya groups equal strongly ambiguous classes, giving short proofs

**Remember:** Galois-fixed ideals are products over whole fibres, so the groups agree.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R32, 11R34. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let L/K be a Galois extension of number fields with group G. The class group of L is its group of ideals modulo principal ideals. The relative Pólya group Po(L/K) is the subgroup generated by the classes of the products of all primes of L above one prime of K. A strongly ambiguous class is an ideal class that contains an ideal fixed by G.

**Problem.** The relative Pólya group Po(L/K) is the group of strongly ambiguous classes. Its order is h(K) times the product of the ramification indices, divided by the order of H¹(G, U(L)), where h(K) is the class number of K and U(L) is the unit group of L (Corollary 2.3).

**How the definition helps.** Our own argument: G permutes the primes of L above one prime of K among themselves, so an ideal fixed by G is a product of the generators of the Pólya group, and the equality with strongly ambiguous classes is close to the definition. The work then moves into a known exact sequence of Brumer–Rosen and Zantema, which the abstract says gives short proofs of classical results, such as the order formula. Our own note: Pólya groups matter because a trivial Pólya group of K over ℚ means the integer-valued polynomials on K have a regular basis.

**Paper or page:** [Ostrowski quotients for finite extensions of number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00442). It says: “For L/K a finite Galois extension of number fields, the relative Pólya group Po(L/K) coincides with the group of strongly ambiguous ideal classes in L/K.”

### Locally integrally equivalent number fields have isomorphic class groups

**Remember:** Keep integer information at every prime, and the class group survives.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R33 (Integral representations related to algebraic numbers; Galois module structure of rings of integers), 11R29, 11R42. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

The group G permutes the cosets of H₁ and of H₂, and this gives two permutation modules. The fields are locally integrally equivalent if these modules are isomorphic over the ℓ-adic integers for every prime ℓ.

**Problem.** Locally integrally equivalent number fields have isomorphic ideal class groups. They also have the same zeta function and the same regulator.

**How the definition helps.** The definition keeps integer information at each prime ℓ, and this controls the ℓ-part of the class group. Equality of zeta functions only keeps rational information. In our own remark, fields with the same zeta function can have different class numbers, so the weaker definition does not give the theorem.

### Cartesian conditions preserve Selmer torsion

**Remember:** Pull back the local tests to get the same test on torsion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Remember:** Pair against the units, and every constructible sheaf gets a dual.

For F = ℤ and r = 2, H²(X, ℤ) is the dual of the Galois group of the Hilbert class field (our own). The group Ext¹(ℤ, 𝔾ₘ) is the class group, so this case says that this Galois group is the class group (our own). That is unramified class field theory.

### Tate-modified compact supports make Artin–Verdier duality hold

**Remember:** Tate cohomology at real places removes the 2-torsion that never stops.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let U be an open subscheme of the spectrum of a ring of integers. Compactly supported cohomology of a sheaf on U is defined from a cone, a complex that subtracts the local cohomology at the places outside U. At real places, the definition uses Tate cohomology of the group of order 2 in place of ordinary group cohomology.

**Problem.** Let F be a constructible sheaf on U, one that is locally constant with finite stalks on the pieces of a finite partition. Then the Tate-modified compactly supported cohomology Ĥⁱc(U, F) is finite, is dual to Ext³⁻ⁱ(F, 𝔾ₘ) for every i, and vanishes for i ≥ 4.

**How the definition helps.** Tate cohomology at the real places cancels the 2-torsion that real places add in all high degrees (our own). Without it, the cohomology of the spectrum of ℤ with coefficients ℤ/2 is nonzero in all large degrees, which breaks a duality of dimension 3 (our own). The usual statement avoids this by assuming the number field is totally imaginary. With the modified definition, the theorem holds for every number field and every open U.

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Verdier duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Verdier_duality). It says: “The sum is taken over all places of K, which are not in U, including the archimedean ones.”

Tsfasman and Vlăduţ prove the required limit for the zeta residues. The class number formula supplies the terms for real and complex embeddings. All correction terms vanish when the degree divided by g tends to zero.

### Primitive characters isolate a zeta quotient

**Remember:** Exclude each prime-order subgroup from the character kernel.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let E/F be a cyclic extension of number fields of degree m. Call a complex character of its Galois group primitive if its kernel is trivial. For each divisor d of m, write E(d) for the field fixed by the subgroup of order d.

**Problem.** The product of the Artin L-functions of all primitive characters equals the product over d dividing m of the Dedekind zeta function of E(d) raised to μ(d), where μ is the Möbius function.

**How the definition helps.** The kernel condition selects the desired factors by inclusion-exclusion, in our own explanation. A nontrivial kernel contains a subgroup of prime order. Characters trivial on the subgroup of order d give exactly the characters of its quotient. Their L-functions multiply to the zeta function of E(d) by Artin’s factorization theorem.

### Reflection bounds fields by zeta values

**Remember:** Reflect past zero to expose a positive discriminant power.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Complete the Dedekind zeta function ζₖ(s) by multiplying by exp((s/2)log D) and the gamma factors attached to the field embeddings. Here D is the absolute discriminant of the number field K. The completed function takes equal values at s and 1−s.

**Problem.** Fix a positive integer n, a negative real noninteger s, and B &gt; 0. Only finitely many degree-n number fields up to isomorphism satisfy \|ζₖ(s)\| ≤ B. For real s &gt; 1, infinitely many quadratic fields satisfy this inequality for some common B.

**How the definition helps.** Completion lets us compare the unknown value at s with a positive series at 1−s. In our own fixed-degree argument, reflection contributes the factor exp((½−s)log D), and the remaining gamma ratio takes finitely many nonzero values because only finitely many embedding counts occur. The series at 1−s starts with one and has positive terms, so B bounds D, and Hermite’s theorem gives finiteness. For s &gt; 1 the quadratic Euler products are all bounded by the square of the Riemann zeta function.

**Paper or page:** [On the Northcott property of Dedekind zeta functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13854v1), [On the Northcott property of Dedekind zeta functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13854v1). It says: “The Northcott property does not hold”

### Smoothing clears Stickelberger denominators

**Remember:** Smoothing multiplies by factors that clear denominators.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let H/F be a finite abelian extension with F totally real and H a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field, and let S be a finite set of places containing all infinite and ramified ones. The Stickelberger element has value L(S,χ⁻¹,0) at each character χ, omitting Euler factors at S. Smooth it at a disjoint finite set T of primes by multiplying by 1−Nv·σᵥ⁻¹ for each v in T, where Nv is the residue field size and σᵥ is the automorphism inducing the Nv-th power map on residues.

**Problem.** Suppose only the identity root of unity in H reduces to one at every prime above T. Then the smoothed Stickelberger element has integer coefficients in the basis of Galois automorphisms.

**How the definition helps.** Smoothing excludes fractional coefficients that already occur for the Gaussian rationals, in our own example. For ℚ(i)/ℚ take S to consist of infinity and 2. The trivial character value is zero and the nontrivial value is one half. The unsmoothed element is therefore (1−c)/4, where c is complex conjugation. Integrality after smoothing uses the theorem of Deligne and Ribet and of Cassou-Noguès.

**Paper or page:** [Two encounters with the p-adic Stark conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03299). It says: “The Brumer–Stark conjecture holds over ℤ\[1/2\].”

### Conductor norms sharpen Chebotarev

**Remember:** Measure the Hecke factors over the fixed field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a finite Galois extension L/F with group G, choose an abelian subgroup H meeting a conjugacy class C, and let K be its fixed field, with absolute discriminant D and degree n over ℚ. Let Q be the largest norm of the conductor of a character of H, the smallest finite modulus needed for its Hecke character. The conductor scale is B = DQ exp(n log n).

For L ≠ ℚ and x ≥ Bᵃ, \|π(x)/M(x)−1\| ≤ A(exp(−b log x/log B)+exp(−b√(log x/n))) for positive, absolute, effective constants A, a and b.

**Remember:** Induce one cyclic point to its whole conjugacy class.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let G be the Galois group of a finite extension of number fields, and let C be the conjugacy class of c. Its cyclic subgroup H consists of the powers of c. Induce the point indicator at c by counting elements x of G satisfying x⁻¹gx = c and dividing by \|H\|.

**Problem.** The induced function equals \|G\|/(\|C\|·\|H\|) on C and zero elsewhere. Consequently, prime counts weighted by the class indicator can be studied through abelian L-functions.

**How the definition helps.** Induction expresses the whole class indicator using one point of a cyclic group. Our own calculation counts \|G\|/\|C\| conjugators for each element of C. On H, the point indicator expands in homomorphisms to the unit circle. Artin’s induction identity preserves their L-functions when the base changes to the field fixed by H. Class field reciprocity identifies these functions with Hecke L-functions over that field.

### Null boundaries permit infinite Chebotarev

**Remember:** A boundary of measure zero lets finite quotients approximate the prime density.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Galois group G of an infinite Galois extension is the inverse limit of its finite Galois groups. Give G its translation-invariant probability measure, called Haar measure. Choose a set X stable under conjugation whose boundary has measure zero.

**Problem.** Let L be a possibly infinite Galois extension of a number field K, ramified at only finitely many primes. The proportion of primes with Frobenius in X tends to its Haar measure as the residue field size bound grows.

**How the definition helps.** A boundary of measure zero lets finite quotient conditions approximate X from inside and outside with arbitrarily small differences in measure. Our own argument applies finite Chebotarev to both approximations. In our own counterexample, the cyclotomic ℤ₃-extension of ℚ has Galois group the additive group of 3-adic integers. The countable set of prime Frobenius elements has measure zero but contains the Frobenius of every unramified prime.

### Signed corrections stabilize Chebotarev counts

**Remember:** Subtract the exceptional contribution before measuring relative error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let C be a conjugacy class in the group G of a finite Galois extension L/K of number fields. Write Li for the logarithmic integral and set M(x) = \|C\|Li(x)/\|G\|. Thorner and Zaman bound the remaining contributions relative to this smaller quantity.

**Remember:** Odd torsion cannot see an obstruction of order two.

The paper defines a matching notion, an exceptional extension of local fields. For a totally ramified extension of degree n prime to q, Theorem 1.6 shows it is exceptional exactly when gcd(n, q − 1) = 1.

In our own words, at a rational point the residue field does not grow, so the local degree is the ramification index. The paper proves the needed local facts in three ways, with different tools.

**Remember:** A zero symbol means the norm residue action fixes the division point.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over a local field of positive characteristic, a formal Drinfeld module uses additive power series for scalar multiplication. **Remember:** Remove the factor whose exponent behaves discontinuously in the p-adic distance.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S40 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions), 11M41. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Remember:** Subtract the rescaled Bernoulli weight to cancel the denominator N.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, \\(p\\)-adic integration, etc.)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Problem.** For odd p the regularized distribution is a bounded p-adic measure, even though the original Bernoulli distribution is not.

The original weights add correctly under subdivision of residue classes, and multiplication by c permutes those subdivisions. The corrected weights therefore still add correctly and define a bounded measure (our own argument). With d = a = 1, the original weights have unbounded p-adic absolute value as n grows.

### Disjoint characters preserve hypergeometric purity

**Remember:** Disjoint lists prevent a character from canceling a parameter.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take two length-n lists of multiplicative characters on 𝔽𝓆, with n ≥ 1. Call them disjoint when no character occurs in both. For nonzero tuples x and y with ∏xᵢ = t∏yᵢ, multiply the first characters on xᵢ and the inverse second characters on yᵢ. Multiply by ψ(Σxᵢ − Σyᵢ), where ψ is a nontrivial additive character, and sum over these tuples.

**Problem.** For disjoint lists and t different from zero and one, the sum is a signed trace of n eigenvalues. Each eigenvalue has modulus q raised to (2n − 1)/2, so the sum has modulus at most n times that number.

**How the definition helps.** Disjointness prevents a matching character from canceling between the lists and changing the predicted eigenvalue size. Our own example takes both lists to contain just the trivial character. For t different from zero and one, the sum becomes the sum of ψ((t − 1)y) over nonzero y, which equals −1. Katz’s hypergeometric sheaf theorem gives the rank and absolute values for disjoint lists.

**Paper or page:** [Traces of Hecke Operators via Hypergeometric Character Sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02918). It says: “are algebraic numbers and have the same absolute value”

**Sources:**

- [Katz, Exponential Sums and Differential Equations, Chapter 8](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nmk/wholebookcorrms.pdf)

### Fourier sheaves exclude completion spikes

**Remember:** Exclude additive characters to keep Fourier mass spread out.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 11L26. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Start with a coefficient system on the affine line over 𝔽ₚ, extended across missing points by taking locally invariant vectors. Assume its Frobenius eigenvalues on the regular part have complex absolute value one. Call it a Fourier sheaf if none of its irreducible pieces over the algebraic closure comes from an additive character x ↦ ψ(ax). Include a = 0 in this test.

**Problem.** Write K for the function giving the Frobenius trace at each point. The conductor c adds the rank to the sum of 1 + Swan over all singularities, including any at infinity. On each integer interval of length at most p, the sum of K has modulus O(c²√p log p), with an absolute constant.

**How the definition helps.** Excluding additive characters removes the constituents whose Fourier transforms concentrate at a single frequency. Our own counterexample is the constant function, whose sum on a full interval equals p. The applied cohomology lectures bound the other Fourier coefficients and sum them against those of the interval. Here Swan measures ramification from the field characteristic.

**Wikipedia:** [Quadratic residue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_residue). It says: “for any nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ(n) modulo q and any integers M and N,”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski, Michel and Sawin, Lectures on applied ℓ-adic cohomology](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/applied-ell-adic.pdf)

### Frobenius traces give Kloosterman recurrences

**Remember:** A Kloosterman sum over an extension is the negative trace of a Frobenius power.

*True by definition.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a nonzero element a of a finite field and a nontrivial additive character ψ, a homomorphism from addition to complex multiplication. For each degree n extension, sum ψ(Tr(ax + 1/x)) over its nonzero elements x. The trace Tr adds the field conjugates. Represent these Kloosterman sums using a single cohomology space attached to the function ax + 1/x.

**Problem.** Write S(n) for the sum in degree n. For n ≥ 1, it satisfies S(n+2) = −S(1)S(n+1) − bS(n), where b = (S(1)² + S(2))/2.

**How the definition helps.** In our own deduction, the cohomology description gives all extension sums as negative traces of powers of one two-dimensional operator F. The cited calculation gives dimension two in degree one and zero elsewhere. The cohomological trace formula identifies each sum with −tr(Fⁿ), replacing a separate calculation in every field. The characteristic polynomial of F then gives the recurrence, with b equal to its determinant.

**Paper or page:** [Matrix Kloosterman sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00762). It says: “\\\[\\dim H<sup>i<sub>c</sub></sup>(\\mathbb {A}<sup>1\\setminus</sup> \\mathbb {A}<sup>0</sup>,f\_\\alpha )=\\left \\{\\begin {array}{ll}2, &amp; \\mathrm {if\~} i=1,\\\\ 0, &amp; \\mathrm {if\~} i\\neq 1\\end {array}\\right .\\\]”

**Sources:**

- [Márton Erdélyi and Árpád Tóth, Matrix Kloosterman sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00762)

### Geometric nonisomorphism forces small correlations

**Remember:** Compare sheaves after extending the field to detect the main term.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On an open subset U of the affine line over 𝔽𝓆, take two locally constant systems of vector spaces F and G. Use ℓ-adic coefficients for a prime ℓ different from the characteristic. Assume both systems stay irreducible over the algebraic closure, meaning neither has a proper nonzero invariant subspace there. Call them geometrically distinct if they remain nonisomorphic there.

**Problem.** Assume both systems have weight zero, meaning all pointwise Frobenius eigenvalues have complex absolute value one. For geometrically distinct systems, sum the trace of F times the conjugate trace of G over U(𝔽𝓆). The modulus is O(√q), with constant depending on the ranks, omitted points and local ramification.

**How the definition helps.** Geometric distinction removes the invariant maps between F and G that could produce a term of order q. Our own explanation uses Schur’s lemma for these maps and Deligne’s bound for the remaining terms in the trace formula. Multiplying the Frobenius action by a constant unit scalar can change a system over the base field while preserving every absolute trace.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “where the cohomology groups are replaced by cohomology with coefficients in the sheaf.”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski, Michel and Sawin, Lectures on applied ℓ-adic cohomology](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/applied-ell-adic.pdf)

### Good twists erase boundary terms

**Remember:** A good twist leaves no cohomology at zero or infinity.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F be a locally constant system of r-dimensional ℓ-adic vector spaces on the line with zero removed over 𝔽𝓆, with ℓ prime to q. Twist F by the one-dimensional system associated to a multiplicative character χ through the power covering of the nonzero line. Call χ good if extension by zero agrees with derived direct image on the projective line for this twist. These extensions differ only through local cohomology at zero and infinity.

**Problem.** Over any finite extension field, at most 2r multiplicative characters fail this test. For every good character, ordinary cohomology of the twist agrees with its cohomology with compact supports.

**How the definition helps.** Goodness tests for boundary contributions before computing either cohomology group. Our own explanation takes cohomology on the projective line of the two extensions in the definition. A bad twist must cancel a local character in the part fixed by wild inertia, the characteristic-power part of the local symmetry group. Each boundary has at most r such characters. Twisting the constant system by the trivial character leaves a boundary contribution.

**Paper or page:** [Wasserstein metrics and quantitative equidistribution of exponential sums over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22059). It says: “let 𝒳ᵢ be the set of characters χ : kᵢ× → ℂ× which are “good” for ℱᵢ(1/2)\[1\]”

**Sources:**

- [Katz, Convolution and Equidistribution](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nmk/mellin398.pdf)

### Newton polytopes bound torus sums

**Remember:** Test each face that misses the origin.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a Laurent polynomial f in m variables, take the convex hull Δ of zero and its exponent vectors. For each face missing zero, let h consist of the terms on that face. Call f nondegenerate if the derivatives xᵢ∂h/∂xᵢ never vanish together at a point with all coordinates nonzero over the algebraic closure.

**Problem.** Assume Δ has dimension m and f is nondegenerate. For any nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽𝓆, sum ψ(f(x)) over tuples of nonzero field elements. The modulus is at most √(qᵐ) times the volume of Δ measured in units of 1/m! of a lattice cube.

**How the definition helps.** The face test lets the volume of the actual exponent polytope control the sum. Our own explanation uses the Adolphson–Sperber theorem to concentrate cohomology in one degree and compute its dimension from this volume. Deligne’s estimate bounds each contributing eigenvalue by √(qᵐ). In odd characteristic, (x + y)² fails the top-face test along y = −x. Its full affine sum has modulus q√q, and removing the axes changes it by at most 2q.

**Paper or page:** [Robba's method on exponential sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.02825). It says: “Suppose that f is nondegenerate. Then H(i)=aᵢ for all integer i≥0. Moreover, we have H(k)=0 for k&gt;nM, ∑ₖ₌₀ⁿᴹ H(k)=n! Vol(Δ(f)).”

**Sources:**

- [Robba's method on exponential sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.02825)

### Odd multiplicities force symplectic cancellation

**Remember:** An odd number of standard symplectic factors cannot contain a fixed vector.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a list of fractional linear maps over 𝔽ₚ, meaning invertible changes of variable x ↦ (ax + b)/(cx + d). Call the list normal if some map occurs an odd number of times.

**Problem.** Let F be a middle extension over 𝔽ₚ, a coefficient system extended across singularities by local invariant vectors, with Frobenius eigenvalues of modulus one at regular points. Suppose its geometric symmetry group is the full symplectic group in its standard representation and only the identity preserves F up to scalar twist; then for a normal list, the sum of products of the transformed traces over common finite inputs avoiding poles is O(√p).

**How the definition helps.** Odd multiplicity gives a factor on which the central symmetry −I negates every tensor, ruling out invariant vectors. Our own explanation uses the independence theorem for distinct transformed systems. Deligne’s bound controls the remaining sum in terms of list length and the rank and ramification of F.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “where the cohomology groups are replaced by cohomology with coefficients in the sheaf.”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel, A study in sums of products](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/sums-of-products.pdf)

### Signed multiplicities force special linear cancellation

**Remember:** Count ordinary factors positively and conjugate factors negatively, modulo the rank.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give each occurrence of a fractional linear map x ↦ (ax + b)/(cx + d) a sign, with ad − bc ≠ 0. Its signed multiplicity counts positive occurrences minus negative occurrences. Call the list r-normal if some map has signed multiplicity indivisible by r.

**Problem.** Take a middle extension F over 𝔽ₚ with weight zero and geometric symmetry group SL(r) in its standard representation, where p &gt; r ≥ 3. Geometrically, only the identity preserves F up to scalar twist, and no fractional linear map carries F to its dual up to twist. For an r-normal list over 𝔽ₚ, the complete trace product summed away from poles is O(√p), conjugating traces with negative signs.

**How the definition helps.** Signed multiplicity gives the exponent by which scalar matrices in SL(r), the determinant-one group, act on each tensor factor, and a nonzero exponent modulo r prevents invariant vectors. Our own explanation uses independence of distinct transformed systems and Deligne’s bound. The bound depends on the list length and the rank and ramification of F.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “where the cohomology groups are replaced by cohomology with coefficients in the sheaf.”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel, A study in sums of products](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/sums-of-products.pdf)

### Character spaces isolate Jacobi factors

**Remember:** Each character pair labels its own Frobenius eigenvalue.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T24 (Other character sums and Gauss sums), 14G10. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take the smooth projective Fermat curve with affine equation xᵐ + yᵐ = 1, where m is a prime power dividing q − 1. Multiplying either coordinate by an mth root of unity preserves the curve. Split its first étale cohomology, the vector space recording its zeta numerator, into spaces where these scalings act by fixed characters.

**Problem.** Each pair χ, ψ of nontrivial multiplicative characters of 𝔽q with orders dividing m and nontrivial product labels a one-dimensional space. Frobenius acts there by −∑χ(x)ψ(1 − x), summing over 𝔽q and extending the characters by zero at zero.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, splitting by characters lets us specify which Jacobi sum belongs to each Frobenius eigenvalue. Frobenius preserves the spaces because all the scalings are defined over the base field. Computing their dimensions and identifying their eigenvalues with character sums still requires the cohomological point-count formula.

**Paper or page:** [On the variation of the Frobenius in a non abelian Iwasawa tower](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16774). It says: “The eigenvalues of $\\sigma \_q$ on the eigenspace $M<sub>n</sub>(\\eta )$ are given by the Jacobi sum 

\\\[ -J<sub>q</sub>(\\chi \_1,\\chi \_2) = -\\sum <sub>x \\in \\mathbb F<sub>q</sub></sub>\\chi \_1(x)\\chi \_2(1-x). \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [Asvin G, On the variation of the Frobenius in a non abelian Iwasawa tower](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16774)

### Frobenius preserves strict Waring numbers

**Remember:** Strip off Frobenius before counting the needed powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11T55 (Arithmetic theory of polynomial rings over finite fields), 11P05, 11P55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For polynomials over a finite field of characteristic p, let J(k) contain all finite sums of kth powers. For nonzero m in J(k), bound each base degree by ⌈deg(m)/k⌉. Increase this bound by one if k divides deg(m) and its leading coefficient lies outside the sums of kth powers in the field. Define G(k) as the least summand count sufficient under this bound for every m in J(k) of sufficiently large degree.

**Problem.** For a positive integer k divisible by p, G(k) = G(k/p), with G(1) = 1.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, taking pth powers maps exactly the allowed targets for k/p onto those for k while preserving the base-degree bound. In characteristic p the pth power of a sum is the sum of the pth powers, and the polynomial ring has no nonzero element with pth power zero, so representations correspond in both directions. This map multiplies target degrees by p and permutes the coefficient field, so the exceptional leading-coefficient test also agrees. Using all polynomials as targets would include powers of the variable whose degrees are not divisible by p.

**nLab:** [Frobenius morphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Frobenius+morphism). It says: “the characteristic of the field is used to show (a + b)ᵖ = aᵖ + bᵖ.”

**Sources:**

- [Y.-R. Liu and T. D. Wooley, Waring’s problem in function fields, §1](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~twooley/publ/wpfqt110809.pdf)

## 12 Field theory and polynomials

### Counting roots with multiplicity makes every degree-n polynomial have n roots

**Remember:** A double root is one root that you count twice.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 12D10 (Polynomials in real and complex fields: location of zeros (algebraic theorems)), 30C15. arXiv math.AC, math.CV. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let a be a root of a polynomial p. The multiplicity of a is the largest k such that (x−a)ᵏ divides p.

**Problem.** Over the complex numbers, every polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 has exactly n roots, counted with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** Counting with multiplicity lets the statement hold with no exceptions. Take x³ + 2x² − 7x + 4 = (x+4)(x−1)². As a set, its roots are only −4 and 1, so 'exactly n roots' would be false. With multiplicity, the root 1 counts twice, and the count is 3. The hard part does not become easier: a complex root must exist at all, and that is the fundamental theorem of algebra (our own remark).

**Wikipedia:** [Multiplicity (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplicity_%28mathematics%29). It says: “The notion of multiplicity is important to be able to count correctly without specifying exceptions (for example, double roots counted twice).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Zero coefficients cannot hide sign changes

**Remember:** Skip zeros before counting signs.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 12D10 (Polynomials in real and complex fields: location of zeros (algebraic theorems)), 01A45. arXiv math.HO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Count a polynomial’s sign changes after deleting all zero coefficients. A tempting alternative counts only adjacent coefficients with opposite signs.

**Problem.** For a real polynomial with a nonzero constant term, the positive root count equals the sign count minus a nonnegative even integer. Count roots with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** Deleting zeros counts a sign change across a missing power. In our own example, x² − 1 has one positive root, but neither adjacent coefficient pair changes sign. Our own proof outline uses the fact that multiplying by x − a for positive a adds at least one sign change. For parity, compare the first and last nonzero coefficients. Their signs also give the signs near zero and near positive infinity, and only roots of odd multiplicity reverse the polynomial’s sign.

**Wikipedia:** [Descartes's rule of signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descartes%27s_rule_of_signs). It says: “the number of sign changes in the sequence of the polynomial's coefficients (omitting zero coefficients)”

**Paper or page:** [Gauss's proof of Descartes's rule of signs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04249v2). It says: “Let f(x) be a polynomial with f(0) ≠ 0. There exists a nonnegative even integer ν such that”

**Sources:**

- [Melvyn B. Nathanson, Gauss's proof of Descartes's rule of signs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04249v2)

### Formal differentiation detects repeated roots

**Remember:** At a root, the derivative detects a second copy of the same linear factor.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 12E05 (Polynomials in general fields (irreducibility, etc.)). arXiv math.AC. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** The formal derivative sends constants to zero. For each positive power, multiply the coefficient by the exponent and lower the exponent by one. A root a is repeated when (x − a)² divides the polynomial.

**Problem.** If a is a root of a nonzero polynomial f over a field, then a is a repeated root exactly when f′(a) = 0.

**How the definition helps.** The formal product rule turns the test into one substitution at the root (our own). Write f = (x − a)g by the factor theorem, so the product rule gives f′(a) = g(a) (our own). Apply the factor theorem again to see that g(a) vanishes exactly when x − a divides g (our own). The work is in proving the formal product rule from the rule on powers (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Formal derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_derivative). It says: “Formal differentiation is used in algebra to test for multiple roots of a polynomial.”

**Paper or page:** [Double Root of Polynomial is Root of Derivative](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Double_Root_of_Polynomial_is_Root_of_Derivative). It says: “Then a is a root of f′.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lagrange basis polynomials isolate data points

**Remember:** Each basis polynomial contributes only its own prescribed value at the given inputs.

*True by definition.* MSC 12E05 (Polynomials in general fields (irreducibility, etc.)). arXiv math.AC. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For each distinct input, multiply the linear factors that vanish at every other input. Divide by the value of that product at the chosen input. These Lagrange basis polynomials replace the usual basis of successive powers of x.

**Problem.** Choose n + 1 distinct inputs in a field. Exactly one polynomial of degree at most n takes prescribed values from that field at those inputs.

**How the definition helps.** Each basis polynomial is 1 at its own input and 0 at the others (our own). Distinct inputs make each denominator a product of nonzero differences (our own). Weight each basis polynomial by its prescribed value and add the results (our own). The root bound does the remaining work, since the difference of two solutions would have more roots than its degree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lagrange polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_polynomial). It says: “The interpolating polynomial is unique.”

**Paper or page:** [Lagrange Interpolation Formula/Formulation 1](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Lagrange_Interpolation_Formula/Formulation_1). It says: “Then there exists a unique polynomial P ∈ ℝ\[X\] of degree at most n such that”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Over an algebraically closed field every linear map has an eigenvector

**Remember:** Every characteristic polynomial has a root, so every linear map has an eigenvalue.

*True by definition.* MSC 12E05 (Polynomials in general fields (irreducibility, etc.)), 15A18. arXiv math.AC. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A field F is algebraically closed when every non-constant polynomial with coefficients in F has a root in F.

**Problem.** Every linear map from Fⁿ to itself, for n ≥ 1, has an eigenvector.

**How the definition helps.** A linear map has an eigenvector exactly when its characteristic polynomial has a root, so over an algebraically closed field the theorem is immediate. The article shows that the converse also holds, so the eigenvector property is an equivalent definition of algebraic closure. The real numbers fail: our own example is a rotation of ℝ² by 90°, which has no eigenvector. What stays hard is the fundamental theorem of algebra, which says that ℂ is algebraically closed.

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraically closed field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraically_closed_field). It says: “The field F is algebraically closed if and only if, for each natural number n, every linear map from Fⁿ into itself has some eigenvector.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Every field has a smallest subfield

**Remember:** Keep exactly the elements that every subfield must contain.

*True by definition.* MSC 12E99 (General field theory). arXiv math.AC. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the prime subfield as the intersection of all subfields that share the field's one. An alternative builds it from one using the field operations.

**Problem.** Every field has a unique smallest subfield.

**How the definition helps.** The intersection automatically lies in every subfield, which is the required minimality. In our own proof, zero and one belong to every subfield. The intersection inherits addition, subtraction, multiplication, and inversion of nonzero elements. Constructing the smallest subfield from one instead requires showing that the construction gives exactly this intersection.

**Paper or page:** [Intersection of All Division Subrings is Prime Subfield](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Intersection_of_All_Division_Subrings_is_Prime_Subfield). It says: “Let P be the intersection of the set of all division subrings of K. Then P is the prime subfield of K.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### As the terminal Archimedean ordered field, the reals are unique by definition

**Remember:** Every Archimedean ordered field maps into the reals in exactly one way.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 12J15 (Ordered fields), 26A03. arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** An Archimedean ordered field is an ordered field in which no element is larger than every natural number. The real numbers are the terminal one, which means that every Archimedean ordered field has exactly one order-preserving field homomorphism into it.

**Problem.** All constructions of the real numbers give the same field, up to a unique isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** A terminal object is unique up to a unique isomorphism, so uniqueness holds by definition. The classical theorem says that any two complete ordered fields are isomorphic, and its proof builds the isomorphism by hand (our own). Here that work moves into existence, which needs a construction such as Dedekind cuts or Cauchy sequences. One must also show that the constructed field receives exactly one map from each Archimedean ordered field. The nLab cites Fred Richman for this description.

**nLab:** [real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/real+number). It says: “We speak of the such field because it is unique up to unique isomorphism by definition of terminal object.”

**Sources:**

- [Fred Richman, Real numbers and other completions, Mathematical Logic Quarterly 54 (2008) 98–108](https://doi.org/10.1002/malq.200710024)

### Asking that −1 is not a sum of squares characterizes orderable fields

**Remember:** If −1 is no sum of squares, some ordering exists.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 12D15 (Fields related with sums of squares (formally real fields, Pythagorean fields, etc.)), 12J15. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A field is formally real if −1 is not a sum of squares in it. Artin and Schreier showed that this is the same as having an ordering that makes the field an ordered field.

**Problem.** A field can be ordered exactly when −1 is not a sum of squares. Every formally real field also sits inside a real closed field, one with no larger formally real algebraic extension.

**How the definition helps.** The sum-of-squares condition is purely algebraic, so it can be checked inside the field and stated as a list of first-order sentences, while the definition by existence of an ordering quantifies over sets, as the page says. One direction is easy, because squares are positive in every ordering. The other direction uses Zorn's lemma to enlarge the sums of squares to a positive cone, the set of positive elements of an ordering. Artin used these fields in 1927 to solve Hilbert's seventeenth problem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Formally real field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formally_real_field). It says: “It is also easy to see that a field that admits an ordering must satisfy these three properties.”

**Sources:**

- [Emil Artin and Otto Schreier, Algebraische Konstruktion reeller Körper, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 5 (1927)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02952512)

### A monic greatest common divisor does not change when the field grows

**Remember:** Normalize the gcd to be monic and it ignores the field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 12E05 (Polynomials in general fields (irreducibility, etc.)), 13F07. arXiv math.RA, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Over a field, a greatest common divisor of two polynomials is unique only up to a nonzero constant factor. The usual convention takes the monic one, with leading coefficient 1.

**Problem.** Let E be an extension field of F, and let P and Q have coefficients in F. Then their monic greatest common divisor over E equals their monic greatest common divisor over F.

**How the definition helps.** The theorem says that the two greatest common divisors are equal, and this only makes sense when the gcd is one fixed polynomial, which the monic convention ensures (our own reading). Then the Euclidean algorithm, done in F, gives the same answer as in E, so the gcd lies in F\[X\]; this argument is our own. Without the convention, the statement could only say that the two differ by a constant. A useful corollary, in our own reading, is that two polynomials over F have a common root in some extension exactly when their gcd over F is not constant.

**Paper or page:** [GCD of Polynomials does not depend on Base Field](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/GCD_of_Polynomials_does_not_depend_on_Base_Field). It says: “Let: gcd {P, Q} = R in F\[X\] gcd {P, Q} = S in E\[X\]. Then R = S. In particular, S ∈ F\[X\].”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, GCD of Polynomials does not depend on Base Field](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/GCD_of_Polynomials_does_not_depend_on_Base_Field)

### Defining the discriminant by root differences makes repeated roots visible

**Remember:** A product of squared root gaps vanishes exactly when two roots meet.

*True by definition.* MSC 12E05 (Polynomials in general fields (irreducibility, etc.)). arXiv math.AC, math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let f be a polynomial over a field with degree n ≥ 2 and leading coefficient a. List its roots r₁, …, rₙ in a field where f factors into linear terms, repeating each root according to its multiplicity. Define the discriminant as a²ⁿ⁻² times the product of (rᵢ − rⱼ)² over all pairs i &lt; j. Another definition uses the coefficients, giving b² − 4ac for a quadratic ax² + bx + c.

**Problem.** The discriminant of f is zero if and only if f has a repeated root. If f has real coefficients and all its roots are real and distinct, the discriminant is positive.

**How the definition helps.** The product definition makes a repeated root exactly a zero factor, and for real distinct roots the squared differences and the even power of a are positive. These facts are not visible directly in a coefficient formula. The work moves into proving that the product agrees with the coefficient formula. The root expression is symmetric under permutations of the roots, so the theorem on symmetric polynomials and the relations between roots and coefficients write it in terms of the coefficients.

**Wikipedia:** [Discriminant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant). It says: “This expression for the discriminant is often taken as a definition. It makes clear that if the polynomial has a multiple root, then its discriminant is zero,”

### Finite fields as Frobenius fixed fields make intersections use greatest common divisors

**Remember:** A point fixed by two powers is fixed by their greatest common divisor.

*True by definition.* MSC 12E20 (Finite fields (field-theoretic aspects)), 12F10. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Fix an algebraic closure K of the field with p elements. The Frobenius map σ raises each element to the pth power, and it is an automorphism of K. Define the subfield of size pⁿ as the set of elements that σⁿ fixes. The usual definition takes the subfield with exactly pⁿ elements.

**Problem.** The intersection of the finite subfields of degrees m and n has degree gcd(m, n) over the prime field.

**How the definition helps.** With the fixed-field definition, an intersection of subfields is the fixed set of a group of powers of σ (our own). The elements fixed by σᵐ and σⁿ are those fixed by the subgroup they generate (our own). By Bézout’s identity, this subgroup is generated by σ to the power gcd(m, n) (our own). The work moves to proving that σ is bijective on K and that σⁿ has exactly pⁿ fixed points (our own).

**nLab:** [finite field](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/finite+field). It says: “may be defined to be the fixed field of the automorphism σⁿ: K → K.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A commutative unital ring with exactly two ideals is a field

**Remember:** A field has two ideals, and the zero ring has only one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 12E99 (General field theory), 13A15. arXiv math.RA, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A field is a commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 in which every nonzero element has an inverse. An ideal is an additive subgroup that is closed under multiplication by every ring element.

**Problem.** A commutative ring with unity is a field exactly when its only ideals are {0} and the whole ring, and these two are different.

**How the definition helps.** Because a field must have 1 ≠ 0, being a field matches having exactly two ideals. Our own sketch: if a ≠ 0, then Ra is not {0}, so Ra = R and 1 = ra. Our own remark: the zero ring has only one ideal, so the rule 1 ≠ 0 makes the count exactly two. ProofWiki shows that commutativity is needed; the ring of 2 × 2 real matrices has only two two-sided ideals but has zero divisors (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [Commutative and Unitary Ring with 2 Ideals is Field](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Commutative_and_Unitary_Ring_with_2_Ideals_is_Field), [Field has 2 Ideals](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Field_has_2_Ideals), [Non-Commutative Ring with Unity and 2 Ideals not necessarily Division Ring](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Non-Commutative_Ring_with_Unity_and_2_Ideals_not_necessarily_Division_Ring). It says: “That is, such that (R, +, ∘) has no non-null proper ideals. Then (R, +, ∘) is a field.”

### Sending 1 to 1 makes every field homomorphism injective

**Remember:** A field map that keeps 1 cannot collapse anything.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 12E99 (General field theory), 13B10, 13A35. arXiv math.RA, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A field homomorphism is a map between fields that keeps sums and products. Many authors also require that it sends 1 to 1. In a field, 1 is not equal to 0.

**Problem.** Every homomorphism between fields that sends 1 to 1 is injective. So a surjective one is an isomorphism, and the Frobenius map x ↦ xᵖ is injective in characteristic p.

**How the definition helps.** Asking that 1 goes to 1 rules out the zero map, which is the only field map that is not injective. The reason is that the kernel of a ring map is an ideal, and a field has only two ideals. The ProofWiki page keeps the zero map as a second case; in our own reading, the condition 1 ↦ 1 removes it. The theorem then has no exceptions, and the surjective case and the Frobenius case follow at once.

**Paper or page:** [Field Homomorphism is either Trivial or Injection](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Field_Homomorphism_is_either_Trivial_or_Injection), [Surjective Field Homomorphism is Field Isomorphism](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Surjective_Field_Homomorphism_is_Field_Isomorphism), [Frobenius Endomorphism on Field is Injective](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Frobenius_Endomorphism_on_Field_is_Injective). It says: “Then φ is either an injection or the trivial homomorphism.”

### Constructible numbers sit at the top of towers of degree-2 steps

**Remember:** A compass solves only quadratic equations, so each step doubles the degree.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 12F05 (Algebraic field extensions), 51M04. arXiv math.AC, math.MG. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A real number is constructible if you can reach it with straightedge and compass, starting from 0 and 1. In algebra, this means it lies at the top of a tower of fields that starts at ℚ. Each step in the tower is a field extension of degree 2.

**Problem.** Doubling the cube and trisecting a general angle are impossible with straightedge and compass (Wantzel, 1837).

**How the definition helps.** The definition turns a question about geometry into a question about degrees of field extensions. The tower gives \[ℚ(γ):ℚ\] = 2ʳ, so the degree of a constructible number is a power of 2. The number ∛2 has degree 3, so the cube cannot be doubled. Trisecting 60° needs cos 20°, a root of an irreducible cubic, so it has degree 3 too.

**Wikipedia:** [Constructible number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructible_number). It says: “It follows from this decomposition that the degree of the field extension \[ℚ(γ):ℚ\] is 2ʳ, where r counts the number of quadratic extension steps.”

**Sources:**

- [P. L. Wantzel, Recherches sur les moyens de reconnaître si un Problème de Géométrie peut se résoudre avec la règle et le compas, Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées 2 (1837), 366–372](http://www.numdam.org/item/JMPA_1837_1_2__366_0/)

### Defining field trace as a matrix trace makes it linear

**Remember:** Add the multiplication maps, then add their traces.

*True by definition.* MSC 12F05 (Algebraic field extensions), 11R04. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a finite field extension L of K, multiplication by an element a is a K-linear map of L. Define the trace of a as the matrix trace of this map. Another definition adds the roots of the minimal polynomial of a, each counted \[L : K(a)\] times.

**Problem.** The field trace is linear over the base field.

**How the definition helps.** With the matrix-trace definition, the theorem is the linearity of matrix trace (our own). Multiplication by xa + yb is x times multiplication by a plus y times multiplication by b (our own). With the root-sum definition, the roots for a + b are not simply sums of roots for a and b (our own). The Napkin proves that the two definitions agree for number fields, and the work moves there.

**Paper or page:** [Theorem 2.8. (Morally correct definition of norm and trace)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “the trace of α equals the trace”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining normal extensions as splitting fields makes composita normal

**Remember:** Combine the polynomial families to combine their splitting fields.

*True by definition.* MSC 12F05 (Algebraic field extensions), 12F10. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define a normal extension of K as a splitting field of a family of polynomials over K. That is the field generated over K by all roots of those polynomials. Another definition asks that every irreducible polynomial over K with one root in the extension splits there.

**Problem.** The compositum of normal algebraic extensions in a common algebraic closure is normal. The compositum is the smallest field containing them all.

**How the definition helps.** With the splitting-field definition, the compositum is generated by all roots of the combined families, so it is a splitting field (our own). The work moves to proving that splitting fields pass the other test (our own).

**nLab:** [normal field extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/normal+field+extension). It says: “A field extension K ⊂ L is said to be normal if L is the splitting field of a family of polynomials in K\[x\].”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Norms as products over embeddings compose down towers of separable extensions

**Remember:** Group the conjugates by their restriction to the middle field.

*True by definition.* MSC 12F05 (Algebraic field extensions), 12F10. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let L be a finite separable extension of K, and fix an algebraic closure of K. Define the norm of an element a as the product of σ(a) over all field maps σ from L to the closure that fix K. Another definition uses the determinant of multiplication by a.

**Problem.** Take finite separable extensions K ⊂ L ⊂ M. The norm from M to K is the norm from M to L followed by the norm from L to K.

**How the definition helps.** With the embedding definition, transitivity is a regrouping of one product (our own). Sort the field maps from M by their restrictions τ to L; the maps above one τ multiply to τ applied to the norm from M to L (our own). Multiplying over all τ gives the norm from L to K of that norm (our own). The work moves to counting the extensions of each τ, and to agreement with the determinant definition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 9.20.5.](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BIJ). It says: “Let M/L/K be a tower of finite extensions of fields.”
