### Cleft extensions are crossed products, the trivial bundles of Hopf–Galois theory

**Remember:** A global section turns a principal bundle into a twisted product.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 16T05 (Hopf algebras and their applications), 58B32, 16S35. arXiv math.QA, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An H-comodule algebra A with coinvariants B is cleft when there is a comodule map γ: H → A with a convolution inverse γ⁻¹. That means γ(h₍₁₎)γ⁻¹(h₍₂₎) = ε(h)1 = γ⁻¹(h₍₁₎)γ(h₍₂₎). The map γ plays the role of a global section of a principal bundle.

**Problem.** For a Hopf algebra H over a field, A is cleft exactly when it is a crossed product of B and H. The crossed product is twisted by an action of H on B and an invertible 2-cocycle. Both conditions are equivalent to B ⊂ A being H-Galois with A ≅ B ⊗ H as left B-modules and right H-comodules.

**How the definition helps.** The cleaving map γ directly gives the twisted action h ▷ b = γ(h₍₁₎) b γ⁻¹(h₍₂₎) and the cocycle σ(h,k) = γ(h₍₁₎)γ(k₍₁₎)γ⁻¹(h₍₂₎k₍₂₎). Then b ⊗ h ↦ bγ(h) is an isomorphism from the crossed product to A. So one condition, an invertible section, says at once that the bundle is trivial and that its algebra is a crossed product. The work moves into the theorems of Doi and Takeuchi and of Blattner, Cohen and Montgomery.

**Paper or page:** [Some interactions between Hopf Galois extensions and noncommutative rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.12860), [Differential Calculi on Quantum Principal Bundles over Projective Bases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.03481). It says: “(i) There exists an invertible 2-cocycle and an action of H on A<sup>co H</sup> such that A≅A<sup>co H</sup> \#\_σ H. (ii) The extension A<sup>co H</sup> ⊂ A is H-cleft. (iii) A<sup>co H</sup> ⊂ A is a H-Galois extension and has the normal basis property.”

**Sources:**

- [Y. Doi and M. Takeuchi, Cleft comodule algebras for a bialgebra, Communications in Algebra 14 (1986) 801–817](https://doi.org/10.1080/00927878608823337)

### Defining Nichols algebras by a maximal ideal forbids primitives above degree one

**Remember:** A new higher primitive would give a larger ideal to remove.

*True by definition.* MSC 16T05 (Hopf algebras and their applications), 17B37. arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Yetter–Drinfeld module V over a Hopf algebra is both a module and a comodule, with a compatibility law. The law gives a braiding that swaps tensor factors, so the tensor algebra T(V) becomes a braided Hopf algebra. Define the Nichols algebra as T(V) divided by the largest graded Hopf ideal that lies in degrees two and higher. The alternative characterization asks for a graded braided Hopf algebra generated in degree one whose primitives are exactly V.

**Problem.** The primitive elements of the Nichols algebra of V are exactly the elements of V. An element x is primitive when Δ(x) = 1 ⊗ x + x ⊗ 1.

**How the definition helps.** The maximal-ideal definition leaves no room for a new primitive element. Suppose that a homogeneous primitive of degree at least two survives (our own argument). The primitives in degrees two and higher span a Yetter–Drinfeld submodule, and they generate a Hopf ideal in those degrees. Its preimage in T(V) is a larger ideal of the allowed kind, which contradicts maximality (our own argument). The work moves into showing that the sum of all allowed ideals is again allowed, so a largest one exists. The quoted lemma, which cites Andruskiewitsch and Schneider, states the alternative characterization.

**Paper or page:** [Eight classes of new Hopf algebras of dimension 128 without the Chevalley property](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.01991v1). It says: “R(0) = k, R(1) = V, R(1) generates the algebra R, P(R) = V.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dual coproducts encode product identities

**Remember:** One tensor coefficient holds one product identity.

*True by definition.* MSC 16T05 (Hopf algebras and their applications), 11M32. arXiv math.QA, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Encode a linear evaluation φ on words as the series F = ∑ φ(w) w. For the shuffle or the stuffle product ∗, the dual coproduct Δ gives ΔF the coefficient φ(u ∗ v) at u ⊗ v.

**Problem.** Over a commutative ℚ-algebra, a linear evaluation φ with φ(empty word) = 1 preserves ∗ exactly when ΔF = F ⊗ F.

**How the definition helps.** The dual coproduct puts every product identity in one coefficient of ΔF. In our own proof, compare the coefficient of u ⊗ v on both sides. The work for multiple zeta values lies in finding the right coproduct and proving the shuffle or stuffle identity for the evaluation.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “Δ∗◇(Genφ(𝒜)) = Genφ(𝒜) ⊗ Genφ(𝒜).”

**Sources:**

- [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1)

### Faithfully flat Galois extensions give descent for relative Hopf modules

**Remember:** On a principal bundle, equivariant modules upstairs are just modules downstairs.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 16T05 (Hopf algebras and their applications), 58B32. arXiv math.QA, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let E be an H-comodule algebra with coinvariants U. The extension U ⊂ E is H-Galois when the canonical map from E ⊗ E over U to E ⊗ H is bijective. A relative Hopf module is an E-module M with a compatible H-coaction, the algebraic version of an equivariant vector bundle on the total space.

**Problem.** Let U ⊂ E be H-Galois, with E faithfully flat as a right U-module. Then M ↦ E ⊗ M over U is an equivalence from U-modules to relative Hopf modules, with inverse given by taking coinvariants.

**How the definition helps.** The Galois bijection between E ⊗ E over U and E ⊗ H identifies relative Hopf modules with descent data for the ring map U → E. So the theorem becomes ordinary faithfully flat descent for noncommutative rings. In the commutative case it says that equivariant quasi-coherent sheaves on a torsor descend to its base.

**nLab:** [Schneider's theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Schneider%27s+theorem). It says: “Hence the categories of comodules are equivalent and the theorem hence boils down to the standard faithfully flat descent (for noncommutative rings) or comonadicity criterium in comonadic version.”

**Sources:**

- [H.-J. Schneider, Principal homogeneous spaces for arbitrary Hopf algebras, Israel Journal of Mathematics 72 (1990) 167–195](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02764619)

### Quantum torsors recover their Hopf algebra from the Galois object alone

**Remember:** A torsor knows its structure group, so you need not supply it.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 16T05 (Hopf algebras and their applications), 58B32. arXiv math.QA, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A quantum torsor, in the sense of Grunspan and Schauenburg, is an algebra T with an algebra map μ: T → T ⊗ Tᵒᵖ ⊗ T. The map μ satisfies associativity-type axioms. It generalizes the operation (x, y, z) ↦ xy⁻¹z of a heap, which describes a torsor without naming its group.

**Problem.** Every faithfully flat H-Galois object T is a quantum torsor, and the Hopf algebra Hᵣ(T) built from the torsor structure alone is isomorphic to H. Conversely, a faithfully flat quantum torsor is a Galois object over Hᵣ(T).

**How the definition helps.** The torsor map μ is the inverse Galois map composed with the coaction, so the structure Hopf algebra becomes something T determines, not extra data. From μ one builds Hᵣ(T) inside Tᵒᵖ ⊗ T by a descent condition, and also a left Hopf algebra Hₗ(T) that makes T a bi-Galois object. The work moves into faithfully flat descent, in Schauenburg's proof.

**Paper or page:** [Some interactions between Hopf Galois extensions and noncommutative rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.12860), [Some interactions between Hopf Galois extensions and noncommutative rings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.12860). It says: “Let T be a faithfully flat H-Galois object. Then T is a quantum K-torsor with associated map μ:T → T ⊗ Tᵒᵖ ⊗ T defined by”

**Sources:**

- [P. Schauenburg, Hopf-Galois and bi-Galois extensions, in Galois Theory, Hopf Algebras, and Semiabelian Categories, Fields Institute Communications 43 (2004) 469–515](https://doi.org/10.1090/fic/043/22)

### Quasi-Hopf algebras describe monoidal categories with a nontrivial associator

**Remember:** Coassociativity holds only up to φ, and φ becomes the associator of modules.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 16T05 (Hopf algebras and their applications), 16T10, 18M15. arXiv math.QA, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A quasi-bialgebra is an algebra A with a comultiplication that is coassociative only up to conjugation by an invertible element φ in A ⊗ A ⊗ A. The element φ must satisfy a pentagon identity. A quasi-Hopf algebra also has an antipode that satisfies suitable axioms.

**Problem.** The modules over a quasi-Hopf algebra form a monoidal category whose associativity isomorphisms are given by φ, so they need not be trivial. Conversely, a finite tensor category with a quasi-fiber functor is the module category of a quasi-Hopf algebra.

**How the definition helps.** The element φ lets a category with a nontrivial associator still be the module category of an algebra. For an ordinary Hopf algebra, the forgetful functor to vector spaces is monoidal (a fiber functor). For a quasi-Hopf algebra it is only a quasi-fiber functor, whose product map need not be associative, and φ measures this failure. In our reading of Drinfeld, the monodromy of the Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations gives a quasi-Hopf structure on U(𝔤)\[\[ħ\]\], and proving it equivalent to the quantum group is still real work.

**nLab:** [quasi-Hopf algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quasi-Hopf+algebra), [Drinfeld-Kohno theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Drinfeld-Kohno+theorem). It says: “In RCFT, the monoidal categories appearing can be, by Tannaka reconstruction considered as categories of modules of Hopf algebra-like objects where the flexibility of associativity coherence in building a theory were natural thus leading to quasi-Hopf algebras.”

**Sources:**

- [Vladimir Drinfeld, Quasi-Hopf algebras, Algebra i Analiz 1:6 (1989) 114–148 (English: Leningrad Math. J. 1 (1990) 1419–1457)](http://www.mathnet.ru/php/getFT.phtml?jrnid=aa&paperid=53&what=fullt&option_lang=rus) (link not checked)
- [Toshitake Kohno, Monodromy representations of braid groups and Yang-Baxter equations, Ann. Inst. Fourier 37 (1987) 139–160](http://www.numdam.org/item?id=AIF_1987__37_4_139_0)

### Removing products gives Leibniz

**Remember:** Discard left-hand products and the coaction becomes a derivation.

*True by definition.* MSC 16T05 (Hopf algebras and their applications), 11M32. arXiv math.QA, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let H be a connected graded Hopf algebra over ℚ, and let H₊ be its part of positive weight. Define D<sub>m</sub> by applying the coproduct and then projecting the left factor onto the weight-m part of H₊/H₊², the elements modulo products.

**Problem.** For each m &gt; 0, D<sub>m</sub> is a derivation: D<sub>m</sub>(ab) = D<sub>m</sub>(a)(1 ⊗ b) + (1 ⊗ a)D<sub>m</sub>(b).

**How the definition helps.** Projecting the coproduct removes precisely the cross terms that would spoil the product rule. In our own proof, expand Δ(a)Δ(b). Its left factor survives only when exactly one input supplies positive weight there. The weight-zero terms of the two coproducts are 1 ⊗ a and 1 ⊗ b. The Hopf algebra construction supplies the multiplicative coproduct.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “is a derivation with respect to ∗”

**Sources:**

- [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1)

### Quasitriangular Hopf algebras give solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation

**Remember:** The universal R-matrix is exactly a braiding on the module category.

*True by definition.* MSC 16T10 (Bialgebras), 16T25, 18M15. arXiv math.QA, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A bialgebra H is quasitriangular if it has an invertible element R in H ⊗ H with two properties. First, the flipped coproduct of h equals R Δ(h) R⁻¹ for all h. Second, (Δ ⊗ id)(R) = R₁₃R₂₃ and (id ⊗ Δ)(R) = R₁₃R₁₂, where R₁₃ means R placed in the first and third tensor factors.

**Problem.** In a quasitriangular bialgebra, R satisfies the quantum Yang–Baxter equation R₁₂R₁₃R₂₃ = R₂₃R₁₃R₁₂. So every H-module gives a solution of this equation, and hence representations of the braid groups.

**How the definition helps.** Drinfeld chose the axioms so that R gives a braiding on modules by construction. The map v ⊗ w ↦ flip(R·(v ⊗ w)) is an H-linear isomorphism that satisfies the hexagon identities. So the module category is braided monoidal: it has a natural way to swap tensor factors that is compatible with the tensor product. The quantum Yang–Baxter equation then follows from the axioms in a few lines, as a corollary. The hard work moves to building examples, such as the quantized enveloping algebras, and to showing that they have a universal R-matrix.

**nLab:** [quasitriangular bialgebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quasitriangular+bialgebra), [quantum group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quantum+group). It says: “equipped with just the right structure such as to make its category of modules into a braided monoidal category/symmetric monoidal category.”

**Sources:**

- [Vladimir Drinfeld, Quantum groups, Proc. ICM 1986, Vol. 1 (1987) 798–820; expanded version J. Soviet Math. 41 (1988) 898–915](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01247086)
- [Shahn Majid, Quasitriangular Hopf algebras and Yang–Baxter equations, Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 5 (1990) 1–91](https://doi.org/10.1142/S0217751X90000027)

### Totally nonnegative integers turn the narrow class group into a Picard group

**Remember:** Build positivity into the ring, and the narrow class group appears by itself.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 16Y60 (Semirings), 11R29. arXiv math.AG, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An algebraic integer of a number field is totally nonnegative when it is at least 0 under every real embedding. These integers form a semiring, a ring without subtraction. Its reflexive Picard group is the group of reflexive rank-one modules up to isomorphism.

**Problem.** The reflexive Picard group of the semiring of totally nonnegative integers of a number field is the narrow class group of the field.

**How the definition helps.** Positivity is built into the semiring, so the sign condition of the narrow class group comes for free. In the ordinary class group, a principal ideal may have a generator of any sign (our own). The cost is new module theory over semirings. There, not all usual definitions of a vector bundle agree, although all usual definitions of a line bundle do.

**Paper or page:** [Facets of module theory over semirings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18645v3). It says: “We also show that the narrow class group of a number field can be recovered as a reflexive Picard group of its subsemiring of totally nonnegative algebraic integers.”

**Sources:**

- [James Borger, Jaiung Jun, Facets of module theory over semirings, arXiv:2405.18645v3 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18645v3)

## 17 Nonassociative rings and algebras

### Power associativity gives exponent laws

**Remember:** All products of one element take their parentheses from an associative subalgebra.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17A05 (Power-associative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** An algebra is power-associative if the subalgebra generated by each element is associative. The weaker test that (xx)x equals x(xx) checks only third powers.

**Problem.** In a power-associative algebra, xᵐxⁿ = xᵐ⁺ⁿ for all positive integers m and n.

**How the definition helps.** The usual exponent law applies in the associative subalgebra generated by x. Our own counterexample uses a commutative algebra on basis e, f, g with ee = f and ff = g. All other basis products are zero. Commutativity gives agreement at degree three, but (ee)(ee) = g and e(e(ee)) = 0. The work is to prove associativity within each subalgebra generated by one element.

**nLab:** [power-associative algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/power-associative+algebra). It says: “it may be that all possible ways of parenthesizing the expression for xⁿ are equal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Alternating brackets exclude a characteristic two counterexample

**Remember:** Alternation implies anticommutativity even when 2 is zero.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B01 (Identities, free Lie (super)algebras), 17B50. arXiv math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Require a Lie bracket to be alternating, meaning \[x,x\] = 0 for every x. As usual, require bilinearity and the Jacobi identity, \[x,\[y,z\]\] + \[y,\[z,x\]\] + \[z,\[x,y\]\] = 0. The weaker condition \[x,y\] = −\[y,x\] is called anticommutativity. Over fields where 2 is nonzero, it is equivalent to alternation.

**Problem.** Every Lie bracket is anticommutative. In characteristic two, anticommutativity and the Jacobi identity do not suffice for a Lie bracket.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding \[x+y,x+y\] = 0 makes anticommutativity immediate. In characteristic two, anticommutativity only says that the bracket is symmetric. On a space with basis e,f over the field with two elements, set \[e,e\] = f and make all other basis brackets zero (our own). This bracket is symmetric and satisfies Jacobi because every bracket value is a multiple of f, which brackets to zero (our own). It is not alternating, so the weaker axiom would admit it (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra). It says: “If the field does not have characteristic 2, then anticommutativity implies the alternating property, since it implies \[x,x\]=−\[x,x\].”

**Paper or page:** [Lie Algebra is Anticommutative](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Lie_Algebra_is_Anticommutative). It says: “Let L be a Lie algebra. Then L is anticommutative:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Jacobi as a product rule gives the adjoint representation

**Remember:** The product rule for brackets says that the adjoint operators preserve brackets.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B01 (Identities, free Lie (super)algebras), 17B10. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Lie bracket is bilinear and satisfies \[x,x\] = 0 and the Jacobi identity. Write adₓ for the operator b ↦ \[x,b\]. Impose Jacobi in product-rule form, \[x,\[a,b\]\] = \[\[x,a\],b\] + \[a,\[x,b\]\]. The usual cyclic form says that \[x,\[a,b\]\] + \[a,\[b,x\]\] + \[b,\[x,a\]\] = 0.

**Problem.** The map x ↦ adₓ preserves brackets, using the commutator AB − BA as the bracket of operators.

**How the definition helps.** The product-rule axiom states exactly that x ↦ adₓ preserves brackets once we move the last term to the left (our own). The result is (adₓ adₐ − adₐ adₓ)(b) = \[\[x,a\],b\] (our own). The only work in replacing the cyclic axiom is using \[a,b\] = −\[b,a\] to rearrange its terms (our own).

**nLab:** [Jacobi identity](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+identity). It says: “If the bracket \[−,−\] is skew-symmetric the Jacobi identity for all triples is equivalent to the Leibniz identity that for all x,a,b, the linear map adₓ = \[x,−\] : 𝔤 → 𝔤 is a derivation”

**Wikipedia:** [Adjoint representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjoint_representation). It says: “This last identity says that ad is a Lie algebra homomorphism; i.e., a linear mapping that takes brackets to brackets.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ruling out abelian ideals makes the adjoint representation faithful

**Remember:** The centre is an abelian ideal, so it vanishes.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras), 17B05. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call a finite-dimensional Lie algebra 𝔤 semisimple if it has no nonzero abelian ideal. An ideal I satisfies \[𝔤,I\] ⊆ I, and it is abelian when \[I,I\] = 0. In characteristic zero an equivalent definition requires a nondegenerate Killing form. This form pairs x and y by the trace of the product of the operators \[x,−\] and \[y,−\].

**Problem.** For a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 in characteristic zero, the adjoint representation x ↦ \[x,−\] is injective.

**How the definition helps.** The no-abelian-ideals definition rules out a nonzero centre immediately, since the centre is an abelian ideal. The centre is exactly the kernel of x ↦ \[x,−\] (our own). Starting with the Killing form, one instead shows that the centre pairs to zero with every element, then uses nondegeneracy (our own). The work moves to Cartan’s criterion, which connects nondegeneracy to the absence of nonzero solvable ideals (our own). A solvable ideal becomes zero after repeated bracketing with itself, so its last nonzero stage is an abelian ideal (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra). It says: “The center of a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 is trivial (since the center is an abelian ideal). In other words, the adjoint representation ad is injective.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Killing squares gives Lie quotients

**Remember:** Kill the squares to get a Lie bracket in every characteristic.

*True by definition.* MSC 17A32 (Leibniz algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A left Leibniz algebra has a bilinear bracket in which left multiplication satisfies the product rule. Define its Lie quotient by dividing out the linear span of the squares \[x,x\]. This imposes alternation, not just a sign change when swapping inputs.

**Problem.** Every bracket-preserving linear map from a left Leibniz algebra to a Lie algebra factors uniquely through its Lie quotient.

**How the definition helps.** Our own proof uses the span of squares because every map into a Lie algebra sends each square to zero. Usually one takes the smallest ideal containing the squares. To see why their span suffices, use the product rule twice. It gives \[\[x,x\],y\] = 0 and \[y,\[x,x\]\] = \[u,x\] + \[x,u\], where u = \[y,x\]. The latter sum equals the square of x + u minus their individual squares. Thus brackets preserve the span on both sides. In the quotient, alternation turns the product rule into the Jacobi identity, and every given map descends uniquely.

**nLab:** [Leibniz algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Leibniz+algebra). It says: “the maximal Lie algebra quotient”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Louis Loday and Teimuraz Pirashvili. Universal enveloping algebras of Leibniz algebras and (co)homology (1993).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01445099)

### Anisotropic composition norms give division

**Remember:** A product of nonzero norms cannot be zero.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17A75 (Composition algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A unital composition algebra over a field has an identity and a nondegenerate quadratic norm satisfying N(xy) = N(x)N(y). Nondegeneracy means that only zero pairs to zero with every vector under the form N(x + y) − N(x) − N(y). The norm is anisotropic if only zero has norm zero.

**Problem.** In a finite-dimensional composition algebra with anisotropic norm, multiplication by any nonzero element is invertible on both sides.

**How the definition helps.** Our own argument uses multiplicativity to show that the product of two nonzero elements has nonzero norm. Left and right multiplication by a nonzero element are therefore injective, hence invertible in finite dimension. For our own counterexample, take two-by-two matrices with the determinant as norm. The diagonal matrices with diagonals (1,0) and (0,1) are nonzero and multiply to zero.

**nLab:** [composition algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/composition+algebra). It says: “A fundamental dichotomy is whether or not the composition algebra has zero divisors, i.e., elements v such that N(v) = 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Cartan subalgebras as maximal toral makes the rank well defined

**Remember:** Maximal toral, not maximal abelian, gives one rank for each algebra.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B05 (Structure theory for Lie algebras and superalgebras), 17B20. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Cartan subalgebra is a nilpotent subalgebra, one where long enough brackets vanish, that is its own normalizer. The normalizer is the set of elements whose bracket with it stays in it. In a semisimple Lie algebra over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, this is the same as a maximal toral subalgebra. A subalgebra is toral if every element x has ad(x) diagonalizable.

**Problem.** Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, all Cartan subalgebras of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra are conjugate under automorphisms. So their common dimension, the rank, is an invariant.

**How the definition helps.** Asking for diagonalizable elements, not just commuting ones, picks out a class of subalgebras that are all alike. Maximal abelian subalgebras do not have one dimension. The page gives sl₂ₙ(ℂ), whose Cartan subalgebras have dimension 2n − 1, but which has an abelian subalgebra of dimension n². One such subalgebra is the matrices with an n × n block in the top right corner and zeros elsewhere (our own). The conditions on the field matter too: over ℝ, the page says, sl₂(ℝ) has two Cartan subalgebras that are not conjugate. What stays hard is the conjugacy theorem itself.

**Wikipedia:** [Cartan subalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan_subalgebra). It says: “The dimension of a Cartan subalgebra is not in general the maximal dimension of an abelian subalgebra, even for complex simple Lie algebras.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Invariant pairings identify the center

**Remember:** Move the bracket across the pairing to detect central elements.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B05 (Structure theory for Lie algebras and superalgebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A metric Lie algebra has a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form B that is invariant. Here invariance means B(\[x,y\],z) = B(x,\[y,z\]). An arbitrary inner product does not require this rule.

**Problem.** In a finite-dimensional metric Lie algebra, the center is the orthogonal complement of the span of all brackets.

**How the definition helps.** Invariance gives B(z,\[x,y\]) = B(\[z,x\],y), so orthogonality to every bracket tests whether z is central (our own). Nondegeneracy means only zero pairs to zero with every y (our own). Give the real Heisenberg algebra an orthonormal basis x,y,z with \[x,y\]=z and z central (our own). Its bracket span is the z-axis, whose perpendicular plane is different from the center, the z-axis (our own).

**nLab:** [metric Lie algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/metric+Lie+algebra). It says: “is symmetric and invariant under the adjoint action, hence is an invariant polynomial on 𝔤”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Fundamental weights make integral weights the integer combinations of a basis

**Remember:** Coroots test integrality; fundamental weights are their dual basis.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B10 (Representations of Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras, algebraic theory (weights)), 17B22. arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let 𝔤 be a complex semisimple Lie algebra, with roots the nonzero weights of its adjoint representation. For a root α, the coroot is α∨ = 2α/(α, α). The fundamental weights ω₁, …, ωₙ are the basis dual to the simple coroots α₁∨, …, αₙ∨. A weight λ is algebraically integral if (λ, α∨) is an integer for every root α.

**Problem.** A weight is algebraically integral if and only if it is an integer combination of the fundamental weights. It is dominant integral if also (λ, α∨) ≥ 0 for every positive root α. That holds exactly when these integers are all nonnegative.

**How the definition helps.** The coefficient of λ on ωᵢ is (λ, αᵢ∨) by the dual basis property, so integrality on the simple coroots is integrality of the coefficients. The work moves into another fact: if λ is integral on the simple coroots, it is integral on all coroots. That holds because the simple coroots form a base of the dual root system, so every coroot is an integer combination of them (our own). The scaling 2α/(α, α) makes the coroots a root system too, with the same group of reflections, the Weyl group (our own). With this, the theorem of the highest weight indexes the irreducible representations by n-tuples of nonnegative integers (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weight (representation theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weight_%28representation_theory%29), [Root system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_system). It says: “An element λ is then algebraically integral if and only if it is an integral combination of the fundamental weights.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Induction gives Verma modules their universal property

**Remember:** Induction turns a choice of highest weight vector into a module map.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B10 (Representations of Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras, algebraic theory (weights)). arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let 𝔟 be a Borel subalgebra of a complex semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤, made of a Cartan subalgebra 𝔥 and the positive root spaces. For a weight λ, let 𝔟 act on a line ℂλ by λ on 𝔥 and by zero on the positive root spaces. The Verma module is the induced module M(λ) = U(𝔤) ⊗ ℂλ, with the tensor product over U(𝔟).

**Problem.** Every 𝔤-module generated by a vector of weight λ killed by the positive root spaces is a quotient of M(λ).

**How the definition helps.** The induced definition gives the map by the tensor product's universal property, with no need to choose a basis (our own). Maps from M(λ) into V correspond to 𝔟-maps ℂλ → V, which select vectors of weight λ killed by the positive root spaces (our own). The map is onto when the selected vector generates V. A basis-first construction instead builds the module from ordered products of negative root vectors applied to one generator (our own). The work of producing this basis and showing M(λ) is nonzero lies in the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem on ordered products in U(𝔤) (our own).

**nLab:** [Verma module](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Verma+module). It says: “Given a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field F with Borel subalgebra 𝔟 ⊂ 𝔤 a Verma module is the induced module”

**Wikipedia:** [Verma module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verma_module). It says: “If V is any representation generated by a highest weight vector of weight λ, there is a surjective 𝔤-homomorphism W\_\\lambda\\to V.”

**Sources:**

- [D.-N. Verma, Structure of certain induced representations of complex semisimple Lie algebras, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 74 (1968) 160–167](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9904-1968-11921-4)

### Verma modules give an irreducible module of every highest weight

**Remember:** Build the largest module of weight λ first, then cut it down.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B10 (Representations of Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras, algebraic theory (weights)). arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let 𝔤 be a complex semisimple Lie algebra with a Borel subalgebra 𝔟, made of a Cartan subalgebra 𝔥 and the positive root spaces. For a linear form λ on 𝔥, the Verma module of weight λ is U(𝔤) ⊗ ℂλ over U(𝔟), where 𝔟 acts on the line ℂλ through λ.

**Problem.** For every linear form λ on 𝔥, the Verma module of weight λ has a unique irreducible quotient. So there is exactly one irreducible module of highest weight λ, up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** The Verma module is defined by a universal property, so every module generated by a vector of highest weight λ is a quotient of it. It has a unique maximal submodule, so it has a unique irreducible quotient. The theorem of the highest weight then reduces to one question: for which λ is this quotient finite dimensional? The answer is the dominant integral weights, and this step is the remaining real work.

**Wikipedia:** [Verma module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verma_module), [Theorem of the highest weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem_of_the_highest_weight). It says: “In any case, the Verma module gives—for any λ, not necessarily dominant or integral—a representation with highest weight λ. The price we pay for this relatively simple construction is that Wλ is always infinite dimensional.”

**Sources:**

- [Verma, D.-N. (1968). Structure of certain induced representations of complex semisimple Lie algebras. Bulletin of the AMS 74, 160–167.](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1968-11921-4)
- [Bernshtein, I. N., Gel'fand, I. M., Gel'fand, S. I. (1971). Structure of representations generated by vectors of highest weight. Functional Analysis and Its Applications 5, 1–8.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01075841)

### Abelian Lie algebras are not simple, so semisimple means no abelian ideals

**Remember:** The line is too simple to be simple.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras), 17B05. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A simple Lie algebra is a non-abelian Lie algebra with no ideals other than 0 and itself. An ideal is a subspace I with \[x, y\] in I for every x in the algebra and y in I. A semisimple Lie algebra is a direct sum of simple ones.

**Problem.** Over a field of characteristic 0, a finite-dimensional Lie algebra is a direct sum of simple ones if and only if it has no nonzero abelian ideals. This holds if and only if its Killing form tr(ad x ad y) is nondegenerate.

**How the definition helps.** Leaving out the one-dimensional Lie algebra makes 'direct sum of simples' the same as 'no abelian ideals'. The following example is our own. The one-dimensional algebra has no proper nonzero ideals, so by the bare condition it would be simple. Then ℝ would be semisimple, yet it is its own abelian ideal and its Killing form is zero. The exclusion is the same move as leaving 1 out of the primes, which is also our own comparison. What stays hard is Cartan's criterion and the Killing–Cartan classification of the simple algebras.

**Wikipedia:** [Simple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Lie_algebra), [Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra). It says: “In algebra, a simple Lie algebra is a Lie algebra that is non-abelian and contains no nonzero proper ideals.”

### Chevalley's integral basis builds the finite groups of Lie type uniformly

**Remember:** Integer structure constants let every simple Lie algebra make finite groups.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras), 20G40. arXiv math.RT, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Chevalley basis of a complex simple Lie algebra is a basis in which all the structure constants are integers. With it, exponentials of root elements make sense over any field. These generate the Chevalley group of that type over that field.

**Problem.** For each complex simple Lie algebra and each finite field, the construction gives a finite group of that type. This group is simple apart from a few small cases. One construction gives the classical groups and the exceptional types E₆, E₇, E₈, F₄ and G₂.

**How the definition helps.** One integral construction replaces a separate construction for each family, so existence and simplicity can be stated and proved for all types together. Before Chevalley's 1955 paper, groups of type G₂ and E₆ were known from Dickson's work. Chevalley's construction gave groups for all the exceptional Lie algebras. The twisted groups of Steinberg, Suzuki and Ree need extra automorphisms of the diagram or the field, so they are not covered directly. Some of the smallest groups are not perfect, so the simplicity theorem has a short list of exceptions.

**Wikipedia:** [Group of Lie type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Lie_type). It says: “Chevalley constructed a Chevalley basis (a sort of integral form but over finite fields) for all the complex simple Lie algebras”

### Defining Lie algebras by Serre relations lifts diagram symmetries

**Remember:** A symmetry of the relations permutes the generators.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras). arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the complex semisimple Lie algebra of a Cartan matrix by generators eᵢ, fᵢ, hᵢ and the Chevalley–Serre relations. The matrix records the pairings of simple roots with simple coroots. Another approach starts from the Lie algebra and reads these pairings from its root decomposition.

**Problem.** Every permutation of the indices that preserves the Cartan matrix gives an automorphism of the Lie algebra. The automorphism permutes the generators eᵢ, fᵢ and hᵢ in the same way.

**How the definition helps.** A permutation that preserves the matrix sends each defining relation to another defining relation. So it defines a map on the presented algebra, and its inverse permutation gives the inverse map. That is our own argument. The work goes into the theorem that the relations present the Lie algebra, so no further relations hold. Without the presentation, one would use the isomorphism theorem for semisimple Lie algebras, in our own comparison.

**nLab:** [Cartan matrix](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cartan+matrix). It says: “In fact, 𝔤 is presented by generators eᵢ, fᵢ, hᵢ and the relations”

### Starting each classical family at the right rank makes the list non-redundant

**Remember:** Start B at two, C at three, D at four, and nothing repeats.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras), 17B22. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The four classical families of complex simple Lie algebras are Aₙ = slₙ₊₁, Bₙ = so₂ₙ₊₁, Cₙ = sp₂ₙ and Dₙ = so₂ₙ. The index n is the rank. By convention each family starts at a fixed lowest rank: 1, 2, 3 and 4.

**Problem.** Every complex simple Lie algebra is exactly one of Aₙ, Bₙ, Cₙ, Dₙ with these ranges, or one of the five exceptional algebras. No algebra appears twice in the list, and every entry is simple.

**How the definition helps.** The lower bounds on n remove exactly the small cases where two families meet or the algebra is not simple. The coincidences are so₃ ≅ sl₂, sp₂ ≅ sl₂, sp₄ ≅ so₅ and so₆ ≅ sl₄ (our own list). D₂ = so₄ is so₃ ⊕ so₃, so it is not simple, and D₁ = so₂ is abelian (our own). The page says that a lower start gives a redundant list with exceptional isomorphisms. With the bounds, the classification is a clean list with each algebra once. What stays hard is the classification itself, through root systems and Dynkin diagrams.

**Wikipedia:** [Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra). It says: “The enumeration of the four families is non-redundant and consists only of simple algebras if n ≥ 1 for Aₙ, n ≥ 2 for Bₙ, n ≥ 3 for Cₙ, and n ≥ 4 for Dₙ.”

### Reduced crystallographic root systems are exactly those that Dynkin diagrams classify

**Remember:** Integer Cartan numbers and no doubled roots leave only A to G.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B22 (Root systems), 17B20. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A root system is a finite set of nonzero vectors that spans a Euclidean space. It is closed under the reflection in the hyperplane orthogonal to each of its vectors. It is reduced if the only multiples of a root α in the set are α and −α. It is crystallographic if 2(α,β)/(α,α) is an integer for all roots α and β.

**Problem.** Every irreducible reduced crystallographic root system is one of Aₙ, Bₙ, Cₙ, Dₙ, E₆, E₇, E₈, F₄ or G₂. These are also exactly the root systems of the complex simple Lie algebras.

**How the definition helps.** The two extra conditions limit the angles between roots to a short list, and that keeps the classification short. Without integrality, the ten unit vectors toward the vertices of a regular decagon pass the axioms; they form type I₂(5), and H₃ and H₄ arise in the same way (our own). Without reducedness, the system BCₙ, which holds both eᵢ and 2eᵢ, is allowed (our own). Both conditions hold for the roots of a complex semisimple Lie algebra, so nothing that matters for Lie theory is lost.

**Wikipedia:** [Root system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_system). It says: “Other authors omit condition 2; then they call root systems satisfying condition 2 reduced. In this article, all root systems are assumed to be reduced and crystallographic.”

**Sources:**

- [Killing, W. (1888). Die Zusammensetzung der stetigen endlichen Transformationsgruppen. Mathematische Annalen 33, 1–48.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01444109)

### Root reflections make the Weyl group visibly finite

**Remember:** A linear map that fixes a spanning set is the identity.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B22 (Root systems), 20F55. arXiv math.RT, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A root system has a finite spanning set Φ of vectors in a Euclidean space. Reflection across the hyperplane perpendicular to any root permutes Φ. Define the Weyl group as the group generated by these reflections. For root systems from compact connected Lie groups, another description uses the quotient N(T)/T.

**Problem.** The Weyl group of a root system is finite.

**How the definition helps.** The reflection definition makes the Weyl group act by permutations of a finite set. Since the roots span, only the identity fixes all of them (our own). This puts the Weyl group inside a finite permutation group (our own). In the other description, T is a maximal connected abelian subgroup and N(T) is the group of elements that conjugate T to itself. The quotient proof shows that N(T) is compact and has T as its identity component (our own). Comparing the definitions requires the theorem that identifies the quotient with the reflection group (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weyl group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_group). It says: “By the definition of a root system, each s\_\\alpha preserves Φ, from which it follows that W is a finite group.”

### Defining enveloping algebras as left adjoints makes them preserve free products

**Remember:** Left adjoints preserve coproducts, and free products are coproducts.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 18A40. arXiv math.RA, math.CT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the universal enveloping algebra U(g) of a Lie algebra g by a universal property. Lie maps from g into an associative algebra A, with bracket ab − ba, match algebra maps U(g) → A. So U is left adjoint to the functor from associative algebras to Lie algebras. The explicit definition presents U(g) by generators x in g and relations xy − yx = \[x, y\].

**Problem.** The enveloping algebra of a free product of Lie algebras is the free product of their enveloping algebras. A free product is the coproduct, so maps out of it are independent maps out of each factor.

**How the definition helps.** Every left adjoint preserves coproducts, and both free products are coproducts in their categories. That is our own argument; the nLab quote gives only the adjunction. In our own account, the work moves to showing that the explicit presentation has the universal property. With the presentation alone, one would compare two presentations by hand.

**nLab:** [universal enveloping algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+enveloping+algebra). It says: “which is the left adjoint to the forgetful functor”

### Defining enveloping algebras universally makes direct sums give tensor products

**Remember:** Commuting Lie summands become commuting tensor factors.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the universal enveloping algebra U(g) of a Lie algebra g by a universal property. Lie maps from g into an associative algebra A, with bracket ab − ba, match algebra maps U(g) → A. The explicit definition presents U(g) inside the tensor algebra, the algebra of words in vectors.

**Problem.** Over a field, the enveloping algebra of a direct sum g ⊕ h of Lie algebras is the tensor product U(g) ⊗ U(h).

**How the definition helps.** Both sides have the same maps into any associative algebra A. These are pairs of maps from g and from h whose images commute, because \[g, h\] = 0 in the direct sum. That is our own argument. In our own account, the work moves to the universal property of the tensor product of algebras, which also uses commuting images. The usual proof without the universal property compares bases from the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem, in our own comparison.

### Free Lie algebras yield tensor algebras

**Remember:** Two extension rules in a row give the free associative algebra.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 17B01. arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A free Lie algebra on a set extends each assignment of its generators uniquely to a bracket-preserving linear map into any Lie algebra. An associative algebra becomes a Lie algebra under the bracket \[a,b\] = ab − ba. An enveloping algebra extends each Lie map into such a target uniquely to a unital associative algebra map.

**Problem.** The enveloping algebra of the free Lie algebra on a set is the free unital associative algebra on that set.

**How the definition helps.** The two extension rules say that every assignment of the generators into an associative algebra extends uniquely to an algebra map (our own). The work moves to proving that the constructions by generators and relations have their stated extension rules (our own).

### Restricted enveloping algebras enforce powers

**Remember:** Put power preservation in the quotient, and every module respects it.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Work over a field of prime characteristic p. A restricted Lie algebra has a chosen power operation P. A restricted representation assigns operators so that brackets become commutators and P(x) acts by the p-fold iterate of the operator for x. The restricted enveloping algebra imposes xᵖ = P(x) in the ordinary enveloping algebra.

**Problem.** Modules over the restricted enveloping algebra are exactly the restricted representations.

**How the definition helps.** An ordinary representation factors through this quotient exactly when each added relation acts as zero (our own). Take a one-dimensional Lie algebra with zero power map and let its basis element act as the identity (our own). Its p-fold iterate is the identity, so this ordinary representation fails the added relation (our own). The correspondence for ordinary enveloping algebras supplies the starting point (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Restricted Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restricted_Lie_algebra). It says: “Restricted representations of 𝔤 are equivalent to modules over the restricted enveloping algebra.”

### The Casimir tensor gives a basis-free central element

**Remember:** The identity map makes no choice of basis.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 17B10. arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra 𝔤 with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form B. Assume B is invariant, so B(\[x,y\],z) + B(y,\[x,z\]) = 0. The identification with the dual given by B turns the identity on 𝔤 into a tensor in 𝔤 ⊗ 𝔤. Multiply the tensor factors in U(𝔤), the associative algebra generated by 𝔤 with xy − yx = \[x,y\].

**Problem.** The resulting Casimir element is independent of the basis and commutes with every element of U(𝔤).

**How the definition helps.** The tensor definition makes basis independence immediate because the identity map uses no basis (our own). The usual formula sums XᵢXⁱ for a basis Xᵢ and its B-dual basis Xⁱ (our own). The adjoint action, which acts by brackets on 𝔤, fixes the identity in the space of linear maps (our own). Since B is invariant, the corresponding tensor is fixed too (our own). Multiplication carries this action to commutators, so its image commutes with all the generators (our own). The work lies in comparing this tensor with the basis formula and in finding B (our own). For a semisimple Lie algebra, Cartan’s criterion ensures that its Killing form is nondegenerate.

**Wikipedia:** [Casimir element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casimir_element). It says: “Although the definition relies on a choice of basis for the Lie algebra, it is easy to show that Ω is independent of this choice.”

### The enveloping algebra turns the diagonal into a coproduct

**Remember:** The diagonal gives the coproduct without checking relations again.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 16T05. arXiv math.RA, math.QA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let 𝔤 be a Lie algebra over a field k. Its enveloping algebra U(𝔤) comes with a map from 𝔤 that turns brackets into commutators xy − yx. Every linear map from 𝔤 to an associative algebra with this property extends uniquely to an algebra map from U(𝔤). A presentation instead uses generators from 𝔤 and imposes xy − yx = \[x,y\] as relations.

**Problem.** U(𝔤) is a Hopf algebra with coproduct x ↦ x ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ x, counit x ↦ 0 and antipode x ↦ −x for x in 𝔤.

**How the definition helps.** The universal property turns the diagonal 𝔤 → 𝔤 × 𝔤 into the coproduct once we identify U(𝔤 × 𝔤) with U(𝔤) ⊗ U(𝔤). That identification uses the fact that maps from the two factors have commuting images (our own). The diagonal and zero map yield the coproduct and counit identities (our own). The antipode extends x ↦ −x and reverses multiplication, so its cancellation identity holds on generators and then on products (our own). The presentation-based proof instead checks directly that the proposed maps respect the relations (our own).

**nLab:** [universal enveloping algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+enveloping+algebra). It says: “The coproduct Δ: U(L) → U(L × L) ≅ U(L) ⊗ U(L) is induced by the diagonal map L → L × L”

**Sources:**

- [J. W. Milnor and J. C. Moore, On the structure of Hopf algebras, Annals of Mathematics 81 (1965) 211–264](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970615)

### The universal enveloping algebra makes Lie algebra representations into modules

**Remember:** A representation of 𝔤 is the same as a module over U(𝔤).

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 17B10. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤) is the associative algebra generated by a Lie algebra 𝔤 with the rule xy − yx = \[x, y\]. It has a universal property. Every Lie algebra map from 𝔤 into an associative algebra, with the commutator as bracket, extends uniquely to an algebra map from U(𝔤).

**Problem.** Representations of 𝔤 on V are the same as U(𝔤)-modules. So central elements of U(𝔤) act on every representation, and as scalars on finite-dimensional irreducible ones over ℂ. An example is the Casimir element, a fixed quadratic expression in a basis.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the associative algebra to be End(V) in the universal property gives the extension of each representation at once. So all of ring and module theory, including induced modules and central characters, applies to Lie algebras. The Casimir element, which commutes with everything, is the tool for Weyl's complete reducibility theorem. The work moves into the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem, which says that ordered monomials in a basis of 𝔤 form a basis of U(𝔤). Only that theorem shows that 𝔤 itself sits inside U(𝔤).

**Wikipedia:** [Universal enveloping algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_enveloping_algebra). It says: “The universal property of the enveloping algebra immediately implies that every representation of 𝔤 acting on a vector space V extends uniquely to a representation of U(𝔤).”

### Defining Lie algebras by dual-number points makes Lie commute with kernels

**Remember:** A tangent vector of a kernel is a tangent vector killed by the map.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B45 (Lie algebras of linear algebraic groups), 14L15. arXiv math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a group scheme G over a field k, define Lie(G) as the kernel of G(k\[ε\]) → G(k). Here k\[ε\] adds an element ε with ε² = 0, and the map sets ε to zero. Another definition uses derivations of the coordinate ring that are invariant under left translations.

**Problem.** Take a map of affine group schemes G → H over a field. The Lie algebra of its kernel is the kernel of the map of Lie algebras. Here the kernel is the scheme kernel, which may have nilpotent functions.

**How the definition helps.** Both sides are the points of G over k\[ε\] that reduce to the identity and map to the identity in H. Milne gives this argument (his 12.12). In our own example, the map x ↦ xᵖ on the additive group in characteristic p has derivative zero. Its scheme kernel has Lie algebra k, but the kernel as a variety is trivial. So the statement needs the scheme kernel. The work goes into comparing points over k\[ε\] with invariant derivations (Milne §12e), in our own account.

### Dual numbers expose derivations in the automorphism group

**Remember:** The coefficient of ε is the product rule.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B45 (Lie algebras of linear algebraic groups), 17B40. arXiv math.AG, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a field k, the dual numbers are the ring k\[ε\] with ε² = 0. For a group defined by polynomial equations, take solutions over the dual numbers that reduce to the identity at ε = 0. These solutions describe the tangent space at the identity and can detect tangent directions that ordinary curves miss (our own).

**Problem.** Let A be a finite-dimensional unital associative k-algebra. The Lie algebra of its algebra automorphism group scheme consists of the derivations of A. These are linear maps D satisfying D(xy) = D(x)y + xD(y), with bracket given by the commutator of linear maps.

**How the definition helps.** The dual-number definition makes each candidate 1 + εD, so one product expansion gives exactly the derivation rule. The inverse is 1 − εD, and the rule gives D(1) = 0, so no extra conditions remain (our own). The comparison with the usual algebraic tangent space is the linearization of polynomial equations at the identity (our own). Keeping the mixed term in the group commutator with two independent parameters gives the bracket DE − ED (our own). The same first-order method gives the trace-zero condition for SLₙ, the group of determinant-one matrices, by expanding its determinant (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra). It says: “Indeed, writing out the condition that (1+εD)(xy) ≡ (1+εD)(x)·(1+εD)(y) (mod ε²) (where 1 denotes the identity map on A) gives exactly the definition of D being a derivation.”

### Invariant derivations give Lie algebras a pth power

**Remember:** All the middle binomial coefficients vanish in characteristic p.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B50 (Modular Lie (super)algebras), 14L15, 17B45. arXiv math.RA, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the Lie algebra of an affine group scheme G as the derivations of its coordinate algebra that commute with left translations. A derivation is a linear map D with D(fg) = D(f)g + fD(g). The tangent-space definition instead uses first-order directions at the identity.

**Problem.** Over a field of characteristic p &gt; 0, the Lie algebra of an affine group scheme has a natural restricted Lie algebra structure. This adds a pth power operation with the laws of pth powers in an associative algebra.

**How the definition helps.** In the derivation model, the power operation is Dᵖ, the composition of D with itself p times (our own). Applying the product rule repeatedly gives binomial coefficients, and all the middle coefficients vanish in characteristic p (our own). Thus Dᵖ is a derivation and still commutes with left translation (our own). The required identities follow from those for pth powers and commutators of linear operators (our own). The work that the tangent-space model hides is identifying a tangent vector at the identity with the derivation obtained by left translation (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Restricted Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restricted_Lie_algebra). It says: “When k has characteristic p&gt;0, then iterating a derivation p times yields a derivation, and this makes Derₖ(A) into a restricted Lie algebra.”

### Zero center makes powers unique

**Remember:** Only central elements can hide the difference of two powers.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B50 (Modular Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A restricted Lie algebra over a field of prime characteristic p has a chosen power map P. Write ad(x) for the operator sending y to \[x,y\]. One axiom says ad(P(x)) is the p-fold iterate of ad(x). The center consists of the elements whose bracket with every element is zero.

**Problem.** A Lie algebra with zero center has at most one restricted power map.

**How the definition helps.** Two possible powers have identical brackets with every element, so their difference lies in the center (our own). A one-dimensional abelian algebra over the field with p elements instead admits both the zero power map and the identity (our own). The work still lies in proving that a power map exists and satisfies the other restricted rules (our own).

### As codifferentials, L∞-algebras turn all higher Jacobi identities into D² = 0

**Remember:** Put all the brackets into one differential D; the Jacobi identities become D² = 0.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras), 18M70. arXiv math.QA, math.AT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An L∞-algebra on a graded vector space 𝔤 is a coderivation D on the free graded cocommutative coalgebra ∨•𝔤. D must have degree −1 and satisfy D² = 0. A coderivation is the dual of a derivation: a map that obeys a Leibniz rule for the coproduct. The components of D are the brackets \[−\], \[−,−\], \[−,−,−\], and so on.

**Problem.** A family of brackets on 𝔤 satisfies all the higher Jacobi identities exactly when the coderivation D that it defines on ∨•𝔤 satisfies D² = 0. Morphisms of L∞-algebras are then the maps of differential graded coalgebras.

**How the definition helps.** One equation, D² = 0, holds all the higher Jacobi identities at once. Lada and Stasheff observed that the brackets extend uniquely to a coderivation, and that the Jacobi identities are equivalent to D² = 0. For finite type, the dual is the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra, which links L∞-algebras with Sullivan models in rational homotopy theory. The sign bookkeeping does not disappear; it moves into the proof that the two definitions agree.

**nLab:** [L-infinity-algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/L-infinity-algebra). It says: “The higher Jacobi identity is equivalently the condition that D² = 0.”

### Abelian extensions classified by H² make the Levi decomposition a vanishing statement

**Remember:** Levi splits off the semisimple part because H² of semisimple algebras vanishes.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B05. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let 𝔰 be a Lie algebra and M an 𝔰-module. H²(𝔰,M) is the set of classes of extensions 0 → M → 𝔤 → 𝔰 → 0 in which M is an abelian ideal with the given action. The class is zero exactly when the extension splits, that is, when 𝔤 has a subalgebra mapping isomorphically onto 𝔰.

**Problem.** Let 𝔤 be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero, with radical 𝔯 (its largest solvable ideal). Then 𝔤 = 𝔰 ⋉ 𝔯 for a semisimple subalgebra 𝔰, so 𝔤 = 𝔰 ⊕ 𝔯 as vector spaces (Levi).

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, a Levi subalgebra is a splitting of 0 → 𝔯 → 𝔤 → 𝔤/𝔯 → 0, so it exists once the class in H² is zero. This replaces Levi's construction of the complement by hand. For abelian 𝔯, Whitehead's second lemma gives H²(𝔤/𝔯, 𝔯) = 0, and induction on dim 𝔯 gives the general case (our own summary). The work went into Whitehead's second lemma, which is proved with the Casimir element.

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology), [Whitehead's lemma (Lie algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead%27s_lemma_%28Lie_algebra%29). It says: “Similarly, Whitehead's second lemma states that under the conditions of the first lemma, also H²(𝔤,V) = 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cocycles detect split central extensions

**Remember:** The extension splits when a change of section erases the bracket error.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A central extension of Lie algebras is a surjective map whose kernel brackets to zero with everything. A linear section s chooses a lift s(x) of each quotient element x. Its bracket error is \[s(x),s(y)\] − s(\[x,y\]), which belongs to the kernel. Jacobi makes the error a cocycle, meaning its cyclic sum on pairs (\[x,y\],z) vanishes.

**Problem.** The extension splits when some section preserves brackets. This happens exactly when its degree-two cohomology class on the quotient, with coefficients in the kernel, is zero.

**How the definition helps.** The class groups together bracket errors from different linear sections, so zero means a section preserves brackets (our own). Replacing s by s+f for a linear map f into the kernel subtracts f(\[x,y\]) from the error (our own). These corrections are exactly the maps identified with zero in degree-two cohomology (our own). The work lies in this change-of-section formula and the cocycle calculation (our own).

**nLab:** [Lie algebra extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+extension). It says: “The condition on μ₂ to be a 2-cocycle is precisely the condition that this formula satisfies the Jacobi identity.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cohomology turns Weyl’s splitting problem into vanishing

**Remember:** A zero extension class means a splitting that respects the action.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B10, 17B20. arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An extension of V by W is a module E with submodule W and quotient V. Encode an extension by choosing a linear map s from V back into E that lifts each vector. The failure of s to respect the action gives a class in H¹(𝔤, Hom(V,W)), the first Lie algebra cohomology of the space of linear maps. This class records the failure up to changes of s.

**Problem.** Over a semisimple Lie algebra in characteristic zero, every finite-dimensional module is a direct sum of irreducible modules. This follows from Whitehead's first lemma, H¹(𝔤, M) = 0 for every finite-dimensional module M.

**How the definition helps.** The extension class turns finding an invariant complement into asking whether one class vanishes (our own). For a submodule W of E, take V = E/W and M = Hom(V, W) with the action x·f = x ∘ f − f ∘ x (our own). Whitehead's lemma makes the class zero, so the lift can be adjusted to respect the action, and its image is an invariant complement (our own). The direct proof instead builds an invariant projection with the Casimir operator (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weyl's theorem on complete reducibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl%27s_theorem_on_complete_reducibility). It says: “The theorem is an easy consequence of Whitehead's lemma”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### Defining cohomology as Ext lets the Casimir kill all cohomology

**Remember:** The Casimir is zero on k and invertible on V, so Ext vanishes.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B10. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The cohomology Hⁿ(𝔤,M) is Extⁿ from the trivial module k to M over the universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤). That is the associative algebra whose modules are the 𝔤-modules. An element z of the center of U(𝔤) acts on these Ext groups through either variable, and the two actions are equal.

**Problem.** Let 𝔤 be a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero. If V is a finite-dimensional irreducible module on which 𝔤 acts nontrivially, then Hⁿ(𝔤,V) = 0 for every n.

**How the definition helps.** With the Ext definition, a central element acts on cohomology through either variable, and the two actions agree (our own). The Casimir element, a central element built from an invariant form, acts by zero on k and invertibly on V, so Ext is zero. With the cochain definition, one would instead build an explicit contracting homotopy (our own). The work went into the fact that the Casimir acts invertibly on a nontrivial irreducible module in characteristic zero.

**Wikipedia:** [Whitehead's lemma (Lie algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead%27s_lemma_%28Lie_algebra%29), [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “further let V be irreducible under the 𝔤-action and let 𝔤 act nontrivially, so 𝔤 · V ≠ 0. Then H<sup>q</sup>(𝔤,V) = 0 for all q ≥ 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Lie cohomology by exterior forms gives a commutative product

**Remember:** A differential with the product rule passes the wedge product to cohomology.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA, math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** With trivial coefficients, Lie algebra cohomology is the cohomology of the exterior algebra on g\*, whose differential is the dual of the bracket extended by the graded product rule. The derived functor definition uses Ext groups over the enveloping algebra, with the Yoneda product that splices extensions.

**Problem.** Lie algebra cohomology with trivial coefficients is a graded commutative ring. The product comes from the wedge product of forms.

**How the definition helps.** The exterior algebra is graded commutative, and the differential obeys the product rule. So closed forms multiply to closed forms, and a boundary times a closed form is a boundary. That is our own argument. The nLab adds that d² = 0 holds exactly when the bracket satisfies the Jacobi identity. In our own account, the work moves to two comparisons. This complex must compute the Ext groups, and the wedge product must match the Yoneda product, whose commutativity is not obvious.

**nLab:** [Chevalley-Eilenberg algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Chevalley-Eilenberg+algebra). It says: “the graded-commutative dg-algebra structures on ∧•𝔤∗ are precisely in bijection with Lie algebra structures on 𝔤”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Derivations modulo inner derivations make Levi factors conjugate

**Remember:** Two Levi factors differ by a derivation, and derivations are inner.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B05. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let 𝔰 be a Lie algebra and M an 𝔰-module. H¹(𝔰,M) is the space of derivations (linear maps f with f(\[x,y\]) = x·f(y) − y·f(x)) modulo the inner derivations x ↦ x·m. When an extension of 𝔰 by an abelian ideal M splits, any two splittings differ by such a derivation.

**Problem.** In a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero, any two Levi subalgebras are conjugate (Malcev). The conjugating automorphism has the form exp(ad z), with z in the nilradical.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, conjugacy of Levi subalgebras becomes the vanishing of H¹, and one need not build the automorphism by hand (our own). For an abelian radical 𝔯, two Levi subalgebras differ by a derivation from 𝔤/𝔯 to 𝔯, which Whitehead's first lemma makes inner, x ↦ \[x,z\]. Then exp(ad z) = 1 + ad z moves one onto the other, and induction gives the general case (our own summary). The work went into Whitehead's first lemma, H¹(𝔰,M) = 0 for finite-dimensional M over a semisimple 𝔰.

**Wikipedia:** [Levi decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi_decomposition), [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “Moreover, Malcev (1942) showed that any two Levi subalgebras are conjugate by an (inner) automorphism of the form exp(ad(z)) where z is in the nilradical (Levi–Malcev theorem).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Derived invariants give the cohomology long exact sequence

**Remember:** The long exact sequence comes from the general theorem for derived functors.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 18G15. arXiv math.RA, math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field k, the invariants of a module M are the vectors killed by all of 𝔤. Define Lie algebra cohomology as the right derived functors of invariants. To compute these, take invariants on an injective resolution, an exact sequence of injective modules starting with an embedding of M. The cochain definition instead uses alternating multilinear maps from copies of 𝔤 to M with a prescribed differential.

**Problem.** A short exact sequence of 𝔤-modules gives a long exact sequence in Lie algebra cohomology.

**How the definition helps.** With derived invariants, this is the general long exact sequence theorem for right derived functors (our own). The cochain proof instead checks that a short exact sequence of modules gives a short exact sequence of cochain complexes (our own). The comparison uses a free resolution of the trivial module over U(𝔤), the associative algebra that encodes the bracket by commutators (our own). The Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem on ordered products in U(𝔤) provides the basis needed to prove the resolution is exact (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “Equivalently, these are the right derived functors of the left exact invariant submodule functor”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### Invariant forms are cocycles, so the Killing 3-form gives nonzero H³

**Remember:** Invariant forms are closed and never exact on reductive Lie algebras.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B20. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Koszul wrote the differential on the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra Λ𝔤\* as d = ½ Σ eⁱ ∧ θ(eᵢ). Here θ is the coadjoint action and (eᵢ), (eⁱ) are dual bases. So d is zero on 𝔤-invariant forms.

**Problem.** For a finite-dimensional reductive Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field of characteristic zero, H\*(𝔤;k) is isomorphic to the algebra of 𝔤-invariant forms in Λ𝔤\*. In particular, for semisimple 𝔤 the form ⟨x,\[y,z\]⟩ gives a nonzero class in H³(𝔤;k), so the vanishing of H¹ and H² stops at degree 3.

**How the definition helps.** Written in Koszul's form, the differential is visibly zero on invariant forms, so every invariant form is a cocycle at once. The work went into showing that invariant forms meet every class exactly once. This uses that 𝔤 acts trivially on cohomology and that Λ𝔤\* is completely reducible, so the noninvariant part is acyclic.

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “For instance for 𝔤 a semisimple Lie algebra, there is the Killing form ⟨−,−⟩. The corresponding 3-cocycle is μ := ⟨−,\[−,−\]⟩ ∈ CE(𝔤)”

**Sources:**

- [J.-L. Koszul, Homologie et cohomologie des algèbres de Lie, Bull. Soc. Math. France 78 (1950) 65–127](https://doi.org/10.24033/bsmf.1410)

### Invariants in two stages give the Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence

**Remember:** Take 𝔥-invariants, then 𝔤/𝔥-invariants, and derive the composite.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 18G40. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Hⁿ(𝔤,M) is the n-th right derived functor of the invariants functor that sends M to its 𝔤-invariants. For an ideal 𝔥 of 𝔤, taking 𝔤-invariants is the same as taking 𝔥-invariants and then 𝔤/𝔥-invariants.

**Problem.** For an ideal 𝔥 of a Lie algebra 𝔤 and a 𝔤-module M, there is a spectral sequence from H\*(𝔤/𝔥; H\*(𝔥;M)) to H\*(𝔤;M). Its low-degree terms give the five-term inflation-restriction exact sequence.

**How the definition helps.** With cohomology defined as a derived functor, the spectral sequence is Grothendieck's spectral sequence for a composite of two functors. The check is that 𝔥-invariants send injective 𝔤-modules to injective 𝔤/𝔥-modules, being right adjoint to the exact inflation functor. Restriction to 𝔥 also keeps injective modules, because U(𝔤) is free over U(𝔥) (our own). Hochschild and Serre instead built the sequence by filtering the cochain complex.

**nLab:** [Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hochschild-Serre+spectral+sequence). It says: “The invariants can be computed in two stages, hence as the composite of two functors”

**Paper or page:** [Kurosh theorem for certain Koszul Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03034). It says: “the inflation-restriction sequence (namely, the 5-term sequence induced by the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence) associated with the exact sequence of ℕ-graded 𝔽-Lie algebras 0→I→ℱ→ℒ→0”

**Sources:**

- [G. Hochschild and J.-P. Serre, Cohomology of Lie algebras, Ann. of Math. 57 (1953) 591–603](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969740)

### Left-invariant forms make Lie algebra cohomology the cohomology of compact groups

**Remember:** Average forms over a compact group, and only Lie algebra data remain.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 57T10. arXiv math.RT, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of a real Lie algebra 𝔤 is the exterior algebra Λ𝔤\* of alternating forms, with differential dω(x₀,…,xₙ) = Σ ± ω(\[xᵢ,xⱼ\], …). For a Lie group G it is exactly the complex of left-invariant differential forms on G with the de Rham differential.

**Problem.** For a compact connected Lie group G, the de Rham cohomology of G is isomorphic to the Lie algebra cohomology H\*(𝔤;ℝ). This fails without compactness: the group ℝ is contractible, but H¹ of its Lie algebra is ℝ.

**How the definition helps.** Because the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex is the complex of left-invariant forms, the theorem only says that invariant forms compute de Rham cohomology. The work went into the averaging argument. Integrating over G with Haar measure projects onto invariant forms. Translations act trivially on cohomology because G is connected.

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “Using an averaging process, this complex can be replaced by the complex of left-invariant differential forms.”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### Relative cochains are invariant forms, so relative cohomology computes compact homogeneous spaces

**Remember:** Invariant forms on G/K are exactly the relative cochains.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 57T15. arXiv math.RT, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Lie algebra 𝔤 with subalgebra 𝔨, the relative cochains are the 𝔨-invariant elements of Λ(𝔤/𝔨)\*, with the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential. Their cohomology is the relative Lie algebra cohomology H\*(𝔤,𝔨).

**Problem.** Let G be a compact connected Lie group and K a closed connected subgroup. Then the de Rham cohomology of G/K is isomorphic to H\*(𝔤,𝔨;ℝ).

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, a relative cochain is the value at the base point of a G-invariant form on G/K. So the relative complex is the complex of G-invariant forms. The work went into the averaging argument over the compact group G, as for G itself (our own summary).

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “consisting of the 𝔥-invariant elements in the tensor product of V with the exterior algebra of the coset 𝔤/𝔥.”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### The Chevalley–Eilenberg resolution makes cohomology vanish above the dimension

**Remember:** No alternating forms above dim 𝔤, so no cohomology there.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B35. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Chevalley–Eilenberg resolution of the trivial module k is the complex U(𝔤) ⊗ Λⁿ𝔤 of free U(𝔤)-modules, with a Koszul-type differential. Its Hom into M is the complex of alternating forms on 𝔤 with values in M.

**Problem.** For a Lie algebra 𝔤 of finite dimension d over a field, Hⁿ(𝔤,M) = 0 for every module M and every n &gt; d. Hence Ext over U(𝔤) between any two modules vanishes above degree d, so U(𝔤) has global dimension at most d.

**How the definition helps.** With the Chevalley–Eilenberg resolution, the cochains in degree n are alternating n-forms, and there are none above degree d. The bound for all modules follows because Ext from N to M equals Lie algebra cohomology with coefficients in Hom(N,M) (our own). The work went into proving the resolution exact, which reduces by the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt filtration to the exactness of the Koszul complex of a polynomial ring.

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “Lie algebra cohomology and homology were defined by Chevalley-Eilenberg with a help of concrete Koszul-type resolution”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)
