### Dedekind real numbers are always Cauchy complete

**Remember:** A cut gives all rational bounds at once, so no choices are needed.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 26E40 (Constructive real analysis), 03F60. arXiv math.LO, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Dedekind real number is a located cut (L, U): L is the set of rationals below the number and U the set of rationals above it. Located means that for rationals a &lt; b, either a is in L or b is in U. A Cauchy real number is instead an equivalence class of Cauchy sequences of rationals.

**Problem.** The Dedekind real numbers are Cauchy complete, even without countable choice: every Cauchy sequence of Dedekind reals converges to a Dedekind real.

**How the definition helps.** A cut describes a real number by all its rational bounds at once, so no sequence of choices is needed. Without countable choice, a Cauchy sequence of Cauchy reals need not converge to a Cauchy real. One cannot lift it to a sequence of representing sequences in order to diagonalize, and Lubarsky constructs a countermodel. The Cauchy reals keep one advantage: they make sense in predicative mathematics, where the Dedekind reals need power sets.

**nLab:** [Cauchy real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cauchy+real+number), [Dedekind cut](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Dedekind+cut). It says: “a Cauchy sequence (even a modulated one) of Cauchy real numbers need not converge to another Cauchy real number (though it always does converge to a Dedekind real number, since the Dedekind real numbers are always Cauchy complete).”

**Sources:**

- [Robert S. Lubarsky, On the Cauchy completeness of the constructive Cauchy reals, Electronic Notes in Theoretical Computer Science 167 (2007) 225–254](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.entcs.2006.09.012)

### With lower reals, every inhabited set has a supremum constructively

**Remember:** Know a number only from below, and a supremum is just a union.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 26E40 (Constructive real analysis), 03F60. arXiv math.LO, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A lower real number is an inhabited, open, downward-closed set of rational numbers: the set of rationals below the number. Inhabited means that one can show an element of the set, and open means that the set has no largest element. The set may be all of ℚ, which stands for +∞. Upper reals are defined in the same way with upward-closed sets.

**Problem.** Constructively, every inhabited set of lower reals has a supremum, namely the union of their sets of rationals. For the usual real numbers, a bounded inhabited set need not have a supremum constructively.

**How the definition helps.** For lower reals, the supremum of an inhabited set is simply the union of their sets of rationals, and this union is again a lower real. The price is that, constructively, the order on lower reals is not total. The comparison law, that a &lt; b implies a &lt; c or c &lt; b, also fails. So lower reals are less well behaved than the usual located reals.

**nLab:** [one-sided real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/one-sided+real+number). It says: “Explicitly, the supremum of any inhabited set of lower reals is a lower real and the infimum of any inhabited set of upper reals is an upper real.”

**Sources:**

- [J. Z. Reichman, Semicontinuous real numbers in a topos, Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra 28 (1983) 81–91](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-4049(83)90075-0)

### The genuine integral of cogerm forms ignores second-order terms

**Remember:** Sum the form on small steps of the curve, as in a Riemann sum.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 26A39 (Denjoy and Perron integrals, other special integrals), 58A10. arXiv math.CA, math.DG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A cogerm 1-form ω, such as dx, \|dx\|, dx² or d²x, assigns a number to each germ of a curve. Its genuine integral along a curve is the gauge limit of Riemann sums of ω applied to the small steps of the curve. Call ω o(dx) if its value on a step of size h is much smaller than h.

**Problem.** The genuine integral of every o(dx) form, such as dx² or d²x, is zero. So the trapezoid integrand f(x) dx + ½ f′(x) dx² has the same genuine integral as f(x) dx.

**How the definition helps.** The genuine integral uses Riemann sums of ω itself, so terms that are small on each step add up to something small. On a fine enough partition, each term of the sum for an o(dx) form is smaller than ε·Δtᵢ. The naive integral ∫ ⟨ω \| cₜ⟩ dt gives d²x the integral (x∘c)′(b) − (x∘c)′(a), which is in general not zero. The cost is that the genuine integral satisfies the fundamental theorem of calculus only for differentials of functions.

**nLab:** [cogerm differential form](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/cogerm+differential+form). It says: “The answer 0 given by the genuine integral is preferable if we regard dx as a "first-order change in x", so that dx² or d²x are "second-order" quantities and hence ought to be negligible.”

### Flat directions block convex smoothing

**Remember:** A flat direction can repeat a corner across infinite space.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 26B25 (Convexity of real functions of several variables, generalizations). arXiv math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Consider a finite convex function on Euclidean space. Its graph contains a full line if the function is affine along some entire straight line. A locally Lipschitz gradient changes by at most a constant times distance near each point.

**Problem.** Let f be a convex function on Euclidean space whose gradient is not already locally Lipschitz. For every ε &gt; 0, some convex function with locally Lipschitz gradient differs from f on a set of measure below ε exactly when the graph of f contains no full line.

**How the definition helps.** Excluding full lines rules out a corner that repeats unchanged along an infinite direction (our own). For f(x,y) = \|x\|, a small disagreement area forces agreement at points arbitrarily far up and down almost every vertical line (our own). Convexity then makes the approximation constant on those lines, so it agrees with \|x\| everywhere, corner included (our own). The cited theorem proves sufficiency.

**Paper or page:** [C²-Lusin approximation of convex functions: one variable case](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22975v2). It says: “The graph of f does not contain any line isometric to ℝ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Retained slopes preserve contact

**Remember:** Keep the touching slope and you keep the value.

*True by definition.* MSC 26B25 (Convexity of real functions of several variables, generalizations). arXiv math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be a convex function on Euclidean space with closed epigraph, the set on or above its graph. Allow +∞ but require a finite value somewhere. Choose a compact set of slopes admitting at least one affine function below f everywhere. Define g as the supremum of all such affine functions with slopes in that set.

**Problem.** The function g has a global Lipschitz bound, meaning its changes are bounded by a constant times distance. It equals f at x exactly when an allowed affine function touches f there.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping a touching affine function forces equality at its contact point (our own). The largest allowed slope norm bounds every change in g per unit distance (our own). For the converse, compactness gives a maximizing slope because the best affine value at x depends upper semicontinuously on the slope (our own). That value is the infimum over y of f(y) plus the slope applied to x − y (our own). Allowing every slope recovers the usual affine representation of f by the Fenchel–Moreau theorem (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Singularities of Fitzpatrick and convex functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09954v3). It says: “∂f(x) ∩ C ≠ ∅ ⇔ f(x) = f꜀(x)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A weak Jacobian for maps with jumps tracks vortices of circle-valued maps

**Remember:** Use the weak Jacobian to keep track of what jumps carry.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 26B30 (Absolutely continuous real functions of several variables, functions of bounded variation), 49Q15, 49J45. arXiv math.AP. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A map u of bounded variation has a derivative that is a finite measure, which can charge jump curves. The paper defines the 2 × 2 minors of its gradient as limits of smooth minors along smooth maps that converge strictly to u. On a jump, the limit averages over the segment between the two one-sided values of u. For smooth maps the weak Jacobian is the usual Jacobian determinant.

**Problem.** Take maps u into the unit circle with energy ∫\|∇u\|² plus 1/ε times the jump length, bounded by C\|log ε\|. Then a subsequence of weak Jacobians tends in the flat norm to π times a finite sum of integer-weighted Dirac masses. The energy divided by \|log ε\| Γ-converges to π times the total mass of that sum.

**How the definition helps.** The weak Jacobian is defined for maps with jumps, so the compactness theorem can track defects in the same terms as for Sobolev maps. Our own observation is that the pointwise Jacobian of an S¹-valued map is zero almost everywhere, so it cannot see the vortices. The work is to prove compactness, identify the point masses and obtain the limiting energy.

**Paper or page:** [A new approach to topological singularities via a weak notion of Jacobian for functions of bounded variation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14746v1). It says: “such a notion extends the standard definition of Jacobian determinant to non-Sobolev maps.”

**Sources:**

### Height absorbs variation weights

**Remember:** Make a weight the height of an extra coordinate.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 26B30 (Absolutely continuous real functions of several variables, functions of bounded variation). arXiv math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On an open subset of Euclidean space, take a positive weight w whose strict upper level sets are open. Above each point x, use the vertical interval 0 &lt; t &lt; w(x). Give every point in that interval the value f(x). Weighted variation integrates w against the total mass measure of the derivative defined by integration by parts.

**Problem.** Suppose both the weighted integral of \|f\| and the weighted variation of f are finite. The ordinary integral of the lifted absolute value and its ordinary variation equal the respective weighted quantities.

**How the definition helps.** Each vertical interval contributes its length w(x) when we integrate the lifted absolute value (our own). For variation, the lifting theorem shows that only horizontal changes contribute. Integrating their mass up each interval gives the same factor w(x) (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Weighted Bounded Variation Revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14105v1). It says: “is an isometric embedding”

### Derivative growth bounds make Taylor data unique

**Remember:** With the right derivative bounds, a flat point forces a zero function.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 26E10 (\\(C<sup>\\infty\\</sup>)-functions, quasi-analytic functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take positive weights Mₖ with M₀ = 1 whose successive ratios are nondecreasing and tend to infinity. In the corresponding class, one constant C ≥ 1 bounds the absolute kth derivative everywhere by Mₖ times the (k + 1)st power of C. Require the sum of the reciprocals of the successive ratios to diverge.

**Problem.** Two functions in this class on a closed interval coincide if their values and all their derivatives agree at one interior point.

**How the definition helps.** The Denjoy–Carleman theorem makes the divergent sum a test for uniqueness from derivatives at one point. Our own counterexample for a convergent sum is the smooth bump exp(−1/(1 − x²)) on \|x\| &lt; 1, extended by zero. Weights that bound its derivatives on \[−2,2\] can be chosen with ratios at least k², so the reciprocal sum is finite. At the interior point 1 the bump and zero have the same derivatives of every order.

**Wikipedia:** [Quasi-analytic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quasi-analytic_function). It says: “the only function in it having all its partial derivatives equal to zero at a point is the function identically equal to zero.”

**Paper or page:** [Ultradifferentiable extension theorems: a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01061v2). It says: “∑ₖ 1/μₖ = ∞.”

### Convergence at every nonstandard point makes Cauchy's proof correct

**Remember:** Convergence everywhere, nonstandard points included, is uniform convergence.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 26E35 (Nonstandard analysis), 40A30, 26A15. arXiv math.CA, math.HO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Read 'the sequence fₙ(x) converges for every x' so that x also ranges over hyperreal points. The hyperreals are the numbers of nonstandard analysis, and they include points infinitely close to a real number. Then fₙ(x + h) must be infinitely close to the limit f∞(x + h) for every infinite n, even when h is infinitesimal.

**Problem.** If continuous functions fₙ converge at every hyperreal point, their limit is continuous. Under this reading, Cauchy's 1821 proof of his sum theorem works as written.

**How the definition helps.** In nonstandard analysis, a sequence converges uniformly exactly when it converges at every hyperreal point. So under this reading Cauchy's hypothesis is uniform convergence, and his proof with infinitesimals is correct. The counterexamples, such as the Fourier series near x = 1/n, fail to converge at some nonstandard point. This is a reading of history; the mathematical content is the equivalence of the nonstandard and the ε–N forms of uniform convergence.

**nLab:** [Cauchy sum theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cauchy+sum+theorem). It says: “By this analysis, Cauchy's notion of convergence everywhere is our modern notion of uniform convergence, not pointwise convergence, and his theorem is true”

### The HoTT book real numbers are complete because limits are constructors

**Remember:** Every Cauchy approximation has a limit because "limit" is a constructor.

*True by definition.* MSC 26E40 (Constructive real analysis), 03B38. arXiv math.LO, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The HoTT book real numbers are a higher inductive-inductive type. Such a type is generated by constructors for its points and for equalities between them, defined together with a relation. Here the generators are the rationals, a limit lim for every Cauchy approximation, and a rule that identifies two points that are ε-close for every ε &gt; 0. Equivalently, they are the initial sequentially complete Archimedean ordered field.

**Problem.** The HoTT book real numbers are sequentially Cauchy complete, even without countable choice. So analytic functions such as exp, sin and cos are well defined on them.

**How the definition helps.** In the higher inductive-inductive type, limits are constructors, so completeness holds by definition and no choice is needed. The naive quotient of regular Cauchy sequences is complete only if every sequence of reals lifts to a sequence of representing Cauchy sequences. That lift needs countable choice. The remaining work is to develop the order and the arithmetic on this type.

**nLab:** [HoTT book real number](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/HoTT+book+real+number). It says: “The analytic functions, such as the exponential function, the sine function, and the cosine function are well defined in the HoTT book real numbers, since all regular Cauchy sequences converge in the HoTT book real numbers.”

**Remember:** Change scale, then use Jensen on the midpoint map.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 26E60 (Means), 26B25. arXiv math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f be continuous and strictly increasing on an interval. Define the mean of a list by averaging its f-values with nonnegative weights totaling one, then applying the inverse of f. For u and v in the range, let H(u,v) be f at the midpoint of their inverse images.

**Problem.** For two lists with common weights, compare the mean of their coordinatewise midpoints with the midpoint of their means. The first never exceeds the second, for any lists and weights, exactly when H is concave.

**How the definition helps.** Applying f turns the comparison of means into Jensen’s inequality for H on pairs of transformed entries (our own). Every pair in the range has inverse images, so the mean comparisons also give every weighted concavity inequality for H (our own).

### Time scales prove the discrete and continuous Weyl–Titchmarsh theories at once

**Remember:** One derivative that is a difference on ℤ covers both worlds.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 26E70 (Real analysis on time scales or measure chains), 34N05, 34B24. arXiv math.CA, math.SP. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A time scale is any nonempty closed subset of the real line. The paper uses the nabla derivative, which looks backward. If t has a nearest point ρ(t) &lt; t on its left, the derivative is (f(t) − f(ρ(t)))/(t − ρ(t)). Otherwise it is the usual limit of difference quotients, so on ℝ it is the usual derivative and on ℤ a backward difference.

**Problem.** Weyl–Titchmarsh theory holds for singular linear Hamiltonian systems on a half-line of a Sturmian time scale: nested matrix discs sort them into limit point and limit circle cases. On ℝ and on ℤ this gives the continuous and the discrete theories at once.

**How the definition helps.** A single derivative that is a limit on ℝ and a difference on ℤ lets one proof cover both settings. Before, the two theories had parallel but separate proofs (our own remark). The price is extra terms in product rules, from the gap to the neighbouring point (our own remark).

**Paper or page:** [Unifying discrete and continuous Weyl-Titchmarsh theory via a class of linear Hamiltonian systems on Sturmian time scales](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.4040v1), [Floquet multipliers and the stability of periodic linear differential equations: a unified algorithm and its computer realization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.04447v8). It says: “These results unify and extend certain classic and recent results on the subject in the continuous and discrete cases, respectively, to Sturmian time scales.”

**Sources:**

- [Douglas R. Anderson, Unifying discrete and continuous Weyl-Titchmarsh theory via a class of linear Hamiltonian systems on Sturmian time scales, arXiv:1001.4040 (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.4040v1)
- [Mengda Wu, Yonghui Xia, Ziyi Xu, Floquet multipliers and the stability of periodic linear differential equations: a unified algorithm and its computer realization, arXiv:2201.04447 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.04447v8)
- [Hilger, Analysis on Measure Chains — A Unified Approach to Continuous and Discrete Calculus, Results in Mathematics 18 (1990), 18–56](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf03323153)

## 28 Measure and integration

### Measure zero describes exactly the Riemann integrable functions

**Remember:** Countably many tiny intervals can hide a set of measure zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 26A42. arXiv math.CA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** A set of real numbers has measure zero if, for every ε &gt; 0, countably many intervals with total length less than ε cover it.

**Problem.** Lebesgue–Vitali theorem: a bounded function on \[a,b\] is Riemann integrable exactly when its points of discontinuity form a set of measure zero.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, the answer fits in one short sentence and needs no full Lebesgue measure or integral. It shows at once that monotone functions are integrable, because they have only countably many discontinuities. Countable covers matter: the rationals in \[0,1\] have measure zero, but finitely many intervals of small total length cannot cover them (our own remark).

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_integral). It says: “A bounded function on a compact interval \[a, b\] is Riemann integrable if and only if it is continuous almost everywhere (the set of its points of discontinuity has measure zero, in the sense of Lebesgue measure).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dynkin systems make two measures that agree on intervals agree everywhere

**Remember:** Agreement sets form a Dynkin system, so check measures on a π-system.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, \\(\\sigma\\)-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 28A12. arXiv math.CA, math.PR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Dynkin system (or λ-system) on a set Ω is a family of subsets that contains Ω. It is closed under differences B minus A when A ⊆ B, and under increasing countable unions. A π-system is a family closed under finite intersections. The π-λ theorem says that a Dynkin system containing a π-system contains the σ-algebra it generates.

**Problem.** Two probability measures that agree on a π-system agree on the σ-algebra it generates. So a law on the real line is fixed by its distribution function. Lebesgue measure is the only Borel measure that gives each interval its length.

**How the definition helps.** The family of sets on which two probability measures agree is always a Dynkin system, so the π-λ theorem applies to it at once. This family need not be a σ-algebra, because agreement on A and B does not give agreement on A ∪ B. So a direct proof that it contains all Borel sets fails. What stays hard is the π-λ theorem itself, a short but careful set-theoretic argument.

**Wikipedia:** [Dynkin system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynkin_system), [Pi-system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pi-system). It says: “One application of Sierpiński-Dynkin's π-λ theorem is the uniqueness of a measure that evaluates the length of an interval (known as the Lebesgue measure)”

**Sources:**

- [W. Sierpiński, Un théorème général sur les familles d'ensembles, Fundamenta Mathematicae 12 (1928) 206–210](https://doi.org/10.4064/fm-12-1-206-210)

### Intersecting σ-algebras lets generators test measurability

**Remember:** The sets with measurable preimages form a σ-algebra containing the generators.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, \\(\\sigma\\)-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 28A20. arXiv math.CA, math.PR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A σ-algebra on X contains X and is closed under complements and countable unions. The σ-algebra generated by a family of subsets is the intersection of all σ-algebras containing that family. A map is measurable if the preimage of each set in the target σ-algebra belongs to the source σ-algebra.

**Problem.** Let the σ-algebra on Y be generated by a family 𝒢. A map from a space with a σ-algebra to Y is measurable exactly when each set in 𝒢 has a measurable preimage.

**How the definition helps.** The intersection definition lets us test just the generators instead of describing all the generated sets. The sets whose preimages are measurable form a σ-algebra because preimages preserve complements and countable unions. If it contains the generators, it contains the intersection in the definition. This is our own proof of the criterion. A construction that adds sets in successive stages would instead check that each operation preserves the preimage condition. The work here is just checking that intersections of σ-algebras are σ-algebras.

**Paper or page:** [Mapping Measurable iff Measurable on Generator](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Mapping_Measurable_iff_Measurable_on_Generator). It says: “That is, the preimage of every generator under f is a measurable set.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Keeping signed measures finite makes them a vector space

**Remember:** No infinite values means no ∞ − ∞, so signed measures add.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions), 46E27. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A signed measure is a countably additive set function on a σ-algebra that may take negative values. A finite signed measure takes only real values. An extended signed measure may take the value +∞ or the value −∞, but not both.

**Problem.** Finite signed measures form a real vector space, and a Banach space under the total variation norm. So the Riesz representation theorem can identify the dual of the continuous functions vanishing at infinity with the finite regular signed measures.

**How the definition helps.** Finite values make the sum of two signed measures defined on every set, so the space is closed under addition. The definition excludes adding a measure with value +∞ on a set to one with value −∞ on the same set, where the sum would be ∞ − ∞. The Jordan decomposition writes each signed measure as a difference of two positive measures, which gives the total variation norm.

**Wikipedia:** [Signed measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signed_measure). It says: “Finite signed measures form a real vector space, while extended signed measures do not because they are not closed under addition.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Singularity makes Jordan decomposition unique

**Remember:** Separate the signs so neither measure can hide mass behind the other.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Jordan decomposition writes a signed measure as the difference of two positive measures. These measures must be mutually singular. This means there are disjoint measurable sets such that each measure is zero outside its own set.

**Problem.** A finite signed measure has exactly one Jordan decomposition.

**How the definition helps.** Disjoint carriers let one recover the positive part on any set by taking the largest signed mass of its measurable subsets (our own). Intersecting with the positive carrier attains that bound (our own). Apply the same argument to the negative of the signed measure to recover the negative part (our own). Existence of the carriers is the Hahn decomposition theorem (our own). Without singularity, even the zero measure is the difference of any finite positive measure and itself (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hahn decomposition theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hahn_decomposition_theorem). It says: “Note that the Jordan decomposition is unique, while the Hahn decomposition is only essentially unique.”

**Paper or page:** [Positive and Negative Parts of Signed Measure are Mutually Singular](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Positive_and_Negative_Parts_of_Signed_Measure_are_Mutually_Singular). It says: “Then μ⁺ and μ⁻ are mutually singular.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Atomless measures take every intermediate value

**Remember:** Without indivisible pieces, every smaller mass can be cut out.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A finite measure is atomless if each measurable set of positive measure contains a measurable subset of strictly smaller positive measure.

**Problem.** Every measurable set A in a finite atomless measure space has a measurable subset of any prescribed mass between zero and μ(A).

**How the definition helps.** Atomlessness lets one split any positive piece instead of having to take it whole, in our own explanation. In our own example, a Dirac probability measure puts all its mass on one point and cannot give any subset mass one half. Sierpiński’s theorem assembles exact masses by extending a nested family of subsets with prescribed masses.

**Wikipedia:** [Atom (measure theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom_%28measure_theory%29). It says: “there exists a measurable subset B of A such that μ(B) = b.”

**Sources:**

- [Wacław Sierpiński. Sur les fonctions d'ensemble additives et continues. Fundamenta Mathematicae 3 (1922), 240–246.](https://doi.org/10.4064/fm-3-1-240-246)

### Carathéodory's measurability condition builds additivity into the definition

**Remember:** A measurable set cuts every other set into two pieces whose sizes add up.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let μ\* be an outer measure on X, a monotone and countably subadditive size function on all subsets with μ\*(∅) = 0. A set E is Carathéodory measurable when μ\*(A) = μ\*(A ∩ E) + μ\*(A ∖ E) for every subset A of X.

**Problem.** The measurable sets form a σ-algebra (a family of sets closed under complements and countable unions). On these sets μ\* is countably additive, so it is a measure.

**How the definition helps.** The definition keeps exactly the sets that split every set additively, so finite additivity is almost the definition. Short arguments then give countable additivity and closure under countable unions. Some sets must be left out, because no translation-invariant countably additive length is defined on all subsets of ℝ. What stays hard is to show that intervals and Borel sets pass the test.

**Wikipedia:** [Outer measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_measure), [Carathéodory's extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory%27s_extension_theorem). It says: “The purpose of constructing an outer measure on all subsets of X is to pick out a class of subsets (to be called measurable) in such a way as to satisfy the countable additivity property.”

**Sources:**

- [C. Carathéodory, Vorlesungen über reelle Funktionen, Teubner (1918; 2nd ed. 1927)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-663-15768-7)

### Completing a product measure makes every subset of a null set measurable

**Remember:** A subset of nothing should also count as nothing.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A35. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A measure space is complete if every subset of a set of measure zero is measurable. The completion of a measure space adds all subsets of null sets and extends the measure, giving them measure zero.

**Problem.** Two-dimensional Lebesgue measure is the completion of the product of one-dimensional Lebesgue measure with itself. In a complete space, any function equal almost everywhere to a measurable function is itself measurable.

**How the definition helps.** Completeness builds the rule that subsets of null sets are null into the measure space, so statements up to null sets need no extra checks. In the plain product, {0} × A, with A a Vitali set, lies inside the null set {0} × ℝ but is not measurable. The cost is that the completed product is not a product σ-algebra, so Fubini's theorem gives measurable sections only for almost every point (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Complete measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_measure). It says: “So this "two-dimensional Lebesgue measure" as just defined is not complete, and some kind of completion procedure is required.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Lebesgue, Intégrale, Longueur, Aire, Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata 7 (1902)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02420592)

### Countable covers give the rationals measure zero, unlike Jordan content

**Remember:** Countably many points cost nothing when covers may be countable.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Jordan content measures a bounded set by finite unions of boxes from inside and outside, and a set is Jordan measurable if the two agree. Lebesgue outer measure uses countable covers by intervals instead. Lebesgue measure agrees with Jordan content wherever the latter is defined.

**Problem.** Every countable set of reals has Lebesgue measure zero. The rationals in \[0, 1\] are such a set, but they are not Jordan measurable.

**How the definition helps.** Countable covers let the n-th point get an interval of length ε/2ⁿ, so a countable set has outer measure at most ε for every ε (our own). Jordan content allows only finite covers. Each rational point has content zero, but the boundary of the rationals in \[0, 1\] is all of \[0, 1\], so they have no Jordan content. The page says that for this reason Jordan content is not a true measure.

**Wikipedia:** [Peano–Jordan measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano%E2%80%93Jordan_measure). It says: “Intuitively however, the set of rational numbers is a "small" set, as it is countable, and it should have "size" zero. That is indeed true, but only if one replaces the Jordan measure with the Lebesgue measure.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Lebesgue, Intégrale, Longueur, Aire, Annali di Matematica Pura ed Applicata 7 (1902)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02420592)

### Measure 0 for the empty set excludes only constant infinite functions

**Remember:** If the empty set is not 0, everything is infinite.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A10. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A countably additive function on a σ-algebra gives the union of countably many disjoint sets the sum of their values. A measure is a countably additive function with values in \[0, +∞\] that gives the empty set the value 0.

**Problem.** A countably additive function f with extended real values has f(∅) = 0, or f is constant +∞, or f is constant −∞.

**How the definition helps.** The condition μ(∅) = 0 removes a single bad case. Writing ∅ as a countable union of copies of ∅ shows that f(∅) is 0 or infinite. Adding ∅ to any set A then shows that an infinite f(∅) makes f(A) infinite. So for nonnegative functions, the only excluded example is the function that is +∞ everywhere (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Countably Additive Function Dichotomy by Empty Set](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Countably_Additive_Function_Dichotomy_by_Empty_Set), [Measure of Empty Set is Zero](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Measure_of_Empty_Set_is_Zero). It says: “Then the exactly one of the following is true: (1): f(∅) = 0 (2): f(∅) = +∞. Moreover, f(A) = +∞ for all A ∈ 𝒜.”

**Sources:**

- [ProofWiki, Countably Additive Function Dichotomy by Empty Set](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Countably_Additive_Function_Dichotomy_by_Empty_Set)
- [ProofWiki, Measure of Empty Set is Zero](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Measure_of_Empty_Set_is_Zero)

### Measuring only some sets keeps length countably additive

**Remember:** Measure theory keeps countable additivity by refusing to measure every set.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A measure is defined only on a σ-algebra of measurable sets, not on every subset. (A σ-algebra is a family of sets that is closed under complements and countable unions.) Lebesgue measure λ is countably additive and translation invariant on its measurable sets. Countably additive means that the measure of a countable disjoint union is the sum of the measures.

**Problem.** No function on all subsets of ℝ gives each interval its length, is translation invariant and is countably additive.

**How the definition helps.** Vitali's set V has no possible length, so length can only be defined on some sets. V has one point in \[0, 1\] from each class of reals that differ by a rational. Its translates by the rationals in \[−1, 1\] are disjoint, cover \[0, 1\] and lie inside \[−1, 2\]. Countable additivity would make a sum of infinitely many copies of λ(V) lie between 1 and 3, which is impossible.

**Wikipedia:** [Vitali set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitali_set), [Outer measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_measure). It says: “So V cannot have been measurable after all, i.e., the Lebesgue measure λ must not define any value for λ(V).”

**Sources:**

- [R. M. Solovay, A model of set-theory in which every set of reals is Lebesgue measurable, Ann. of Math. 92 (1970), 1–56, doi:10.2307/1970696](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970696)

### Metric outer measures make every Borel set measurable

**Remember:** Additive on sets far apart gives every Borel set measurable.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A78. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Two sets in a metric space are positively separated if they are at positive distance from each other. An outer measure μ is a metric outer measure if μ(A ∪ B) = μ(A) + μ(B) for all such pairs. Hausdorff measures are built from covers by small sets and are metric outer measures.

**Problem.** For a metric outer measure, every closed set, and hence every Borel set, satisfies Carathéodory's measurability condition. So each Hausdorff measure restricts to a true measure on the Borel sets.

**How the definition helps.** Additivity for separated sets is the geometric form of Carathéodory's condition, so closed sets pass the condition with a short argument. With covers of one fixed size, the outer measure can fail this additivity (our own). Taking covers by sets of diameter at most δ, and then letting δ go to 0, makes the result a metric outer measure. Then the Borel σ-algebra comes for free from Carathéodory's theorem. What stays hard is computing Hausdorff measures and dimensions of particular sets.

**Wikipedia:** [Metric outer measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_outer_measure). It says: “Consequently, all the Borel subsets of X — those obtainable as countable unions, intersections and set-theoretic differences of open/closed sets — are μ-measurable.”

**Sources:**

- [F. Hausdorff, Dimension und äußeres Maß, Mathematische Annalen 79 (1918)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01457179)

### Right continuity gives Stieltjes measures

**Remember:** Match right continuity with intervals that include their right endpoints.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 26A42. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a real nondecreasing function g, assign mass g(t) − g(s) to each bounded interval (s, t\]. Require g to be right-continuous, meaning its values approaching any point from the right tend to its value there.

**Problem.** These masses determine a unique measure on the Borel sets of the line, the sets generated by open intervals. Every bounded interval has finite mass.

**How the definition helps.** Right continuity makes the masses of shrinking intervals (s, s + 1/n\] tend to zero, as countable additivity requires (our own). With compactness, this gives countable additivity on intervals, and the extension theorem gives the unique Borel measure (our own). If g is one on the positive reals and zero elsewhere, every interval (0, 1/n\] gets mass one (our own). Their intersection is empty, which contradicts continuity of a finite measure (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue–Stieltjes integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue%E2%80%93Stieltjes_integration). It says: “Define w((s, t\]) = g(t) − g(s) and w({a}) = 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The cover definition of Lebesgue measure makes translation invariance immediate

**Remember:** Slide the cover, and its total length stays the same.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the Lebesgue outer measure of a set of reals as the infimum of the total lengths of its countable covers by intervals. Another construction extends the length of half-open intervals to a measure on Borel sets by an abstract extension theorem.

**Problem.** Translating a Borel subset of the real line does not change its Lebesgue measure.

**How the definition helps.** Translating a cover by intervals gives a cover of the translated set with the same total length, so the infimum does not change. This argument is our own; the nLab gives only the cover formula. With the abstract extension, one instead needs the theorem that measures agreeing on intervals agree on Borel sets, in our own account. In both constructions, the real work is proving that Borel sets are measurable and that intervals get their length.

**nLab:** [Lebesgue measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lebesgue+measure). It says: “\|B\| = inf {∑ⱼ₌₁∞ \|Iⱼ\| : B ⊆ ⋃ⱼ₌₁∞ Iⱼ}.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Almost uniform convergence gives Egorov’s theorem one exceptional set

**Remember:** Finite measure lets the sets of late errors shrink to measure zero.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Convergence is almost uniform if, for every ε &gt; 0, convergence is uniform outside some measurable set of measure less than ε.

**Problem.** On a finite measure space, suppose real measurable functions converge to a real measurable limit outside a set of measure zero. Then they converge almost uniformly.

**How the definition helps.** Almost uniform convergence lets one exceptional set absorb the errors at every accuracy (our own). For each k, the points where some error after index N exceeds 1/k form sets that decrease to measure zero as N grows (our own). Finite total measure makes their measures tend to zero, so one N per k can be chosen with measures summing to less than ε (our own). Outside the union of these sets, convergence is uniform (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Egorov's Theorem](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Egorov's_Theorem). It says: “Then fₙ converges a.u. to f.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Borel sets on the target make measurable functions compose

**Remember:** Pull back only Borel sets, so a Borel map after it is safe.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 28A05. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Lebesgue measurable function f goes from ℝ with the Lebesgue sets to ℂ with the Borel sets. The preimage of each Borel set must be Lebesgue measurable. So the σ-algebra on the source is large, but the one on the target is only the Borel sets.

**Problem.** If f is Lebesgue measurable and g is Borel measurable, then g ∘ f is Lebesgue measurable. In particular, continuous functions of measurable functions, and sums and products of measurable functions, are measurable.

**How the definition helps.** Composition is measurable when the outer function pulls Borel sets back to sets on which the inner function is measurable. With Borel sets on the target, this holds for every Borel outer function. If both functions used Lebesgue sets on the target, the composition could fail to be measurable, as the page says. The standard example uses the Cantor function to send a non-measurable set onto a null set (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Measurable function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measurable_function). It says: “Indeed, two Lebesgue-measurable functions may be constructed in such a way as to make their composition non-Lebesgue-measurable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Large-power norms find essential suprema

**Remember:** Large powers detect every height that occurs on positive measure.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The essential supremum is the least upper bound that holds outside a set of measure zero. Unlike the ordinary supremum, it ignores changes confined to a set of measure zero. The p-norm is the pth root of the integral of the absolute value raised to power p.

**Problem.** On a probability space, the p-norms of a measurable function tend to the essential supremum of its absolute value as p tends to infinity. Both norms and limit may equal infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Ignoring sets of measure zero removes peaks that no integral can detect (our own). For example, the indicator of one point in \[0, 1\] has supremum one but every p-norm zero (our own). Each height below the essential supremum is exceeded on a set of positive measure, and the pth root of that measure tends to one (our own). The essential supremum bounds every norm because the space has measure one (our own).

**nLab:** [essential supremum](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/essential+supremum). It says: “But we ignore things that happen only on a null set.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Tail infima prove Fatou

**Remember:** Take the infimum before integrating, then let the tail move.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a sequence of extended real numbers, the limit inferior is its smallest subsequential limit. Equivalently, take the infimum of each tail, then the supremum of these infima.

**Problem.** For nonnegative measurable functions, the integral of their pointwise limit inferior is at most the limit inferior of their integrals.

**How the definition helps.** The tail formula gives increasing measurable functions without choosing a subsequence at each point (our own). Each tail infimum has integral at most the infimum of the integrals over that tail (our own). Monotone convergence identifies the limit of these integrals with the integral of the pointwise limit inferior (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Fatou's Lemma for Integrals/Positive Measurable Functions](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Fatou's_Lemma_for_Integrals/Positive_Measurable_Functions). It says: “∫ lim inf fₙ dμ ≤ lim inf ∫ fₙ dμ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Lebesgue integral lets limits pass inside the integral

**Remember:** Lebesgue slices the range, not the domain, so limits keep their integrals.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 28A20. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The Lebesgue integral of a measurable function is built from the measures of the sets where the function takes given values, by approximation with simple functions. A pointwise limit of measurable functions is measurable, so it has a Lebesgue integral.

**Problem.** If nonnegative measurable functions increase to f, their integrals tend to the integral of f (monotone convergence). If fₙ → f pointwise and an integrable g bounds every \|fₙ\|, then the integrals of fₙ tend to that of f (dominated convergence).

**How the definition helps.** A limit of measurable functions is measurable, so the limit always has an integral to compare with. For the Riemann integral this fails: the indicators of the first k rationals in \[0, 1\] each have Riemann integral 0, but their limit, the Dirichlet function, has none (our own example). A condition is still needed: fₙ = n on (0, 1/n\] has integral 1 for each n but tends to 0. The hard work moves into the construction of Lebesgue measure.

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral), [Dominated convergence theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominated_convergence_theorem). It says: “The main purpose of the Lebesgue integral is to provide an integral notion where limits of integrals hold under mild assumptions.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Lebesgue, Intégrale, longueur, aire, Ann. Mat. Pura Appl. 7 (1902), 231–359, doi:10.1007/BF02420592](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02420592)
- [H. Lebesgue, Leçons sur l'intégration et la recherche des fonctions primitives, Gauthier-Villars, Paris, 1904](https://archive.org/details/leconegrarecher00leberich)

### Requiring σ-finite measures makes Tonelli's theorem true

**Remember:** σ-finite spaces can be cut into countably many finite pieces.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 28A12. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A measure space is σ-finite when it is a countable union of sets of finite measure.

**Problem.** For two σ-finite measure spaces and a non-negative measurable function on their product, the two iterated integrals are equal, and they equal the integral against the product measure.

**How the definition helps.** σ-finiteness rules out examples where the two iterated integrals differ. Take \[0, 1\] with Lebesgue measure and \[0, 1\] with counting measure, which is not σ-finite. The indicator of the diagonal x = y has iterated integral 0 in one order and 1 in the other. So no product measure can make Tonelli's theorem hold there.

**Wikipedia:** [Fubini's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fubini%27s_theorem). It says: “This shows that Tonelli's theorem can fail for spaces that are not σ-finite no matter which product measure is chosen.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Standard Borel spaces always have conditional distributions

**Remember:** Standard Borel spaces are the measurable spaces of Polish spaces.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, \\(\\sigma\\)-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 60A10, 60B05. arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measurable space is standard Borel if its σ-algebra is the Borel σ-algebra of some Polish topology. A Polish topology is one given by a complete separable metric. Up to isomorphism, the standard Borel spaces are the countable discrete spaces and ℝ.

**Problem.** On a standard Borel probability space, every sub-σ-algebra has a regular conditional distribution. Every Markov kernel between standard Borel spaces has a Bayesian inverse, unique almost surely.

**How the definition helps.** On standard Borel spaces, conditional distributions exist with no extra hypothesis, and the sub-σ-algebra need not be countably generated. In the language of Markov categories, the category BorelStoch has conditionals. The nLab notes that in the larger category Stoch of all measurable spaces, conditionals can fail to exist. Standard Borel spaces are also closed under countable products and under the Giry monad, so the restriction costs little.

**nLab:** [standard Borel space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/standard+Borel+space), [Markov kernel](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Markov+kernel), [Markov category](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Markov+category). It says: “They provide a setting for many constructions in probability theory, including conditional probability, disintegration, and countable products.”

**Sources:**

- [Chris Preston, Some notes on standard Borel and related spaces (2008), arXiv:0809.3066](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.3066)

### The partition definition of total variation makes it the least dominating measure

**Remember:** A dominating measure pays for every partition at once.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a signed or complex measure μ, define its total variation \|μ\|(A) as the supremum of Σ\|μ(Aᵢ)\| over finite measurable partitions of A. Another definition, for signed measures, adds the positive and negative parts of the Jordan decomposition.

**Problem.** Always \|μ(A)\| ≤ \|μ\|(A). Every positive measure ν with \|μ(A)\| ≤ ν(A) for all measurable A satisfies \|μ\|(A) ≤ ν(A).

**How the definition helps.** With the partition definition, both claims take one line, in our own proof. If ν dominates μ, each partition sum Σ\|μ(Aᵢ)\| is at most Σν(Aᵢ) = ν(A). The partition with one part gives \|μ(A)\| ≤ \|μ\|(A). The work moves into proving that the partition supremum is countably additive, in our own account. With the Jordan definition, one would first need the Hahn decomposition, which splits the space into a positive set and a negative set.

**Paper or page:** [Total Variation is Smallest Measure exceeding Modulus of Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Total_Variation_is_Smallest_Measure_exceeding_Modulus_of_Measure). It says: “\|μ(A)\| ≤ ν(A) for each A ∈ Σ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Total variation adds both signs

**Remember:** Count both signs as positive mass.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite signed measure μ has a Hahn decomposition into sets P and N, where measurable subsets of P have mass ≥ 0 and those of N have mass ≤ 0. The total variation is \|μ\|(A) = μ(A ∩ P) − μ(A ∩ N). Another definition takes the supremum of Σ\|μ(Aᵢ)\| over finite measurable partitions of A.

**Problem.** The total variation of a finite signed measure is a nonnegative measure.

**How the definition helps.** The formula adds two nonnegative measures, so it gives a measure. In our own comparison, the Hahn decomposition theorem supplies P and N. The triangle inequality bounds every partition sum by μ(A ∩ P) − μ(A ∩ N). Splitting A along P and N attains the bound, so the two definitions agree and the value does not depend on the choice of P and N.

**Paper or page:** [Variation of Signed Measure is Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Variation_of_Signed_Measure_is_Measure). It says: “Then \|μ\| is a measure.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Finite mass controls small sets

**Remember:** With finite mass, control at zero also controls nearby values.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let μ and ν be measures on the same measurable space, with ν finite. Absolute continuity means that ν vanishes on every measurable set of μ-mass zero.

**Problem.** If ν is finite and absolutely continuous with respect to μ, then for every ε &gt; 0 there is δ &gt; 0 with ν(A) &lt; ε whenever μ(A) &lt; δ.

**How the definition helps.** Finite total mass makes ν continuous on decreasing sequences of sets. In our own proof, if the bound fails for some ε, choose sets Aₙ with μ(Aₙ) ≤ 2⁻ⁿ and ν(Aₙ) ≥ ε. The unions of the tails decrease to a set of μ-measure zero but keep ν-measure at least ε, a contradiction. Our own counterexample without finiteness takes ν as counting measure on the positive integers and μ({n}) = 2⁻ⁿ.

**Paper or page:** [Characterization of Absolutely Continuous Measures](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Characterization_of_Absolutely_Continuous_Measures). It says: “for each ε &gt; 0 there exists δ &gt; 0 such that for each A ∈ Σ with μ(A) &lt; δ, we have ν(A) &lt; ε.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Localizable measures are exactly where the main measure theorems hold

**Remember:** Localizable means measurable sets modulo null sets form a complete Boolean algebra.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A60, 28A25. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measure is semifinite if every set of infinite measure contains a subset of finite positive measure. A measure is localizable if it is semifinite and every collection of measurable sets has an essential union. An essential union is a smallest measurable set that contains each set of the collection up to null sets. Equivalently, the Boolean algebra of measurable sets modulo null sets is complete (every subset of it has a least upper bound).

**Problem.** For a semifinite measure, the Radon–Nikodym theorem, the Hahn decomposition and the duality L∞ ≅ (L¹)\* each hold exactly when the measure is localizable.

**How the definition helps.** Localizability is exactly the condition that these theorems need, not just a sufficient one. Textbooks state them for σ-finite measures, but they hold for every localizable measure. The Segal–Kelley theorem gives the converse, and that equivalence is the real content.

**nLab:** [localizable measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/localizable+measure), [categories of measure theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/categories+of+measure+theory), [Radon–Nikodym derivative](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym+derivative). It says: “The takeaway from this result is that without the localizability property much of the measure theory as we know is false, so it is completely reasonable to require it from the start.”

**Sources:**

- [Irving E. Segal, Equivalences of measure spaces, American Journal of Mathematics 73:2 (1951) 275](https://doi.org/10.2307/2372178)
- [John L. Kelley, Decomposition and representation theorems in measure theory, Mathematische Annalen 163:2 (1966) 89–94](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02052840)

### Truly continuous measures give Radon–Nikodym without σ-finiteness

**Remember:** Truly continuous means absolute continuity controlled by one set of finite measure.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 28A25. arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ν be a finitely additive set function and μ a measure. Then ν is truly continuous with respect to μ if, for every ε &gt; 0, there are a set E of finite μ-measure and a δ &gt; 0 with this property: \|ν(F)\| &lt; ε whenever μ(E ∩ F) &lt; δ. Equivalently, ν is countably additive and absolutely continuous, and every set of positive ν-measure contains a subset of finite μ-measure and positive ν-measure.

**Problem.** On any measure space, ν has a density with respect to μ, meaning ν(E) = ∫<sub>E</sub> f dμ for some integrable f and all measurable E, exactly when ν is truly continuous with respect to μ.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition the Radon–Nikodym theorem becomes an exact 'if and only if' on every measure space, with no σ-finiteness hypothesis. Ordinary absolute continuity is not enough, as the nLab's counterexample shows. Take counting measure on the countable–cocountable σ-algebra of an uncountable set, and let ν be 0 on countable sets and 1 on the others. In the σ-finite case, for countably additive ν, true continuity reduces to absolute continuity.

**nLab:** [Radon–Nikodym derivative](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon%E2%80%93Nikodym+derivative). It says: “The following example shows that the condition of being truly continuous is necessary in the non-σ-finite case.”

**Sources:**

- [David H. Fremlin, Measure Theory, Volume 2, Chapter 23](https://www1.essex.ac.uk/maths/people/fremlin/mt.htm)

### Measure densities multiply

**Remember:** Changing the reference measure twice multiplies the two weights.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A15 (Abstract differentiation theory, differentiation of set functions), 28A25. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A density dν/dμ is a nonnegative function whose integral against μ over each measurable set equals its ν-measure. A measure is σ-finite if countably many sets of finite measure cover its space.

**Problem.** Let ν, μ and λ be σ-finite positive measures on one measurable space. Suppose ν vanishes on every set of μ-measure zero and μ vanishes on every set of λ-measure zero. Then dν/dλ equals (dν/dμ)(dμ/dλ) outside a set of λ-measure zero, using finite versions of the densities.

**How the definition helps.** The integral definition allows the second weight to replace integration against the intermediate measure (our own). Check that substitution on indicators, then extend it to nonnegative functions by monotone convergence (our own). Apply it to the first weight restricted to any measurable set (our own). Existence and uniqueness of the resulting weight belong to the Radon–Nikodym theorem (our own).

**nLab:** [absolutely continuous measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/absolutely+continuous+measure). It says: “This measure f ν is absolutely continuous with respect to ν.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Continuous sections keep substitution measurable

**Remember:** Approximate the input by countably many values before substituting it.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 26B40. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Ω be an open subset of Euclidean space and let W(x, y) be real-valued, with y in a Euclidean space. A Carathéodory function is Lebesgue measurable in x for each y. Outside one set of x of measure zero, it is continuous in y.

**Problem.** For each Lebesgue measurable map u from Ω into the space of y values, x ↦ W(x, u(x)) is Lebesgue measurable.

**How the definition helps.** Continuity in y lets substitution preserve pointwise limits outside one set of measure zero (our own). Approximate u pointwise by measurable maps with countably many values, and substitute into each (our own). For failure under separate measurability, take a nonmeasurable set A on the line, and let W(x, y) be one if x = y lies in A and zero otherwise (our own). Each section is measurable, but W(x, x) is the indicator of A (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Carathéodory function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carath%C3%A9odory_function). It says: “the mapping ξ ↦ W(x, ξ) is continuous for almost every x ∈ Ω.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining convergence in measure by truncated distances makes it metrizable

**Remember:** Cap each pointwise error at one, then integrate.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A20 (Measurable and nonmeasurable functions, sequences of measurable functions, modes of convergence), 46E30. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the topology of convergence in measure by the pseudometrics that integrate min{\|f − g\|, 1} over sets of finite measure. A pseudometric is a distance that may be zero between different functions. The usual definition asks that μ{\|fₙ − f\| &gt; ε} tend to zero for each ε &gt; 0.

**Problem.** On a finite measure space, convergence in measure comes from one metric on measurable functions, once functions equal almost everywhere are identified.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, on a finite measure space one may integrate over the whole space, so one pseudometric defines the topology. Wikipedia states this. Identifying functions that are equal almost everywhere turns that pseudometric into a metric, in our own account. The work is the equivalence with the usual ε test, in our own account. It splits the integral where \|f − g\| is below or above ε.

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence in measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_in_measure). It says: “When μ(X) &lt; ∞, we may consider only one metric ρ<sub>X</sub>, so the topology of convergence in finite measure is metrizable.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining the Lebesgue integral by horizontal slices gives the layer cake formula

**Remember:** Add up the areas of the horizontal slabs.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A25 (Integration with respect to measures and other set functions), 26A42. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonnegative measurable f, let F(t) be the measure of the set where f &gt; t. Define the integral of f as the improper Riemann integral of F over (0, ∞), allowing the value ∞. The usual construction takes the supremum of integrals of simple functions below f. A simple function takes finitely many values, each on a measurable set.

**Problem.** Let f be nonnegative and measurable. Its integral equals the integral over t from 0 to ∞ of μ{f &gt; t}, also when both are infinite.

**How the definition helps.** With the slice definition, this formula is the definition itself, and Wikipedia says the integral may be defined this way. The work is proving that the slice integral agrees with the simple-function integral, in our own account. One checks it for simple functions and then passes to increasing limits with the monotone convergence theorem, in our own account.

**Wikipedia:** [Lebesgue integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebesgue_integral). It says: “The Lebesgue integral may then be defined as the improper Riemann integral of f∗:”

### Bounded mass controls vague tests

**Remember:** A uniform mass bound keeps small tails small in the integral.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Measures converge vaguely if their integrals converge against every continuous function that is zero outside a compact set. A function on the line vanishes at infinity if it tends to zero as \|x\| grows. Require a single finite upper bound on all total masses.

**Problem.** Suppose finite positive Borel measures on the line converge vaguely to a finite measure and have uniformly bounded masses. Their integrals converge against every continuous function vanishing at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** A compactly supported test can approximate a vanishing test uniformly, and the mass bound controls every integral error. In our own proof, multiply the test by a cutoff that equals one on a large interval and dies away outside it. In our own counterexample, mass n at n converges vaguely to zero. Its integral against f(x) = 1/(1 + \|x\|) tends to one.

**Paper or page:** [Vague Convergence of Uniformly Bounded Sequence of Finite Borel Measures implies Convergence of Integrals of Bounded Continuous Functions Vanishing at Infinity](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Vague_Convergence_of_Uniformly_Bounded_Sequence_of_Finite_Borel_Measures_implies_Convergence_of_Integrals_of_Bounded_Continuous_Functions_Vanishing_at_Infinity). It says: “∫ f dμₙ → ∫ f dμ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lipschitz tests bound closed-set masses

**Remember:** Fade a closed set’s indicator to zero just beyond its boundary.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures). arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Lipschitz function bounds each change in value by a fixed multiple of the distance between inputs. Borel probability measures are defined on the sets generated by open sets. They converge weakly if their integrals converge to the proposed limit measure’s integrals for every bounded continuous function. Equivalently, one can use only bounded Lipschitz functions.

**Problem.** Suppose probability measures converge on all bounded Lipschitz tests. On each closed set, their masses have limit superior at most its mass under the limit measure.

**How the definition helps.** Bounded Lipschitz tests include functions that decrease to the indicator of any closed set C, such as max(0, 1 − n·dist(x, C)) (our own). For fixed n, the integral bounds the mass of C from above and converges by hypothesis (our own). Letting n grow and applying bounded convergence to the limit measure gives the bound (our own). The equivalence with all bounded continuous tests is part of the Portmanteau theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Convergence of measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergence_of_measures). It says: “lim sup Pₙ(C) ≤ P(C) for all closed sets C of space S”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Countable covers by finite rectangles determine product measures

**Remember:** Countably many finite rectangles let their masses determine the whole product.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measure is σ-finite if countably many measurable sets of finite mass cover its space. The product σ-algebra is the smallest collection containing measurable rectangles and closed under complements and countable unions.

**Problem.** For two σ-finite measures, exactly one measure on the product σ-algebra assigns each rectangle the product of its side masses. Use zero for zero times infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Finite-mass rectangles exhaust the product, so the uniqueness theorem for finite measures applies on each of them; the extension theorem gives existence (our own). For our own counterexample, take length and counting measure on \[0, 1\]. Summing the lengths of horizontal sections gives the diagonal mass zero. Adding length along the diagonal gives it mass one but leaves every rectangle's mass unchanged.

**Wikipedia:** [Product measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_measure). It says: “In fact, when the spaces are σ-finite, the product measure is uniquely defined, and for every measurable set E,”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining product measure by integrating sections makes Tonelli's equality hold by construction

**Remember:** Measure each slice, then integrate the slice measures.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For σ-finite measure spaces, define the product measure of a measurable set E as the integral over x of ν(Eₓ). Here Eₓ is the vertical section of E at x. The rectangle construction instead extends the rule that E₁ × E₂ has measure μ(E₁)ν(E₂).

**Problem.** For σ-finite measures, the integral of a nonnegative measurable function on the product equals the iterated integral, first over y and then over x.

**How the definition helps.** For indicator functions of sets, which equal one on the set and zero elsewhere, the equality is the definition itself, in our own account. Sums and the monotone convergence theorem extend it to all nonnegative measurable functions, in our own proof. The work is proving that x ↦ ν(Eₓ) is measurable and that the formula defines a measure. The other order of integration needs the uniqueness of product measures, which uses σ-finiteness.

**Paper or page:** [Existence of Product Measures](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Existence_of_Product_Measures). It says: “ρ₁(E) = ∫<sub>X</sub> ν(E<sub>x</sub>) dμ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Fiber averages contract integral norms

**Remember:** Average over each fiber before taking the norm.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A50 (Integration and disintegration of measures). arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The image law assigns each set the probability of its inverse image. Disintegration expresses the original probability as an average of conditional probabilities, one on almost every fiber. Define the fiber average of a function by integrating it against each conditional probability.

**Problem.** Let a Borel map carry a probability on one complete separable metric space to its image law on another. For 1 ≤ p &lt; ∞, the Lᵖ norm of the fiber average is at most the original Lᵖ norm.

**How the definition helps.** Using conditional probabilities makes Jensen’s inequality available on each fiber. Our own proof bounds the pth power of the absolute average by the average of the absolute pth power. Integrating gives the norm bound. The alternative definition uses a measure density for each function. Disintegration supplies one measurable family of probabilities that works for all functions.

**Paper or page:** [A note about charts built by Eriksson-Bique and Soultanis on metric measure spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07010v1). It says: “{\\rm Pr}\_\\varphi (f)(y) = \\int \_\\mathsf{X}f(x)\\, \\mathrm d\\mathfrak m<sub>y</sub>(x)\\quad \\mathfrak m\_\\mathsf{Y}-\\text{a.e.},\\quad \\forall f\\in {\\rm L}<sup>p</sup>(\\mathfrak m\_\\mathsf{X}),”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### New densities reweight fiber laws

**Remember:** Weight each fiber, then move its total weight to the image law.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A50 (Integration and disintegration of measures). arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A disintegration gives a conditional probability on almost every fiber of a map. Averaging these probabilities against the image law recovers the original probability. A probability density here means a nonnegative measurable function whose integral is one.

**Problem.** Let m be a probability on a complete separable metric space, φ a Borel map into another, and ρ a probability density. The image of ρm has density equal to the fiber average of ρ against the image of m. Where this average is positive and finite, the new conditional law is ρ times the old one, divided by the average.

**How the definition helps.** The fiber description splits reweighting into two operations, changing the image law and normalizing each conditional probability. Our own proof substitutes this formula into the defining integral for disintegration. The normalizing factor cancels the new image density. Fibers with zero or infinite average have zero mass under the new image law. Uniqueness of disintegration identifies the result without constructing conditional laws afresh.

**Wikipedia:** [Disintegration theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disintegration_theorem). It says: “for every Borel-measurable function f : Y → \[0,∞\]”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Shared fibers glue couplings

**Remember:** Take products within fibers and average over the shared coordinate.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A50 (Integration and disintegration of measures). arXiv math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A coupling is a joint probability with prescribed coordinate laws. For each value of the shared coordinate, take the conditional laws of the two outer coordinates. Define a joint law by multiplying these conditional laws and averaging their product against the shared law.

**Problem.** Two couplings on complete separable metric spaces with a common middle law have a joint law on three coordinates. The joint law has the original couplings as its adjacent marginals.

**How the definition helps.** The product of the conditional laws gives both required marginals because each factor has mass one. Here a marginal means the law obtained by keeping only the specified coordinates. Our own proof integrates out one factor, then averages the other against the shared law. Disintegration supplies measurable conditional laws. The two adjacent marginals alone need not determine a unique joint law.

**Paper or page:** [Hypergraph Co-Optimal Transport: Metric and Categorical Properties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.03904v3). It says: “π′ ⊠ π (dx × dx′ × dx″) = π′ₓ′(dx″) πₓ′(dx) μ′(dx′).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Standard probability spaces make every measure-algebra map come from a point map

**Remember:** Standard spaces have enough points, so set maps come from point maps.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A60 (Measures on Boolean rings, measure algebras), 60A10. arXiv math.PR, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A probability space is standard if, after removing null sets, it is isomorphic to one of three things. These are an interval with Lebesgue measure, a countable set of atoms, or a disjoint union of both. The measure algebra is the Boolean algebra of measurable sets, with sets that differ by a null set treated as equal.

**Problem.** On standard probability spaces, every homomorphism of measure algebras is induced by a measure-preserving map of points. So on these spaces one can pass between maps of events and maps of points, up to null sets.

**How the definition helps.** A standard space has no missing points, so a map defined on events can be realized by a map on points. The definition excludes spaces such as the perforated interval, a set of inner measure 0 and outer measure 1 with the induced measure. Its events match those of the interval, but some of its points are missing. On the perforated circle, rotations act on events but not on points.

**Wikipedia:** [Standard probability space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_probability_space). It says: “It may seem that every homomorphism of measure algebras has to correspond to some measure preserving map, but it is not so. However, for standard probability spaces each F corresponds to some f.”

**Sources:**

- [V. A. Rokhlin, On the fundamental ideas of measure theory, Mat. Sbornik 25 (67) (1949), 107–150; English translation, AMS Translations 71 (1952), 1–54](http://ma.huji.ac.il/~matang02/rohlin.pdf)

### Flat norms contract boundaries

**Remember:** Take a boundary and only the small remainder survives.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A current acts on smooth differential forms and can represent an oriented region. Its mass norm measures its size without allowing it to move. The flat norm of T takes the infimum of the sum of masses of R and S over decompositions T = R + ∂S.

**Problem.** The boundary operator is a contraction for the flat norm on Euclidean currents of finite flat norm.

**How the definition helps.** The flat norm allows a boundary to cost only the mass of a filling. Our own proof starts with T = R + ∂S and takes boundaries to obtain ∂T = ∂R. Thus R fills ∂T, at cost at most the original sum of masses. Taking the infimum gives the contraction. The mass norm alone gives no such estimate. A short oriented segment has two boundary points whatever its length.

**Wikipedia:** [Current (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_%28mathematics%29). It says: “they are close in the flat norm if they coincide up to a small deformation.”

**Sources:**

- [Herbert Federer and Wendell H. Fleming, Normal and Integral Currents (1960)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970227)

### Lipschitz charts preserve rectifiability

**Remember:** A Lipschitz map composes with charts and preserves Hausdorff null sets.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A countably m-rectifiable set is covered, except for an m-dimensional Hausdorff null set, by countably many Lipschitz images from subsets of ℝᵐ. One can instead use smooth charts in Euclidean space.

**Problem.** A Lipschitz map between metric spaces sends a countably m-rectifiable set to a countably m-rectifiable set, for m ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** Lipschitz charts remain Lipschitz after composition, even when differentiable charts would lose differentiability. Our own proof also tracks the exceptional set. If the map multiplies distances by at most L, it multiplies each covering diameter by at most L. Its image therefore still has zero m-dimensional Hausdorff measure. In Euclidean space the equivalence with continuously differentiable charts carries the additional work.
