**Wikipedia:** [Rectifiable set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifiable_set). It says: “Equivalently, the fᵢ may be taken to be Lipschitz continuous without altering the definition.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Normal components count boundary crossings

**Remember:** The projected area factor turns a boundary integral into a crossing count.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set has finite perimeter when the distributional derivative of its indicator is a finite vector measure. Its variation measures its size without cancellation. The reduced boundary consists of points where the derivative divided by its variation on shrinking centered balls is defined and approaches a unit normal.

**Problem.** Let E be a bounded set of finite perimeter in ℝⁿ. Integrate the absolute last component of its normal over the reduced boundary with respect to (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure. This equals the integral, over horizontal coordinates, of the number of reduced boundary points on each vertical line.

**How the definition helps.** The reduced boundary provides the normal needed to state the projection formula even for sets without a smooth boundary. Our own derivation uses De Giorgi’s theorem, which gives a tangent plane at almost every reduced boundary point. Projecting that plane horizontally scales area by the absolute last component of the normal. The area formula integrates this factor and counts each point in each fiber.

**Paper or page:** [The Petty projection inequality for sets of finite perimeter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07103v1). It says: “\\int\_{\\partial<sup>\\ast</sup>E}g(x)\|\\nu<sup>E<sub>y</sub></sup>(x)\|d\\mathcal{H}<sup>n-1</sup>(x)=\\int\_{\\mathbb{R}<sup>n-1</sup>}dx<sup>\\prime</sup>\\int\_{(\\partial<sup>\\ast</sup>E)\_{x<sup>\\prime</sup>}}g(x<sup>\\prime</sup>,y)d\\mathcal{H}<sup>0</sup>(y).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced boundaries ignore null holes

**Remember:** Removing a null set does not change the measured boundary.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory). arXiv math.CA, math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set has finite perimeter if the distributional derivative of its indicator is a finite vector measure. This derivative tests the indicator by integration against derivatives of smooth functions. Its total variation measures the size of the derivative without cancellation. At a reduced boundary point, the derivative divided by its variation on shrinking centered balls is defined and tends to a unit vector.

**Problem.** Changing a set of finite perimeter on a Lebesgue null set preserves its reduced boundary. Its perimeter measure equals normalized (n−1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure restricted to that boundary in ℝⁿ.

**How the definition helps.** The reduced boundary uses only the derivative measure, which ignores changes on null sets. Our own example removes a countable dense subset from an open ball. Every point inside the ball then belongs to the topological boundary, but the reduced boundary stays on the sphere. De Giorgi’s structure theorem identifies surface measure there with perimeter for general sets of finite perimeter.

**Paper or page:** [Rectifiability; a survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00540v3). It says: “Let E ⊂ ℝⁿ be a set of finite perimeter. Then ∂∗E is (n−1)-rectifiable”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Covering fixes packing premeasure

**Remember:** Pack each piece, then take the cheapest countable cover.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Packing premeasure takes the supremum of sums of diameter powers over disjoint small balls centered on the set. It then shrinks the diameter cutoff to zero. Packing measure takes the infimum of the sums of premeasures over all countable covers.

**Problem.** Packing measure is countably subadditive and gives countable sets zero measure in every positive dimension. Packing premeasure need not do either.

**How the definition helps.** Taking countable covers lets each singleton contribute zero, even when disjoint balls around a dense set have large total diameter. Our own example uses rational grid points in \[0,1\]. At arbitrarily small scales, disjoint balls centered there have total diameter at least one-half. The one-dimensional packing premeasure is therefore positive. Covering by singletons gives packing measure zero, and combining covers proves countable subadditivity.

**Wikipedia:** [Packing dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_dimension). It says: “the packing measure of S is the infimum of the packing pre-measures of countable covers of S.”

**Sources:**

- [Claude Tricot, Two definitions of fractional dimension (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1017/s0305004100059119)

### Diameter powers reveal dimension

**Remember:** On small sets, raising the exponent makes every cover cheaper.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures), 28A80. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For s ≥ 0, cover the set by countably many nonempty sets of diameter at most δ. Take the infimum of the sums of their diameters raised to s, charging one per set when s = 0. Let δ decrease to zero to obtain the unnormalized Hausdorff measure at exponent s. The Hausdorff dimension is the infimum of exponents where this measure vanishes.

**Problem.** For a subset of Euclidean space, Hausdorff measure is infinite below its dimension and zero above it. At the dimension itself, it can be zero, finite positive, or infinite.

**How the definition helps.** The same cover compares costs at two exponents (our own). For t &lt; s, the cost at s is at most the cost at t times δ raised to s − t (our own). Thus finite measure at t forces zero measure at s (our own). This gives one cutoff without first computing any of the measures (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Strictly Positive Hausdorff Measure implies Infinite Lower Dimensional Measure](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Strictly_Positive_Hausdorff_Measure_implies_Infinite_Lower_Dimensional_Measure). It says: “ℋˢ(F) &gt; 0 ⇒ ∀ t ∈ \[0, s) : ℋᵗ(F) = +∞”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Frostman bounds force positive measure

**Remember:** If each covering set carries little mass, the whole cover must cost enough.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.MG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Frostman probability of exponent s assigns each ball of radius r at most Crˢ, for a fixed C. Hausdorff measure takes the least sum of diameter powers over covers, then sends the allowed diameters to zero.

**Problem.** A Borel subset of Euclidean space carrying a Frostman probability of exponent s &gt; 0 has positive s-dimensional Hausdorff measure.

**How the definition helps.** The ball bound replaces a search through all covers with an estimate on each member of any cover. Our own proof encloses each member of positive diameter in a ball of at most twice that diameter. Singletons have zero mass. Summing the ball bounds gives a positive lower bound for every cover’s cost. The converse for compact sets requires Frostman’s lemma, which constructs the measure.

**Paper or page:** [A Study Guide to "Kaufman and Falconer estimates for radial projections"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11847v1). It says: “If a Borel set X supports an s-Frostman probability measure μ, then ℋˢ(X) &gt; 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Hausdorff dimension respects countable unions

**Remember:** A countable union of sets of measure zero still has measure zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At each scale δ, take the infimum of sums of s-th powers of diameters over countable covers with diameters at most δ. Letting δ decrease to zero gives s-dimensional Hausdorff measure up to normalization. Hausdorff dimension is the infimum of exponents giving zero measure. Box dimension instead counts boxes of one size at a time.

**Problem.** The Hausdorff dimension of a countable union is the supremum of the dimensions of its members.

**How the definition helps.** Above the supremum, every member has measure zero, so the union has measure zero. In our own proof, monotonicity gives the reverse inequality. Countable subadditivity comes from joining the countable covers with a summable error budget. In our own comparison, each singleton has box dimension zero, but the rationals in \[0, 1\] have box dimension one.

**Wikipedia:** [Hausdorff dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_dimension). It says: “If X=\\bigcup<sub>i\\in I</sub>X<sub>i</sub> is a finite or countable union, then \\dim\_{\\operatorname{Haus}}(X) =\\sup<sub>i\\in I</sub> \\dim\_{\\operatorname{Haus}}(X<sub>i</sub>).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Mass bounds give dimension bounds

**Remember:** A cover must pay enough to carry all the mass.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each countable cover, add the s-th powers of its set diameters. Take the infimum over covers with diameters at most δ, then let δ decrease to zero. This defines s-dimensional Hausdorff measure up to normalization. Hausdorff dimension is the infimum of exponents giving zero measure.

**Problem.** Suppose a finite measure gives a Borel set F on the line positive mass. For some C and s &gt; 0, each sufficiently small closed interval has mass at most C times its diameter to power s. Then F has Hausdorff dimension at least s.

**How the definition helps.** The diameter bound turns each covering cost into an upper bound on the mass covered, up to the factor C. In our own proof, enclose each covering set in a closed interval of the same diameter. Summing the interval bounds shows that every sufficiently fine cover costs at least μ(F)/C. The s-dimensional measure is therefore positive. Finding a measure with the interval bound is the work in applications.

**Paper or page:** [Constructing self-similar subsets within the fractal support of Lacunary Wavelet Series for their multifractal analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17712). It says: “μ(U) ≤ c \|U\|ᵗ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Packing dimension respects countable unions

**Remember:** Cover each piece first, then put all the covers together.

*True by definition.* MSC 28A78 (Hausdorff and packing measures), 28A80. arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a bounded nonempty set, let N(r) count the fewest radius-r balls that cover it. Its upper box dimension is the limit superior of log N(r) divided by log(1/r) as r decreases to zero. For each countable cover by bounded sets, take the supremum of their upper box dimensions. In Euclidean space the infimum over these covers equals packing dimension, usually defined using disjoint balls.

**Problem.** The packing dimension of a countable union of subsets of Euclidean space equals the supremum of their packing dimensions.

**How the definition helps.** The countable cover definition lets one combine the covers of all pieces into one cover (our own). For any number above the supremum, choose covers whose dimensions stay below that number (our own). Monotonicity gives the reverse inequality (our own). The theorem equating modified box dimension with the packing measure definition carries the real work (our own). Ordinary upper box dimension is zero for each point, but it is one for the rationals in \[0, 1\] (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Packing dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packing_dimension). It says: “the packing dimension of S is equal to the upper modified box dimension of S”

**Sources:**

- [Claude Tricot Jr., Two definitions of fractional dimension (1982)](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305004100059119)

### Disjoint pieces give unique addresses

**Remember:** The first place where two addresses differ puts them in disjoint pieces.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A80 (Fractals), 37B10. arXiv math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Consider finitely many injective contractions on a compact metric space. Their attractor is the unique nonempty compact set A equal to the union of its images. Strong separation means those images are pairwise disjoint. An address is an infinite list of maps whose successive compositions, applied to A with the first map outermost, contain the point.

**Problem.** If the space and the family are nonempty and strong separation holds, each point of A has exactly one address.

**How the definition helps.** Disjoint images determine the first map uniquely, and injectivity determines the point to use at the next step. Our own proof repeats this choice inside A to construct the entire address. The contraction mapping theorem supplies the attractor. Without separation, the two half-size copies of \[0,1\] meet at 1/2, giving our own example of two addresses.

**Paper or page:** [Applications of the Tarski-Kantorovitch Fixed-Point Principle to the study of Infinite Iterated Function Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.04650v1). It says: “the canonical projection π : Λ(I) → A is bijective.”

**Sources:**

- [Applications of the Tarski-Kantorovitch Fixed-Point Principle to the study of Infinite Iterated Function Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.04650v1)

### Graph norms let closed operators commute with integrals

**Remember:** Integrate the point and its image together.

*True by definition.* MSC 28B05 (Vector-valued set functions, measures and integrals). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let T be a linear operator from part of one Banach space into another. Suppose its graph is closed in the product space. Give its domain the graph norm ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖. The Bochner integral uses approximations by measurable functions with finitely many values, with error measured by the integral of the norm.

**Problem.** If f takes values in the domain of T and both f and Tf are Bochner integrable, T commutes with integration. In particular, the integral of f belongs to the domain.

**How the definition helps.** The graph norm makes T bounded on its domain even when the original norm does not. Our own proof integrates the pair (f, Tf) in the product space. Its integral belongs to the closed graph because simple approximations can take their values there. The two coordinates of the integral therefore satisfy the required identity.

**Paper or page:** [A Representation of Matrix-Valued Harmonic Functions by the Poisson Integral of Non-commutative BMO Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.11752v2). It says: “T\\left(\\int \_E f(x)\\, d\\mu (x) \\right)=\\int \_E T(f(x))\\, d\\mu (x),”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Separable range rules out invisible vectors

**Remember:** A separable range lets scalar tests detect strong measurability.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28B05 (Vector-valued set functions, measures and integrals). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Banach-valued function is weakly measurable if every continuous linear functional gives a measurable scalar function. It is essentially separably valued if its values outside a null set lie in a separable subspace. Strong measurability means it is an almost everywhere norm limit of simple functions.

**Problem.** Pettis's theorem says that weak measurability gives strong measurability when the range is essentially separable.

**How the definition helps.** A separable subspace has a countable dense set, which lets scalar tests yield measurable simple approximations in Pettis’s theorem. Our own example on the Lebesgue interval sends t to the unit vector at coordinate t in ℓ²(\[0,1\]). Each continuous linear functional has only countably many nonzero coordinates, so its value is zero almost everywhere. Distinct unit vectors have distance √2, so a separable subspace contains only countably many of them.

**Paper or page:** [Kernel-Summability Methods and the Silverman-Toeplitz Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.06770v3). It says: “A function v : E → X is strongly measurable if, and only if, the two following conditions are satisfied: v is weakly measurable; v is essentially separably valued.”

**Sources:**

- [B. J. Pettis, On integration in vector spaces (1938)](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1938-1501970-8)

### Stone's condition lets an abstract Daniell integral come from a measure

**Remember:** Truncate at height one, and the integral finds its measure.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C05 (Integration theory via linear functionals (Radon measures, Daniell integrals, etc.), representing set functions and measures), 28A12. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Daniell starts from a vector lattice T₀ of functions, closed under maximum and minimum, and a positive linear functional I on it. The functional must be continuous under monotone limits: if φₙ decreases to 0, then I(φₙ) tends to 0. Stone's condition asks that min(φ, 1) is in T₀ whenever φ is.

**Problem.** Under Stone's condition, there are a σ-algebra 𝒜 on X and a measure μ on 𝒜 such that I(φ) is the integral of φ against μ for every φ in T₀. This is the Daniell–Stone theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Stone's condition lets one cut functions off at height one, so indicator functions of sets can be reached as limits. The integral then gives a measure on those sets. The convergence theorems need no measure at all and are proved first. Applied to the Riemann integral of continuous functions with compact support, this route gives Lebesgue measure (our own remark).

**Paper or page:** [The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1), [The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1). It says: “with the property that χX ∧ φ ∈ T₀ whenever φ ∈ T₀. Let I be an I-integral on T₀. Then there is a σ-algebra 𝒜 on X and a measure μ on 𝒜”

**Sources:**

- [Adriaan de Clercq, The Daniell Integral: Integration without measure, arXiv:2211.14964 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.14964v1)

### Compatible finite quotient averages give Haar measure on profinite groups

**Remember:** On each finite quotient, average with equal weight for every point.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 20E18. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A profinite group is an inverse limit of finite groups with the discrete topology. On functions that factor through a finite quotient G/N, define the integral as the ordinary average over that quotient. The usual definition asks for a translation invariant regular Borel probability measure, called Haar probability measure.

**Problem.** These finite averages determine Haar probability measure on any profinite group, without using Haar’s general existence theorem.

**How the definition helps.** The finite averages make translation invariance immediate because translations permute each finite quotient (our own). Passing to a finer quotient does not change the average, since each fibre has the same number of points (our own). Functions from finite quotients are uniformly dense in the continuous functions, so the averages extend to a positive linear functional (our own). The Riesz representation theorem makes it integration against a regular Borel probability measure (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Compact group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_group). It says: “In the profinite case there are many subgroups of finite index, and Haar measure of a coset will be the reciprocal of the index.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Haar measure on Baire sets makes the regularity conditions unnecessary

**Remember:** On Baire sets, invariant measures are regular for free.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 43A05. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A left Haar measure on a locally compact group is a nonzero left-invariant measure. On Borel sets it must be finite on compact sets, outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular on open sets. The Baire sets form the σ-algebra generated by compact sets that are countable intersections of open sets.

**Problem.** Every locally compact group has a left Haar measure, unique up to a positive constant. On the Baire sets this can be stated without any regularity condition.

**How the definition helps.** Baire measures that are finite on compact sets are automatically regular, so on Baire sets the regularity part holds by itself. On Borel sets, regularity must be assumed, and Haar measure can fail inner regularity. Take the circle times the real line with the discrete topology, and the closed set {1} × \[0, 1\]. Its compact subsets are finite and have measure 0, but the set itself does not.

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “Some authors define a Haar measure on Baire sets rather than Borel sets. This makes the regularity conditions unnecessary as Baire measures are automatically regular.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Haar, Der Massbegriff in der Theorie der kontinuierlichen Gruppen, Annals of Mathematics 34 (1933)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968346)

### Left invariant volume forms give Haar measure on Lie groups

**Remember:** Translate a volume form at the identity to get invariant volume everywhere.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 22E15. arXiv math.DG, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On an n-dimensional Lie group, choose a nonzero alternating n-linear form on the tangent space at the identity. Move it by left translation to get a smooth volume form ω on the group. Its absolute value defines a measure by integration. The general definition of left Haar measure asks for a nonzero regular Borel measure unchanged by left translation.

**Problem.** Every Lie group has a left Haar measure, given by its left invariant volume form.

**How the definition helps.** The volume form makes invariance automatic because left translation preserves the form. Integrating its absolute value then gives a positive measure on nonempty open sets and a finite measure on compact sets (our own). Standard integration of a smooth density gives regularity, which means approximation by open and compact sets (our own). This replaces Haar’s general existence proof with the construction and integration of a smooth form.

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “On an n-dimensional Lie group, Haar measure can be constructed easily as the measure induced by a left-invariant n-form. This was known before Haar's theorem.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Haar, Der Massbegriff in der Theorie der kontinuierlichen Gruppen, Annals of Mathematics 34 (1933)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968346)

### The Haar scaling definition makes compact groups unimodular

**Remember:** Left translation cannot rescale the finite mass of the whole group.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C10 (Set functions and measures on topological groups or semigroups, Haar measures, invariant measures), 22C05. arXiv math.FA, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ν be right Haar measure, a nonzero measure on a locally compact Hausdorff group that is unchanged by right translation. Its modular function Δ assigns to g the factor with ν(g⁻¹S) = Δ(g)ν(S). Unimodular means Δ equals 1 everywhere. The equivalent definition asks for a Haar measure that is both left and right invariant.

**Problem.** The modular function is multiplicative. Every compact Hausdorff group is unimodular.

**How the definition helps.** Defining Δ by scaling makes multiplicativity a composition law, since two translations multiply their scaling factors (our own). For compact G, the whole group has finite positive Haar measure, and a translation leaves it unchanged. So Δ(g) = 1. The usual argument instead needs Δ to be a continuous homomorphism into the positive reals, which have no nontrivial compact subgroup (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Haar measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haar_measure). It says: “Thus, by uniqueness up to a constant scaling factor of the Haar measure, there exists a function Δ from the group to the positive reals, called the Haar modulus, modular function or modular character”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Inner regularity is what Kolmogorov's extension theorem needs beyond Euclidean spaces

**Remember:** Compact sets inside every event let finite laws glue into one process.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 60G05, 28A35. arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A measure on a topological space is inner regular if each set has measure equal to the supremum over the compact sets inside it. A consistent family gives a probability measure on each finite product. These measures agree under the projections between products.

**Problem.** A consistent family of inner regular probability laws on the finite products of Hausdorff spaces extends to a unique probability measure on the product σ-algebra of the infinite product. Borel probability measures on Polish spaces are inner regular, so the Euclidean case needs no extra condition.

**How the definition helps.** Inner regularity lets the proof use compact sets. Nested compact sets with the finite intersection property have a common point, which gives countable additivity. Without such a condition the extension can fail; a known example is due to Andersen and Jessen (our own). The measure lives only on the product σ-algebra, so events that depend on uncountably many coordinates stay outside it.

**Wikipedia:** [Kolmogorov extension theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov_extension_theorem). It says: “In fact, any collection of measurable spaces together with a collection of inner regular measures defined on the finite products of these spaces would suffice, provided that these measures satisfy a certain compatibility relation.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Kolmogoroff, Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung, Springer, 1933](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-49888-6)

### Measures that respect directed unions of open sets have a support

**Remember:** τ-additive: the measure of a directed union of open sets is the supremum.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 28A12. arXiv math.FA, math.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Borel measure μ on a topological space is τ-additive if, for every directed family of open sets, the measure of their union is the supremum of their measures. A family is directed if any two members are contained in a third member.

**Problem.** Every τ-additive Borel measure has a support, a smallest closed set of full measure.

**How the definition helps.** τ-additivity says directly that the union of the null open sets is null, because the null open sets form a directed family. The complement of that union is the support. For a general Borel measure, the union of all null open sets can fail to be null. Every Radon measure on a Hausdorff space is τ-additive, so the definition covers the usual examples.

**nLab:** [tau-additive measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/tau-additive+measure), [valuation (measure theory)](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/valuation+%28measure+theory%29), [correspondence between measure and valuation theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/correspondence+between+measure+and+valuation+theory). It says: “the union of all null open sets is null”

**Sources:**

- [Tobias Fritz, Paolo Perrone, Sharwin Rezagholi, Probability, valuations, hyperspace: Three monads on Top and the support as a morphism (2019); arXiv:1910.03752](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.03752)

### Proper maps keep Radon measures locally finite

**Remember:** Compact inverse images keep mass finite near every target point.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)). arXiv math.GN. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Radon measure is locally finite and approximates Borel sets from inside by compact sets. A proper continuous map has compact inverse images of compact sets. Its pushforward assigns each Borel set the measure of its inverse image.

**Problem.** A proper continuous map between locally compact Hausdorff spaces sends a Radon measure to a Radon measure in the inner-regular convention.

**How the definition helps.** Properness makes the inverse image of a compact neighborhood compact, so the image measure stays locally finite. Our own proof approximates the inverse image of a Borel set from inside by compact sets. Their images give compact subsets of the target set with at least as much image measure. Our own counterexample sends the whole real line to one point, which receives infinite Lebesgue mass under the pushforward.

**nLab:** [Radon measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon+measure). It says: “is a Borel measure m on X such that m is locally finite and inner regular on all Borel subsets.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Proper maps preserve Radon measures

**Remember:** Compact sets cannot collect infinite mass from far away.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)). arXiv math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A proper map has compact inverse images of compact sets. On locally compact metric spaces, use Radon measures that are finite on compact sets and approximate Borel sets from inside by compact sets.

**Problem.** A continuous proper map between locally compact metric spaces sends a Radon measure to a Radon measure.

**How the definition helps.** Properness makes each compact target set receive only the finite mass of its compact inverse image. In our own specialization, each target point has a compact neighborhood, so its inverse image also has finite mass. To approximate a Borel set from inside, first approximate its inverse image by compact sets. Their continuous images are compact and capture at least the same mass. In our own counterexample, a constant map sends the entire length of the line to one point.

**nLab:** [Radon measure](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Radon+measure). It says: “The pushforward measure H∗μ is a Radon measure on Y defined as follows.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regularity makes the measure in the Riesz representation theorem unique

**Remember:** Regularity picks one measure for each positive functional on continuous functions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C15 (Set functions and measures on topological spaces (regularity of measures, etc.)), 28C05. arXiv math.CA, math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Borel measure is outer regular when the measure of each Borel set is the infimum of the measures of open sets that contain it. It is inner regular when each open set, and each Borel set of finite measure, has the supremum over compact subsets as its measure. A regular measure has both properties and gives each compact set finite measure.

**Problem.** Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space. The Riesz–Markov–Kakutani theorem says that each positive linear functional on the compactly supported continuous functions on X is integration against a unique regular Borel measure. It also identifies the dual of C₀(X) with the regular complex Borel measures.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity makes a measure depend only on its values on compact sets, and integrals of continuous functions fix those values (our own summary). The page gives a counterexample on the ordinals up to the first uncountable ordinal Ω, with the order topology. Evaluation at Ω is integration against the point mass at Ω. It is also integration against the non-regular Dieudonné measure, which gives measure 1 to Borel sets containing a closed unbounded set and measure 0 to the point Ω.

**Wikipedia:** [Riesz–Markov–Kakutani representation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riesz%E2%80%93Markov%E2%80%93Kakutani_representation_theorem). It says: “Without the condition of regularity the Borel measure need not be unique.”

**Sources:**

- [S. Kakutani, Concrete representation of abstract (M)-spaces, Annals of Mathematics 42 (1941), 994–1024](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968778)

### Finite energy protects Brownian null sets

**Remember:** A continuous shift can be too rough to preserve Brownian null sets.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C20 (Set functions and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces (Wiener measure, Gaussian measure, etc.)). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Consider Brownian paths starting at zero on \[0,1\]. Their Cameron–Martin space consists of paths obtained by integrating a square-integrable function from zero to each time t.

**Problem.** Brownian path measure and its translate have the same null sets for shifts in the Cameron–Martin space. All other continuous shifts starting at zero give mutually singular measures.

**How the definition helps.** Square-integrable derivatives identify exactly the shifts that preserve Brownian null sets. Our own example uses the continuous shift t ↦ √t. Its derivative has square 1/(4t), whose integral diverges at zero. The Cameron–Martin theorem gives singularity here, meaning that some set has full original probability and zero translated probability.

**Paper or page:** [Notions of null sets in infinite-dimensional Carnot groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14524v1). It says: “A Gaussian measure γ is quasi-invariant under translation by elements of its Cameron–Martin space H.”

**Sources:**

- [R. H. Cameron and W. T. Martin, Transformations of Wiener Integrals Under Translations (1944)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969276)

### Linear functional tests show continuous linear maps preserve Gaussian laws

**Remember:** Compose a linear functional with the operator to test the image law.

*True by definition.* MSC 28C20 (Set functions and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces (Wiener measure, Gaussian measure, etc.)), 60G15. arXiv math.PR, stat.ML. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A separable Banach space is a complete normed vector space with a countable dense set. A probability law on such a space is Gaussian if every continuous linear functional sends it to a normal law. A linear functional maps vectors to real numbers, and a constant counts as normal with variance zero.

**Problem.** A continuous linear map B between separable Banach spaces sends each Gaussian law to a Gaussian law. The output means and covariances of linear tests come from composing those tests with B.

**How the definition helps.** The functional definition makes preservation a composition rule (our own). If L tests the output, then L∘B is a continuous linear functional on the input, where the Gaussian condition already gives normality (our own). The finite-dimensional density approach cannot work here because infinite-dimensional Banach spaces have no Lebesgue measure. The work shifts to constructing the original Gaussian law and checking that the operator is continuous on the chosen spaces (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Gaussian measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_measure). It says: “Even so, it is possible to define Gaussian measures on infinite-dimensional spaces, the main example being the abstract Wiener space construction.”

**Paper or page:** [Gaussian Process Priors for Systems of Linear Partial Differential Equations with Constant Coefficients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.14319v4). It says: “be a linear continuous map. Then B∗γ is a Gaussian measure”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Weighted spaces carry Gaussian sequences

**Remember:** Independent standard Gaussians fit in weighted ℓ², not in ordinary ℓ².

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28C20 (Set functions and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces (Wiener measure, Gaussian measure, etc.)). arXiv math.FA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A cylinder law specifies consistent joint laws for finite lists of coordinates. Choose positive weights with finite sum. The weighted space consists of sequences whose weighted sum of squares is finite, with norm equal to its square root.

**Problem.** Independent standard Gaussian coordinates define a Borel probability on the weighted space, but not on ordinary ℓ².

**How the definition helps.** Summable weights give the squared norm finite expectation, which makes it finite almost surely. Our own proof starts with the countable product of standard Gaussian laws. The truncated sequences converge almost surely in weighted norm, so their limit defines a random element of that space. In ordinary ℓ² the squared norm diverges almost surely because the average of the first n squares tends to one. The strong law of large numbers supplies this last step.

**Wikipedia:** [Abstract Wiener space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_Wiener_space). It says: “the cylinder set measure on B, unlike the cylinder set measure on H, will extend to a countably additive measure”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Sober measurable spaces make measurable Gelfand duality hold by definition

**Remember:** Sober: every zero-one measure is a point, just as every point of a locale is.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A05 (Classes of sets (Borel fields, \\(\\sigma\\)-rings, etc.), measurable sets, Suslin sets, analytic sets), 46L05. arXiv math.FA, math.OA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A zero-one measure is a measure that takes only the values 0 and 1. A measurable space X is sober if every zero-one measure on it is the Dirac measure of exactly one point. Equivalently, the map X → Sp(L∞(X)) that sends x to evaluation at x is an isomorphism. Here L∞(X) is the algebra of all bounded measurable functions on X, and Sp(L∞(X)) is its spectrum.

**Problem.** The functors L∞ and Sp give a duality between sober measurable spaces and spatial σ-C\*-algebras, the commutative σ-C\*-algebras of the form L∞(X). A σ-C\*-algebra is a C\*-algebra closed under countable bounded monotone suprema.

**How the definition helps.** Sober spaces are defined as exactly the spaces on which the duality holds, so the duality is automatic. The functors L∞ and Sp form an idempotent adjunction, and for such an adjunction the objects on which the unit is an isomorphism form one side of an equivalence. The work is in proving that the adjunction is idempotent. Every standard Borel space is sober, while the invariant σ-algebra of an ergodic system is in general not.

**nLab:** [sober measurable space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/sober+measurable+space), [measurable Gelfand duality](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/measurable+Gelfand+duality). It says: “As usual with idempotent adjunctions, we have that the center is equivalently given by”

**Sources:**

- [Tobias Fritz, Antonio Lorenzin, Categories of abstract and noncommutative measurable spaces, Advances in Mathematics 488 (2026) 110793; arXiv:2504.13708](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13708)

### Take inclusion-exclusion as an axiom of constructive measures

**Remember:** Use the formula you actually need as the axiom.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A10 (Real- or complex-valued set functions), 03F60. arXiv math.CA, math.LO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take the two-set inclusion-exclusion law μ(A ∪ B) + μ(A ∩ B) = μ(A) + μ(B) as an axiom of a measure, in place of additivity on disjoint sets.

**Problem.** In constructive mathematics, a measure with the two-set law as an axiom satisfies the inclusion-exclusion formula for every finite family of sets.

**How the definition helps.** If the law you need is an axiom, its constructive proof is no longer a problem. Classically the two-set law follows from additivity, but constructively that proof fails. With the two-set law as an axiom, the general finite formula follows by the usual induction. On Cheng spaces, the law also follows from finite additivity and one extra rule, so there the choice of axiom makes no difference.

**nLab:** [inclusion-exclusion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/inclusion-exclusion), [Cheng space](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cheng+space). It says: “On the other hand, we may adopt (\*) as the proper clause in the definition of measure.”

**Sources:**

- [Errett Bishop, Henry Cheng, Constructive measure theory, Memoirs of the AMS 116 (1972)](https://doi.org/10.1090/memo/0116)
- [Errett Bishop, Douglas Bridges, Constructive Analysis, Grundlehren 279, Springer (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-61667-9)

### The Carathéodory extension theorem becomes a Kan extension of transformations

**Remember:** Extending a premeasure is a Kan extension.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A12 (Contents, measures, outer measures, capacities), 18A40. arXiv math.CT, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A premeasure is a countably additive function on a Boolean algebra of sets. An outer measure is a monotone, countably subadditive function on all subsets. The paper treats both as transformations between poset-valued functors. Lax and colax transformations satisfy inequalities where strict transformations satisfy equalities.

**Problem.** A premeasure on a Boolean algebra of sets extends to a measure on the σ-algebra it generates. In the paper's language, this extension is a Kan extension of strict transformations.

**How the definition helps.** A Kan extension is the best extension of a map along another map, so extending a premeasure becomes a universal construction. The paper proves a general extension result for transformations between poset-valued functors. It then checks that the transformations that come from measures satisfy its conditions. In our own remark, the measure-theoretic estimates do not disappear but move into this check.

**Paper or page:** [A categorical proof of the Carathéodory extension theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01720). It says: “To prove this result categorically, we represent (pre)measures and outer measures by certain (co)lax and strict transformations. The Carathéodory extension then corresponds to a Kan extension of strict transformations.”

**Sources:**

- [Ruben Van Belle, A categorical proof of the Carathéodory extension theorem, arXiv:2210.01720 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01720)

### Area lifts preserve nonlinear integrals

**Remember:** Adjoin volume before measuring the size of a vector measure.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures), 28B05. arXiv math.FA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The total variation of a vector measure measures mass without cancellation. Strict convergence means convergence against continuous tests together with convergence of total variation masses. Lift a vector measure by adjoining Lebesgue measure on the domain as its first coordinate. Area-strict convergence means strict convergence of these lifted measures.

**Problem.** Consider finite vector measures on the closure of a bounded Euclidean domain. Under area-strict convergence, integrals of continuous functions of position and unit direction against lifted total variation converge. The unit direction is the density of the lifted measure relative to its variation.

**How the definition helps.** The lift detects concentrations that ordinary strict convergence misses. The cited lemma constructs concentration even under strict convergence. In our own example, divide \[0,1\] into n equal intervals. Put density n on the first 1/n fraction of each interval and zero elsewhere. These measures converge strictly to Lebesgue measure, but their lifted masses tend to two instead of √2. Our own deduction applies Reshetnyak’s continuity theorem directly to the strictly converging lifts.

**Paper or page:** [Relaxation of functionals with linear growth: interactions of emerging measures and free discontinuities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12687v1). It says: “vε → σ weakly∗ and strictly in ℳ(Ω̄; ℝᵈ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Comparing distribution functions up to constants characterizes vague convergence of signed measures

**Remember:** Compare masses of intervals, not mass accumulated from minus infinity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A33 (Spaces of measures, convergence of measures), 28A20. arXiv math.PR, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Finite signed measures μₙ on ℝ converge vaguely to μ when ∫ f dμₙ → ∫ f dμ for every continuous f with compact support. The distribution function of μ is F(x) = μ((−∞, x\]). The abstract's notion is convergence in Lebesgue measure up to constants: Fₙ + cₙ → F in measure for some constants cₙ.

**Problem.** Finite signed measures μₙ on ℝ converge vaguely to μ exactly when two things hold. Their total variations on each bounded interval are bounded uniformly in n, and Fₙ + cₙ → F in Lebesgue measure on each bounded interval for some constants cₙ.

**How the definition helps.** Vague convergence cannot see mass that escapes to infinity, and the free constants cₙ remove this blind spot from the distribution functions (our own). For example, the unit mass at −n converges vaguely to zero (our own). Its distribution function is 1 at each fixed point for large n, while the limit has distribution function 0, so cₙ = −1 is needed (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Vague and basic convergence of signed measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11377v1). It says: “it is locally uniformly bounded in variation and the corresponding sequence of distribution functions either converges in Lebesgue measure up to constants, converges basically, or converges almost basically.”

**Sources:**

- [Michael Staněk, Vague and basic convergence of signed measures, arXiv:2406.11377 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11377v1)

### Virtual continuity replaces Luzin's theorem in several variables and gives traces

**Remember:** Delete small sets one coordinate at a time, not in the square.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 28A35 (Measures and integrals in product spaces), 46E35. arXiv math.FA, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f(x, y) be a measurable function on a product X × Y of two probability spaces. The function f is virtually continuous if it is continuous, for suitable metrics, on a product X′ × Y′ of large subsets. For any ε &gt; 0, each of X′ and Y′ may miss a set of measure ε, as in Theorem 3 of the paper. So what remains is always a product of two large sets, not an arbitrary large subset of X × Y.

**Problem.** Bounded virtually continuous functions on X × Y have well-defined integrals against singular measures, such as the measure on the diagonal x = y. Suitable Sobolev functions are virtually continuous, so this gives their traces.

**How the definition helps.** Deleting small sets in each coordinate separately respects the product structure, so restrictions to the diagonal still make sense. Luzin's theorem deletes an arbitrary small set of the product, which may contain the whole diagonal. A function changed on the diagonal alone is the same element of L¹, so ordinary measurable functions have no trace (our own remark).

**Paper or page:** [Virtual continuity of the measurable functions of several variables, and Sobolev embedding theorems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.3523v2), [Virtual continuity of the measurable functions of several variables, and Sobolev embedding theorems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.3523v2), [Virtual continuity of the measurable functions of several variables, and Sobolev embedding theorems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.3523v2), [Virtual continuity of the measurable functions of several variables, and Sobolev embedding theorems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.3523v2). It says: “The search of right analogue of the Luzin theorem leads to a notion of virtually continuous functions of several variables. This probably new notion appears implicitly in the statements like embeddings theorems and traces theorems for Sobolev spaces.”

**Sources:**

- [Anatoly Vershik, Pavel Zatitskiy, Fedor Petrov, Virtual continuity of the measurable functions of several variables, and Sobolev embedding theorems, arXiv:1307.3523 (2013), Funct. Anal. Appl. 2013, no. 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.3523v2)

### Compact strictly localizable measurable spaces are dual to commutative von Neumann algebras

**Remember:** Compact is Radon without topology; strictly localizable is σ-finite without countability.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28A60 (Measures on Boolean rings, measure algebras), 46L10, 28A05. arXiv math.FA, math.OA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An enhanced measurable space (X, M, N) is a set X with a σ-algebra M and a σ-ideal N ⊆ M of negligible sets. It is compact if some compact class K ⊆ M has a non-negligible member inside every non-negligible measurable set. A compact class is a family of sets in which every countable subfamily with the finite intersection property has a non-empty intersection. It is strictly localizable if it is a disjoint union (coproduct) of σ-finite enhanced measurable spaces.

**Problem.** The category of compact strictly localizable enhanced measurable spaces is equivalent to the opposite of the category of commutative von Neumann algebras.

**How the definition helps.** Each of the two conditions removes one obstacle to the duality. Strict localizability lets maps of Boolean algebras of measurable sets lift to maps of spaces. Compactness excludes the nLab's counterexample, a set of real-valued-measurable cardinality where the identity map has no essential image. The deep step is a theorem of Fremlin that, under these conditions, all maps are localizable.

**nLab:** [categories of measure theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/categories+of+measure+theory), [commutative von Neumann algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/commutative+von+Neumann+algebra), [measurable locale](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/measurable+locale). It says: “These properties eliminate pathologies and ensure the following desirable properties of objects and morphisms.”

**Sources:**

- [Dmitri Pavlov, Gelfand-type duality for commutative von Neumann algebras, Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra 226:4 (2022) 106884; arXiv:2005.05284](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.05284)
- [Edward Marczewski, On compact measures, Fundamenta Mathematicae 40 (1953) 113–124](https://doi.org/10.4064/fm-40-1-113-124)

### Metric tangent measures let one test rectifiability in any complete metric space

**Remember:** Blow up both distances and mass to see the local model.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28A75 (Length, area, volume, other geometric measure theory), 28A78, 53C23. arXiv math.MG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** To blow up a measure at a point, scale distances by 1/r, rescale the measure to match, and let r tend to zero. A tangent is a limit of these rescaled spaces with their measures and marked points, in a sense defined for any metric space. For doubling measures this agrees with measured Gromov–Hausdorff convergence, where spaces become close inside one common space. A set is n-rectifiable if countably many Lipschitz images of subsets of ℝⁿ cover it, apart from a set of n-dimensional Hausdorff measure zero.

**Problem.** Take a set E of finite n-dimensional Hausdorff measure in a complete metric space. E is n-rectifiable exactly when almost every point has positive lower density and one tangent: ℝⁿ with a norm and scaled Hausdorff measure. Positive lower density means the measure of E in a ball of radius r stays above a fixed multiple of rⁿ as r shrinks.

**How the definition helps.** The new tangents need no ambient Euclidean space, so the characterization can be stated in any complete metric space. Preiss's tangent measures live in the surrounding Euclidean space, so they do not apply in general. The paper proves that its definition agrees with Preiss's when the ambient space is Euclidean. The hard part is to turn the small-scale models into countably many Lipschitz maps that cover the set. The paper does this in Theorem 1.1, from bi-Lipschitz approximations at small scales.

**Paper or page:** [Characterising rectifiable metric spaces using tangent spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12371v3). It says: “We also introduce a generalisation of Preiss's tangent measures that is suitable for the setting of arbitrary metric spaces and formulate our characterisation in terms of tangent measures.”

**Sources:**

- [David Bate, Characterising rectifiable metric spaces using tangent spaces, arXiv:2109.12371v3 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12371v3)

### Countable tests fix weak density versions

**Remember:** Countably many scalar tests can share one exceptional null set.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 28B05 (Vector-valued set functions, measures and integrals). arXiv math.FA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A weak-star density takes values in the dual of a Banach space. It represents a vector measure when testing against each original-space vector gives the corresponding scalar measure density. Separability lets these tests use a single countable dense set.

**Problem.** On a finite Lebesgue interval, two weak-star densities of the same vector measure agree almost everywhere if the original Banach space is separable.

**How the definition helps.** A countable dense set lets every scalar uniqueness argument use the same exceptional null set. Our own proof removes the union of those null sets and extends equality to every vector by continuity. For our own counterexample take X = ℓ¹(\[0,1\]) and let the density at t evaluate a vector at coordinate t. Each vector has countable support, so each scalar test vanishes almost everywhere on the Lebesgue interval. The density therefore represents the zero measure although its norm equals one everywhere.

**Paper or page:** [Global entropy solutions to a degenerate parabolic-parabolic chemotaxis system for flux-limited dispersal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03887v3). It says: “If X is separable, then any ζ₁ and ζ₂ that satisfy the conditions on ζ coincide a.e. in {g &gt; 0}.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prevalence gives infinite-dimensional spaces a measure meaning of almost every

**Remember:** Test along finite-dimensional slices, and almost every works without a big measure.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 28C20 (Set functions and measures and integrals in infinite-dimensional spaces (Wiener measure, Gaussian measure, etc.)), 37C20. arXiv math.CA, math.DS. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Borel set S in a real topological vector space V is prevalent if some finite-dimensional subspace P works as a probe. That is, for every v in V, Lebesgue-almost every p in P has v + p in S. A set is shy if its complement is prevalent, and in ℝⁿ shy means Lebesgue measure zero.

**Problem.** Shy sets behave like null sets: subsets, translates and countable unions of shy sets are shy, and prevalent sets are dense. In this sense, almost every Cᵏ map of ℝⁿ has only hyperbolic periodic points.

**How the definition helps.** The definition needs Lebesgue measure only on finite-dimensional slices, so it needs no measure on the big space. An infinite-dimensional space has no useful translation-invariant measure like Lebesgue measure (our own). Prevalence differs from the Baire category notion of generic: the Liouville numbers form a residual set of Lebesgue measure zero. The work moves to finding a probe space for each property (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Prevalent and shy sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prevalent_and_shy_sets), [Generic property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generic_property). It says: “the notions of prevalence and shyness are notions of almost everywhere and measure zero that are well-suited to the study of infinite-dimensional spaces”

**Sources:**

- [B. R. Hunt, T. Sauer, J. A. Yorke, Prevalence: a translation-invariant almost every on infinite-dimensional spaces, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 27 (1992) 217–238](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-1992-00328-2)

## 30 Functions of a complex variable

### Conjugation makes the complex modulus multiplicative

**Remember:** Conjugation respects products, so the squared modulus does too.

*True by definition.* MSC 30A99 (General properties of functions of one complex variable). arXiv math.CV. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** For z = x + iy, its complex conjugate is z̄ = x − iy. Define the modulus by \|z\| = √(z z̄), the nonnegative square root of the real number z z̄. The coordinate definition is \|z\| = √(x² + y²).

**Problem.** For all complex numbers z and w, \|zw\| = \|z\|\|w\|.

**How the definition helps.** The conjugate definition makes the squared modulus of a product a rearrangement of factors. Conjugation sends zw to z̄w̄, so \|zw\|² = (z z̄)(w w̄) = \|z\|²\|w\|². Taking nonnegative square roots gives the result. With coordinates, one would instead expand the squares of the real and imaginary parts of zw (our own comparison). The work moves into showing from complex multiplication that conjugation respects products (our own explanation).

**Wikipedia:** [Absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value). It says: “\|z\| = √(z · z̄).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A complex derivative as an i-linear map gives Cauchy–Riemann at once

**Remember:** The derivative's value on i is i times its value on 1.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 30A05 (Monogenic and polygenic functions of one complex variable), 26B05. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Identify ℂ with ℝ². Call f complex differentiable at z if it has a real linear approximation L there with L(iv) = iL(v) for every vector v. The usual definition takes the limit of (f(z + h) − f(z))/h over complex h → 0.

**Problem.** Let f = u + iv be complex differentiable at a point. Then ∂u/∂x = ∂v/∂y and ∂u/∂y = −∂v/∂x at that point.

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, the equations are just L(i) = iL(1) written in coordinates (our own). Here L(1) = ∂u/∂x + i∂v/∂x and L(i) = ∂u/∂y + i∂v/∂y (our own). Since iL(1) = −∂v/∂x + i∂u/∂x, comparing real and imaginary parts gives both equations (our own). The work moves into the lemma that the two definitions agree (our own). It holds because a real linear map that commutes with i is multiplication by one complex number (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cauchy–Riemann equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Riemann_equations). It says: “the partial derivatives of u and v exist and satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations at that point.”

**Paper or page:** [Cauchy-Riemann Equations/Necessary Condition](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Cauchy-Riemann_Equations/Necessary_Condition). It says: “The following two equations, known as the Cauchy-Riemann equations, hold for the partial derivatives of u and v:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Wirtinger derivative test makes holomorphic functions harmonic

**Remember:** One factor of the Laplacian already vanishes on holomorphic functions.

*True by definition.* MSC 30A05 (Monogenic and polygenic functions of one complex variable), 31A05. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a continuously differentiable function, define D = ½(∂/∂x − i∂/∂y) and E = ½(∂/∂x + i∂/∂y), the two Wirtinger operators. Call the function holomorphic if E sends it to zero. The usual definition uses a complex difference quotient.

**Problem.** The real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic. Their second partial derivatives in x and y sum to zero.

**How the definition helps.** The Wirtinger definition makes harmonicity follow from a factorization. On twice continuously differentiable functions, the Laplacian, the sum of the two second partial derivatives, is 4DE. This factorization follows by expanding the product and canceling the equal mixed partial derivatives. Since Ef = 0, the Laplacian of f is zero, so both parts have zero Laplacian. This is our own calculation. The equivalence with the difference quotient uses real differentiability, and the power series theorem supplies the second derivatives.

**Wikipedia:** [Wirtinger derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wirtinger_derivatives). It says: “The second Wirtinger derivative is also related with complex differentiation; ∂f/∂z̄ = 0 is equivalent to the Cauchy-Riemann equations in a complex form.”

**Paper or page:** [Real and Imaginary Parts of Holomorphic Function are Harmonic](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Real_and_Imaginary_Parts_of_Holomorphic_Function_are_Harmonic). It says: “Then u and v are harmonic functions.”

**Sources:**

- [W. Wirtinger, Zur formalen Theorie der Funktionen von mehr komplexen Veränderlichen, Mathematische Annalen 97 (1927), 357–375](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01447872)

### Differentiation preserves a power series radius

**Remember:** An nth root makes the derivative’s factor n vanish in the limit.

*True by definition.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable), 40A30. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the radius of convergence of ∑ aₙ(z − c)ⁿ as 1/limsup \|aₙ\|<sup>(1/n)</sup>, with 1/0 = ∞ and 1/∞ = 0. Geometrically, it is the supremum of the distances from c at which the series converges.

**Problem.** A complex power series and its termwise derivative have the same radius of convergence.

**How the definition helps.** The coefficient rule makes the extra factor n harmless, since its nth root tends to one (our own). Apply the rule to the derivative multiplied by the variable minus the center to align the powers (our own). That multiplication does not change convergence off the center (our own). The work goes into the Cauchy–Hadamard theorem, which gets the disk from the coefficient rule (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Radius of Convergence of Derivative of Complex Power Series](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Radius_of_Convergence_of_Derivative_of_Complex_Power_Series). It says: “Then R = R′.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Holomorphic as one power series on a disk gives antiderivatives there

**Remember:** Integrate each power, and the radius of convergence stays the same.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable), 30A05. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** On an open disk, describe a holomorphic function by one power series about the centre that converges on the whole disk. The usual definition asks for a complex derivative at each point. A theorem of Cauchy says that the two agree on disks.

**Problem.** Every holomorphic function on an open disk has an antiderivative defined throughout the disk.

**How the definition helps.** With one series on the whole disk, integrating term by term gives an explicit antiderivative (our own). The series of aₙ(z − c)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) has the same radius of convergence as the series for f, and differentiating it term by term gives back f (our own). The work moves into the theorem that a holomorphic function on a disk has one series valid on the whole disk, which rests on Cauchy's integral formula.

**Wikipedia:** [Analyticity of holomorphic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analyticity_of_holomorphic_functions). It says: “The argument, first given by Cauchy, hinges on Cauchy's integral formula and the power series expansion of the expression”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Log-convexity controls reciprocal signs

**Remember:** Nondecreasing coefficient ratios control the signs in the reciprocal series.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable). arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A positive sequence is log-convex if its ratios of successive terms never decrease. This is stronger than requiring positive coefficients in a power series.

**Problem.** For a power series of positive radius with positive log-convex coefficients, its reciprocal has nonpositive coefficients beyond the constant.

**How the definition helps.** Nondecreasing ratios provide the comparisons needed to keep every later reciprocal coefficient nonpositive. Our own explanation uses the identity f(x)(1/f(x)) = 1. Comparing coefficients gives a recurrence, and Kaluza’s sign test follows by induction. Our own counterexample has coefficients 1, 1, ½, ¼, …. Its reciprocal has quadratic coefficient 1 − ½ = ½.

**Paper or page:** [On Kaluza's sign criterion for reciprocal power series](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.5337v3). It says: “b₀ = 1/a₀ &gt; 0 and bₙ ≤ 0 for all n ∈ {1, 2, …}.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Power series make holomorphic functions differentiable to every order

**Remember:** Differentiate the power series term by term to get another power series.

*True by definition.* MSC 30B10 (Power series (including lacunary series) in one complex variable), 30E20. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call a function analytic if it equals a convergent power series near each point of its open domain. The usual definition of holomorphic asks for a complex derivative at every point.

**Problem.** Every holomorphic function has complex derivatives of all orders, and those derivatives are holomorphic.

**How the definition helps.** The power series definition makes each derivative analytic by termwise differentiation. The new series has the same radius of convergence, so we can repeat the step indefinitely. This is our own deduction from the equivalence of analyticity and complex differentiability. The hard part of that equivalence is Goursat’s theorem, which removes the continuity assumption from Cauchy’s integral theorem. Cauchy’s integral formula then gives the power series.

It says: “The theorem that every continuously complex-differentiable function is analytic is soft and due to Augustin Cauchy; the theorem that every complex-differentiable function is continuously differentiable is hard and due essentially to Édouard Goursat”

### Germs turn multivalued functions such as log z into true functions

**Remember:** Do not continue the value; continue the germ, and every branch gets its own point.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 30B40 (Analytic continuation of functions of one complex variable), 30F99. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A germ of an analytic function at a point z₀ is its power series at z₀. The set of all germs gets a topology. In it, a basic open set is the set of germs of one analytic function at all points of a disc. A connected component of this space is a Riemann surface, and on it the analytic continuation of a function is one single-valued function.

**Problem.** Analytic continuation of a germ, such as a germ of log z or √z, is a single-valued holomorphic function on the connected component of the space of germs that contains it.

**How the definition helps.** On the space of germs, each branch of the function is a different point, so continuation can never give two values at one point. In the plane, continuing log z once around the origin changes its value by 2πi, so the result is a 'multivalued function'. On its component of the space of germs, the logarithm is one function f with exp(f(z)) = z. What stays hard is to decide when continuation along different paths gives the same result, which is the monodromy theorem.

**Wikipedia:** [Analytic continuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_continuation), [Riemann surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_surface). It says: “The idea of finding the maximal analytic continuation of a function in turn led to the development of the idea of Riemann surfaces.”

**How the definition helps.** The added point ∞ gives each Möbius transformation a value at every point and a preimage of every point, so each one is a bijection. On the plane alone, z ↦ 1/z is undefined at 0 and never takes the value 0 (our own example). The condition ad − bc ≠ 0 excludes the constant maps. ### Counting zeros with multiplicity makes the argument principle exact

**Remember:** Count each zero by its multiplicity, and the winding gives the count.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 30C15 (Zeros of polynomials, rational functions, and other analytic functions of one complex variable (e.g., zeros of functions with bounded Dirichlet integral)), 30E20. arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A zero of f at a has multiplicity k if f(z) = (z − a)ᵏ g(z) with g(a) ≠ 0. A pole of order m is a point where f(z) = (z − a)⁻ᵐ h(z) with h(a) ≠ 0. Counting with multiplicity means each zero or pole is counted k or m times.

A count without multiplicity fails: for f(z) = z² on the unit circle, the integral is 2, but there is only one distinct zero (our own example). Multiplicity also makes the count stable under small changes of f, which is Rouché's theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Argument principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument_principle). It says: “where Z and P denote respectively the number of zeros and poles of f inside the contour C, with each zero and pole counted as many times as its multiplicity and order, respectively, indicate.”

### Requiring orientation makes conformal maps exactly the holomorphic ones

*True by definition.* MSC 30E20 (Integration, integrals of Cauchy type, integral representations of analytic functions in the complex plane). arXiv math.CV. Level 2: later undergraduate.

It says: “\\int \_T<sup>2T</sup>\\bigg\|\\sum <sub>p\\leqslant x</sub>\\frac{a(p)}{p<sup>1/2+it</sup>}\\bigg\|<sup>2k</sup>dt\\ll Tk!\\bigg(\\sum <sub>p\\leqslant x</sub>\\frac{\|a(p)\|<sup>2}{p}\\bigg</sup>)<sup>k</sup>.”

**Definition.** A disk automorphism is a holomorphic bijection from the disk onto itself. A finite Blaschke product is a product of finitely many such maps times a constant of modulus one. The number of factors is its degree. The positive-degree products are exactly the proper holomorphic disk maps, meaning inverse images of compact sets are compact.

**Problem.** Precomposing or postcomposing a nonconstant finite Blaschke product with a disk automorphism preserves its class and degree.

**How the definition helps.** Use the proper-map characterization, since composing with a homeomorphism preserves properness (our own). The homeomorphism also preserves the degree, which counts preimages of any disk point with multiplicity (our own). To prove the characterization, factor out the finite list of zeros (our own). Apply the maximum principle to the quotient and its reciprocal, whose boundary moduli tend uniformly to one (our own).

**Remember:** Zeros of bounded functions approach the circle fast enough to give a finite sum.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 30C15 (Zeros of polynomials, rational functions, and other analytic functions of one complex variable (e.g., zeros of functions with bounded Dirichlet integral)). arXiv math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A sequence in the unit disk meets the Blaschke condition if the sum of its distances to the unit circle is finite. This is stronger than requiring no accumulation point inside the disk.

**Problem.** A sequence in the disk, counted with repetitions, is the complete zero list of a nonzero bounded holomorphic function on the disk exactly when it satisfies the Blaschke condition.

**How the definition helps.** The finite sum rules out sequences that approach the circle too slowly (our own). The points 1 − 1/n for n ≥ 2 have no interior accumulation point, but their distances have divergent sum (our own). Jensen’s formula gives the necessary bound from the circular averages of the logarithm of the modulus (our own). Conversely, the sum ensures local uniform convergence of the normalized product with the prescribed zeros, after factoring out zeros at zero (our own).

### Cross-ratio distortion gives the Schwarzian derivative its chain rule

**Remember:** Cross-ratio distortion ratios multiply under composition, so their leading corrections add.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 30C45 (Special classes of univalent and multivalent functions of one complex variable (starlike, convex, bounded rotation, etc.)), 51B10. arXiv math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For distinct points z₁, z₂, z₃, z₄ approaching z, use the cross-ratio R = ((z₃ − z₁)(z₄ − z₂))/((z₃ − z₂)(z₄ − z₁)). Divide the cross-ratio of their images under f by R. The Schwarzian Sf at z is six times the coefficient of (z₁ − z₂)(z₃ − z₄) in the leading distortion term. The usual formula is Sf = (f″/f′)′ − ½(f″/f′)².

**Problem.** Where the holomorphic functions and the composite are defined and their derivatives are nonzero, S(f∘g) = ((Sf)∘g)·(g′)² + Sg. In particular, Möbius maps have zero Schwarzian wherever finite.

**How the definition helps.** The distortion definition gives the chain rule because the distortion ratio for a composite is the product of two ratios. The leading corrections add because each is already quadratic in the small differences. For f after g, the two differences each gain a factor of g′ to first order, giving the square in the formula. The article gives the expansion and its implication, and the multiplication step is our own explanation. The work moves into the Taylor calculation that identifies the coefficient with the differential formula.

**Wikipedia:** [Schwarzian derivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzian_derivative). It says: “This immediately yields the chain rule S(f∘g) = ((Sf)∘g)·(g′)² + Sg.”

### Normalizing univalent functions makes the Bieberbach coefficient bound statable

**Remember:** Fix f(0) = 0 and f′(0) = 1, then \|aₙ\| ≤ n.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 30C55 (General theory of univalent and multivalent functions of one complex variable), 30C50. arXiv math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A schlicht function is a one-to-one holomorphic function f on the unit disc with f(0) = 0 and f′(0) = 1. So f(z) = z + a₂z² + a₃z³ + … . Any one-to-one holomorphic g becomes schlicht after (g − g(0))/g′(0).

**Problem.** De Branges's theorem, once the Bieberbach conjecture, says that every schlicht function has \|aₙ\| ≤ n for all n ≥ 2. The Koebe function z/(1 − z)², with aₙ = n, shows that the bound is sharp.

**How the definition helps.** The normalization removes the freedom of scaling and translation, which would otherwise make the coefficients unbounded. Without it, cf is one-to-one for every c ≠ 0 and has coefficients caₙ, so no bound can hold (our own). The normalization also makes the class compact, since by Hurwitz's theorem a limit of one-to-one functions is one-to-one or constant (our own link). The hard part was the proof, which de Branges completed in 1985.

**Wikipedia:** [De Branges's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Branges%27s_theorem), [Hurwitz's theorem (complex analysis)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz%27s_theorem_%28complex_analysis%29). It says: “The statement concerns the Taylor coefficients aₙ of a univalent function, i.e., a one-to-one holomorphic function that maps the unit disk into the complex plane, normalized as is always possible so that a₀=0 and a₁=1.”

**Remember:** Two distortions multiply, and reversing a map swaps the bounds.

*True by definition.* MSC 30C62 (Quasiconformal mappings in the complex plane). arXiv math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For K ≥ 1, a plane homeomorphism is K-quasiconformal if it changes every curve family’s modulus by factors between 1/K and K. A nonnegative Borel density is admissible when its line integral along each locally rectifiable curve in the family is at least one. Modulus is the infimum of the area integrals of squared admissible densities. The differential definition bounds the ratio of the major and minor axes of infinitesimal ellipses.

**Problem.** The composition of quasiconformal maps with bounds K and L has bound KL. The inverse of a map with bound K has bound K.

**How the definition helps.** Apply the modulus inequalities successively for composition (our own). For inversion apply them to the inverse image of each curve family and exchange the inequalities (our own). The hard step is the equivalence between the modulus definition and the analytic definition using weak derivatives (our own).

### Geometric and analytic quasiconformality agree, so each proof can choose

**Remember:** Distortion of shapes and the Beltrami bound are the same condition.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 30C62 (Quasiconformal mappings in the complex plane), 30F60. arXiv math.DG, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the geometric sense, a K-quasiconformal map is a homeomorphism that changes the conformal modulus of each quadrilateral by at most a factor K. The modulus is a conformal invariant, like the ratio of the sides of a rectangle. In the analytic sense, it is a homeomorphism with weak derivatives that satisfy \|∂f/∂z̄\| ≤ k\|∂f/∂z\| almost everywhere, where k = (K−1)/(K+1). The theorem adds that these derivatives are locally square-integrable.

**Problem.** For a homeomorphism between plane domains, the geometric and the analytic definitions of K-quasiconformality are equivalent.

**How the definition helps.** Each definition makes some theorems immediate, and the equivalence lets every proof use the easier one. With the geometric definition, the inverse of a K-quasiconformal map is K-quasiconformal by definition (our own). Compositions multiply the constants, also by definition (our own). The analytic definition links the maps to the Beltrami equation ∂f/∂z̄ = μ ∂f/∂z (our own). The work moves into the proof that the two definitions agree.

**Paper or page:** [Survey on the Canonical Metrics on the Teichmüller Spaces and the Moduli Spaces of Riemann Surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00761). It says: “The geometric and the analytic definitions of K-quasiconformality are equivalent.”
