The work lies in finding variables and coefficients that reproduce the original equations and checking the diffusion and boundary inequalities.

**Paper or page:** [A Skew-Symmetric Energy Stable Almost Dissipation Free Formulation of the Compressible Navier-Stokes Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12038v2). It says: “C + Cᵀ = 0”

**Sources:**

- [Jan Nordström, A Skew-Symmetric Energy Stable Almost Dissipation Free Formulation of the Compressible Navier-Stokes Equations.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.12038v2)

### Relative energy blocks branching gas flows

**Remember:** Compare to the tangent at the state you want to track.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 76N10 (Existence, uniqueness, and regularity theory for compressible fluids and gas dynamics). arXiv math.AP, physics.flu-dyn. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a gas whose pressure depends only on density, define relative energy with two terms. Use half the density times squared velocity error. Add the internal energy per volume minus its tangent line at the comparison density. Total energy alone does not measure error from that state.

**Problem.** Consider a gas whose pressure is proportional to a power of density with exponent greater than one. Suppose a comparison solution satisfies the regularity and vacuum conditions of Theorem 1.4. Every weak solution satisfying its energy inequality with the same initial data has the same density and momentum.

**How the definition helps.** In our own reading, relative energy measures precisely the errors that must vanish, even where velocity alone has no physical meaning. Strict convexity detects density differences. The kinetic term then detects velocity differences wherever density is positive. The hard estimates justify comparison near vacuum and control the growth of relative energy. Starting from zero relative energy forces it to stay zero.

**Paper or page:** [Weak-Strong Uniqueness for the Isentropic Euler Equations with Possible Vacuum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.16560v1). It says: “ϱ = r and ϱu = rv in \[0, T\] × ℝᴺ.”

**Sources:**

- [Shyam Sundar Ghoshal, Animesh Jana and Emil Wiedemann, Weak-Strong Uniqueness for the Isentropic Euler Equations with Possible Vacuum.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.16560v1)

### Subtracting surface motion saves derivatives

**Remember:** Subtract what the moving coordinates contribute.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 76N30 (Waves in compressible fluids). arXiv math.AP, physics.flu-dyn. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In coordinates that flatten the moving water surface, the Alinhac good unknown of a field is four surface derivatives of the field minus a correction. The correction is the physical vertical derivative of the field times four surface derivatives of the coordinate map.

**Problem.** Suppose the vertical derivative of the coordinate map stays above a positive constant. Then the integrated squared size of four surface derivatives of the field is bounded using its good unknown, four surface derivatives of the map, and the largest first vertical derivative of the field.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, the correction removes the fourth derivative caused by moving the coordinates. Adding the correction back gives the stated bound by the triangle inequality. The substantive estimates control the errors when the fluid equations differentiate this corrected quantity.

**Paper or page:** [Compressible Gravity-Capillary Water Waves with Vorticity: Local Well-Posedness, Incompressible and Zero-Surface-Tension Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03600v5). It says: “be the Alinhac good unknowns associated with the smooth function f”

**Sources:**

- [Chenyun Luo and Junyan Zhang, Compressible Gravity-Capillary Water Waves with Vorticity: Local Well-Posedness, Incompressible and Zero-Surface-Tension Limits.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.03600v5)

### Pair coordinates isolate collision angles

**Remember:** At fixed center and speed, a collision only changes the angle.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 76P05 (Rarefied gas flows, Boltzmann equation in fluid mechanics). arXiv math.AP, physics.flu-dyn. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Describe two particle velocities by their average, their relative speed, and the direction of their difference. In two dimensions a single angle describes that direction. Exchanging the particles changes the angle by half a turn.

**Problem.** For a smooth positive symmetric pair density, the angular collision operator contributes a nonpositive rate of change to angular Fisher information. This information measures squared angular derivatives of log density, weighted by density and inverse squared relative speed.

**How the definition helps.** In our own reading, the coordinates reduce collisions at fixed average velocity and relative speed to changes in one angle. Lemma 3.3 pairs each angle with a possible outgoing angle. The resulting integral is minus a squared difference of angular derivatives with nonnegative weights. Deriving that identity supplies the sign.

**Paper or page:** [On the monotonicity of the Fisher information for the Boltzmann equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01183v1). It says: “where θ is an angular variable and F is π-periodic with respect to θ”

**Sources:**

- [Cyril Imbert, Luis Silvestre and Cédric Villani, On the monotonicity of the Fisher information for the Boltzmann equation.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01183v1)

### Density sorting measures excess energy

**Remember:** Compare with the lowest energy that preserves the density distribution.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 76S05 (Flows in porous media; filtration; seepage). arXiv math.AP, physics.flu-dyn. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Sort the density by height, with heavier fluid below lighter fluid. Keep the volume occupied by each density range unchanged. Define excess energy as the gravitational energy above that of the sorted density.

**Problem.** For the incompressible porous flow of Park's Theorem 1.1, near a density that decreases linearly with height, the integrated squared difference from the sorted density is at most a constant times the excess energy. So decay of excess energy gives convergence to the sorted density.

**How the definition helps.** Sorting provides one reference state for the whole motion because transport preserves the volume of each density range. Proposition 2.5 bounds the integrated squared density difference by a constant times the excess energy for these small perturbations. In our own account, taking square roots converts energy decay into density convergence. Proving the comparison and the energy decay requires separate estimates.

**Paper or page:** [Stability analysis of the incompressible porous media equation and the Stokes transport system via energy structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14187v2). It says: “the solution ρ(t) converges to the vertical rearrangement of the initial data”

**Sources:**

- [Jaemin Park, Stability analysis of the incompressible porous media equation and the Stokes transport system via energy structure.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14187v2)

### Relative energy controls the incompressible limit

**Remember:** Compare two flows by charging for their difference, not their separate energies.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 76T06 (Liquid-liquid two component flows), 76D05. arXiv math.AP, physics.flu-dyn. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Relative energy measures how far a fluid state lies from a reference state. Integrate half the density times the squared velocity difference and half the squared difference of the order-s composition derivatives. These derivatives weight each spatial frequency by its magnitude to the power s. Add the integral of the convex composition energy above its tangent at the reference composition.

**Problem.** On a periodic cube, compare the paper’s weak solutions with a smooth incompressible solution on a fixed interval of regularity. Initial compositions have equal means and converge in the norm controlling their mean-square derivatives through order s. With uniformly bounded initial energies and initial velocities converging in mean square, relative energy tends uniformly to zero as the density contrast vanishes.

**How the definition helps.** Relative energy expresses convergence of velocity and composition through one estimate. Weak solutions satisfy the equations after integration against smooth test functions. In our own words, convexity makes the tangent subtraction nonnegative. The work goes into bounding relative energy by a constant times the initial relative energy plus the density contrast.

**Paper or page:** [Weak solutions and incompressible limit of a quasi-incompressible Navier--Stokes/Cahn--Hilliard model for viscous two-phase flows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08090v1). It says: “E(φα, uα \| φ, u)(τ) ≔ ∫𝕋³ ½ρα\|u − uα\|²(τ) dx + ∫𝕋³ ½\|Λˢφ − Λˢφα\|²(τ) dx + ∫𝕋³ (Φ(φα) − Φ′(φ)(φα − φ) − Φ(φ))(τ) dx”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

## 78 Optics, electromagnetic theory

### Parallel chief rays stabilize magnification

**Remember:** If chief rays are parallel, changing object depth does not change their image positions.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A05 (Geometric optics). arXiv physics.optics. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The chief ray passes through the center of the opening that limits a bundle of rays. An object-space telecentric lens makes chief rays on the object side parallel to the optical axis.

**Problem.** In the small-angle ray model, hold the lens and detector fixed. Moving an object along the axis preserves the magnification measured by chief-ray positions on the detector.

**How the definition helps.** Parallel chief rays from points of the same lateral height follow the very same incoming line. In our own explanation, that line follows the same path through the lens and hits the same detector point. The work lies in positioning the limiting opening to obtain parallel rays. The image may lose focus.

**Wikipedia:** [Telecentric lens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecentric_lens). It says: “The entrance pupil is located at infinity, and chief rays before the objective are parallel to the optical axis.”

### Reduced radiance stays constant

**Remember:** Divide power by conserved ray volume and the ratio stays constant.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A05 (Geometric optics). arXiv physics.optics. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define radiance as power per projected area per solid angle. Define reduced radiance by dividing by the square of the refractive index. This is power per unit étendue, the weighted size of a ray bundle.

**Problem.** Reduced radiance is constant along a ray in lossless geometric optics with no ray splitting or scattering.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation uses conservation of both the power and the étendue of the same narrow bundle. Our own explanation puts the work in showing that ray propagation preserves this weighted measure, even when the unweighted area and angular spread change.

### Reduced ray angles give unit determinants

**Remember:** Index times angle keeps the ray map’s determinant at one.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A05 (Geometric optics). arXiv physics.optics. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For rays close to the optical axis, describe a ray by its height and nθ. Here θ is its small angle to the axis, and n is the speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in the medium.

**Problem.** In centered paraxial optics, propagation and refraction in one meridian give a ray transfer matrix of determinant one in these coordinates.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying the angle by n cancels the index ratio in the ordinary transfer determinant in our own calculation. With angle alone, refraction at a flat boundary gives the incident index divided by the outgoing index. Our own argument uses the small-angle refraction law and multiplication of determinants along the optical system.

**Remember:** A ray’s travel time need not be the shortest nearby time.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 78A05 (Geometric optics). arXiv physics.optics. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define a geometric ray by stationary travel time under small path changes with fixed endpoints. Stationary means that the first-order change vanishes. This replaces the rule that a ray always takes the least time.

**Problem.** At a smooth mirror in a uniform medium, a reflected ray makes equal angles with the surface normal, even when nearby paths take less time.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, shifting the reflection point along the mirror makes the travel-time derivative compare the two tangential ray components. Stationarity makes these components equal, giving the reflection law in our own calculation. A sufficiently concave mirror admits reflected paths whose travel time can decrease under a small change. The stationary rule covers them too.

**Wikipedia:** [Fermat's principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_principle). It says: “In order to be true in all cases, this statement must be weakened by replacing the "least" time with a time that is "stationary”

### Complex beam parameters add distance

**Remember:** One complex number tracks beam width and curvature as distance adds.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A10 (Physical optics). arXiv physics.optics. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a beam with a Gaussian intensity profile, combine its radius w and wavefront curvature radius R in one number q. Define 1/q = 1/R − iλ/(πw²), with wavelength λ in the medium. At radius w the intensity falls to exp(−2) times its central value.

**Problem.** In a uniform medium, the small-angle wave model sends q to q + d after propagation through distance d.

**How the definition helps.** The complex coordinate turns separate changes of width and curvature into addition of distance. Our own explanation uses the Gaussian solution of the small-angle wave equation. It gives q a constant imaginary part and a real part equal to distance from the beam waist.

### Jones matrices compose by multiplication

**Remember:** Put the matrix of the first optical element on the right.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A10 (Physical optics). arXiv physics.optics. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a fully polarized beam at one frequency, record the two complex electric field amplitudes perpendicular to its direction of travel. A linear element that preserves full polarization acts on this pair by a Jones matrix. This replaces separate tracking of the polarization ellipse and phase.

**Problem.** For a beam passing through a chain of linear elements, the chain’s Jones matrix is their product, with the first element on the right.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, multiplying matrices composes their actions on the field amplitudes. Our own calculation needs each element’s action on two basis inputs and matching bases between adjacent elements.

### Mueller matrices discard global phase

**Remember:** A common phase cancels when a field multiplies its conjugate.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A10 (Physical optics). arXiv physics.optics. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Represent polarization by the matrix of averaged products of field components with conjugated field components. A Mueller matrix acts on the four real coordinates of this matrix, rather than on the field amplitudes.

**Problem.** Multiplying a Jones matrix, which acts on field amplitudes, by a common phase leaves its induced Mueller matrix unchanged.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation uses the polarization update C ↦ JCJ†, where J† is the conjugate transpose. The phase in J cancels the opposite phase in J†. Our own explanation puts the work in deriving this update and converting the product matrix to the four real polarization coordinates.

**Definition.** Measure each wave’s average power per unit area crossing the interface. Divide the reflected and transmitted amounts by the incident amount to obtain reflectance and transmittance. These ratios include the angle of propagation.

**Problem.** Consider one plane wave striking a flat boundary between lossless homogeneous dielectrics, with nonzero incident power across it. With no surface sources, reflectance plus transmittance equals one.

**How the definition helps.** Using crossing power as the numerator turns the sum rule into the energy balance at the interface. Our own explanation uses the normal component of the energy flow to derive that balance. Squared electric field ratios alone omit the impedance and angle factors.

### Normalized coherence gives fringe visibility

**Remember:** At equal power, fringe contrast measures the magnitude of the normalized correlation.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A10 (Physical optics). arXiv physics.optics. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Average the product of one complex field and the conjugate of the other. Divide by the geometric mean of their average intensities to obtain their degree of coherence. Fringe visibility is the intensity range divided by the sum of the maximum and minimum intensities.

**Problem.** For two scalar beams of equal nonzero average intensity at the detector, fringe visibility equals the magnitude of their degree of coherence.

**How the definition helps.** Normalizing the field correlation makes its magnitude equal to the measured contrast when the intensities match. In our own derivation, varying only the relative phase makes the interference term swing between opposite extrema. Expanding the average intensity gives the stated ratio.

**Remember:** A polarization imbalance cannot exceed the light that carries it.

**Definition.** Represent the electric field perpendicular to the beam by a two-component complex vector. Average its outer product with its conjugate transpose to form the polarization matrix. Its trace is total intensity. The other Stokes parameters are the diagonal difference and twice the real and imaginary parts of one off-diagonal entry, using a fixed sign convention.

**Problem.** The length of the last three Stokes parameters cannot exceed total intensity. Every four-tuple with nonnegative intensity that meets this bound is realizable as a mixture of polarized beams.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, positivity makes the determinant nonnegative, which bounds the length of the three polarization parameters by total intensity. Our own example (1, 2, 0, 0) violates the bound and gives a negative intensity in one direction. Conversely, our own construction uses the eigenvectors as polarized beams and the nonnegative eigenvalues as their intensities.

**Remember:** The exterior derivative of an exterior derivative is zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A25 (Electromagnetic theory (general)), 35Q61, 58A10. arXiv math-ph, physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Write the electromagnetic field strength as F = dA. Here A is a potential 1-form, which assigns a linear measurement to each spacetime direction. The exterior derivative d turns A into a 2-form, which measures oriented area elements. The vector formulation instead starts with separate electric and magnetic fields.

**Problem.** Every field strength F = dA satisfies the homogeneous Maxwell equations dF = 0. In vector form, magnetic fields have zero divergence, and a changing magnetic field induces electric circulation.

**How the definition helps.** The potential makes both equations automatic because dF = d(dA) = 0. The vector proof uses separate identities for divergence and curl. The converse takes the Poincaré lemma, which gives a potential for any closed form on a smoothly contractible region (our own). A global potential can fail to exist when there is nonzero magnetic flux through a closed surface (our own).

### The electromagnetic tensor makes Maxwell’s equations Lorentz covariant

**Remember:** Tensor equations hold in every inertial frame if they hold in one.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A25 (Electromagnetic theory (general)), 83A05. arXiv math-ph, physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Combine the electric and magnetic fields into the electromagnetic tensor F, an antisymmetric array with two spacetime indices. The tensor formulation also combines charge and current densities into one spacetime vector. The usual vector formulation separates electric from magnetic and time from space.

**Problem.** The transformed fields and sources satisfy Maxwell’s equations in every inertial frame if they satisfy them in one. Lorentz transformations relate these frames and preserve the spacetime interval.

**How the definition helps.** The tensor definition makes covariance immediate because a Lorentz transformation changes both sides of each tensor equation by the same rule. With separate electric and magnetic vectors, one must check their mixing under a change of frame. The work moves into checking that the tensor equations reproduce the four vector equations (our own).

### The Lorenz gauge turns Maxwell's equations into wave equations

**Remember:** One gauge choice, and the potentials obey plain wave equations.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 78A25 (Electromagnetic theory (general)), 78A40. arXiv physics.class-ph, math-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The Lorenz gauge is the condition that the four-divergence of the electromagnetic four-potential is zero. In terms of the scalar potential φ and the vector potential A, this is ∇·A + (1/c²) ∂φ/∂t = 0.

**Problem.** In the Lorenz gauge, Maxwell's equations for the potentials become separate inhomogeneous wave equations, one for φ and one for each component of A. Their sources are the charge density and the components of the current density, and the form is visibly Lorentz invariant.

**How the definition helps.** The potentials are fixed only up to a gauge transformation, so we may impose one condition, and the Lorenz condition separates the equations while staying Lorentz invariant. The Coulomb gauge instead gives a scalar potential that responds instantly and is not Lorentz covariant. The Lorenz gauge still leaves some gauge freedom, by solutions of the wave equation, so it does not fix the gauge completely.

**Wikipedia:** [Gauge fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauge_fixing). It says: “It is unique among the constraint gauges in retaining manifest Lorentz invariance.”

**Definition.** Consider a straight, uniform hollow guide with a bounded, simply connected cross-section and a perfectly conducting wall. Fill it with a homogeneous isotropic dielectric. A transverse electromagnetic mode has both fields perpendicular to the guide axis.

**Problem.** At positive frequency, such a guide supports no nonzero transverse electromagnetic mode.

**How the definition helps.** Power conservation becomes equality of the squared vector norms for every input. Our own explanation assumes independent channels whose powers add and equal finite numbers of incoming and outgoing channels. A square linear map preserving that norm is unitary.

**Problem.** At fixed frequency, lossless reversible propagation in isotropic geometric optics preserves the étendue of a ray bundle between transverse sections without clipping or splitting.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, identifying étendue with phase space volume lets Liouville’s volume preservation theorem give conservation directly. **Remember:** Image contrast at each frequency comes from overlapping two shifted pupils.

**Remember:** Taking the Hodge star switches the two vacuum equations.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A25 (Electromagnetic theory (general)). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On oriented four-dimensional Lorentzian spacetime, combine the electric and magnetic components into one antisymmetric field F, a two-form. The metric defines the Hodge star ⋆, which exchanges complementary pairs of directions.

**Problem.** If F solves the source-free Maxwell equations, so does ⋆F.

**How the definition helps.** The two-form description writes both vacuum equations in the same way, dF = 0 and d⋆F = 0, where d denotes exterior differentiation. In our own proof, replacing F by ⋆F exchanges these equations because ⋆⋆F = −F. The work lies in identifying the two equations with Maxwell’s component equations.

**Definition.** On a compact oriented Riemannian manifold without boundary, fix the integrals of a closed field F over all closed cycles of its degree. These fluxes specify its cohomology class. Closed means dF = 0, where d is exterior differentiation.

**Problem.** Let F have degree k in dimension n, and let j be an exact form of degree n − k + 1. Exact means that j is an exterior derivative. Each class contains one closed F satisfying d⋆F = j, where ⋆ is the metric’s Hodge star.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing the fluxes prevents adding a nonzero harmonic field, one satisfying both homogeneous equations. Our own example is a constant area form on a flat torus with zero current. The Hodge decomposition gives existence and shows that a harmonic field with zero fluxes vanishes.

**Remember:** The derivative of the current vanishes because the current is itself a derivative.

**Paper or page:** [Symmetry-induced quasicrystalline waveguides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.14906v1). It says: “T(ω)⁻¹ = ST(ω)S”

**Sources:**

- [Bryn Davies, Richard V Craster — Symmetry-induced quasicrystalline waveguides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.14906v1)

### Transfer traces detect band gaps

**Remember:** A trace beyond two in magnitude gives one growing mode and one shrinking mode.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 78A48 (Composite media; random media in optics and electromagnetic theory). arXiv physics.optics. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a periodic scalar wave equation, define T to map the field and its slope across one period. Assume T is real and has determinant one.

**Problem.** At a real frequency, the repeated medium has an exponentially growing and an exponentially decaying mode exactly when \|tr T\| &gt; 2.

**How the definition helps.** One matrix describes every period, so its eigenvalues give the growth factors. Our own derivation uses the characteristic polynomial λ² − tr(T)λ + 1. Its roots have magnitudes on opposite sides of one exactly when \|tr T\| &gt; 2.

**Paper or page:** [Symmetry-induced quasicrystalline waveguides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.14906v1), [Symmetry-induced quasicrystalline waveguides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.14906v1). It says: “In this case, \|tr(T)\| &gt; 2 and T is said to be hyperbolic.”

**Sources:**

- [Bryn Davies, Richard V Craster — Symmetry-induced quasicrystalline waveguides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.14906v1)

### Envelope extraction preserves waveguide stability

**Remember:** Removing a unit phase does not change the stability constant.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A50 (Antennas, waveguides in optics and electromagnetic theory). arXiv math.NA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write the field as a known oscillation times an unknown function called its envelope. For real k, multiply by exp(ikz) to pass from field to envelope at axial position z.

**Problem.** If the original operator satisfies ‖Au‖ ≥ α‖u‖ in the paper’s integral square norms, the envelope operator satisfies the same bound, and conversely.

**How the definition helps.** Changing to the envelope preserves both norms because the oscillation has magnitude one. Our own explanation transfers the operator domain by the same multiplication. The original waveguide estimate supplies the value of α.

**Paper or page:** [Stability Analysis for Electromagnetic Waveguides. Part 1: Acoustic and Homogeneous Electromagnetic Waveguides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04521v2). It says: “bounded below if and only if operator A is bounded below, and the corresponding boundedness below constants are identical”

**Sources:**

- [Jens Markus Melenk, Leszek Demkowicz, Stefan Henneking — Stability Analysis for Electromagnetic Waveguides. Part 1: Acoustic and Homogeneous Electromagnetic Waveguides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04521v2)

### Transparent boundaries preserve exterior solutions

**Remember:** The exact boundary map carries the whole exterior problem to the surface.

*True by definition.* MSC 78A45 (Diffraction, scattering), 78M10. arXiv math.NA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The transparent boundary map on a sphere around the obstacle sends the tangential electric field of an outgoing exterior wave to its magnetic boundary data. It is exact, unlike a local absorbing rule.

**Problem.** For time-harmonic Maxwell scattering, impose this map on the scattered field at the sphere. The resulting bounded problem has as its solution the restriction of the full solution.

**How the definition helps.** The map enforces exactly the boundary data of an outgoing exterior field. In our own explanation, this replaces an approximate local rule and lets the inner and outer fields join. The work lies in solving the exterior problem uniquely and expressing its map as an infinite series.

**Paper or page:** [An Adaptive Finite Element DtN Method for Maxwell's Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09203v1). It says: “an exact transparent boundary condition is introduced and the scattering problem is reduced equivalently into a bounded domain.”

**Sources:**

- [Gang Bao, Mingming Zhang, Xue Jiang, Peijun Li, Xiaokai Yuan — An Adaptive Finite Element DtN Method for Maxwell's Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09203v1)

### Born fields reveal Fourier arcs

**Remember:** Each propagating detector frequency samples one point on the object’s Fourier arc.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 78A46 (Inverse problems (including inverse scattering) in optics and electromagnetic theory). arXiv physics.optics. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Born approximation replaces the total field inside the scattering source by the incoming wave. The resulting scattered field depends linearly on the object’s contrast, its departure from the background medium.

**Problem.** Illuminate a bounded, compactly supported contrast with a scalar plane wave in two dimensions. Beyond the object, measure the Born field along a line perpendicular to the incoming direction. Its propagating Fourier components give the contrast transform on a shifted circular arc, up to a known factor.

**How the definition helps.** Replacing the unknown field by a plane wave turns its product with the contrast into a shift in Fourier coordinates. Our own explanation uses the outgoing response to a point source to obtain the arc and the factor. The theorem concerns the approximate field itself.

**Paper or page:** [Diffraction Tomography, Fourier Reconstruction, and Full Waveform Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07921v2). It says: “\\mathcal{F}<sub>1</sub>u<sup>{\\mathrm{Born}}</sup>(k<sub>1</sub>, r\_{\\mathrm{M}}) = \\sqrt{2 \\pi } \\frac{\\i \\mathrm e<sup>{\\i</sup> \\kappa r\_{\\mathrm{M}}}}{2 \\kappa } \\mathcal{F}f\\left(k<sub>1</sub>, \\kappa -k<sub>0</sub> \\right).”

**Sources:**

- [Florian Faucher, Clemens Kirisits, Michael Quellmalz, Otmar Scherzer, Eric Setterqvist — Diffraction Tomography, Fourier Reconstruction, and Full Waveform Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07921v2)

### Untwisting reduces helical mode dimension

**Remember:** Follow the helix and separate out the phase along its length.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 78A50 (Antennas, waveguides in optics and electromagnetic theory). arXiv physics.optics. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Describe a circular helical waveguide in coordinates that follow its bending and rotation. Assume its cross section and refractive index profile stay fixed in those coordinates. A transverse scalar mode has a fixed cross-sectional shape multiplied by a phase that advances uniformly along the guide.

**Problem.** For the paper’s scalar wave equation with zero boundary values, finding such modes with real propagation constant reduces to a cross-sectional equation. The propagation constant, or phase change per unit length, enters at most quadratically.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the moving coordinates make the mode profile and wave equation coefficients independent of distance along the helix. Each longitudinal derivative introduces one factor of the propagation constant in our own calculation. The second-order wave equation therefore gives at most two factors. The paper derives the transformed equation and proves equivalence in both directions.

**Paper or page:** [Guided modes of helical waveguides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03276v1). It says: “Next, exploiting the constant torsion and curvature of the Frenet frame of a circular helix, the 3D eigenproblem is further reduced to a two-dimensional (2D) eigenproblem on the waveguide cross section.”

**Sources:**

- [Jay Gopalakrishnan and Michael Neunteufel, Guided modes of helical waveguides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.03276v1)

### Compatible derivatives preserve Gauss’s law

**Remember:** Two successive discrete derivatives vanish, so the Gauss constraint cannot drift.

*True by definition.* MSC 78M10 (Finite element, Galerkin and related methods applied to problems in optics and electromagnetic theory). arXiv math.NA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a closed surface, choose mesh versions of gradient and curl so that curl after gradient gives zero. Define charge from the initial electric field and the accumulated current in the same mesh equations.

**Problem.** As time varies continuously, the mesh electric field satisfies Gauss’s law. Its discrete divergence equals the charge at each time.

**How the definition helps.** Testing the field update against a mesh gradient removes the curl term, leaving exactly the prescribed charge update. Our own explanation uses the same projected current in both updates. Lemma 13 supplies the zero composition for the paper’s mesh spaces.

**Paper or page:** [A polytopal discrete de Rham complex on manifolds, with application to the Maxwell equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16130v3), [A polytopal discrete de Rham complex on manifolds, with application to the Maxwell equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16130v3). It says: “\\langle \\underline{E}<sub>h</sub>(t),\\underline{{\\mathrm{d}}}<sup>0<sub>r</sup>,h</sub>\\underline{{v}}<sub>h</sub><sup>0\\rangle</sup> = -\\langle \\rho \_h(t),\\underline{{v}}<sub>h</sub><sup>0\\rangle</sup>”

**Sources:**

- [Jérôme Droniou, Marien Hanot, Todd Oliynyk — A polytopal discrete de Rham complex on manifolds, with application to the Maxwell equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16130v3)

### Vertex quadrature gives local mass solves

**Remember:** Sample products at vertices and the mass matrix separates by vertex.

*True by definition.* MSC 78M10 (Finite element, Galerkin and related methods applied to problems in optics and electromagnetic theory). arXiv math.NA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A mass matrix records integrals of products of basis fields on a mesh. Replace each integral with a weighted sum over vertices. Choose the paper’s basis fields, each nonzero at just one sampled vertex.

**Problem.** The mass matrix in the Maxwell time step has one diagonal block for each vertex.

**How the definition helps.** Products of basis fields assigned to different vertices vanish at every sample point. Our own explanation groups the fields by vertex to obtain the blocks. The remaining work is to show that sampling gives a norm comparable to exact integration.

**Paper or page:** [A Yee-like finite-element scheme for Maxwell's equations on unstructured grids](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01182v1). It says: “with one block per vertex of the mesh coupling all degrees of freedom not vanishing at this vertex”

**Sources:**

- [Herbert Egger, Bogdan Radu — A Yee-like finite-element scheme for Maxwell's equations on unstructured grids](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01182v1)

### Combined fields avoid false resonances

**Remember:** An imaginary wavenumber removes false cavity resonances from the boundary equation.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 78M15 (Boundary element methods applied to problems in optics and electromagnetic theory). arXiv math.NA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Describe the scattered field by electric and magnetic sources on the conductor’s surface. Combine their exterior boundary values with interior boundary values computed at a purely imaginary wave number.

**Problem.** For a bounded perfect conductor with a locally Lipschitz graph as boundary, the paper’s combined equation has at most one solution per positive wave number.

**How the definition helps.** The interior terms prevent a standing wave inside the conductor from creating a false solution of the boundary equation. Our own example is a spherical cavity at a frequency where it supports a standing wave. The proof uses exterior uniqueness and a positive lower bound for the interior operators.

**Paper or page:** [An operator preconditioned combined field integral equation for electromagnetic scattering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02289v3). It says: “has at most one solution”

**Sources:**

- [Van Chien Le, Kristof Cools — An operator preconditioned combined field integral equation for electromagnetic scattering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02289v3)

### A discrete product preserves energy balance

**Remember:** Use a product that respects the discrete derivative to keep the energy law.

*True by definition.* MSC 78M20 (Finite difference methods applied to problems in optics and electromagnetic theory). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In Sushch’s model, store electromagnetic field values on oriented vertices, edges, faces, and cells of a spatial grid. Time stays continuous. Combine the values using the model’s cup product, a multiplication that respects the derivative product rule on the grid.

**Problem.** For the paper’s spatially discrete Maxwell system in a vacuum with a current, energy loss equals outgoing flux plus work on the current.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the cup product lets one expand the net energy flux using the grid’s derivative product rule. Maxwell’s equations and the model’s relations between fields then give the energy change and the work on the current. Our own comparison requires those relations as well as the product rule to recover the balance from sampled fields.

**Paper or page:** [On a semi-discrete model of Maxwell's equations in three and two dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26427v1). It says: “dᶜ(E∪H) = −½ d/dt(E∪D+B∪H) − E∪J.”

**Sources:**

- [Volodymyr Sushch, On a semi-discrete model of Maxwell's equations in three and two dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26427v1)

### Compatible differences enforce zero divergence

**Remember:** Take a discrete divergence of the eigenvalue equation to get zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 78M20 (Finite difference methods applied to problems in optics and electromagnetic theory). arXiv math.NA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a grid, let C approximate curl and D approximate divergence. Choose their difference formulas together so that DC = 0.

**Problem.** Let L = CMCᵀ be the paper’s matrix for applying curl twice with a weight matrix M. Every eigenvector of L with nonzero eigenvalue has zero discrete divergence.

**How the definition helps.** The choice DC = 0 makes DL zero before any eigenvectors are computed. In our own proof, applying D to Lv = λv gives λDv = 0. Constructing compatible grid formulas supplies the essential identity.

**Paper or page:** [Kernel compensation method for Maxwell eigenproblem with mimetic finite difference discretization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19379v1). It says: “then discrete divergence-free condition Bvₕ = 0 holds.”

**Sources:**

- [Chenhao Jin, Yinhua Xia, Yan Xu — Kernel compensation method for Maxwell eigenproblem with mimetic finite difference discretization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.19379v1)

## 80 Classical thermodynamics, heat transfer

### Kelvin's temperature scale makes the Carnot efficiency universal

**Remember:** In a reversible engine, the ratio of temperatures is the ratio of heats.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A05 (Foundations of thermodynamics and heat transfer), 80A10. arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Kelvin's thermodynamic temperature is defined by reversible engines. If a reversible engine takes heat Q₁ from one reservoir and gives heat Q₂ to another, then T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂. One reference point fixes the unit.

**Problem.** This temperature does not depend on any particular substance. Every reversible engine between two reservoirs has efficiency 1 − T(cold)/T(hot).

**How the definition helps.** Kelvin defined temperature by the ratio that Carnot's theorem fixes, so the efficiency formula holds by definition. Carnot's theorem says that all reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency. So the ratio of heats depends only on the reservoirs, and 1 − Q(cold)/Q(hot) equals 1 − T(cold)/T(hot). The physics that remains is to show that this scale agrees with the ideal-gas thermometer.

**Wikipedia:** [Thermodynamic temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermodynamic_temperature). It says: “it is this definition of the thermodynamic temperature that enables us to represent the Carnot efficiency in terms of T(H) and T(C)”

**Sources:**

- [Thomson, W. (Lord Kelvin) (1848). On an absolute thermometric scale founded on Carnot's theory of the motive power of heat. Philosophical Magazine, October 1848.](https://zapatopi.net/kelvin/papers/on_an_absolute_thermometric_scale.html)

### The zeroth law of thermodynamics makes temperature well defined

**Remember:** Temperature is the label of an equivalence class.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A05 (Foundations of thermodynamics and heat transfer), 80A10. arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** The zeroth law says that two systems each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other. With reflexivity, this makes thermal equilibrium an equivalence relation.

**Problem.** There is a quantity, temperature, that is equal for two systems exactly when they are in thermal equilibrium.

**How the definition helps.** An equivalence relation sorts all systems into disjoint classes, so a temperature is just a label for a class. The existence of temperature is thus close to a restatement of the law. A thermometer in equilibrium with a system reads the class of that system. The law gives no order of hotness and no preferred numerical scale.

**Wikipedia:** [Zeroth law of thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeroth_law_of_thermodynamics). It says: “It makes the relation of thermal equilibrium between systems an equivalence relation, which can represent equality of some quantity associated with each system.”

**Sources:**

- [Carathéodory, C. (1909). Untersuchungen über die Grundlagen der Thermodynamik. Mathematische Annalen 67, 355–386.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01450409)

### Enthalpy gives heat at constant pressure

**Remember:** Add pressure times volume to turn constant-pressure heating into a state change.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define enthalpy as internal energy plus pressure times volume. Use it in place of internal energy for heating a closed system at constant pressure.

**Problem.** Consider a closed system whose only work is expansion against a constant pressure equal to the system pressure. The heat supplied equals its enthalpy increase when bulk kinetic and potential energies stay fixed.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, the increase in pressure times volume exactly accounts for expansion work. The first law then turns the sum of internal energy change and expansion work into the heat supplied.

**Wikipedia:** [Enthalpy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy). It says: “at constant pressure the enthalpy change equals the energy exchanged with the environment by heat.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Thermal resistances add in series

**Remember:** The same heat crosses each layer, so the temperature drops add.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A19 (Diffusive and convective heat and mass transfer, heat flow). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define a layer’s thermal resistance as its temperature drop divided by the steady rate of heat flow through it. For a flat layer of thickness L, area A, and constant thermal conductivity k, this gives L/(kA). Conductivity measures heat transport within the material.

**Problem.** In steady one-dimensional conduction with no internal heat sources, the total resistance of layers in series equals the sum of their resistances. Perfect contact introduces no extra resistance.

**How the definition helps.** Our own calculation adds the temperature drops and divides by the common heat flow to get the sum of resistances. Our own account puts the work in deriving each resistance from Fourier’s law and using steady energy balance to equate the flows.

**Wikipedia:** [Thermal conductance and resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_conductance_and_resistance). It says: “When resistances are in series, the total resistance is the sum of the resistances:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Bit reset costs heat

**Remember:** The heat bound pays for lost uncertainty, not for changing a bit.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 80A05 (Foundations of thermodynamics and heat transfer). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A perfect reset sends both values of a bit to one fixed value. Assume the two initial values are equally likely, have equal internal entropy, and have no correlations with other systems. Require the final memory state to have the same internal entropy as either initial value.

**Problem.** Let the controller return to its initial state, with a single bath at absolute temperature T taking up all exported entropy. Resetting the bit sends at least kT ln 2 of heat to the bath, where k is Boltzmann’s constant.

**How the definition helps.** Our own entropy balance uses the reset definition to count exactly k ln 2 of lost memory entropy. The second law requires the bath to gain at least that much. In our own counterexample, an auxiliary blank bit takes the original value as the first bit resets. This reversible swap preserves their joint entropy.

**Wikipedia:** [Landauer's principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landauer%27s_principle). It says: “erasure resets a memory that may be in either of two distinguishable physical states into a fixed state”

**Sources:**

- [Rolf Landauer, Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183)

### Energy potentials yield Maxwell relations

**Remember:** Choose the right potential, then swap the order of differentiation.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a simple compressible system of fixed composition, write internal energy U in terms of entropy S and volume V. Temperature T and negative pressure −P are its respective partial derivatives. Define three further potentials by H = U + PV, F = U − TS, and G = H − TS.

**Problem.** Suppose each potential has continuous second derivatives in its own variables. Each gives one Maxwell relation between measurable derivatives. For F(T,V), the volume derivative of entropy at fixed temperature equals the temperature derivative of pressure at fixed volume.

**How the definition helps.** Each potential gives two observable quantities as its first derivatives, so exchanging the differentiation order relates their rates of change. Our own example uses F in place of U because dF = −S dT − P dV. The physical input is the equilibrium energy balance dU = T dS − P dV.

**Wikipedia:** [Maxwell relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell_relations). It says: “the order of differentiation of an analytic function of two variables is irrelevant”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Enthalpy survives insulated throttling

**Remember:** A throttle trades flow work against internal energy.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define specific enthalpy as h = u + Pv, where u and v are internal energy and volume per unit mass. The term Pv includes the work of pushing fluid into or out of a region at pressure P.

**Problem.** Suppose fluid flows steadily through an insulated valve with negligible changes in speed and height. If no moving part exchanges work with the fluid, its specific enthalpy stays constant. An ideal gas with positive heat capacity then keeps its temperature.

**How the definition helps.** In our own balance, enthalpy groups the internal energy and pressure work that travel together through the valve. Our own account puts the work in the steady flow energy balance. The temperature claim separately uses that ideal gas enthalpy depends only on temperature.

**Wikipedia:** [Joule–Thomson effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joule%E2%80%93Thomson_effect). It says: “In a Joule–Thomson expansion the enthalpy remains constant.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gibbs energy tracks total entropy

**Remember:** At fixed temperature and pressure, rising total entropy means falling Gibbs energy.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define Gibbs energy as internal energy plus pressure times volume minus temperature times entropy. Use it to compare a closed system’s equilibrium states at the same positive temperature and pressure as its surroundings.

**Problem.** Suppose the system exchanges heat with one temperature reservoir and does only expansion work against the fixed external pressure. Gibbs energy cannot increase in a spontaneous change between these states.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, Gibbs energy combines the system and surroundings terms in the total entropy change. The reservoir loses the heat gained by the system, while the first law accounts for expansion work. Our own calculation gives ΔG = −TΔSₜₒₜ, so the second law gives ΔG ≤ 0.

**Wikipedia:** [Gibbs free energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs_free_energy). It says: “The equation can be also seen from the perspective of the system taken together with its surroundings”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Grand potential gives bulk pressure

**Remember:** Subtract the temperature and particle terms, leaving the pressure term.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For one species in equilibrium, subtract TS and μN from internal energy U to obtain the grand potential Ω. Here T is temperature, S is entropy, and N counts particles. The chemical potential μ is the derivative of U with respect to N at fixed S and volume V. The new potential uses T, V and μ as independent variables.

**Problem.** Suppose internal energy U is differentiable and scales linearly when entropy, volume and particle number all scale together. For this homogeneous bulk system, Ω = −PV, where P is pressure.

**How the definition helps.** Our own calculation cancels two terms from the extensive internal energy using the definition of the grand potential. Euler’s theorem gives U = TS − PV + μN because U scales linearly with its extensive variables. Our own account puts the physical work in justifying that scaling, which neglects surface and other finite-size effects.

**nLab:** [Legendre transformation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Legendre+transformation). It says: “Some of the standard choices are enthalpy H, Helmholtz free energy F, Gibbs free energy G, internal energy U, etc.”

**Wikipedia:** [Grand potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_potential). It says: “all extensive quantities (particle number, energy, entropy, potentials, ...) must grow linearly with volume”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Helmholtz energy bounds work

**Remember:** The decrease in Helmholtz energy bounds the work the system can deliver.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let a closed system exchange heat with one bath at constant temperature T. At each equilibrium endpoint at temperature T, define Helmholtz energy by F = U − TS, using internal energy U and entropy S.

**Problem.** Between equilibrium states of a closed system in one heat bath at fixed temperature, delivered work is at most −ΔF. A reversible path, when available under the same constraints, achieves the bound.

**How the definition helps.** Our own derivation collects the two terms that bound the work in F. In our own calculation, conservation of energy gives delivered work Q − ΔU, where Q is heat input. Our own account puts the physical work in the second law for the system and bath, which gives Q ≤ TΔS.

**Wikipedia:** [Helmholtz free energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz_free_energy). It says: “the total amount of work that can be extracted in an isothermal process is limited by the free-energy decrease”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Homogeneity of the energy turns Euler's theorem into the Gibbs–Duhem equation

**Remember:** Scale the whole system, and its intensive variables lose one freedom.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics), 82B30. arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech, math-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Extensive variables, such as entropy S, volume V and particle numbers Nᵢ, add up over the parts of a system. A system is homogeneous when its internal energy U(S, V, N₁, …) is first-order homogeneous. That means that multiplying all extensive variables by λ multiplies U by λ.

**Problem.** Gibbs–Duhem equation: S dT − V dP + Σ Nᵢ dμᵢ = 0, where T is temperature, P pressure and μᵢ the chemical potentials. So the intensive variables cannot all change independently.

**How the definition helps.** Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions gives U = TS − PV + Σ μᵢNᵢ at once. Comparing its differential with the fundamental relation dU = T dS − P dV + Σ μᵢ dNᵢ leaves the Gibbs–Duhem equation. So the equation is nearly the definition of homogeneity. What stays hard is to justify extensivity for real matter, which needs forces of short range (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Gibbs–Duhem equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs%E2%80%93Duhem_equation). It says: “The Gibbs−Duhem equation applies to homogeneous thermodynamic systems. It does not apply to inhomogeneous systems such as small thermodynamic systems”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Measuring hotness by β = 1/kT puts negative temperatures above infinite ones

**Remember:** Heat always flows from smaller β to larger β.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics), 82B30. arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech, math-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Thermodynamic temperature is defined by 1/T = dS/dE, the change of entropy per change of energy. Thermodynamic beta, or coldness, is β = 1/(kT), where k is Boltzmann's constant. When entropy falls as energy rises, as in a system of spins with bounded energy, T is negative.

**Problem.** Heat flows from the system with the smaller β to the system with the larger β, with no exceptions. Stated with T this fails, because a system at negative temperature is hotter than any system at positive temperature.

**How the definition helps.** When energy dE passes from system 1 to system 2, the total entropy changes by k(β₂ − β₁)dE (our own derivation). The second law needs this to be positive, so heat flows toward larger β. As the energy rises, β runs continuously from +∞ through 0 to −∞, while T jumps from +∞ to −∞. Negative temperature needs an upper bound on the energy, so ordinary gases cannot have it (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Negative temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_temperature). It says: “Because it avoids the abrupt jump from +∞ to −∞, β is considered more natural than T.”

**Sources:**

- [N. F. Ramsey, Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics at Negative Absolute Temperatures, Physical Review 103 (1956), 20–28](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.103.20)
- [E. M. Purcell and R. V. Pound, A nuclear spin system at negative temperature, Physical Review 81 (1951), 279–280](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.81.279)

### Reduced Gibbs energy reveals enthalpy

**Remember:** Temperature scaling turns the Gibbs derivative into an enthalpy measurement.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** At positive absolute temperature T, divide Gibbs energy G by T. Write G = H − TS, where S is entropy. Enthalpy H is internal energy plus pressure times volume.

**Problem.** At fixed pressure and composition, the temperature derivative of G/T is −H/T² in a smooth equilibrium phase.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by temperature puts both terms of G = H − TS into the quotient rule, where the entropy terms cancel. Our own calculation uses the equilibrium identity dG/dT = −S at fixed pressure and composition. It gives d(G/T)/dT = (−TS − G)/T² = −H/T².

**Wikipedia:** [Gibbs–Helmholtz equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibbs%E2%80%93Helmholtz_equation). It says: “The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation can be derived by this second master equation”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Restricting the third law to perfect crystals excludes residual entropy

**Remember:** One ground state means zero entropy at zero temperature.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics), 82B30. arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech, math-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A perfect crystal of a pure substance is one with a unique ground state. So it has exactly one microstate at absolute zero.

**Problem.** For every perfect crystal, the entropy S tends to 0 as T tends to 0. For glasses and for crystals with frozen disorder, such as ice, the entropy near absolute zero stays positive.

**How the definition helps.** With a unique ground state, Boltzmann's formula S = k ln Ω, where Ω counts the microstates, gives k ln 1 = 0. So the law is nearly the definition of 'perfect'. The word 'perfect' excludes glasses and crystals with defects or frozen disorder, such as ice, which keep a residual entropy. Pauling explained the residual entropy of ice by the many ways to place its hydrogen atoms (our own, from Pauling's paper).

**Wikipedia:** [Third law of thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_law_of_thermodynamics). It says: “Some crystals form defects which cause a residual entropy. This residual entropy disappears when the kinetic barriers to transitioning to one ground state are overcome.”

**Sources:**

- [L. Pauling, The Structure and Entropy of Ice and of Other Crystals with Some Randomness of Atomic Arrangement, Journal of the American Chemical Society 57 (1935), 2680–2684](https://doi.org/10.1021/ja01315a102)

### A logarithmic mean gives heat flow

**Remember:** Average the temperature gap logarithmically when the gap changes exponentially along the exchanger.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 80A19 (Diffusive and convective heat and mass transfer, heat flow). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let a and b be the positive temperature differences between the hot and cold streams at the two ends of a heat exchanger. Define their logarithmic mean as (a − b)/log(a/b) when they differ. For equal gaps, use their common value.

**Problem.** Consider steady parallel or counterflow without heat loss or heat conduction along the streams. Assume constant overall transfer coefficient and constant heat capacity rates, meaning heat carried per unit time per degree. The heat transfer rate equals coefficient times exchange area times the logarithmic mean.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, this mean equals the average temperature gap over the exchange area. The stream energy balances make the gap exponential in cumulative exchange area, including a constant gap as a limiting case in our own derivation.

**Wikipedia:** [Logarithmic mean temperature difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logarithmic_mean_temperature_difference). It says: “When the two temperature differences are equal, this formula does not directly resolve, so the LMTD is conventionally taken to equal its limit value”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Effusivity weights contact temperature

**Remember:** The material with higher effusivity pulls the contact temperature closer to its own.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 80A19 (Diffusive and convective heat and mass transfer, heat flow). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define thermal effusivity as √(kc), where k is thermal conductivity and c is heat capacity per unit volume. Conductivity relates heat flow to a temperature gradient. Heat capacity measures the energy needed for a unit temperature rise.

**Problem.** Two homogeneous half-spaces placed in perfect planar contact have constant interface temperature. With uniform initial temperatures and constant material properties, that temperature is the mean weighted by the two effusivities.

**How the definition helps.** Effusivity gives each material’s weight in the formula for the shared contact temperature. In our own derivation, the heat equation gives each side’s heat flux as its effusivity times its temperature drop divided by √(πt). Matching the fluxes cancels the common time factor in our own calculation.

**Wikipedia:** [Thermal effusivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_effusivity). It says: “the temperature at the contact surface Tₘ will be a weighted mean based on their relative effusivities.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Area weighting makes view factors reciprocal

**Remember:** Swap emitter and receiver after restoring the area used to normalize.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A21 (Radiative heat transfer). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Suppose every point on each surface emits equally per unit area, with power per solid angle proportional to the cosine from the normal. The view factor is the fraction of emitted power reaching the other surface directly through transparent space. Multiply this fraction by the emitting area.

**Problem.** For two diffusely emitting surfaces, each view factor times its emitting area is unchanged when the surfaces swap roles.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, multiplying by area removes the emitter’s normalization and leaves a symmetric integral over visible point pairs. Its kernel contains both projection cosines divided by π times the squared separation. Exchanging the points therefore preserves the integral in our own proof. The physical step derives the kernel from diffuse emission and straight ray paths.

**Wikipedia:** [View factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/View_factor). It says: “Aᵢ Fᵢ→ⱼ = Aⱼ Fⱼ→ᵢ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Radiosity linearizes enclosure radiation

**Remember:** Track all outgoing radiation, and each reflection reuses the same unknown.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 80A21 (Radiative heat transfer). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Radiosity is the total radiant power leaving a surface per unit area, including emission and reflection. A diffuse surface sends radiation in each direction with intensity proportional to the cosine of its angle from the surface normal.

**Problem.** Consider an enclosure with opaque surfaces at known temperatures and a medium that transmits all radiation between them. Assume each surface emits and reflects diffusely, with wavelength-independent properties and uniform radiosity. Then the unknown surface radiosities satisfy a linear system.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, each surface receives a linear combination of the outgoing radiosities, weighted by the fractions that reach it. Our own calculation adds its emission to a fixed fraction of that incoming radiation to obtain its outgoing total. Our own account puts the work in deriving those fractions and justifying the diffuse gray model.

**Wikipedia:** [Radiosity (radiometry)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiosity_%28radiometry%29). It says: “this summation for each surface will generate N linear equations with N unknown radiosities”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gibbs energy gives coexistence slopes

**Remember:** Along coexistence, equal Gibbs energies change at the same rate.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A22 (Stefan problems, phase changes, etc.). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a pure substance, use molar Gibbs energy g = u + Pv − Ts. Here u, v, and s are internal energy, volume, and entropy per mole. This replaces internal energy in entropy and volume coordinates with a function of temperature T and pressure P.

**Problem.** Suppose two phases coexist along a smooth pressure curve P(T). Its slope is Δs/Δv wherever their molar volumes differ. Take both differences in the same phase order.

**How the definition helps.** In our own differential argument, equal Gibbs energies change at the same rate along the coexistence curve. Our own calculation subtracts dg = v dP − s dT in the two phases to obtain Δv dP = Δs dT. Our own account puts the work in the equilibrium criterion, which equates the molar Gibbs energies.

**Wikipedia:** [Clausius–Clapeyron relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clausius%E2%80%93Clapeyron_relation). It says: “Their chemical potentials are related by μα = μβ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Carathéodory's approach defines heat as energy change minus adiabatic work

**Remember:** Heat is whatever energy change work does not explain.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 80A05 (Foundations of thermodynamics and heat transfer), 80A10. arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Internal energy U is measured by adiabatic work, which is work done through walls that let no heat pass. The heat Q into a body is defined as the part of ΔU that the work W done on the body does not account for. So Q = ΔU − W.

**Problem.** With heat defined this way, the first law ΔU = Q + W holds for every process without taking heat as a primitive notion.

**How the definition helps.** With heat defined this way, the energy balance of the first law holds by definition. Before Carathéodory, textbooks treated heat, temperature and thermal equilibrium as jointly primitive notions. In our own reading, the physical content moves into one claim. The claim is that the adiabatic work between two states does not depend on the path, so U is a function of state.

**Wikipedia:** [Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat). It says: “Although Carathéodory himself did not state such a definition, following his work it is customary in theoretical studies to define heat”

**Sources:**

- [Carathéodory, C. (1909). Untersuchungen über die Grundlagen der Thermodynamik. Mathematische Annalen 67, 355–386.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01450409)

### Entropy inversion preserves stability

**Remember:** The same stability test survives when energy and entropy trade places.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 80A05 (Foundations of thermodynamics and heat transfer). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write equilibrium entropy as S(E,x), where E is energy and x collects the remaining variables. When entropy increases strictly with energy, solve for energy as a function of entropy and x.

**Problem.** Suppose S is continuously differentiable and concave on an open convex domain, with positive energy derivative. Its inverse energy function is convex on every convex subset of its domain.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, exchanging energy and entropy lets the same chord compare both functions. Concavity places the chord below the entropy graph. Since entropy increases with energy, reaching the chord’s entropy requires at most the chord’s energy in our own argument.

**Paper or page:** [A note on relations between convexity and concavity of thermodynamic functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24440v1). It says: “If ϕᵤ₁(u)&gt;0 for all u∈D, then we can use the same transformation but the properties are switched,”

**Sources:**

- [Mária Lukáčová-Medvid’ová, Ferdinand Thein, Gerald Warnecke and Yuhuan Yuan, A note on relations between convexity and concavity of thermodynamic functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.24440v1)

### Exergy measures lost useful work

**Remember:** Each unit of entropy generated costs T₀ units of useful work.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A10 (Classical and relativistic thermodynamics). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Consider a closed system with fixed composition and negligible changes in speed and height. Its surroundings have constant temperature T₀ and pressure P₀. Form U + P₀V − T₀S from internal energy U, volume V and entropy S. Define exergy by subtracting the value of this expression at equilibrium with the surroundings.

**Problem.** When heat exchange is only with the environment at T₀, the exergy drop equals the useful work delivered plus T₀ times the entropy generated. Useful work excludes the work against ambient pressure.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, exergy absorbs both the ambient-pressure work and the entropy term from the energy balance. Our own account puts the physical work in the entropy balance for heat at the bath temperature. The second law makes the loss nonnegative.

**Wikipedia:** [Exergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exergy). It says: “exergy is always destroyed when a process is non-ideal or irreversible”

**Sources:**

- [Joaquim Anacleto, Lost work and exergy: two views of the same concept](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6404/ad2101)

### Entropy forces give transport positivity

**Remember:** Use the entropy gradient so production becomes a quadratic form.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A17 (Thermodynamics of continua). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A flux measures the amount of a conserved quantity crossing unit area per unit time. Pair each flux with the spatial gradient of the entropy density derivative with respect to that quantity’s density. For energy, the force is the gradient of inverse absolute temperature.

**Problem.** Near equilibrium, suppose fluxes depend linearly on independently variable forces through a matrix L. The second law requires that the symmetric part of L have a nonnegative quadratic form.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the force and flux choices make entropy production the quadratic form of the transport matrix. Our own calculation discards the antisymmetric part because it contributes zero to that form. Our own account puts the work in deriving the local entropy balance, which fixes the force and flux pairs.

**Wikipedia:** [Onsager reciprocal relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onsager_reciprocal_relations). It says: “since the entropy production must be non-negative, the Onsager matrix of phenomenological coefficients L₍αβ₎ is a positive semi-definite matrix.”

**Sources:**

- [Lars Onsager, Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I.](https://doi.org/10.1103/physrev.37.405)

### A common tangent gives equal areas

**Remember:** A straight coexistence segment cancels the two pressure areas.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A22 (Stefan problems, phase changes, etc.). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At fixed temperature, plot the uniform phase’s Helmholtz free energy per mole against volume per mole. Allow mixtures by taking the largest convex function below this graph. In a coexistence interval, this function follows a straight line that touches the two pure phases.

**Problem.** If the supporting line touches two smooth points, its negative slope is the coexistence pressure. The signed areas between the original pressure curve and this pressure cancel on that interval.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, the straight segment fixes the free energy difference as slope times volume change. Pressure equals minus the volume derivative, so integrating pressure gives the same difference with opposite sign. Subtracting the constant coexistence pressure then gives zero signed area in our own proof. The physical step in our own comparison justifies the straight segment by mixing bulk phases with negligible interface energy per mole.

**Wikipedia:** [Maxwell construction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxwell_construction). It says: “This line is the one for which the two areas, I and II, shown in the figure, are equal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Chemical potential drives phase separation

**Remember:** Let concentration flow down the derivative of its free energy.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A22 (Stefan problems, phase changes, etc.). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let c denote concentration, and integrate f(c) + κ\|∇c\|²/2 over space to define energy E, with κ positive. The second term penalizes concentration gradients. Define chemical potential μ so a small change δc gives first-order energy change ∫μ δc. For periodic boundaries, integration by parts gives μ = f′(c) − κΔc, where Δ is the Laplacian.

**Problem.** Suppose concentration changes only by flow with flux −M∇μ, where M is a nonnegative coefficient measuring mobility. For a smooth solution with periodic boundaries, E cannot increase.

**How the definition helps.** Our own calculation writes the energy derivative as the integral of chemical potential times concentration change rate. Our own next step uses the flux −M∇μ and periodicity to get minus the integral of M\|∇μ\|². Our own account puts the modeling work in choosing the energy and using its derivative in the flux law.

**Wikipedia:** [Cahn–Hilliard equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahn%E2%80%93Hilliard_equation). It says: “The proof relies essentially on the existence of a Lyapunov functional.”

**Sources:**

- [John W. Cahn and John E. Hilliard, Free Energy of a Nonuniform System. I. Interfacial Free Energy](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1744102)

### Independent components fix phase counts

**Remember:** Count independent chemical amounts, not names on the reaction list.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 80A22 (Stefan problems, phase changes, etc.). arXiv cond-mat.stat-mech. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Count independent chemical components instead of counting every species. Each independent equilibrium reaction removes one independent species count when there are no other composition constraints. The components give enough independent amounts to describe the composition of every phase.

**Problem.** At regular equilibrium with temperature and pressure as the only external controls, F = C − P + 2. Here C counts independent components and P counts phases. F counts freely variable properties, such as temperature or composition, that do not depend on system size.

**How the definition helps.** Our own count uses independent components to give each phase C − 1 composition variables. Adding temperature and pressure and subtracting C(P − 1) independent equilibrium conditions gives the rule. In our own example, solid calcium carbonate, solid calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas coexist. One reaction relates the three species, leaving two components and one freedom. Counting all three species would predict two freedoms.

**Wikipedia:** [Phase rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_rule). It says: “the minimum number of independent species necessary to define the composition of all phases of the system.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Stored latent heat gives the interface law

**Remember:** Count the heat of melting even when the temperature stays fixed.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A22 (Stefan problems, phase changes, etc.). arXiv physics.class-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Consider a material at rest that melts at a fixed temperature. Describe stored thermal energy per unit volume by its enthalpy, including the heat needed to melt a unit volume. At melting temperature this gives distinct values for solid and liquid.

**Problem.** For smooth phases and a smooth melting front at the melting temperature, weak energy conservation gives the Stefan condition. The heat flux jump supplies the latent heat required to move the front.

**How the definition helps.** In our own balance, moving the interface converts a known volume and therefore accounts for its melting heat automatically. For a unit area, the stored energy jump times the normal speed equals the net heat flux into the front. Our own derivation integrates energy conservation across a shrinking layer around the front, replacing a separately imposed boundary law.

**Wikipedia:** [Stefan problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_problem). It says: “the discontinuity of heat flux at the boundary must be accounted for by the rate of latent heat release”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Heat polynomials satisfy diffusion automatically

**Remember:** Choose basis functions that already solve the heat equation.

*True by definition.* MSC 80A23 (Inverse problems in thermodynamics and heat transfer). arXiv math.NA, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define the nth heat polynomial as n factorial times the coefficient of zⁿ in exp(zx + z²t). Use these polynomials instead of ordinary powers to fit the temperature behind a moving melting front.

**Problem.** Every finite linear combination of heat polynomials solves the heat equation ∂ₜu = ∂ₓ²u.

**How the definition helps.** Our own check shows that the generating function solves the heat equation for every z. Differentiating once in time or twice in space multiplies it by z². Comparing powers of z gives the equation for every basis polynomial. Ordinary powers of position alone lack this property.
