- [H. Bondi, M. G. J. van der Burg, and A. W. K. Metzner (1962), Gravitational waves in general relativity, VII. Waves from axi-symmetric isolated system](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1962.0161)
- [R. K. Sachs (1962), Gravitational waves in general relativity VIII. Waves in asymptotically flat space-time](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1962.0206)

### Bulk symmetries act conformally at infinity

**Remember:** A bulk symmetry preserves the boundary metric up to scale.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C30 (Asymptotic procedures (radiation, news functions, \\(\\mathcal \\)-spaces, etc.) in general relativity and gravitational theory). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A conformal compactification adds a boundary where a smooth function Ω vanishes with nonzero differential. Multiplying the interior metric by Ω² gives a smooth nondegenerate metric there. Changing Ω rescales the induced boundary metric by a positive function. A Killing field generates local maps preserving the metric.

**Problem.** Consider a smooth conformal compactification with timelike boundary, meaning its induced metric has one negative direction. Any interior Killing field extending smoothly to the boundary generates local maps preserving the boundary metric up to positive rescaling.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping the boundary metric up to scale absorbs the change of Ω under the symmetry (our own explanation). Write h for the rescaled metric and K for the field. In the interior, the derivative of h along the flow equals 2K(Ω)h/Ω. Taking its trace shows that K(Ω)/Ω extends smoothly. Thus K(Ω) vanishes on the boundary, so the flow stays there and changes the induced metric only by scale.

**Paper or page:** [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661). It says: “then it is tangent to ℐ”

**Sources:**

- [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661)

### Cotton curvature supplies boundary stress

**Remember:** Cotton–York curvature already obeys the boundary constraints.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C30 (Asymptotic procedures (radiation, news functions, \\(\\mathcal \\)-spaces, etc.) in general relativity and gravitational theory). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On an oriented three-dimensional Lorentzian manifold, the Cotton–York tensor measures how the curvature varies. First subtract one quarter of the scalar curvature times the metric from the Ricci tensor, the trace of the curvature tensor. Take the covariant derivative and contract its derivative index and first tensor index with the volume form to obtain the curl.

**Problem.** A conformal boundary specifies its metric only up to multiplication by a positive function. A constant multiple of its Cotton–York tensor has zero trace and divergence for each metric h. Changing h to Ω²h multiplies this covariant tensor by Ω⁻¹, as required for boundary stress data in three dimensions.

**How the definition helps.** Choosing the boundary tensor as a multiple of curvature satisfies the constraints for every boundary metric at once. The Cotton–York identities give its symmetry, vanishing trace and vanishing divergence. Its rescaling law makes the prescription consistent across all representatives. The work lies in proving those curvature identities (our own assessment).

**Paper or page:** [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661), [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661). It says: “is symmetric, trace-free with respect to the metric h and divergence-free for the Levi-Civita connection D of h.”

**Sources:**

- [Geometric reflective boundary conditions for asymptotically Anti-de Sitter spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20661)

### Dominant energy bounds total momentum

**Remember:** Keep local energy large enough to pay for local momentum.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C40 (Gravitational energy and conservation laws; groups of motions). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Initial data describe spatial geometry and its bending in spacetime at one time. The gravitational constraint equations determine local energy density μ and momentum density J from these data. The dominant energy condition requires μ ≥ \|J\| everywhere.

**Problem.** Take smooth complete three-dimensional initial data without boundary, with integrable energy and momentum densities satisfying the dominant energy condition. Assume metric error decays as 1/r and bending as 1/r², gaining one inverse power per derivative through orders two and one respectively. Then total energy is at least total momentum magnitude.

**How the definition helps.** The density bound makes the energy term in the positive mass proof nonnegative. In our own example, take zero bending and multiply the Euclidean metric by (1 − a/√(1 + r²))⁴, with 0 &lt; a &lt; 1. The resulting complete geometry has total energy −2a and zero momentum. Our own sign check uses μ\|v\| + J · v ≥ 0 for every vector v. The proof still needs a global estimate connecting this local sign to energy at infinity.

**Paper or page:** [The case of equality for the spacetime positive mass theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01984v3). It says: “Suppose (M,g,k) is a complete asymptotically flat initial data set satisfying the dominant energy condition (DEC) μ ≥ \|J\|. Then E ≥ \|P\|.”

**Sources:**

- [Sven Hirsch and Yiyue Zhang, The case of equality for the spacetime positive mass theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01984v3)

### Nearly round spheres recover total mass

**Remember:** Going to infinity does not make a fixed oval shape round.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C40 (Gravitational energy and conservation laws; groups of motions), 53C21. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let r be the minimum distance of a surrounding sphere from a fixed point. Nearly round spheres have maximum distance and intrinsic diameter bounded by Cr and area bounded by Cr², for a common constant C. Subtract the average principal curvature times the identity from the shape operator to obtain B, which measures unequal bending. For decay exponent t, both r¹⁺ᵗ‖B‖ and r²⁺ᵗ‖∇B‖ stay bounded, where ∇ measures change along the surface.

**Problem.** Assume a three-dimensional end approaches Euclidean space with two derivatives at decay rate t &gt; ½ and has integrable scalar curvature. Along nearly round spheres escaping to infinity, the Hawking mass calculated from area and mean curvature tends to the total mass at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Near roundness excludes a persistent shape error that can swamp the mass being measured. In our own example, dilate a nonspherical ellipsoid in flat space. By Gauss–Bonnet, its integrated squared mean curvature stays above the round value by a fixed positive amount. The Hawking mass multiplies this deficit by a factor proportional to the square root of area, so it tends to minus infinity although flat space has zero total mass.

**nLab:** [ADM mass](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/ADM+mass). It says: “a notion of total mass contained in asymptotically flat spacetimes.”

**Paper or page:** [On the behavior of quasi-local mass at the infinity along nearly round surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.0678v1). It says: “\\lim<sub>r\\rightarrow \\infty </sub>m<sub>H</sub>(\\Sigma r)=m{ADM}(M).”

**Sources:**

- [Yuguang Shi, Guofang Wang, and Jie Wu (2009), On the behavior of quasi-local mass at the infinity along nearly round surfaces](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10455-009-9169-5)

### Choosing the right time flow makes Kerr–de Sitter wave expansions provable

**Remember:** Choose the time flow before splitting the wave into modes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes), 58J45. arXiv math.AP, gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Kerr–de Sitter spacetime models a rotating black hole in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. A stationary Killing field is a vector field whose flow preserves the metric and acts as a time direction. A quasinormal mode is a smooth wave that changes by a factor exp(−iσt) along the flow of a chosen stationary Killing field. The paper allows several such fields, among them the fields that generate the horizons.

**Problem.** In a subextremal Kerr–de Sitter spacetime, the mode frequencies form a discrete set of complex numbers. Waves then have an expansion in quasinormal modes up to a decay rate set by the trapped light rays.

**How the definition helps.** A suitable choice of time flow gives a family of operators that are Fredholm, so the standard Fredholm theory applies. Fredholm means that the kernel and cokernel have finite dimension and the range is closed. The earlier paper by the same authors proved the expansion with one such choice. This paper shows that many other choices work too. The control of the trapped light rays is still separate work.

**Paper or page:** [Stationarity and Fredholm Theory in Subextremal Kerr-de Sitter Spacetimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09213v2). It says: “One central ingredient in the argument was a new definition of quasinormal modes, where a non-standard choice of stationary Killing vector field had to be used in order for the Fredholm theory to be applicable.”

**Sources:**

- [Oliver Petersen, András Vasy, Stationarity and Fredholm Theory in Subextremal Kerr-de Sitter Spacetimes, arXiv:2306.09213 (2024), SIGMA 20 (2024), 052, 11 pages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09213v2)
- [Oliver Petersen, András Vasy, Wave equations in the Kerr–de Sitter spacetime: the full subextremal range, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 27 (2025)](https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1448)

### Rescaling makes horizon inversion isometric

**Remember:** Divide by radius squared to turn horizon inversion into an isometry.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C57 (Black holes). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Consider the exterior of a nonrotating charged black hole whose charge magnitude equals its mass M in geometric units. Define r by the area 4πr² of each sphere. Divide the spacetime metric by r². The inversion keeps time and angles fixed and sends r − M to M²/(r − M).

**Problem.** The inversion preserves the rescaled metric. On the extended exterior it exchanges the future horizon with the boundary reached by outgoing light, and similarly for the past.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by r² cancels the position-dependent change in the original metric under inversion. In our own calculation, the transformed sphere radius is Mr/(r − M). The original metric gains exactly the square of the ratio of transformed to original radius. The separate boundary argument identifies where incoming and outgoing rays end.

**Paper or page:** [Peeling at extreme black hole horizons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.14574v1). It says: “It fixes the photon sphere and exchanges the future event horizon ℋ⁺ and the future null infinity ℐ⁺”

**Sources:**

- [Jack Borthwick, Eric Gourgoulhon and Jean-Philippe Nicolas, Peeling at extreme black hole horizons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.14574v1)

### A quadratic test detects type D

**Remember:** Two distinct polynomial roots rule out a Jordan block.

*True by definition.* MSC 83C60 (Spinor and twistor methods in general relativity and gravitational theory; Newman-Penrose formalism). arXiv gr-qc, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** At a point of an oriented four-dimensional spacetime, the trace-free part of curvature defines an operator W on a three-dimensional complex space. Its elements are self-dual two-forms, which the metric’s Hodge star sends to i times themselves. In the operator classification, Petrov type D means W is diagonalizable with eigenvalues λ, λ and −2λ for some nonzero λ.

**Problem.** Suppose tr(W²) ≠ 0 and set λ = −tr(W³)/tr(W²). The curvature has Petrov type D exactly when W² + λW − 2λ²I = 0, where I is the identity.

**How the definition helps.** The operator definition replaces the geometric search for repeated lightlike directions with a polynomial test (our own explanation). For the stated spectrum, taking traces gives the displayed value of λ. Conversely, λ cannot vanish because the equation would imply W² = 0. The polynomial has distinct roots λ and −2λ, so W is diagonalizable. Its zero trace forces multiplicities two and one. The geometric work is proving agreement with the classification by lightlike directions.

**Paper or page:** [An ideal conformally covariant characterization of the Kerr conformal structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04783). It says: “is of “genuine” Petrov type D (Petrov type D, but not any of its specializations) if and only if\\begin{equation}  \\tilde{a}\\neq 0\\; ,\\quad \\tilde{\\mathcal{D}}<sub>abcd</sub>=0\\; ,  \\end{equation}”

**Sources:**

- [An ideal conformally covariant characterization of the Kerr conformal structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04783)

### Curvature blocks twice differentiable extensions

**Remember:** Curvature can diverge where first derivatives still extend continuously.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C75 (Space-time singularities, cosmic censorship, etc.). arXiv gr-qc. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An extension identifies a spacetime with a proper open subset of a larger spacetime while preserving its metric. A C² extension has metric coefficients with continuous second derivatives in smooth coordinates. A C¹ extension requires only continuous first derivatives.

**Problem.** Each interior Lorentzian Hawking–Page metric in the cited family extends across its specified lightlike boundary with continuous first derivatives. No extension across that boundary has continuous second derivatives.

**How the definition helps.** Requiring two continuous derivatives rules out extensions whose curvature diverges in a regular frame (our own explanation). A C² metric has continuous curvature components in every smooth local frame. The cited paper proves that the sectional curvature blows up at the boundary for every extension. Constructing the C¹ extension and establishing that obstruction are the substantive results.

**Paper or page:** [Extensions of Lorentzian Hawking--Page Solutions with Null Singularities, Spacelike Singularities, and Cauchy horizons of Taub--NUT type](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06134), [Extensions of Lorentzian Hawking--Page Solutions with Null Singularities, Spacelike Singularities, and Cauchy horizons of Taub--NUT type](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06134). It says: “For any extension of the Lorentzian Hawking–Page vacuum solution, the sectional curvature blows up along C₀⁻.”

**Sources:**

- [Extensions of Lorentzian Hawking--Page Solutions with Null Singularities, Spacelike Singularities, and Cauchy horizons of Taub--NUT type](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06134)

### Strict trapping rules out flat cylinders

**Remember:** Rays that only stay parallel need not ever meet.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 83C75 (Space-time singularities, cosmic censorship, etc.), 83C57. arXiv gr-qc, math.DG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Cauchy surface meets every inextendible slower-than-light path once. Inside it, consider a compact separating surface without boundary. It is outer trapped if outgoing perpendicular light rays initially shrink every small area element. Weak outer trapping allows the initial rate to vanish.

**Problem.** Assume a spacetime has a spacelike Cauchy surface and nonnegative Ricci curvature in every light direction. Suppose a connected outer trapped surface separates that slice and the outer component has noncompact closure. Then some future light ray ends at finite affine parameter, the parameter for which its velocity transports parallel to itself.

**How the definition helps.** Strict shrinking excludes parallel outgoing rays, which can persist forever. In our own example, identify opposite faces periodically in two spatial directions of flat spacetime. At fixed time and fixed remaining coordinate, the resulting torus has constant area along its outgoing rays. Every ray extends forever. The theorem uses strict shrinking to focus the rays and the noncompact outer side to deduce incompleteness.

**Paper or page:** [Rigidity aspects of Penrose's singularity theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11315v3). It says: “outer trapped (i.e., θ⁺ &lt; 0)”

**Sources:**

- [Rigidity aspects of Penrose's singularity theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11315v3)

## 85 Astronomy and astrophysics

### Distance modulus adds to magnitude

**Remember:** The logarithmic distance correction adds to a source’s absolute magnitude.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A04 (General questions in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR, astro-ph.GA. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Flux is received power per unit area. Magnitude measures brightness on a scale where multiplying flux by 100 subtracts five magnitudes. Absolute magnitude is the magnitude an isotropic source would have at ten parsecs, a standard astronomical distance. Define the distance modulus as five times the base-ten logarithm of luminosity distance divided by ten parsecs.

**Problem.** Sum the light over all wavelengths and assume transparent propagation. Apparent magnitude equals absolute magnitude plus the distance modulus.

**How the definition helps.** The logarithm makes inverse-square dilution an additive correction. In our own derivation, luminosity distance is the distance that gives the measured flux from the source power by inverse-square dilution. Taking the magnitude difference then gives exactly the distance modulus.

**Wikipedia:** [Distance modulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance_modulus). It says: “the observed brightness of a light source is related to its distance by the inverse square law”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Redshift factors multiply

**Remember:** Consecutive wavelength ratios multiply along a light path.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 1: early undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the redshift factor 1 + z as the received wavelength divided by the emitted wavelength. Use this ratio instead of the fractional change z.

**Problem.** The total redshift factor equals the product of the factors measured on consecutive parts of the same light path. Use the same observer at each shared endpoint.

**How the definition helps.** Using ratios makes consecutive shifts multiply because the shared wavelength cancels. In our own proof, the middle observer measures the same light signal for both ratios. Predicting each ratio from motion or cosmic expansion requires a separate physical calculation.

**Wikipedia:** [Redshift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redshift). It says: “corresponding to the fractional change in wavelength (positive for redshifts, negative for blueshifts), and by the wavelength ratio 1 + z”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Flat spectra have zero AB color

**Remember:** A flat flux density has the same AB magnitude in every filter.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A04 (General questions in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR, astro-ph.GA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Flux density per unit frequency measures received power per unit area and frequency interval. The AB magnitude scale uses a logarithm of the filter-averaged flux density and assigns zero magnitude to the same reference flux density in every filter. A color is the difference between magnitudes in two filters.

**Problem.** A source with constant flux density per unit frequency has zero AB color between any two properly calibrated filters.

**How the definition helps.** The common reference makes a constant flux density yield the same magnitude in every filter. In our own calculation, every normalized filter average of that constant equals the constant itself. A reference star with a varying spectrum would instead establish different flux references across filters. Applying the AB definition to observations requires calibrating each filter.

**Wikipedia:** [AB magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AB_magnitude). It says: “The bandpass AB magnitude is defined so that the zero point corresponds to a bandpass-averaged spectral flux density”

**Sources:**

- [J. B. Oke and J. E. Gunn (1983), Secondary standard stars for absolute spectrophotometry](https://doi.org/10.1086/160817)

### Orbit constants give stellar equilibria

**Remember:** A function of orbit constants stays constant as stars move.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A05 (Galactic and stellar dynamics). arXiv astro-ph.GA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Write the distribution of stars in position and velocity as a function of orbit constants such as energy. Here an orbit constant has the same value at every point along a star’s orbit. This replaces specifying the distribution independently at each position and velocity.

**Problem.** In a time-independent gravitational field, every smooth function of time-independent orbit constants solves the steady collisionless Boltzmann equation. This equation requires the distribution to stay constant along each star’s orbit when encounters are negligible.

**How the definition helps.** Writing the distribution in terms of orbit constants makes its derivative along a star’s path vanish. In our own derivation, this follows by the chain rule. The work lies in finding the orbit constants. If the stars generate the field, their density must also reproduce that field.

**Wikipedia:** [Jeans's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeans%27s_theorem). It says: “any function of the integrals is a steady-state solution”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Squared buoyancy frequency flags instability

**Remember:** Positive squared buoyancy frequency restores a displaced parcel.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A15 (Galactic and stellar structure). arXiv astro-ph.SR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Displace a small parcel of stellar gas vertically without exchanging heat, and compare its buoyancy acceleration with its displacement. At equilibrium define N² as minus the derivative of this acceleration with respect to displacement. This signed quantity is the squared buoyancy frequency.

**Problem.** With constant local coefficients, the linearized displacement oscillates if N² is positive. It has an exponentially growing mode if N² is negative.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping the sign of N² gives both stability tests from the same linear equation. In our own argument, a displacement x satisfies x″ = −N²x. The physical calculation compares the parcel’s density after displacement with the surrounding density.

**Wikipedia:** [Brunt–Väisälä frequency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunt%E2%80%93V%C3%A4is%C3%A4l%C3%A4_frequency). It says: “If a gas parcel is pushed up and N² &gt; 0, the air parcel will move up and down”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Eddington ratios compare accelerations

**Remember:** The same luminosity ratio compares outward radiation and inward gravity.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A25 (Radiative transfer in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR, astro-ph.HE. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Luminosity L is the power a source radiates. For spherical emission, define the Eddington luminosity as 4πGMc/κ, with mass M, gravitational constant G, and light speed c. The opacity κ measures the effective area per unit mass for momentum transfer from light.

**Problem.** Outside a spherical source, use Newtonian gravity and assume constant luminosity and opacity. The ratio of radiation acceleration to gravity equals the ratio of luminosity to Eddington luminosity.

**How the definition helps.** The Eddington luminosity collects all the constants in the acceleration ratio into one reference power. In our own calculation, outward acceleration is κL/(4πr²c) at radius r, while inward acceleration has magnitude GM/r². Their common radius factor cancels. The physical work establishes these acceleration laws for the gas.

**Wikipedia:** [Eddington luminosity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_luminosity). It says: “The limit is obtained by setting the outward radiation pressure equal to the inward gravitational force.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Optical depths add along rays

**Remember:** Transmission multiplies, so optical depth adds.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A25 (Radiative transfer in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For starlight at one wavelength, let transmission be the fraction of incident beam intensity that survives a region. For positive transmission, define optical depth as minus its natural logarithm.

**Problem.** If successive regions only remove light from this beam, their optical depths add.

**How the definition helps.** The negative logarithm turns multiplication of consecutive transmission fractions into addition of optical depths (our own). In each region the exiting beam supplies the incident light for the next (our own). Computing the depths from matter requires a physical law for absorption and scattering out of the beam (our own). With loss proportional to intensity, integrating the local loss coefficient gives the optical depth (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Optical depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_depth). It says: “the transmitted flux decays exponentially with optical depth”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Comoving distances stay fixed

**Remember:** Divide out expansion to keep galaxies that move with it at fixed distances.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the comoving distance as the proper distance on a constant cosmic time slice divided by the scale factor. The scale factor measures the common expansion of space. Proper distance instead measures physical lengths on the slice.

**Problem.** Suppose space looks the same at every point and in every direction at each cosmic time. Two observers following the common expansion stay at constant comoving distance.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by the scale factor cancels the common change in all physical spatial lengths. In our own derivation, the spatial metric equals a fixed metric times the square of the scale factor. The symmetry assumptions justify that form.

**Wikipedia:** [Comoving and proper distances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comoving_and_proper_distances). It says: “Comoving distance factors out the expansion of the universe, giving a distance that does not change in time except due to local factors”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lens Jacobians give signed magnification

**Remember:** The determinant gives the area change and tells whether orientation flips.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A thin lens treats light deflection as occurring in one plane. Its lens map sends each observed image direction to the source direction without deflection. Define signed magnification as the local ratio of image to source angular area, with a minus sign when orientation reverses.

**Problem.** Where the derivative of the lens map is invertible, signed magnification equals the reciprocal of its determinant in local angular area coordinates.

**How the definition helps.** Using oriented areas makes magnification the area factor for the inverse lens map. In our own calculation, the inverse derivative has reciprocal determinant. Relating its absolute value to a flux ratio also requires conservation of surface brightness, the flux per unit solid angle.

**Wikipedia:** [Gravitational lensing formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_lensing_formalism). It says: “The amplification is the inverse of the Jacobian”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Toomre’s ratio detects disk instability

**Remember:** Pressure and rotation prevent local ring collapse when Toomre’s ratio reaches one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 85A05 (Galactic and stellar dynamics). arXiv astro-ph.GA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Consider a rotating gas disk of negligible thickness. Define Toomre’s ratio Q as cₛκ/(πGΣ), where cₛ is sound speed and G is the gravitational constant. Here κ is the frequency of small radial oscillations about a circular orbit, and Σ is mass per unit area.

**Problem.** Consider small local disturbances that are the same at every angle around the disk. For positive κ, cₛ, and Σ, no radial wavelength grows exponentially exactly when Q ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** The ratio Q collects pressure, rotation, and gravity into one test covering every radial wavelength. In our own calculation, squared wave frequency is κ² − 2πGΣ\|k\| + cₛ²k², where k is radial wave number. Its minimum is κ²(1 − 1/Q²). Deriving the wave equation from the gas dynamics supplies the physical work.

**Wikipedia:** [Toomre's stability criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toomre%27s_stability_criterion). It says: “The stability criterion can then simply be stated as, Q ≥ 1 for a disk to be stable against collapse.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Interior mass matches exterior mass

**Remember:** Define the interior mass through the same metric coefficient as outside.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A15 (Galactic and stellar structure). arXiv astro-ph.SR, gr-qc. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a static spherical star, define radius r by sphere area 4πr². Use units where light speed and the gravitational constant equal one. Define enclosed mass m(r) through the radial squared length element (dr)²/(1 − 2m(r)/r).

**Problem.** Match the stellar surface at radius R smoothly to the spherical vacuum solution without a surface layer. The mass inferred from the exterior gravitational field equals m(R).

**How the definition helps.** Using the same radius and metric coefficient on both sides makes the mass comparison immediate. In our own calculation, the exterior radial coefficient is 1/(1 − 2M/R) at the surface. Continuity equates it to the interior coefficient and gives M = m(R). Computing the interior geometry and establishing the match still require the gravitational field equations.

**Wikipedia:** [Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolman%E2%80%93Oppenheimer%E2%80%93Volkoff_equation). It says: “continuity of the metric and the definition of m(r) require that”

**Sources:**

- [J. R. Oppenheimer and G. M. Volkoff (1939), On Massive Neutron Cores](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.55.374)

### Polytropic stars share a scaled profile

**Remember:** Scale the center to one and let the pressure-law index set the shape.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 85A15 (Galactic and stellar structure). arXiv astro-ph.SR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Model a spherical star in gravitational equilibrium by a pressure law P = Kρ⁽¹⁺¹⁄ⁿ⁾, with density ρ and constants K, n &gt; 0. Write d for central density and G for Newton’s gravitational constant. Use the dimensionless density variable θ = (ρ/d)¹⁄ⁿ. Measure radius in units of √((n + 1)K d⁽¹⁄ⁿ⁻¹⁾/(4πG)).

**Problem.** In Newtonian gravity, these stars share one scaled density profile for each index n. For 0 &lt; n &lt; 5, the first zero of θ gives the radius in the chosen units.

**How the definition helps.** The chosen units leave only n in the differential equation for θ (our own). Newtonian gravity and pressure balance supply that equation, called the Lane–Emden equation (our own). Regularity at the center gives θ(0) = 1 and θ′(0) = 0. The remaining work proves uniqueness of this central solution and, for n below five, existence of its first zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lane–Emden equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lane%E2%80%93Emden_equation). It says: “The standard boundary conditions are θ(0) = 1 and θ′(0) = 0.”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Homer Lane, On the theoretical temperature of the Sun, under the hypothesis of a gaseous mass maintaining its volume by its internal heat, and depending on the laws of gases as known to terrestrial experiment (1870).](https://doi.org/10.2475/ajs.s2-50.148.57)

### Rosseland averaging preserves diffusive flux

**Remember:** Transparent frequency ranges carry more of the diffusive flux.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A25 (Radiative transfer in astronomy and astrophysics). arXiv astro-ph.SR, astro-ph.HE. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Opacity measures how strongly matter blocks radiation per unit mass. At each frequency, weight reciprocal opacity by the temperature derivative of the thermal radiation spectrum. Divide the weighted integral by the integral of the weights, then take its reciprocal. This defines the Rosseland mean opacity.

**Problem.** Suppose photons travel only short distances between interactions and radiation is nearly in thermal equilibrium with nearby matter. In the diffusion approximation, the Rosseland mean gives the same total energy flux as the frequency-dependent law.

**How the definition helps.** Averaging reciprocal opacity preserves exactly the factor that multiplies the temperature gradient in the total flux. In our own calculation, each frequency contributes in proportion to its temperature weight divided by its opacity. The underlying transport equation supplies this diffusion law.

**Wikipedia:** [Opacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opacity). It says: “The Rosseland opacity is derived in the diffusion approximation to the radiative transport equation.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Sky power depends on degree

**Remember:** Rotation gives all modes of the same degree the same power.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 85A35 (Statistical astronomy), 85A40. arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Represent a random map of the sky by spherical harmonics, the angular modes on a sphere. Each mode has a degree and an index within that degree. The angular power spectrum assigns each degree the mean squared magnitude of a coefficient at that degree for a sky with rotation-invariant statistics.

**Problem.** For a rotationally invariant random sky with zero mean and finite variance, harmonic coefficients are uncorrelated across distinct modes. Their variance depends only on degree.

**How the definition helps.** The harmonic representation reduces the whole covariance to one number per degree. In our own outline, rotations mix modes within each degree. A rotation-invariant covariance acts as a scalar on each degree and has no terms connecting different degrees. This step uses Schur’s lemma for the rotation group.

**Paper or page:** [Geometric Methods for Spherical Data, with Applications to Cosmology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15278v1). It says: “there exists a family of orthogonal random coefficients”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Conformal time gives constant grid speed

**Remember:** Divide out expansion so light crosses equal grid distances in equal time increments.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Divide each increment of ordinary cosmic time by the expansion scale factor to get an increment of conformal time. Measure radial distance in comoving coordinates, which keep the expansion out of the spatial grid.

**Problem.** Consider an expanding universe that looks the same at every location and in every direction, with flat spatial geometry. In conformal time, radial light crosses the comoving grid at constant speed c. The comoving particle horizon, the greatest distance light could have covered since the Big Bang, equals c times the elapsed conformal time when finite.

**How the definition helps.** Conformal time absorbs the scale factor that changes light’s grid speed in ordinary cosmic time (our own). In conformal time the radial light equation gives a constant speed, so integration gives the horizon distance (our own). The work lies in obtaining the light equation from spacetime geometry and integrating the expansion history to find elapsed conformal time (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Particle horizon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particle_horizon). It says: “the particle horizon is equal to the conformal time η that has passed since the Big Bang, times the speed of light c.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Critical density normalizes flatness

**Remember:** Measure density in critical units and flat space has density one.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Hubble rate H measures fractional expansion per unit time. In units where light speed equals one, define critical density as 3H²/(8πG), where G is Newton’s gravitational constant. Divide total energy density, including vacuum energy, by critical density to obtain the density parameter Ω.

**Problem.** In a universe with uniform, direction-independent expansion governed by the Friedmann equations, assume H is nonzero. Spatial curvature vanishes exactly when Ω equals one.

**How the definition helps.** Measuring density in critical units makes Ω − 1 proportional to spatial curvature (our own). The first Friedmann equation supplies this relation from Einstein’s equations (our own). In ordinary density units the value giving flat space changes with the Hubble rate (our own).

**nLab:** [FRW model](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/FRW+model). It says: “Ω ≔ Ω<sub>R</sub> + Ω<sub>M</sub> + Ω\_Λ = 1 + k/(a²H²)”

**Sources:**

- [Alexander Friedmann, Über die Krümmung des Raumes (1922).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01332580)

### Distance duality gives brightness dimming

**Remember:** Use one distance for flux and another for apparent area.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Luminosity distance converts emitted power to observed flux, the power received per unit area, by inverse-square dilution. For angular diameter distance, divide projected source area by observed solid angle and take the square root.

**Problem.** Suppose photons follow light rays of the spacetime metric and their number is conserved. Observed surface brightness summed over all frequencies equals emitted surface brightness divided by (1 + z)⁴. Here 1 + z is received wavelength divided by emitted wavelength.

**How the definition helps.** Using separate distances for flux and apparent area turns dimming into a squared distance ratio. In our own derivation, dividing received flux by solid angle gives the squared ratio of angular diameter distance to luminosity distance. Etherington’s reciprocity theorem and photon conservation give that ratio as 1/(1 + z)².

**Wikipedia:** [Etherington's reciprocity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etherington%27s_reciprocity_theorem). It says: “The Etherington distance-duality equation is the relationship between the luminosity distance of standard candles and the angular diameter distance.”

**Sources:**

- [I. M. H. Etherington (1933), On the definition of distance in general relativity](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786443309462220)

### Redshift preserves blackbody spectra

**Remember:** A Planck spectrum keeps its shape when frequency and temperature fall together.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology), 85A25. arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Describe thermal radiation by the mean number of photons in a state of frequency ν. At absolute temperature T this number is 1/(exp(hν/(kT)) − 1), where h and k are Planck’s and Boltzmann’s constants.

**Problem.** Suppose thermal radiation travels freely through a uniformly expanding universe. If expansion divides every photon frequency by 1 + z, the radiation remains thermal with temperature divided by 1 + z.

**How the definition helps.** Photon occupation depends only on frequency divided by temperature, so the common frequency shift rescales temperature directly. In our own derivation, free propagation preserves the occupation number along a ray. Substituting the emitted frequency into the original distribution gives the cooler distribution. Proving occupation conservation and the common frequency shift supplies the physical work.

**Wikipedia:** [Cosmic microwave background](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background). It says: “expansion of the universe would cool blackbody radiation while maintaining a thermal spectrum.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced shear hides a mass sheet

**Remember:** Rescale both parts of the shear ratio and its value stays put.

*True by definition.* MSC 85A40 (Astrophysical cosmology). arXiv astro-ph.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A gravitational lens bends light and distorts images. Convergence κ measures local focusing, and shear γ measures directional stretching. Define reduced shear as γ/(1 − κ) wherever κ differs from one.

**Problem.** Take one thin lens and sources at a fixed distance. Multiply the lens mass distribution by a positive factor λ and add a uniform sheet of convergence 1 − λ. This preserves reduced shear, so image shapes alone cannot distinguish the models.

**How the definition helps.** Scaling the lens multiplies its shear by λ, while the uniform sheet adds no shear (our own). The new convergence is λκ + 1 − λ, so 1 − κ also gains a factor of λ (our own). The factors cancel, so reduced shear is unchanged even though raw shear changes (our own). An independent magnification measurement can break the ambiguity.

**Wikipedia:** [Gravitational lensing formalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_lensing_formalism). It says: “this degeneracy can be broken if an independent measurement of the magnification is available”

**Sources:**

- [E. E. Falco, M. V. Gorenstein and I. I. Shapiro, On model-dependent bounds on H(0) from gravitational images: Application of Q0957 + 561A,B (1985).](https://doi.org/10.1086/184422)

## 86 Geophysics

### Buoyancy sign predicts oscillation

**Remember:** Positive N² means oscillation, while negative N² means exponential growth is possible.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics), 86A05. arXiv physics.ao-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Let z measure height upward in a resting fluid with density ρ(z). Assume a displaced fluid parcel keeps its density, and use a constant positive reference density ρ₀ for inertia. Define the signed coefficient N² = −gρ′(z)/ρ₀, where g is gravitational acceleration.

**Problem.** For small vertical parcel displacements in this model, N² &gt; 0 gives oscillations. If N² &lt; 0, the linear equation has an exponentially growing solution.

**How the definition helps.** The signed coefficient puts stable and unstable displacements into one equation (our own). A small vertical displacement x satisfies x″ = −N²x after linearization at its starting height (our own). Deriving this equation requires comparing the parcel’s density with its new surroundings (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brunt–Väisälä frequency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunt%E2%80%93V%C3%A4is%C3%A4l%C3%A4_frequency). It says: “the displacement z′ has oscillating solutions (and N gives our angular frequency).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Geopotential height absorbs varying gravity

**Remember:** Measure altitude by lifting work so gravity drops out of the conversion.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Divide the work per unit mass against gravity from a reference level by a fixed standard gravity. This gives geopotential height instead of geometric height.

**Problem.** Suppose the vertical pressure force balances gravity at every height, a condition called hydrostatic balance. The derivative of pressure with respect to geopotential height then equals minus density times standard gravity, even when local gravity varies.

**How the definition helps.** Both the pressure gradient and the new height increment contain the same local gravity, so it cancels (our own). The work lies in the hydrostatic equation, which follows from vertical force balance (our own). Recovering geometric height still requires the local gravity field (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Geopotential height](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopotential_height). It says: “the simplification obtained by assuming a constant value of gravitational acceleration is the sole reason for defining the geopotential altitude.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Potential temperature survives adiabatic motion

**Remember:** Compare air parcels after bringing them to the same pressure without heating.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Use the temperature an air parcel would reach at a fixed reference pressure after reversible compression or expansion without heat exchange. This is potential temperature, rather than the parcel’s actual temperature at its current pressure.

**Problem.** A dry ideal-gas parcel keeps its potential temperature during reversible motion with no heat exchange.

**How the definition helps.** Moving along a reversible path without heat exchange does not change the parcel’s state at the reference pressure (our own). The work is in thermodynamics, which gives constant entropy on that path and a unique temperature at fixed pressure (our own). Actual temperature changes when the parcel expands or compresses (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Potential temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_temperature). It says: “Potential temperature is conserved for all dry adiabatic processes”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Authalic latitude preserves ellipsoid area

**Remember:** Match the area of each latitude band before drawing the map.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A30 (Geodesy, mapping problems). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The authalic latitude of a point on an ellipsoid of revolution is a latitude on the sphere of the same total area. It is the latitude, in the same hemisphere, at which the band from the equator has the same area as on the ellipsoid. Longitude stays the same.

**Problem.** The authalic latitude map preserves area, so composing it with a spherical equal-area projection gives an equal-area ellipsoid map.

**How the definition helps.** Matching areas from the equator gives equal areas for latitude bands by subtraction (our own). Rotational symmetry splits each band into longitude sectors in proportion to their angular widths (our own). Those sectors determine area, so the whole map preserves it (our own). Computing the latitude requires integrating the ellipsoid’s area element and inverting the resulting monotone function (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Latitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latitude). It says: “gives an equal-area projection to a sphere.”

**Sources:**

- [J. P. Snyder, Map projections: A working manual (1987)](https://doi.org/10.3133/pp1395)

### Chord radius preserves mapped area

**Remember:** Use chord length as the map radius to keep areas unchanged.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A30 (Geodesy, mapping problems). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The spherical Lambert azimuthal equal-area map keeps the bearing from its center. It sets the map radius to the straight chord length from the center to the point. An equidistant map instead uses the distance along the surface.

**Problem.** The spherical Lambert azimuthal map preserves area away from the point opposite its center.

**How the definition helps.** Using chord length makes each map disk equal in area to its spherical cap (our own). On a sphere of radius R, a cap of angular radius θ has area 2πR²(1 − cos θ), which is π times the squared chord length (our own). Preserving bearing gives equal areas for sectors of caps (our own). Subtracting nested sectors then gives equal areas for the polar rectangles that determine area (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambert_azimuthal_equal-area_projection). It says: “It accurately represents area in all regions of the sphere, but it does not accurately represent angles.”

**Sources:**

- [J. P. Snyder, Map projections: A working manual (1987)](https://doi.org/10.3133/pp1395)

### Mercator straightens compass courses

**Remember:** Mercator stretches latitude until a steady compass bearing has a steady slope.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A30 (Geodesy, mapping problems). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The spherical Mercator map uses longitude as its horizontal coordinate. Its vertical coordinate is the integral of the secant of latitude from the equator. A simple latitude-longitude grid instead uses latitude itself as the height.

**Problem.** A course that keeps a constant angle to geographic north maps to a straight line when longitude runs continuously across the map edges.

**How the definition helps.** The chosen height makes the map preserve angles, so a fixed bearing becomes a fixed angle to parallel vertical lines (our own). On the sphere, eastward distance per unit longitude shrinks by the cosine of latitude (our own). Using the secant as the height derivative makes the map stretch equally in both directions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Mercator projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercator_projection). It says: “representing rhumb lines as straight lines”

**Sources:**

- [J. P. Snyder, Map projections: A working manual (1987)](https://doi.org/10.3133/pp1395)

### The geoid follows local level

**Remember:** A level surface is one on which gravity can do no work.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A30 (Geodesy, mapping problems). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The geoid is the level surface of Earth’s effective gravitational potential chosen to fit mean sea level. The effective potential includes the effect of Earth’s rotation. A reference ellipsoid instead approximates Earth’s shape geometrically.

**Problem.** In the reference gravity field, a plumb line meets the geoid at right angles wherever gravity is nonzero.

**How the definition helps.** Gravity is normal to a surface of constant potential because the potential has zero derivative in every tangent direction (our own). The work lies in modeling the gravity field and finding the level that best matches mean sea level (our own). An ellipsoid’s normal need not point along real gravity (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Geoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoid). It says: “the geoid is, by definition, a surface upon which the force of gravity is perpendicular everywhere, apart from temporary tidal fluctuations.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Depth integration removes Ekman viscosity

**Remember:** Integrate the spiral and only the surface stress remains.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A05 (Hydrology, hydrography, oceanography). arXiv physics.ao-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The interior ocean current balances horizontal pressure forces against the effect of Earth’s rotation. Ekman transport is the depth integral of the horizontal current in excess of that interior current.

**Problem.** Consider steady, horizontally uniform flow of constant density away from the equator, with zero stress at the layer base. The transport points perpendicular to nonzero surface wind stress, to its right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere.

**How the definition helps.** Integrating the force balance over depth replaces the unknown internal stress profile by its boundary values (our own). Only the surface stress remains because the bottom stress is zero (our own). The rotation term gives a right-angle rotation of the integrated current with opposite signs in the two hemispheres (our own). The usual velocity-profile calculation needs a law for turbulent friction, which drops out of the integrated balance (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ekman transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekman_transport). It says: “If all flow over the Ekman layer is integrated, the net transportation is at 90° to the right (left) of the surface wind”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Shallow-water potential vorticity follows parcels

**Remember:** Divide the total spin by layer depth to cancel stretching.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A05 (Hydrology, hydrography, oceanography). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Absolute vorticity adds the vertical curl of the horizontal water velocity to the local contribution from planetary rotation. Shallow-water potential vorticity divides that sum by the water depth.

**Problem.** In a smooth rotating shallow-water flow of positive depth, potential vorticity stays constant along each moving parcel. Assume no viscosity, external forcing or water sources.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing absolute vorticity by depth cancels the common effect of horizontal spreading (our own). The momentum equation makes the parcel’s vorticity change at minus its vorticity times the horizontal divergence (our own). Water conservation gives the same equation with depth in place of vorticity (our own). The quotient rule then gives zero, even where vorticity vanishes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Potential vorticity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_vorticity). It says: “The conserved quantity, in parentheses in equation (3), was later named the shallow water potential vorticity.”

**Sources:**

- [Carl-Gustaf Rossby, Relation between variations in the intensity of the zonal circulation of the atmosphere and the displacements of the semi-permanent centers of action (1939).](https://doi.org/10.1357/002224039806649023)

### Fixed rotation prevents geostrophic divergence

**Remember:** With fixed rotation, the divergence of a rotated gradient cancels.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use a flat local model with a fixed nonzero Coriolis parameter, which measures the local effect of planetary rotation. Unlike a model with latitude-dependent rotation, it uses the same parameter everywhere.

**Problem.** Assume the geopotential, the effective gravitational potential per unit mass, has continuous second derivatives on a constant-pressure surface. The horizontal wind that balances rotation against the pressure force then has zero horizontal divergence.

**How the definition helps.** Constant rotation makes the geostrophic wind a fixed multiple of a right-angle rotation of the geopotential gradient (our own). Equality of mixed partial derivatives then gives zero divergence (our own). With rotation strength varying northward, an eastward geopotential gradient instead gives a northward wind whose speed varies northward (our own). The physical work lies in deciding when a constant rotation parameter is accurate enough (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [F-plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-plane). It says: “the Coriolis parameter f, which measures the local effect of the planet's rotation, is a constant”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Layer thickness directs thermal wind

**Remember:** Compare geopotential at two pressure surfaces to find the direction of wind shear.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A10 (Meteorology and atmospheric physics). arXiv physics.ao-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define geopotential thickness between two fixed pressure surfaces as the upper geopotential minus the lower geopotential. Geopotential is the work per unit mass needed to lift air against gravity. This uses pressure surfaces rather than heights above the ground.

**Problem.** Assume gravity balances the vertical pressure force and Earth’s rotation balances the horizontal pressure force. Away from the equator, the upper wind minus the lower wind follows thickness contours wherever their gradient is nonzero.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the geopotential difference combines two wind formulas into one horizontal gradient (our own). At either pressure level, the balanced wind equals the geopotential gradient rotated through a right angle and divided by the local rotation parameter (our own). Subtracting at the same horizontal location gives the rotated thickness gradient, which is tangent to its contours (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Thermal wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_wind). It says: “the thermal wind flows along thickness or temperature contours”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Fault-plane swaps preserve moment tensors

**Remember:** Switch the normal and slip direction and the tensor stays the same.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A15 (Seismology (including tsunami modeling), earthquakes), 74J15. arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Model slip on one flat fault in a solid whose elastic properties are the same in every direction. Let n be the unit normal to the fault and s the unit slip direction within it. Represent the earthquake source by the symmetric matrix M = a(nsᵀ + snᵀ), where a measures the strength of the slip.

**Problem.** Swapping the fault normal and slip direction leaves the source matrix unchanged. Thus the matrix alone cannot identify which of the two planes slipped.

**How the definition helps.** The symmetric matrix makes the ambiguity visible without computing seismic waves in each direction (our own). Swapping the slip direction and fault normal exchanges the two terms and leaves their sum unchanged (our own). The physical work lies in deriving this matrix from slip across an elastic fault (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Focal mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Focal_mechanism). It says: “It is impossible to determine solely from a focal mechanism which of the nodal planes is the fault plane.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### River order gaps survive pruning

**Remember:** Pruning lowers both surviving orders by one and leaves their gap alone.

*True by definition.* MSC 86A05 (Hydrology, hydrography, oceanography). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In the Horton–Strahler order of a binary river tree, headwaters have order one. At a junction the order is the larger incoming order, plus one if the two orders are equal. The ratio T(i, j), for i &lt; j, is the expected number of order-i side branches joining order-j branches, divided by the expected number of order-j branches.

**Problem.** Pruning removes the headwaters and joins segments left with one input. For a coordinated random tree, where T(i, j) does not depend on the maximum order, the ratios are unchanged by pruning exactly when they depend only on j − i.

**How the definition helps.** The order gap stays the same when pruning lowers each surviving order by one (our own). Thus the expected counts are invariant exactly when they are constant along each diagonal of the table of counts (our own). The work is to prove the order shift and use coordination to identify the table entries across tree sizes (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Critical Tokunaga model for river networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02991v1). It says: “the Toeplitz property Tᵢ,ᵢ₊ₖ = Tₖ and Horton prune-invariance”

**Sources:**

- [Yevgeniy Kovchegov, Ilya Zaliapin and Efi Foufoula-Georgiou, Critical Tokunaga model for river networks (2021).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02991v1)
- [Yevgeniy Kovchegov, Ilya Zaliapin and Efi Foufoula-Georgiou, Critical Tokunaga model for river networks (2022).](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.105.014301)

### Steady water keeps discharge and head

**Remember:** A steady current can change depth while keeping discharge and head fixed.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 86A05 (Hydrology, hydrography, oceanography), 65M08. arXiv physics.ao-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For shallow water over a fixed bed, discharge per unit width is q = hu, and total head is E = u²/2 + g(h + b). Here h is depth, u velocity, b bed height and g gravity. The scheme reconstructs the flow from q and E instead of from depth and velocity.

**Problem.** In the paper's frictionless schemes for one-dimensional flow of positive depth, suppose q and E are constant across all cell and point data. Then every stored value has zero time derivative.

**How the definition helps.** For smooth flow, discharge and head turn a spatially varying steady flow into constant data for reconstruction (our own). The proof checks that the discrete transport and bed-slope terms then cancel in both update equations (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A New Approach for Designing Well-Balanced Schemes for the Shallow Water Equations: A Combination of Conservative and Primitive Formulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07809). It says: “qⱼ = qⱼ₊½ ≡ q̂ = Const, Eⱼ = Eⱼ₊½ ≡ Ê = Const, ∀j”

**Sources:**

- [A New Approach for Designing Well-Balanced Schemes for the Shallow Water Equations: A Combination of Conservative and Primitive Formulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07809)

### Convexity removes hidden mass alternatives

**Remember:** Fix density and forbid hollow domains before asking gravity to identify a shape.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 86A22 (Inverse problems in geophysics). arXiv physics.geo-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A density contrast is the difference between a body's density and the background density. The unknown body D lies in a known bounded region Ω whose closure has connected exterior. D is convex with piecewise smooth boundary, and its contrast f is known, integrable and positive on Ω.

**Problem.** Enclose Ω in a convex domain with analytic boundary. Exact gravity measurements on any nonempty patch of that boundary determine D uniquely.

**How the definition helps.** Convexity rules out hollow shells, so a basic exterior-gravity ambiguity disappears (our own). A uniform ball and a concentric hollow spherical shell of equal mass have identical exterior gravity by Newton’s shell theorem (our own). The paper’s Theorem 0.1 does the harder work of proving uniqueness for the whole convex class.

**Paper or page:** [Learning on the correct class for domain inverse problems of gravimetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07393v1). It says: “D is convex, f ∈ L₁(Ω), and 0 &lt; f on Ω.”

**Sources:**

- [Yihang Chen and Wenbin Li, Learning on the correct class for domain inverse problems of gravimetry (2024).](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07393v1)

## 90 Operations research, mathematical programming

### Generalized quantiles handle demand ties

**Remember:** Choose the first stock level where the demand probability reaches the cost ratio.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90B05 (Inventory, storage, reservoirs). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For nonnegative demand D, write F(x) for the probability that D ≤ x. For 0 &lt; p &lt; 1, the generalized quantile is the smallest x with F(x) ≥ p. An ordinary inverse may miss p when F jumps.

**Problem.** Choose a nonnegative stock level before demand is known. Pay a fixed positive cost per unit short and another per unit left over, and assume finite mean demand. The quantile minimizes expected cost when p equals the shortage cost divided by the sum of the two costs.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, allowing F to jump across p puts zero between the left and right slopes of the convex expected cost. Deriving those slopes requires counting the shortage or surplus caused by a small stock increase. If demand is zero or two with equal probability, F never equals one quarter. The generalized quantile still selects zero at that probability.

**Wikipedia:** [Newsvendor model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsvendor_model). It says: “denotes the generalized inverse cumulative distribution function of D.”

**Sources:**

- [E. L. Porteus (2008), The Newsvendor Problem](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-73699-0_7)

### Customer time gives Little’s law

**Remember:** Count one block of customer time either by customer or by clock time.

*True by definition.* MSC 90B22 (Queues and service in operations research). arXiv math.PR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For each customer, measure the part of their stay inside the observation window. Define observed customer time as the sum of these lengths.

**Problem.** For finitely many visits, observed customer time equals the integral over the window of the number present. Suppose the arrival rate and the average stay have finite limits as the window grows. If the customer time lost at the window edges is small compared with the window length, mean occupancy is the product of the two limits.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, clipping each visit lets us count the same pairs of customers and times in either order. Summing by customer gives observed customer time. Summing by time gives the occupancy integral. The work in passing to full stays is controlling the visits crossing the window boundaries.

**Wikipedia:** [Little's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little%27s_law). It says: “multiplied by the average time that a customer spends in the system (W).”

**Sources:**

- [J. D. C. Little (1961), A Proof for the Queuing Formula L = λW](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383)

### Reflected walks give waiting times

**Remember:** Subtract the lowest past level to keep the workload nonnegative.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 90B22 (Queues and service in operations research). arXiv math.PR. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Start with an empty queue and one server that takes customers in arrival order whenever work is waiting. After each arrival, add its service time and subtract the time until the next arrival. Reflect the resulting sum by subtracting its lowest value so far, including the starting zero.

**Problem.** Just before each arrival, the reflected sum equals that customer’s waiting time. The next wait equals the current wait plus the increment, or zero if that sum is negative.

**How the definition helps.** In our own queue argument, subtracting the running minimum gives exactly the usual waiting-time update. When the sum reaches a new low, the server has cleared all waiting work. Otherwise the reflected sum changes by the service time minus the time between arrivals. Starting at zero therefore gives the waiting time at each arrival.

**Paper or page:** [On fluctuation-theoretic decompositions via Lindley-type recursions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.01811v1). It says: “where Wₙ ∼ Sₙ − minₖ∈{0,…,n} Sₖ”

**Sources:**

- [Onno Boxma, Offer Kella, Michel Mandjes, On fluctuation-theoretic decompositions via Lindley-type recursions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.01811v1)

### Longest paths give project duration

**Remember:** Each event waits for its slowest chain of predecessors.

*True by definition.* MSC 90B35 (Deterministic scheduling theory in operations research). arXiv cs.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Draw the project as a finite directed graph with no cycles, one start event and one finish event. Each edge represents a task and carries its duration. Every task lies on a path from start to finish. An event waits for all incoming tasks, and enough resources exist to start all ready tasks immediately.

**Problem.** The earliest project finish equals the longest weighted path from the start to the finish event.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, earliest event times and longest path lengths satisfy the same rule. Each event takes the largest value, over incoming tasks, of the predecessor's time plus the task duration. Applying this rule in dependency order from zero at the start gives both quantities. The modeling work is encoding every precedence constraint and the resource limits.

**Wikipedia:** [Critical path method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_path_method). It says: “A critical path is determined by identifying the longest stretch of dependent activities”

**Sources:**

- [J. E. Kelley Jr. and M. R. Walker (1959), Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling](https://doi.org/10.1145/1460299.1460318)

### Preemption makes earliest deadlines optimal

**Remember:** With pause and resume, urgent work can always go first.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90B35 (Deterministic scheduling theory in operations research). arXiv cs.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For independent jobs on one processor, allow preemption, which means a job can pause and resume without cost. Whenever jobs are ready, run one whose deadline is earliest.

**Problem.** If any schedule meets all release times and deadlines, the preemptive earliest deadline rule does too.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing pauses lets an earlier deadline take priority even when a later job has already started. In our own exchange argument, move ready work with the earliest deadline forward; the displaced work still meets its deadline. In our own counterexample, a three-unit job arrives at zero, due at five, and a one-unit job arrives at one, due at two. Without pauses, starting the first job at once misses the second deadline, but idling until one meets both.

**Wikipedia:** [Earliest deadline first scheduling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earliest_deadline_first_scheduling). It says: “EDF is an optimal scheduling algorithm on preemptive uniprocessors”

**Sources:**

- [W. A. Horn (1974), Some Simple Scheduling Algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1002/nav.3800210113)

### Fractional assignments decompose into matchings

**Remember:** Fractional assignments are mixtures of whole assignments.

*True by definition.* MSC 90B80 (Discrete location and assignment). arXiv cs.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A whole assignment pairs each worker with one job and uses every job once. Define a fractional assignment by drawing a whole assignment at random and recording the probability of each worker–job pair. Equivalently, these probabilities form a nonnegative square matrix whose rows and columns each sum to one.

**Problem.** The minimum linear cost over all fractional assignments equals the cheapest whole assignment’s cost.

**How the definition helps.** In our own argument, the random-assignment definition makes fractional cost an average of whole-assignment costs. This average cannot beat its cheapest term, and choosing that term with probability one attains it. The work lies in proving that every matrix with the stated sums represents such a draw. This is the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem.

**Wikipedia:** [Doubly stochastic matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubly_stochastic_matrix). It says: “the vertices of Bₙ are precisely the permutation matrices.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Basic feasible solutions are vertices, so linear programs need finite search

**Remember:** Some optimum always sits at a vertex, and vertices are finitely many.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 90C05 (Linear programming), 90C49. arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A linear program in standard form minimizes cᵀx subject to Ax = b and x ≥ 0. A basic feasible solution is a feasible x whose nonzero entries belong to linearly independent columns of A. With n variables and m equations there are at most 'n choose m' of them.

**Problem.** If a linear program in standard form has an optimal solution, then it has an optimal basic feasible solution. Each basic feasible solution is a vertex of the feasible polyhedron.

**How the definition helps.** The algebraic definition can be checked with linear algebra, and its geometric meaning, a vertex, is where optima lie. Together they turn optimization into a finite search. The simplex method moves from one basic feasible solution to another until it finds an optimum. What stays hard is that there can be exponentially many vertices (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Basic feasible solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_feasible_solution), [Linear programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_programming). It says: “Geometrically, each BFS corresponds to a vertex of the polyhedron of feasible solutions. If there exists an optimal solution, then there exists an optimal BFS.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Total unimodularity makes every vertex of a linear program integral

**Remember:** Determinants ±1 mean Cramer's rule never divides, so vertices are integers.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C10 (Integer programming), 90C57, 05B20. arXiv math.OC, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A matrix is totally unimodular if every square submatrix has determinant 0, +1 or −1. Examples are the incidence matrix of a bipartite graph and the incidence matrix of a directed graph.

**Problem.** If A is totally unimodular and b is an integer vector, every vertex of {x : Ax ≤ b} has integer entries. So the linear program 'maximize cᵀx subject to Ax ≤ b' has an integer optimum whenever it has an optimum, for every c.

**How the definition helps.** The definition asks exactly for the determinants that Cramer's rule divides by, so vertices come out integral. A vertex solves a square invertible subsystem Bx = b′ taken from the rows of A (our own explanation). Cramer's rule writes each entry of x as a determinant divided by det B = ±1, so x is integral. So integer problems with such matrices, like bipartite matching, can be solved as linear programs.

**Wikipedia:** [Unimodular matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodular_matrix). It says: “Hence if A is totally unimodular and b is integral, every extreme point of the feasible region (e.g. {x \| Ax ≥ b}) is integral and thus the feasible region is an integral polyhedron.”

**Sources:**

- [A. J. Hoffman and J. B. Kruskal, Integral boundary points of convex polyhedra, in Linear Inequalities and Related Systems, Annals of Mathematics Studies 38 (1956), 223–246](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400881987-014)

### Strong quasiconvexity forbids tied minima

**Remember:** Two equal minima would make their midpoint lower than both.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C26 (Nonconvex programming, global optimization). arXiv math.OC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Choose γ &gt; 0 and let z = (1−t)x + ty for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Strong quasiconvexity requires h(z) ≤ max(h(x),h(y)) − γt(1−t)‖x−y‖²/2 for every x and y. Ordinary quasiconvexity requires only h(z) ≤ max(h(x),h(y)).

**Problem.** A real strongly quasiconvex function on a convex set has at most one minimizer.

**How the definition helps.** The positive midpoint gap rules out two different points at the minimum value. In our own counterexample, f(x) = max(0, \|x\| − 1) is quasiconvex but has a whole interval of minima. The work moves to finding a positive modulus γ, rather than just proving that sublevel sets are convex.

**Paper or page:** [Characterizations of Strongly Quasiconvex Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21580v1). It says: “If h is strongly quasiconvex with modulus γ &gt; 0”

**Sources:**

- [Characterizations of Strongly Quasiconvex Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21580v1)

### Diminishing returns bound greedy gains

**Remember:** The best single gain covers at least one share of the remaining gap.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 90C27 (Combinatorial optimization). arXiv cs.DS. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A set score has diminishing returns if adding an absent item gives at least as much gain on a smaller set as on any superset. The item must be absent from both sets. Assume adding items never lowers the score. Starting from the empty set, repeatedly add an item with largest gain.

**Problem.** Choose a budget k from one to the number of items. After k steps, the gain above the empty-set score is at least 1 − 1/e times the best gain with that budget.

**How the definition helps.** Diminishing returns bounds the remaining improvement by k times the best single gain. In our own proof, adding the missing optimal items one by one gives gains that can only shrink, so each greedy step removes at least a fraction 1/k of the remaining gap. In our own counterexample without diminishing returns, two special items together earn 100, and a third item alone earns one. With budget two, greedy earns one, because neither special item earns anything alone.

**Paper or page:** [Incremental space-filling design based on coverings and spacings: improving upon low discrepancy sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05833v1). It says: “Let f be a non-decreasing submodular set function, then, for any given k, 1 ≤ k ≤ C, Algorithm 1 returns a set Xₖ with bounded optimality gap”

**Sources:**

- [Amaya Nogales Gómez, Luc Pronzato, Maria-João Rendas, Incremental space-filling design based on coverings and spacings: improving upon low discrepancy sequences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05833v1)
- [G. L. Nemhauser, L. A. Wolsey and M. L. Fisher (1978), An Analysis of Approximations for Maximizing Submodular Set Functions I](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01588971)

### Touching objectives share envelope slopes

**Remember:** At a smooth contact, the upper envelope and its touching curve share a slope.

*True by definition.* MSC 90C31 (Sensitivity, stability, parametric optimization), 91B02. arXiv math.OC, econ.TH. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Fix a set of feasible choices. Each choice gives an objective curve as the parameter varies. Their pointwise supremum is the value function, also called the upper envelope.

**Problem.** At an interior parameter where the value function and an attaining objective curve are differentiable, their derivatives agree.

**How the definition helps.** Our own proof uses the envelope definition to turn equality at the optimizer into a minimum of the gap between two curves. The gap has derivative zero there, so the slopes agree. Differentiating an optimizing choice would require assumptions about how it moves. The work lies in proving attainment and differentiability when the problem does not already supply them.

**Wikipedia:** [Envelope theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelope_theorem). It says: “the traditional envelope formula holds for optimization problems with arbitrary choice sets at any differentiability point of the value function”

**Sources:**

- [Milgrom and Segal, Envelope Theorems for Arbitrary Choice Sets (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0262.00296)

### Ratio minima become scalar zeros
